Elam.x: The ancient kingdom of southwestern Iran, joining the lowland city of Susa with the highland realm of Anshan, with its own tongue and scripts. For two thousand years the Elamites traded and warred with Mesopotamia, sacked Ur and plundered Babylonia, carrying off Hammurabi's laws, until Ashurbanipal laid Susa waste about 646 B.C.

Akkadian Empire.x: The first empire of Mesopotamia, founded by Sargon of Akkad, who united the Sumerian cities with the Semitic north and campaigned from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean. Under his grandson Naram-Sin its kings called themselves gods; it fell about 2150 B.C. to revolt, drought, and the Gutians.

Middle Kingdom of Egypt.x: Egypt reunited by Mentuhotep II of Thebes and brought to its classical age by the Twelfth Dynasty, whose kings ruled from Itjtawy, conquered Lower Nubia, reclaimed the Faiyum, and left the masterpieces of Egyptian literature. It dissolved under the weaker Thirteenth Dynasty as the Hyksos rose in the Delta.

Assyria.x: The kingdom of the god Ashur on the upper Tigris: a merchant city-state under the Old Assyrian kings, the heart of Shamshi-Adad's realm, then a vassal of Mitanni. From Ashur-uballit I the Middle Assyrian kings made it a great military power, which reached the Mediterranean under Tiglath-Pileser I.
Assyria.gov: Monarchy (the king as vice-regent of Ashur)

Hittites.x: The kingdom of Hatti in central Anatolia, ruled from Hattusa, whose people wrote the oldest recorded Indo-European tongue. Its kings sacked Babylon, destroyed Mitanni, fought Ramesses II at Kadesh, and swore with him the oldest peace treaty whose text survives, before the empire collapsed about 1180 B.C.
Hittites.gov: Monarchy with a council of nobles (pankus)
Hittites.faith: Hittite religion (the thousand gods of Hatti)

New Kingdom of Egypt.x: Egypt at the height of its power, from the expulsion of the Hyksos to the last Ramesside kings: an empire from the Euphrates to the Fourth Cataract, the age of Hatshepsut, Thutmose III, Akhenaten, Tutankhamun, and Ramesses II, of the temples of Karnak and Luxor and the tombs of the Valley of the Kings.
New Kingdom of Egypt.faith: Egyptian religion (Amun-Ra); the Aten alone under Akhenaten

Kingdom of Kush.x: The Nubian kingdom of the middle Nile, ruled first from Napata beneath Jebel Barkal and later from Meroë. Its kings conquered Egypt as the Twenty-fifth Dynasty, and its queens, the Kandakes, defied Rome; rich in gold and iron, it endured for more than a thousand years until Axum overthrew it about A.D. 350.
Kingdom of Kush.gov: Monarchy, with powerful queen mothers and ruling queens

Third Intermediate Period of Egypt.x: Egypt divided after the New Kingdom: the Twenty-first Dynasty ruled the Delta from Tanis while the high priests of Amun governed Thebes, and the Libyan chiefs of the Twenty-second Dynasty, beginning with Shoshenq I, briefly reunited the land before it splintered among rival kings.
Third Intermediate Period of Egypt.gov: Monarchy, with the priesthood of Amun ruling Thebes

Neo-Assyrian Empire.x: The greatest of the Mesopotamian empires, built by the warrior kings of Ashur from Ashurnasirpal II to Ashurbanipal. Ruling from Kalhu and Nineveh by deportation and terror, it held the Near East from Egypt to the Zagros, until the Medes and Babylonians destroyed Nineveh in 612 B.C.

Greek City-States.x: The hundreds of free cities of Greece and the Aegean, Athens, Sparta, Corinth, Thebes, Argos, and many more: rivals in war and in the games, who repelled Persia and gave the world democracy, philosophy, history, and drama, and who fell under Macedon after Chaeronea and under Rome after 146 B.C.
Greek City-States.gov: City-states: kingship, tyranny, oligarchy, and democracy

(Macedonian Empire).x: The whole realm of the Argead kings of Macedon: the kingdom Philip II made master of Greece, and the empire his son Alexander won from the Danube to the Indus and the Nile, held after Alexander's death in 323 B.C. in the name of his heirs until the Successors divided it among themselves.
(Macedonian Empire).gov: Hereditary monarchy with the assembled army

Macedonian Empire.x: The kingdom of the Argead kings of Macedon, raised by Philip II and his phalanx to mastery of Greece and carried by Alexander the Great across the Persian Empire to Egypt, Central Asia, and the Punjab. After 323 B.C. it was fought over by Alexander's generals until Cassander and Demetrius held only Macedon itself.

Scythia.x: The realm of the Scythians, Iranian horse nomads of the Pontic steppe, who swept into the Near East in the seventh century B.C., defeated Darius by retreat, and buried their kings in great barrows with gold of Greek workmanship. Philip II killed their king Ateas in 339 B.C., and the Sarmatians later displaced them.

Carthage.x: The Phoenician city on the Gulf of Tunis that built a maritime empire across North Africa, Sardinia, western Sicily, and southern Spain. Ruled by an oligarchy of merchant families, it fought Syracuse for Sicily and Rome in three Punic Wars, and was destroyed by Scipio Aemilianus in 146 B.C.
Carthage.gov: Oligarchic republic under suffetes and a council of elders

Twenty-sixth Dynasty of Egypt.x: The Saite dynasty, which freed Egypt from Assyria under Psamtik I and ruled from Sais in the Delta, reviving the forms of old art and learning, hiring Greek and Carian mercenaries, and founding the Greek trading town of Naucratis. It fell to Cambyses of Persia at Pelusium in 525 B.C.

Median Kingdom.x: The kingdom of the Medes of northwestern Iran, united by Deioces at Ecbatana, Herodotus says. Under Cyaxares the Medes, with Babylon, destroyed Assyria and pushed west to the Halys, until Cyrus the Persian overthrew Astyages in 550 B.C. and made the Medes partners in his empire.

Neo-Babylonian Empire.x: The Chaldean empire of Nabopolassar and Nebuchadnezzar II, which destroyed Assyria, took Syria and Judah, burned Jerusalem, and rebuilt Babylon with the Ishtar Gate and the great ziggurat. Its last king, Nabonidus, spent ten years in Arabia, and Cyrus took the city without a battle in 539 B.C.

Achaemenid Empire.x: The Persian empire founded by Cyrus the Great and ordered by Darius I into satrapies joined by royal roads, the largest state the world had yet seen, from the Aegean and Egypt to the Indus. Tolerant of the gods of its subjects, it failed to conquer Greece and fell to Alexander the Great.
Achaemenid Empire.gov: Absolute monarchy (King of Kings) with satraps
Achaemenid Empire.faith: Zoroastrianism (Ahura Mazda), tolerant of subject cults

Roman Republic.x: The commonwealth of the Roman people from the expulsion of the kings to the rise of Augustus, governed by annual consuls, the Senate, and the assemblies. Its legions conquered Italy, Carthage, the Hellenistic East, and Gaul, until the civil wars of Marius and Sulla, Pompey and Caesar destroyed it.

Twenty-eighth Dynasty of Egypt.x: The single reign of Amyrtaeus of Sais, who led the Delta in revolt against Persia on the death of Darius II and won back all Egypt by about 400 B.C. He was overthrown by Nepherites I of Mendes, founder of the next dynasty.

Twenty-ninth Dynasty of Egypt.x: The dynasty of Mendes in the Delta, founded by Nepherites I, which kept Egypt free of Persia, allied with Sparta and Athens against the Great King, and fortified the eastern frontier. Its ablest king, Hakor, beat off a Persian invasion.

Thirtieth Dynasty of Egypt.x: The last dynasty of native pharaohs, from Sebennytos in the Delta, under Nectanebo I and Nectanebo II, great builders of temples. It repelled a Persian invasion in 373 B.C. but fell to Artaxerxes III in 343 B.C., after which no native Egyptian ruled all Egypt for more than two thousand years.

Kingdom of Armenia.x: The kingdom of the Armenian highlands, ruled by the Orontids, the Artaxiads, and from the first century A.D. by a branch of the Arsacids. Under Tigranes the Great it was briefly an empire from the Caspian to Syria; caught ever after between Rome and Persia, it became the first Christian kingdom, until Persia ended the monarchy in 428.
Kingdom of Armenia.gov: Hereditary monarchy with great noble houses (nakharars)
Kingdom of Armenia.faith: Armenian paganism and Zoroastrianism, then Christianity from about 301

Kingdom of Lysimachus.x: The realm of Lysimachus, Alexander's bodyguard, who held Thrace from 323 B.C., took the royal title in 306, and after Ipsus added western Asia Minor and later Macedon itself. He founded Lysimachia on the neck of the Thracian Chersonese and fell, nearly eighty years old, at Corupedium in 281 B.C.

Seleucid Empire.x: The largest of the Hellenistic kingdoms, founded by Seleucus I from Babylon and stretching at its height from the Aegean to Bactria. Ruled from Antioch, it planted Greek cities across Asia but lost Iran to the Parthians and Judea to the Maccabees, and Pompey made its last remnant the province of Syria in 64 B.C.
Seleucid Empire.faith: Greek and Babylonian religion; cult of the kings

Ptolemaic Kingdom.x: The Macedonian kingdom of Egypt founded by Ptolemy I, whose house ruled from Alexandria as pharaohs to the Egyptians and as kings to the Greeks, with the Museum and the Library at its capital. Weakened by native revolts and family wars, it ended with the death of Cleopatra VII in 30 B.C.
Ptolemaic Kingdom.faith: Greek and Egyptian religion (Serapis); cult of the kings

Kingdom of Pontus.x: The Persian and Greek kingdom on the southern shore of the Black Sea founded by Mithridates I Ctistes. Under Mithridates VI Eupator it became Rome's most dangerous enemy in the East, massacring the Romans of Asia in 88 B.C. and fighting three wars before Pompey broke it; a client dynasty ruled its eastern part until A.D. 64.
Kingdom of Pontus.faith: Greek and Iranian religion, with the Anatolian cult of Ma

Parthian Empire.x: The Iranian empire of the Arsacid kings, horsemen from the steppe east of the Caspian who took Iran and Mesopotamia from the Seleucids. Its mounted archers destroyed Crassus at Carrhae, and for nearly five centuries it was the rival of Rome in the East, until the Persian Ardashir overthrew it in A.D. 224.
Parthian Empire.gov: Feudal monarchy (King of Kings) with great noble houses
Parthian Empire.faith: Zoroastrianism and Iranian religion, with Greek and Babylonian cults

Roman Empire.x: The empire of the Caesars from Augustus to Theodosius I, master of the whole Mediterranean, from Britain and the Rhine to Egypt and the Euphrates, the Roman Peace of law, roads, and cities. It survived the crisis of the third century, became Christian under Constantine, and was divided between the sons of Theodosius in 395.

Huns.x: The nomad horsemen who came out of the steppes beyond the Volga about A.D. 370, crushed the Alans and the Gothic realm of Ermanaric, and drove the Goths across the Danube into the Roman Empire. Under kings such as Uldin and Rugila they settled on the Hungarian plain and took tribute and service from Rome.
Huns.gov: Tribal kingship, often shared among brothers

Gothia.x: The realm of the Goths north of the lower Danube and the Black Sea, from their first raids on the Roman frontier about A.D. 238 to the coming of the Huns. They harried the empire, killed Decius at Abritus, and later, as the Tervingi in the west and the Greuthungi in the east, received from Wulfila the Gothic Bible.
Gothia.faith: Germanic paganism, with Arian Christianity spreading

Sasanian Empire.x: The second Persian empire, founded by Ardashir I and ruled from Ctesiphon by Kings of Kings who made Zoroastrianism the faith of the realm. For four centuries it fought Rome on equal terms, capturing Valerian and sacking Antioch, until the Arab conquests destroyed it after Qadisiyyah and Nahavand.
Sasanian Empire.gov: Absolute monarchy (King of Kings) with great noble houses

Palmyrene Empire.x: The eastern realm of the caravan city of Palmyra, built on the victories of Odaenathus over Persia and turned against Rome by his widow Zenobia, who took Egypt and most of Asia Minor in the name of her son Vaballathus. Aurelian destroyed it in 272 and 273.

Gallic Empire.x: The breakaway Roman state of the West, proclaimed by the Rhine legions under Postumus in 260, which defended Gaul, Britain, and for a time Spain against the Franks and Alamanni with its own emperors, senate, and consuls, until Tetricus surrendered to Aurelian in 274.

Vandals.x: The East Germanic Vandals, Hasdings and Silings, who lived in Silesia and beyond the Danube, crossed the Rhine in 406 with the Alans and Suebi, and settled in Spain. Under Gunderic and Genseric they took Seville and in 429 crossed to Africa, where they founded the Vandal kingdom.

Eastern Roman Empire.x: The eastern half of the Roman Empire after 395, ruled from Constantinople, which outlived the barbarian invasions that destroyed the West. Under Justinian it reconquered Africa, Italy, and southern Spain and codified Roman law; its emperors were still Romans, though its tongue was becoming Greek.

Western Roman Empire.x: The western half of the Roman Empire after 395, ruled from Milan and then Ravenna by emperors more and more in the hands of their barbarian generals. It lost Britain, Spain, Africa, and Gaul to Goths, Vandals, Franks, and others, and ended when Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus in 476.

Hunnic Empire.x: The empire of the Huns at its height under Rugila, Bleda, and Attila, the Scourge of God, ruling from the Hungarian plain over Germanic and steppe peoples from the Rhine to the Caspian. It wrung tribute from Constantinople and invaded Gaul and Italy, but collapsed after Attila's death and the defeat of his sons at the Nedao in 454.

Visigothic Kingdom.x: The kingdom of the Visigoths, settled in Aquitaine in 418 with its capital at Toulouse, driven into Spain by Clovis in 507, and ruled at last from Toledo. Catholic from Reccared's conversion in 587, it gave Spain its law and its great church councils, until the Arab and Berber invasion of 711 destroyed it.

Ostrogothic Kingdom.x: The kingdom of the Ostrogoths in Italy, founded by Theodoric the Great, who ruled from Ravenna as king of the Goths and viceroy for the emperor, keeping Roman law and the Senate. After his death Justinian's armies under Belisarius and Narses destroyed it in a war of nearly twenty years.

Scandinavian minor kingdoms.x: The petty kingdoms and chieftaincies of Scandinavia in the Migration and Viking ages, among the Danes, the Geats, the Svear, and the peoples of Norway, before the united kingdoms of Denmark, Norway, and Sweden. Their kings raised the Danevirke, raided the Frankish coasts, and received the first Christian missionaries.
Scandinavian minor kingdoms.gov: Petty kingdoms and chieftaincies with assemblies (things)

Avar Khaganate.x: The empire of the Avars, mounted nomads from the steppe who settled on the Hungarian plain in 568 under their khagan Bayan and ruled the Slavs and Gepids. They wrung tribute from Constantinople, besieged it with the Persians in 626, and were broken by the armies of Charlemagne between 791 and 796.

(Kingdom of the Franks).x: The whole realm of the Franks, from the Merovingian kingdom of Clovis and his heirs, divided again and again among their sons, to the Carolingian empire of Pepin, Charlemagne, and Louis the Pious, which stretched from the Ebro to the Elbe and was parted among Louis's sons at Verdun in 843.
rulers: Pepin of Herstal (mayor of the palace)

Kingdom of the Franks.x: The kingdom founded by Clovis I, who united the Franks, won Gaul from the Romans, the Visigoths, and the Burgundians, and took the Catholic faith. Ruled by the Merovingians and then in their name by the mayors of the palace, it passed to the Carolingians in 751 and became under Charlemagne the empire of the West.
rulers: Pepin of Herstal (mayor of the palace)

(Merovingian Empire).x: The Frankish realm of the Merovingian house, sprung by legend from Merovech, from Childeric I and Clovis to the shadow kings whom the mayors of the palace governed. Divided again and again into Austrasia, Neustria, and Burgundy, it embraced nearly all of Gaul and much of Germany.
rulers: Pepin of Herstal (mayor of the palace)

Sumerian City-States.x: The cities of Sumer in the marshy south of Mesopotamia, Uruk, Ur, Lagash, Umma, Kish, and Nippur among them, where writing, the wheel, and monumental temples first appeared. Each served its own god under a king or governor; they were united in turn by Lugal-zage-si, by Sargon of Akkad, and by the Third Dynasty of Ur.

Early Dynastic Period of Egypt.x: The first dynasties of united Egypt, ruling from Memphis after Narmer joined the Two Lands; their kings shaped the royal titles, the hieroglyphic script, and the cult of the god-king, and were buried at Abydos and Saqqara.

Old Kingdom of Egypt.x: Egypt of the Third to Eighth Dynasties, ruled from Memphis: the age of Djoser's Step Pyramid, the pyramids of Giza, the sun temples of Ra, and the Pyramid Texts. After the long reign of Pepi II the governors of the provinces grew too strong and the central state broke apart.

Lower Egypt.x: Northern Egypt in the First Intermediate Period, ruled by the Ninth and Tenth Dynasties from Herakleopolis, whose kings, several of them named Khety, contended with the princes of Thebes for the Two Lands. The Instruction for Merikare, a king's counsel to his son, is set at this court; Mentuhotep II of Thebes ended its rule.

Gutian Dynasty.x: The kings of the Gutians, a people of the Zagros mountains who overran Akkad after the successors of Naram-Sin and held sway over much of Sumer, remembered by the Sumerians as a plague of barbarians. Utu-hengal of Uruk defeated their last king, Tirigan, about 2116 B.C.

Babylonia.x: The land of Babylon in southern Mesopotamia: the Amorite kingdom of Hammurabi, four centuries of Kassite rule, the Second Dynasty of Isin of Nebuchadnezzar I, and the long struggle against Assyria. Through every change of master the city of Marduk remained the holy and learned capital of the Near East.

Canaanite city-states.x: The walled cities of Canaan and the Phoenician coast, Hazor, Megiddo, Shechem, Jerusalem, Gezer, Lachish, Tyre, Sidon, and their neighbors, each under its own king. Canaanites devised the first alphabet; after Thutmose III's victory at Megiddo in 1457 B.C. their kings paid tribute to Egypt.

Hyksos.x: The Hyksos, West Semitic rulers of foreign lands who rose in the eastern Delta about 1650 B.C. and from their capital Avaris held Lower Egypt in close league with the towns of southern Canaan, taking tribute from Thebes. The horse and chariot came to Egypt in their age; Ahmose drove them out about 1540 B.C.

Seventeenth Dynasty of Egypt.x: The Theban kings of the late Second Intermediate Period, vassals of the Hyksos who ruled Upper Egypt from Thebes. Seqenenre Tao died of axe blows in battle against them, and Kamose carried the war to the walls of Avaris; Ahmose, finishing the work, founded the New Kingdom.

Fifteenth Dynasty of Egypt.x: The Hyksos dynasty of Avaris, rulers of Lower and Middle Egypt in the Second Intermediate Period, whose king Khyan left his name on objects found from Knossos to Hattusa and whose king Apepi quarreled with Seqenenre Tao of Thebes. Ahmose ended it by taking Avaris.
Fifteenth Dynasty of Egypt.faith: Egyptian and Canaanite religion (Seth of Avaris)

Sixteenth Dynasty of Egypt.x: One of the obscure lines of kings of the Second Intermediate Period. Manetho's lists made them vassals of the Hyksos in the Delta, while the Danish Egyptologist Kim Ryholt has argued that they were a Theban dynasty between the Thirteenth and the Seventeenth. Their names survive chiefly on scarabs and in the Turin king list.

Mitanni.x: The Hurrian kingdom of upper Mesopotamia, ruled by kings with Indo-Aryan names who invoked Mitra, Varuna, and Indra in their treaties and were masters of the chariot. It held Assyria as a vassal, fought and then married into the house of the pharaohs, and was broken by the Hittite Suppiluliuma I.

Mycenaean Greece.x: The Bronze Age Greek kingdoms of Mycenae, Pylos, Tiryns, Thebes, and Knossos, ruled from palaces whose scribes kept their accounts in Linear B, the oldest written Greek. Warrior lords buried with gold masks and bronze armor traded across the Mediterranean; the palaces fell about 1200 B.C., leaving the memory of Agamemnon's age to Homer.

(Phoenician city-states).x: The whole Phoenician world: Tyre, Sidon, Byblos, and Arvad on the Levant coast, and the colonies and trading posts they planted from Cyprus to Carthage, Sicily, Sardinia, and Gadir beyond the Pillars of Hercules. Seafarers, purple dyers, and merchants, they gave the Mediterranean the alphabet.

Phoenicia.x: The Phoenician cities and their dependencies, with Tyre and Sidon at their head, whose merchants ruled the trade of the Mediterranean in the early Iron Age. Their western outposts, Motya, Panormus, and Soloeis in Sicily among them, passed under the leadership of Carthage as the home cities fell to Assyria and Babylon.

Neo-Hittite states.x: The kingdoms that kept the name and the hieroglyphic Luwian script of the Hittites after the fall of Hattusa: Carchemish, Melid, Gurgum, Kummuh, Hamath, Pattina, and Sam'al, in southeastern Anatolia and northern Syria. Mingled with Aramean newcomers, they were swallowed one by one by the Assyrian empire by 708 B.C.

Greek Dark Ages.x: The four centuries after the fall of the Mycenaean palaces, when writing was forgotten, the people dwindled, and Greeks crossed the Aegean to settle Ionia. Iron replaced bronze, the Geometric style of pottery arose, and at Lefkandi in Euboea a chieftain's burial shows that wealth and seafaring never wholly died.

Kingdom of Israel.x: The kingdom of the Israelites, united under David and Solomon with its capital at Jerusalem, and after the division of about 931 B.C. the northern kingdom of the ten tribes. Under Omri and Ahab it was a power in Syria, ruled from Samaria; Assyria destroyed it in 722 B.C. and carried its people away.
Kingdom of Israel.faith: Worship of the God of Israel, with rival cults of Baal

Phrygia.x: The kingdom of the Phrygians, who came into central Anatolia from the Balkans after the fall of the Hittites and ruled from Gordion on the Sangarius. Its most famous king, Midas, the Mita of the Assyrian records, was remembered by the Greeks for his golden touch; Cimmerian raiders broke the kingdom early in the seventh century B.C.
Phrygia.faith: Phrygian religion (Matar, the Mother of the Gods)

Tabal Kingdom.x: The Neo-Hittite kingdom of the central Anatolian plateau north of the Taurus, in the land later called Cappadocia, whose kings wrote in hieroglyphic Luwian. Caught between Phrygia, Urartu, and Assyria, it paid tribute to Tiglath-Pileser III, and Sargon II deposed its king Ambaris, his own son-in-law, in 713 B.C.

Kingdom of Urartu.x: The kingdom of Biainili around Lake Van, Assyria's great rival in the highlands, which built mighty fortresses, canals, and vineyards and spread from the Euphrates to Lake Urmia and the Ararat plain. Its chief god was Haldi; it faded under the blows of Cimmerians, Scythians, and Medes early in the sixth century B.C.

Twenty-second Dynasty of Egypt.x: The dynasty of Libyan chiefs from Bubastis, founded by Shoshenq I, the Shishak of the Bible, who reunited Egypt and invaded Judah and Israel. Under his successors the kingdom splintered among rival Libyan princes of the Delta, and Piye of Kush found it divided when he came north.

Twenty-third Dynasty of Egypt.x: A rival line of Libyan kings of the eighth century B.C., seated by Manetho's tradition at Leontopolis in the Delta, though its kings held Thebes and many scholars now place their seat in Upper Egypt. Its most notable king, Osorkon III, made his daughter Shepenupet God's Wife of Amun.

Etruscans.x: The Etruscans of central Italy, a people of non-Indo-European speech joined in a league of twelve cities, among them Tarquinii, Caere, Veii, Volsinii, and Clusium. Masters of bronze, painted tombs, and the art of divination, they ruled Rome under the Tarquins and Campania for a time, and were absorbed by Rome by 264 B.C.
Etruscans.gov: League of city-states under kings, later magistrates (zilath)

Lydia.x: The kingdom of western Anatolia ruled from Sardis by the Mermnad kings, whose gold from the Pactolus made the name of Croesus a byword for wealth. The Lydians struck the first coins, subdued the Ionian Greeks, and fixed the Halys as their frontier with Media, until Cyrus took Sardis about 546 B.C.

Phoenician Colonies.x: The Phoenician settlements of the far west around the Strait of Gibraltar, Gadir, Malaka, Sexi, Abdera, and Lixus, founded by Tyre to trade for the silver of Tartessos. When Tyre fell under Babylon, they passed into the orbit of Carthage.

Peloponnesian League.x: The alliance of the Peloponnesian cities, Corinth, Tegea, Elis, and others, under the leadership of Sparta, which led the Greeks against Persia and fought Athens in the Peloponnesian War. Bound to Sparta by separate oaths, its members met in congress to vote on war; it dissolved after Sparta's defeats by Thebes.
Peloponnesian League.gov: Military alliance under Sparta (dual kingship and ephors)

Odrysian Kingdom.x: The kingdom of the Odrysian Thracians, founded by Teres I in the fifth century B.C., which united most of the tribes between the Danube and the Aegean and could put, Thucydides says, 150,000 men in the field under Sitalces. Weakened by division among rival kings, it fell under Philip II of Macedon.

Cimmerian Bosporus.x: The Greek kingdom of the Straits of Kerch, joining Panticapaeum, Phanagoria, and the other Milesian colonies with the native Sindi and Maeotians. Under the Spartocids it fed Athens with Scythian grain; Mithridates VI added it to Pontus, and under Rome it lived on as a client kingdom until the Huns came.

Minaeans.x: The kingdom of Ma'in in the Jawf of northern Yemen, whose merchants ran the incense caravans from southern Arabia to Gaza and Egypt and kept a colony at Dedan in the Hejaz. Its kings ruled from Qarnaw and worshiped at Yathill; it fell under Saba in the first century B.C.

Second Athenian League.x: The naval alliance founded by Athens in 378 B.C. with Chios, Thebes, Byzantium, and other free cities against Spartan domination, pledged not to repeat the abuses of the old Delian empire. It won the sea battle of Naxos, but the Social War of 357 to 355 B.C. broke it, and Philip II ended it after Chaeronea.
Second Athenian League.gov: Alliance under the Athenian democracy, with a congress of allies

Thebes (Boeotian League).x: The Boeotian League under the leadership of Thebes, which, led by Epaminondas and Pelopidas and the Sacred Band, broke Sparta at Leuctra in 371 B.C., freed Messenia, and for a decade was the first power in Greece. Its greatness died with Epaminondas at Mantinea in 362.

Kingdom of Bithynia.x: The kingdom of the Thracian Bithynians on the Asian shore of the Bosporus and the Sea of Marmara, which kept its freedom against Alexander's Successors, invited the Galatians into Asia, and gave refuge to Hannibal. Its last king, Nicomedes IV, bequeathed it to Rome in 74 B.C.

Cyrenaica.x: The Greek cities of eastern Libya, Cyrene, Barca, Euesperides, Taucheira, and Apollonia, rich in grain, horses, and silphium. Ruled by the Ptolemies, at times as a separate kingdom under princes such as Magas, it was bequeathed to Rome by Ptolemy Apion in 96 B.C.
Cyrenaica.gov: Ptolemaic dependency, at times a separate kingdom

Laomedon.x: The satrapy of Syria as held by Laomedon of Mytilene, a boyhood friend of Alexander, under the settlement made at Babylon in 323 B.C. Ptolemy of Egypt drove him out about 319 B.C. and seized Coele-Syria, opening a struggle for the land that lasted more than a century.

Perdiccas.x: The central lands of Alexander's empire, Babylonia and its neighbors, held in the name of the joint kings Philip III and Alexander IV by the regent Perdiccas, to whom the dying Alexander had given his ring. Perdiccas was murdered by his own officers while invading Egypt in 320 B.C., and Babylon passed to Seleucus as satrap.

Athenian Coalition.x: Athens and its Greek allies in their risings against Macedon after Alexander's death: the Lamian War of 323 to 322 B.C., led by Leosthenes, which ended at Crannon, and the Chremonidean War of the 260s, fought with Spartan and Ptolemaic help against Antigonus Gonatas, which ended with the fall of Athens.

Polyperchon.x: The lands held by Polyperchon, the old officer whom Antipater named regent of the kings in 319 B.C. He proclaimed the freedom of the Greek cities to win them from Cassander, but lost Macedon in 316 and ended as a petty lord in the Peloponnese.

Atropatene.x: The kingdom of northern Media, the later Azerbaijan, named for Atropates, the Persian satrap who served Alexander and kept his province as an independent realm after 323 B.C. A land of the Magi ruled from Ganzak, it kept its own kings under Seleucid and later Parthian overlordship.

Colchis.x: The land of the Golden Fleece on the eastern shore of the Black Sea, at the mouth of the Phasis, where Greek colonies traded for gold, timber, and linen with the native kingdom of western Georgia. It minted its own silver coins; it passed in time to Pontus and Rome and became the kingdom of Lazica.

Antigonid Dynasty.x: The realm of the house of Antigonus the One-Eyed in its years of eclipse after Ipsus, when Demetrius the Besieger held Macedon and much of Greece and then, losing Macedon in 288 B.C., only strongholds such as Demetrias and Corinth. His son Antigonus Gonatas won back the Macedonian throne in 277 B.C.

Kingdom of Pergamon.x: The Hellenistic kingdom of the Attalids, founded by Philetaerus, the eunuch who kept the treasure of Lysimachus, and raised to greatness by Attalus I's victories over the Galatians. Allied with Rome, its kings built the great altar of Zeus and a library to rival Alexandria's, and Attalus III bequeathed the kingdom to Rome in 133 B.C.

Galatia.x: The land of the Celtic Galatians in central Anatolia, three tribes, the Tolistobogii, the Tectosages, and the Trocmi, who crossed from Europe in 278 B.C. and terrorized Asia Minor until Attalus I defeated them. Ruled by tetrarchs and then by kings such as Deiotarus, the ally of Pompey, it became a Roman province in 25 B.C.
Galatia.faith: Celtic religion, with the cult of Cybele at Pessinus

Paphlagonia.x: The rugged land between Bithynia and Pontus on the Black Sea, divided among native princes, many of them named Pylaemenes after the Paphlagonian leader of the Iliad. Squeezed between greater neighbors, it fell to Mithridates VI and then to Rome.

Antigonid Macedonia.x: The kingdom of Macedon under the Antigonid house, from Antigonus Gonatas, who defeated the Gauls and restored order, to Philip V and Perseus, who fought Rome. The phalanx that had conquered Asia was broken at Cynoscephalae and Pydna, and in 167 B.C. Rome divided the kingdom into four republics.

Greek Colonies.x: Free Greek cities outside the great Hellenistic kingdoms in the third century B.C., among them the quarrelsome cities of Crete, Knossos, Gortyn, and Lyttos, which sold archers and mercenaries to every king and harbored pirates, and the trading cities of the Aegean and Black Sea coasts.

Illyrian Kingdom.x: The kingdom of the Ardiaei on the eastern Adriatic, whose pirate fleets of light galleys preyed on Italian and Greek shipping. Rome made war on Queen Teuta in 229 B.C. and on Demetrius of Pharos in 219, and ended the kingdom by capturing King Genthius at Scodra in 168 B.C.

Kingdom of Sophene.x: A small Armenian kingdom on the upper Euphrates and Tigris, ruled by a branch of the Orontid house from Arsamosata and Carcathiocerta. Tigranes the Great annexed it to Armenia about 95 B.C.; under Rome it was briefly restored as a client kingdom before it was absorbed into the empire.

Kingdom of Cappadocia.x: The kingdom of the Ariarathid kings on the high plateau of eastern Anatolia, Persian in its nobility and Greek in its court, rich in horses and slaves. Long a Roman ally against Pontus, it was ruled after 95 B.C. by the Ariobarzanids and last by Archelaus, on whose death Tiberius annexed it in A.D. 17.
Kingdom of Cappadocia.faith: Iranian and Anatolian religion (Ma of Comana)

Mauretania.x: The kingdom of the Moors in northwest Africa, from the Atlantic to the river Mulucha, ruled by kings such as Bocchus I, who betrayed Jugurtha to Sulla, and Juba II, the scholar king of Iol Caesarea. Caligula had its last king, Ptolemy, put to death in A.D. 40, and Claudius made it two provinces.
Mauretania.faith: Berber and Punic religion; Roman cults

Kingdom of Numidia.x: The Berber kingdom of the North African interior, united by Masinissa, Rome's ally against Carthage, who turned nomads into farmers and lived to ninety. His grandson Jugurtha bribed the Senate and fought Rome for six years; Juba I sided with Pompey and fell after Thapsus in 46 B.C.

Ankhwennefer.x: The native kingdom of Upper Egypt in the great Theban revolt against the Ptolemies, begun by Horwennefer in 205 B.C. and carried on by Ankhwennefer, who held Thebes with Nubian help. Ptolemaic armies defeated and captured him in 186 B.C.

Rhodes.x: The island republic of Rhodes, the greatest naval and trading power of the Hellenistic Aegean, famed for its Colossus, its law of the sea, and its war on the pirates. Rewarded by Rome with Lycia and Caria after Magnesia, it lost them for wavering in the war against Perseus, and Rome's free port of Delos ruined its trade.

Nabataeans.x: The Arab kingdom of the Nabataeans, desert traders in incense and spices who carved their capital Petra from the rose-red cliffs, mastered the storing of water, and held the caravan roads from the Hejaz to Damascus. Its kings were clients of Rome until Trajan annexed the realm as the province of Arabia in A.D. 106.

Judea.x: The Jewish state won from the Seleucids by the Maccabees and ruled by their Hasmonean heirs as high priests and then kings, who conquered Idumea, Samaria, and Galilee. Pompey made it a client of Rome in 63 B.C., and Herod the Great, king by Rome's grace, rebuilt the Temple on a grand scale.
Judea.gov: High priests and kings, then a Roman client kingdom

Italic Confederation (Social War).x: The confederacy of Italian allies, Marsi, Samnites, Paeligni, Vestini, Lucanians, and others, who rose against Rome in 91 B.C. to win the citizenship. They founded a state called Italia with its capital at Corfinium, a senate, and two consuls, and struck coins showing the Italian bull goring the Roman wolf.

Thracian Kingdom.x: The client kingdom of the Sapaean and Odrysian Thracians under Roman protection, whose kings, such as Rhoemetalces I, fought for Rome in the Balkans and quarreled among themselves. Claudius annexed it as the province of Thrace in A.D. 46 after the murder of Rhoemetalces III.

Caucasian Albania.x: The kingdom of the eastern Caucasus between the Kura and the Caspian, in the land now called Azerbaijan, a league of tribes that met Pompey in battle in 65 B.C. Under Persian overlordship it took Christianity in the fourth century and its own alphabet in the fifth, with its capital at Kabalaka and later Partav.
Caucasian Albania.faith: Caucasian paganism, then Christianity from the fourth century

Kingdom of Osroene.x: The Aramean kingdom of Edessa in northern Mesopotamia, ruled by the Abgarid dynasty between Rome and Parthia. Christian tradition honored Abgar V for his letter to Jesus, and Edessa became the fountainhead of Syriac Christianity before Caracalla annexed the kingdom in A.D. 214.
Kingdom of Osroene.gov: Monarchy (client of Parthia, then of Rome)

Caucasian Iberia.x: The kingdom of eastern Georgia, ruled from Mtskheta on the Kura, which by Georgian tradition Pharnavaz I founded in the third century B.C. Its king Mirian III was converted by Saint Nino in the fourth century, and Vakhtang I Gorgasali, by tradition the founder of Tbilisi, fought Persia; Persia abolished the monarchy about A.D. 580.
Caucasian Iberia.faith: Georgian paganism, then Christianity from the fourth century

Lazica.x: The kingdom of the Laz on the eastern shore of the Black Sea, heir of ancient Colchis, ruled from Archaeopolis. Its king Tzath I was baptized at Constantinople in 522, and the Lazic War of 541 to 562 between Rome and Persia was fought over its fortresses and passes; it ended a Roman dependency.

Goths.x: The Goths in their northern homeland, which their historian Jordanes placed in Scandza and archaeologists trace in the Wielbark culture of the lower Vistula. In the second century A.D. they began the migration toward the Black Sea that brought them to the Roman frontier.

Burgundians.x: The East Germanic Burgundians, who by their own tradition came from Scandinavia and the island of Bornholm, settled between the Oder and the Vistula, and in the third century moved west toward the Main. In 406 they crossed the Rhine with the great migration and founded a kingdom on the middle Rhine.

Norse.x: The peoples of Scandinavia in the Roman Iron Age and the Migration Period, farmers and warriors who traded furs and amber for Roman silver and glass, sank the weapons of defeated armies in their bogs, and carved the first runes. From among them came the Danes, the Geats, and the Svear of later history.

Ripuarian Franks.x: The Rhineland Franks settled around Cologne, as distinct from the Salians to the west. Their king Sigobert the Lame was murdered by his son Chloderic at the urging of Clovis, who then had Chloderic killed in his turn and was raised on a shield as king of the Ripuarians about 509.

Lakhmid Kingdom.x: The Arab kingdom of the Lakhmids at al-Hira on the edge of the Euphrates, Persia's shield against the desert and against Rome's Arab allies. Its court was a center of Arabic poetry and of the Church of the East, until Khosrow II put al-Nu'man III to death about 602 and ended the dynasty.
Lakhmid Kingdom.faith: Arab paganism, then Christianity of the Church of the East

Saxons.x: The Saxon peoples of northern Germany between the Elbe and the Weser, sea raiders who harried the Roman coasts of Britain and Gaul and, with the Angles and Jutes, settled England. Those who stayed at home, governed by a yearly assembly at Marklo, resisted Charlemagne for thirty years, led by Widukind, before their conversion.
Saxons.gov: Tribal confederation with an assembly, without a king

Makuria.x: The Christian Nubian kingdom of the middle Nile, with its capital at Old Dongola, which halted the Arab invaders at the walls of Dongola in 652 and made with them the truce called the baqt. Absorbing Nobatia, it ruled Nubia for seven centuries, until Mamluk attacks and Arab migration brought its decline.

Nobatia.x: The northernmost Nubian kingdom, between the First and Third Cataracts, heir of the Noba and Blemmyes who replaced Meroë. Its king Silko boasted in Greek of his victories over the Blemmyes; converted by Theodora's missionaries in 543, it was joined to Makuria in the seventh century, with its seat at Faras.

Salian Franks.x: The Salian Franks, settled by the emperor Julian in Toxandria in 358, who spread south into Roman Gaul under Chlodio, the half-legendary Merovech, and Childeric I, whose rich grave was found at Tournai in 1653. Childeric's son Clovis made them masters of Gaul.

Visigoths.x: The Visigoths in their wandering years under Alaric, who led them from the Balkans into Italy, sacked Rome in 410, and died in Bruttium; his successors Athaulf and Wallia led them into Gaul and Spain, fighting Rome's enemies, until they were settled in Aquitaine in 418.

Kingdom of the Suebi.x: The kingdom of the Suebi in Gallaecia, in northwestern Spain, founded after their crossing of the Rhine in 406 and ruled from Braga. Their king Rechiar was the first Germanic king to take the Catholic faith; the kingdom turned Arian and back again, and fell to the Visigothic king Leovigild in 585.
Kingdom of the Suebi.faith: Germanic paganism, then Catholic and Arian Christianity, Catholic from about 560

Alans.x: The Iranian-speaking Alans, horse nomads of the Caspian steppe, part of whom were driven west by the Huns and crossed the Rhine with the Vandals and Suebi in 406. In 411 they took Lusitania and Carthaginiensis in Spain; after the Visigoths killed their king Addac in 418, they joined the Hasding Vandals.

Burgundian Kingdom.x: The kingdom of the Burgundians, first on the middle Rhine, where the Huns destroyed it in 436 in the disaster remembered in the Nibelungenlied, then resettled by Aetius in Sapaudia, whence it spread down the Rhone. Its king Gundobad issued the Burgundian law; the Franks conquered it in 534.

Marzpanate of Armenia.x: Persian Armenia after the end of the Arsacid monarchy in 428, governed from Dvin by marzpans, often Armenian princes, under the Sasanian King of Kings. The Armenians rose against forced conversion to Zoroastrianism at Avarayr in 451 and again under Vahan Mamikonian, who won freedom of worship and became marzpan in 485.

(Brythonic Kingdoms).x: The whole company of British kingdoms that rose when Roman rule ended, Gwynedd, Powys, Dyfed, Dumnonia, Rheged, Gododdin, and Strathclyde, speaking the Brittonic tongue that became Welsh, Cornish, and Cumbric. Pressed back by the English, the Welsh princes held out until Edward I conquered Gwynedd in 1282 and 1283.

Brythons.x: The British Celts of the post-Roman island, heirs of Roman Britain, whose kings fought the Anglo-Saxon invaders in the age remembered in the tales of Arthur and the poems of Aneirin and Taliesin. Their kingdoms in Wales, Cornwall, and the north slowly gave way to England, though Welsh princes kept their freedom until the thirteenth century.

Vandal Kingdom.x: The kingdom of the Vandals and Alans in Roman Africa, founded by Genseric with the capture of Carthage in 439, whose fleets ruled the western Mediterranean and sacked Rome in 455. Its Arian kings persecuted the Catholic clergy; Belisarius destroyed it at Ad Decimum and Tricamarum in 533.

(Anglo-Saxon England).x: The whole of the English kingdoms founded by the Angles, Saxons, and Jutes in Britain, Kent, Sussex, Wessex, Essex, East Anglia, Mercia, and Northumbria, converted by the mission of Augustine and the monks of Iona, and united under the kings of Wessex after the Viking wars into the kingdom of England.

Anglo-Saxon England.x: The first English settlements in Britain in the fifth and early sixth centuries, when Angles, Saxons, and Jutes from the coasts of Germany and Denmark took the east and south of the island. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle remembers Hengist in Kent, Ælle in Sussex, and Cerdic in Wessex, though the British victory at Mount Badon checked the advance for a generation.

Ostrogoths.x: The Ostrogoths of the Amal house, freed from the Huns after the Nedao and settled as Roman federates in Pannonia under the brothers Valamir, Theodemir, and Vidimer. Theodemir's son Theodoric, raised as a hostage in Constantinople, led them into the Balkans and then, at Zeno's bidding, into Italy.

Kingdom of Alamannia.x: The land of the Alamanni, a league of Germanic tribes on the upper Rhine and Danube who had raided Gaul and Italy since the third century. Defeated by Clovis about 496 and brought under Frankish rule, they were governed by their own dukes until the Carolingian mayors crushed them at Cannstatt in 746.
Kingdom of Alamannia.gov: Tribal kingship, then a duchy under the Franks

Thuringian states.x: The Thuringians of central Germany, between the Harz and the Danube, a powerful kingdom in the late fifth century, whose queen Basina, by Gregory of Tours's story, left her husband Bisinus to marry the Frankish king Childeric and bore him Clovis.

Kingdom of Odoacer.x: The rule of Odoacer, a Germanic officer of the Roman army who deposed Romulus Augustulus in 476, sent the imperial insignia to Constantinople, and governed Italy as king with the Senate and Roman law intact. Theodoric the Ostrogoth defeated him and killed him at Ravenna in 493.

Kingdom of Soissons.x: The last fragment of Roman rule in northern Gaul, held between the Somme and the Loire by the general Aegidius and his son Syagrius, whom Gregory of Tours calls king of the Romans. Clovis defeated Syagrius at Soissons in 486 and took his realm.

Kingdom of Thuringia.x: The kingdom of the Thuringians in central Germany under Bisinus and his sons Baderic, Berthar, and Hermanafrid, the last of whom married Amalaberga, niece of Theodoric the Great. The Franks destroyed it on the Unstrut in 531, and Hermanafrid was killed at Zülpich soon after.

Lombards.x: The Lombards in their wandering years north of the Alps, on the Elbe, in Moravia, and from about 526 in Pannonia, where under Audoin and Alboin they destroyed the Gepids with Avar help. In 568 Alboin led the whole people into Italy.

Ghassanids.x: The Arab Christian dynasty of the Syrian desert frontier, allies of Rome against Persia and its Lakhmid clients. Justinian made al-Harith ibn Jabalah king over the Arabs of the empire, and the Ghassanids championed the Miaphysite church; their last king, Jabalah ibn al-Ayham, fought the Muslims at the Yarmuk.

Kingdom of the Gepids.x: The kingdom of the Gepids, East Germanic kinsmen of the Goths, who under Ardaric led the subject peoples to break the sons of Attila at the Nedao in 454 and took the old Hunnic lands of Dacia and the Tisza. Masters of Sirmium, they were destroyed in 567 by the Lombards and the Avars.

Kingdom of Wessex.x: The kingdom of the West Saxons, founded by Cerdic in the Chronicle's tradition, which grew from the upper Thames and Hampshire to rule all southern England under Egbert. Its king Alfred the Great held off the Danes, and his son and grandson, Edward the Elder and Æthelstan, made it the kingdom of England.

Kingdom of Mercia.x: The kingdom of the Mercians in the English Midlands, raised to power by the pagan Penda and at its height under Æthelbald and Offa, whose great dyke marked the Welsh border and who styled himself king of the English. Broken by Wessex under Egbert and then by the Danes, Mercia was absorbed by Wessex.

Bavarians.x: The Bavarians, who appear in the sixth century between the Lech and the Enns, ruled under Frankish overlordship by the Agilolfing dukes from Regensburg. Converted by Rupert, Emmeram, and Boniface, the duchy grew strong under Odilo and Tassilo III, whom Charlemagne deposed in 788.

Dál Riata.x: The Gaelic kingdom spanning the North Channel, from Antrim in Ireland to Argyll in Scotland, ruled from the rock fortress of Dunadd. Its king Conall gave Iona to Columba, Áedán mac Gabráin fought the Angles at Degsastan, and from its royal line came Kenneth MacAlpin, king of the Picts and the Scots.

Kingdom of Gwynedd.x: The kingdom of northwest Wales, centered on Snowdonia and Anglesey, which by tradition Cunedda founded and Maelgwn Gwynedd made the first power among the Britons. Under Rhodri the Great, Owain Gwynedd, and the two Llywelyns it led the Welsh, until Edward I conquered it in 1282 and 1283.

Duchy of Thuringia.x: Thuringia as a duchy of the Frankish kingdom after 531, guarding the eastern frontier against the Slavs and Avars. Its duke Radulf defeated King Sigebert III about 640 and ruled almost as a king; under the line of Heden, the last dukes, it gave way to Frankish counts and to the missions of Boniface.

Duchy of Spoleto.x: The Lombard duchy of central Italy, founded by Faroald about 570, which held the Apennines between Rome and Ravenna and was often all but independent of the kings at Pavia. Under Frankish rule its dukes of the house of Guy rose so high that Guy III and his son Lambert were crowned emperors.

Duchy of Benevento.x: The Lombard duchy of southern Italy, founded by Zotto about 571, which held most of the south apart from the Roman coastal cities. Its dukes, among them Grimoald I, who became king of the Lombards, held it against the emperor Constans II; after 774 Arechis II made it an independent principality.

Kingdom of the Lombards.x: The Lombard kingdom of Italy, ruled from Pavia, which held the north and, through the duchies of Spoleto and Benevento, much of the south. Its kings turned Catholic under the influence of Queen Theodelinda, issued the Edict of Rothari, and pressed hard on Rome, until Charlemagne took Pavia and the iron crown in 774.

Breton Kingdoms.x: The British settlers of Armorica, who crossed from Cornwall and Wales in the fifth and sixth centuries and gave Brittany its name and speech. Their chiefs, such as Waroch of the Vannetais and Judicael of Domnonée, defied the Franks, and Morvan and Wiomarc'h fought Louis the Pious before Nominoe united the land.

Frankish Burgundy.x: The Burgundian kingdom of the Merovingian Franks, one of the three realms into which the Frankish lands were divided, on the Saône and the Rhône. Under Theuderic II and his grandmother Brunhild it warred with Austrasia and Neustria, until Clothar II seized it in 613 and reunited the Franks.

Magna Frisia.x: The realm of the Frisians along the North Sea coast from the Scheldt to the Weser, masters of the trade of Dorestad. Its kings Aldgisl and Redbad resisted Frankish power and the Christian mission, until Charles Martel broke them in 734 and Charlemagne absorbed the last free Frisians.

Kingdom of Northumbria.x: The northernmost Anglo-Saxon kingdom, formed by the union of Bernicia and Deira, from the Humber to the Forth. In the seventh century it was the strongest English realm and, with Lindisfarne, Jarrow, and Bede, a light of Christian learning in the West; the Danes took York in 866, and English lords held out at Bamburgh.

Duchy of Alamannia.x: The duchy of the Alamanni between the upper Rhine, the Danube, and the Alps, a Frankish dependency under its own dukes. Gotfrid and his sons Lantfrid and Theudebald strove for independence from the Carolingian mayors, until Carloman's blood court at Cannstatt in 746 ended the duchy.

Samo's Empire.x: The first known union of the western Slavs, raised by the Frankish merchant Samo after the Wends rose against the Avars about 623. Centered on Bohemia, Moravia, and the lands about the middle Danube, it defeated Dagobert's Franks at Wogastisburg and fell apart on Samo's death some thirty-five years later.

Aquitaine.x: The land between the Loire, the Pyrenees, and the Rhône, Roman in speech and law, which repeatedly broke free of the Franks. Its dukes Odo, Hunald, and Waifer defied the Carolingians and fought the Muslims, until Pepin the Short subdued it; Charlemagne then made it a sub-kingdom for his son Louis.
Aquitaine.gov: Kingdom, then duchy, then Carolingian sub-kingdom

Khazaria.x: A Turkic khaganate of the steppe between the Volga, the Don, and the Caucasus, which held back the Arabs in the Caucasus wars and grew rich on the trade from the Baltic to Baghdad. Its ruling class embraced Judaism, the only such state of the Middle Ages, until Sviatoslav of Kiev broke it in 965.
Khazaria.gov: Khaganate, with a sacred khagan and a ruling bek
Khazaria.faith: Tengrism, then Judaism among the ruling class; Islam and Christianity tolerated

Byzantine Empire.x: The Roman Empire in the East, Greek in tongue and Orthodox in faith, ruled from Constantinople for over a thousand years. It held the Arabs at its walls, brought the Slavs to Christianity, kept the learning of antiquity, and outlived the sack of 1204, until the Ottoman Turks stormed its capital in 1453.

Old Great Bulgaria.x: The Bulgar realm founded about 632 by Khan Kubrat on the steppe north of the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov, an ally of Heraclius against the Avars. After Kubrat's death the Khazars broke it apart, and his sons led their hordes away, Asparukh to the Danube and Kotrag toward the Volga.

Neustria and Burgundy.x: The western Frankish kingdom of the Merovingians, Neustria joined with Burgundy, ruled from Paris by the child king Clovis II and his queen Balthild, while real power passed to mayors of the palace such as Erchinoald and Ebroin.
Neustria and Burgundy.gov: Monarchy under mayors of the palace

Carantania.x: A principality of the Alpine Slavs in what became Carinthia and Styria, centered on the Zollfeld and its Prince's Stone. Pressed by the Avars, Prince Boruth sought Bavarian help about 743 and accepted Bavarian overlordship; his successors were baptized, and Carantania passed with Bavaria into the Frankish realm.

First Bulgarian Empire.x: The Bulgar khanate south of the Danube, founded by Asparukh in 681, which fused Turkic Bulgars and Slavs into one people. Under Krum and Simeon it rivaled Byzantium; Boris took the Christian faith, and the schools of Preslav and Ohrid made Slavonic a written tongue. Basil II conquered it by 1018.

Republic of Venice.x: The merchant republic of the lagoons, nominally Byzantine until it grew into the mistress of the Adriatic and the Levant trade. Ruled by an elected doge and, after 1297, a closed patrician Great Council, it built an empire of islands and ports from Dalmatia to Crete and Cyprus, and endured until Bonaparte ended it in 1797.
Republic of Venice.gov: Aristocratic republic under an elected doge

Merovingian Empire.x: The Frankish realm in the last years of Pepin of Herstal, its Merovingian kings mere shadows on the throne. On Pepin's death in 714 civil war broke out among his widow Plectrude, the Neustrians, and his son Charles Martel, who emerged master of all the Franks.
Merovingian Empire.gov: Monarchy under mayors of the palace

(Carolingian Empire).x: The Frankish empire of the Carolingian house, built by Charles Martel and Pepin the Short and brought by Charlemagne to its height, from the Ebro to the Elbe and from the North Sea to Rome. It revived the Western Empire, Latin learning, and the reform of the Church, but was divided among Charlemagne's grandsons at Verdun in 843.

Carolingian Empire.x: The Frankish realm in the first years of Charles Martel's mastery, after his victories over the Neustrians and their mayor Ragenfrid at Amblève, Vinchy, and Soissons. Ruling through puppet Merovingian kings, Charles went on to humble the Saxons, Frisians, and Alamanni and to gather the host that stopped the Muslims near Tours in 732.
Carolingian Empire.gov: Monarchy under the mayor of the palace

Kingdom of Asturias.x: The Christian kingdom founded by Pelayo in the Cantabrian mountains after Covadonga, the first refuge of Spain against the Muslim conquest. From Oviedo, Alfonso II and Alfonso III pushed its frontier to the Duero and fostered the shrine of St. James; in 910 its center moved south to León.

Kingdom of Neustria.x: The western Frankish lands between the Loire and the Scheldt, centered on Paris and Soissons, the old heartland of the Merovingians. By this time its kings were puppets of Charles Martel, who had broken the Neustrian mayor Ragenfrid.
Kingdom of Neustria.gov: Monarchy under the mayor of the palace

Duchy of Croatia.x: The duchy of the Croats on the Dalmatian coast and in its hinterland, under Frankish and then Byzantine sway. Duke Trpimir founded the native dynasty, Branimir won papal recognition of his independence in 879, and Tomislav made it a kingdom about 925.

Papal States.x: The temporal dominion of the popes in central Italy, born of Pepin's donation of 756 and stretching at its height from Rome to Bologna and Ferrara. Defended by excommunication, mercenaries, and the diplomacy of the Curia, it survived the Avignon exile and Napoleon, until Italian troops entered Rome in 1870.

Emirate of Córdoba.x: The independent Umayyad emirate of al-Andalus, founded by Abd al-Rahman I, a survivor of the Abbasid massacre of his house, who reached Spain in 755. From Córdoba his heirs ruled most of the peninsula, raided the Christian north, and raised the Great Mosque, until Abd al-Rahman III proclaimed himself caliph in 929.
Emirate of Córdoba.faith: Sunni Islam; Christian and Jewish subjects

Principality of Serbia.x: The Serbian principality of the early Middle Ages in the hills of Raška, ruled by the house of Vlastimir between Byzantium and Bulgaria; and the modern principality won from the Ottomans in the risings of Karađorđe in 1804 and Miloš Obrenović in 1815, autonomous from 1830 and independent in 1878.

Duchy of Gascony.x: The duchy of the Basques and Gascons between the Garonne and the Pyrenees, fiercely independent of the Franks, kinsmen of the Basques who struck Charlemagne's rearguard at Roncevaux. A native ducal house ruled it from the late ninth century until 1032, after which it passed to the counts of Poitou and was joined to Aquitaine.

Principality of Benevento.x: The Lombard duchy of southern Italy that survived the fall of Pavia in 774, when Duke Arechis II took the title of prince and defied Charlemagne. Divided after 849 into Benevento and Salerno, beset by Saracens, Byzantines, and at last the Normans, its city passed to the pope in 1077.

Viking settlements.x: The lands won and settled by Norse and Danish Vikings in the British Isles: the Danelaw, the kingdoms of York and Dublin, the earldom of Orkney, and the Western Isles. They brought trading towns, place names, and law, and their leaders married into native dynasties until absorbed by English, Scottish, and Irish kings.

Great Moravia.x: The first great state of the western Slavs, on the Morava river, which under Rastislav and Svatopluk ruled Moravia, Slovakia, Bohemia, and lands beyond. It received Cyril and Methodius and the Slavonic liturgy in 863, and was destroyed by the Magyars soon after 900.

Principality of Nitra.x: A Slavic principality in what is now western Slovakia, whose prince Pribina raised the first known church in the land, consecrated by the archbishop of Salzburg. Mojmír of Moravia drove Pribina out about 833 and joined Nitra to Great Moravia.

Kingdom of Pamplona.x: The Basque kingdom of the western Pyrenees founded by Íñigo Arista about 824, later called Navarre. Under Sancho III the Great it dominated Christian Spain from Castile to Aragon, but his realm was split among his sons, and after Sancho IV's murder in 1076 it was shared between Aragon and Castile.

Kingdom of Brittany.x: The Breton realm of the Armorican peninsula, made independent by Nominoe's victory over Charles the Bald at Ballon in 845. His son Erispoe and the usurper Salomon bore the title of king, and Alan the Great beat back the Vikings, but after 907 the Northmen overran the land.

Magyars.x: The confederation of seven Magyar tribes, Finno-Ugric in speech and steppe horsemen in their way of war, who roamed between the Don and the lower Danube in the ninth century. Under Álmos and Árpád they crossed the Carpathians about 895 and took the basin of the Danube for their home.
Magyars.gov: Tribal confederation under a sacral kende and a war leader, the gyula

West Franks.x: The western kingdom of the Franks allotted to Charles the Bald at Verdun in 843, the seed of France. Ravaged by the Vikings and parceled among great vassals, it saw the crown pass back and forth between the last Carolingians at Laon and the Robertian dukes of Paris until Hugh Capet's election in 987.

East Franks.x: The eastern kingdom of the Franks, allotted to Louis the German at Verdun: the lands of the Saxons, Franconians, Swabians, Bavarians, and Thuringians east of the Rhine. Its Carolingian line ended with the death of the boy Louis the Child in 911, when the dukes chose Conrad of Franconia.

Middle Franks.x: The middle kingdom carved out at Verdun for the emperor Lothair I, a long strip from Frisia through Burgundy and Provence to Italy, holding both imperial cities, Aachen and Rome. On Lothair's death in 855 it was split among his three sons, and its northern part, Lotharingia, became the bone of contention between France and Germany.

Emirate of Sicily.x: Muslim Sicily, won from Byzantium over three-quarters of a century from 827 and ruled first by Aghlabid governors from Palermo, then from 948 by the Kalbid emirs under the Fatimids. Citrus, sugar cane, and cotton flourished and Palermo grew into a great city, until feuding emirs called in the Normans, who won the island by 1091.
Emirate of Sicily.faith: Islam, with a large Greek Christian population

Old Kingdom of Norway.x: The kingdom of Norway from Harald Fairhair's union of the coast to the end of its native line in 1387. Its kings made it Christian under the two Olafs, ruled Iceland, Greenland, and the isles of the west at its height under Haakon IV, and after the Black Death drifted into union with Denmark under Queen Margaret.

Giudicato of Arborea.x: The most enduring of the four native kingdoms, or judicates, of medieval Sardinia, ruled from Oristano. Its judges Marianus IV and his daughter Eleanor, lawgiver of the Carta de Logu, waged a long war against the Crown of Aragon for the whole island, until the last judge sold his rights to Aragon in 1420.

Danelaw.x: The lands of England north and east of Watling Street settled by the Danes after the Great Heathen Army, where Danish law and custom held sway: the kingdom of York, the Five Boroughs, and East Anglia. The kings of Wessex won them back between 917 and 954, but Danish law endured there long after.

Rus'.x: The realm of the Varangian Rus' in the north, about Lake Ladoga and Novgorod, where the chronicle says Rurik was called to rule in 862. His kinsman Oleg moved south down the Dnieper and in 882 made Kiev the capital of a united Kievan state.
Rus'.gov: Princely rule of a Varangian dynasty

Lower Burgundy.x: The kingdom of Provence, or Lower Burgundy, seized in 879 by Count Boso of Vienne, the first man not of Carolingian blood to make himself king in the Frankish world. His son Louis the Blind, briefly emperor, was blinded in Italy in 905, and Count Hugh of Arles governed in his name.

Kievan Rus'.x: The realm of the Rurikid princes along the Dnieper and the Volkhov, from Novgorod to Kiev, built on the river trade from the Varangians to the Greeks. Christianized under Vladimir in 988 and given law and cathedrals by Yaroslav the Wise, it splintered among quarreling princes after 1132 and was destroyed by the Mongols in 1237 to 1240.
Kievan Rus'.gov: Monarchy of the Rurikid house, succession by seniority
Kievan Rus'.faith: Slavic paganism, then Orthodox Christianity from 988

Kingdom of Italy.x: The Lombard crown of Italy, fought over by native princes after the Carolingians until Otto the Great joined it to the German kingship in 961; thereafter the emperors were kings of Italy in name while its cities governed themselves. The title revived under Napoleon, and in the united kingdom of the House of Savoy from 1861 to 1946.
Kingdom of Italy.gov: Monarchy, later nominal under the emperors

Upper Burgundy.x: The kingdom founded by the Welf count Rudolf, crowned at the abbey of St. Maurice in 888, in the lands of the Jura and western Switzerland. His son Rudolf II briefly held Italy and acquired Provence, uniting the two Burgundies into the Kingdom of Arles.

(West Francia).x: The West Frankish kingdom and its great fiefs in the last century of the Carolingians: Normandy, Brittany, Aquitaine, Burgundy, Flanders, and the Robertian march about Paris. Its kings, Carolingian and Robertian by turns, held little beyond Laon and Paris, until the election of Hugh Capet in 987 founded the French monarchy.

Duchy of Bohemia.x: The duchy of the Czechs under the Přemyslid house, centered on the castle of Prague. Bořivoj received baptism, Wenceslaus was martyred and became the nation's saint, and Boleslaus I and II extended its power into Moravia, Silesia, and Kraków while acknowledging the German king as overlord.

County of Barcelona.x: The chief of the Catalan counties of the old Spanish March, made hereditary by Wilfred the Hairy, who died fighting the Muslims in 897. Drifting from the Frankish crown after Almanzor's sack of 985, the counts led the Catalans toward the Ebro and in 1137 joined their house to the kingdom of Aragon.

Nitra.x: The principality of Nitra, an appanage of Great Moravia in the west of present Slovakia, held at the end of the ninth century by Svatopluk II, younger son of Svatopluk I, who rose against his brother Mojmír II. It fell to the Magyars in the first years of the tenth century.

Principality of Hungary.x: The realm of the Magyars after the conquest of the Carpathian basin, a confederation of horse-riding tribes whose raids terrorized Europe until the Lechfeld in 955. Prince Géza invited missionaries and made peace with the Empire, and his son Stephen, crowned in 1000, turned it into the Christian kingdom of Hungary.
Principality of Hungary.gov: Tribal principality of the Árpád house

Kingdom of Lower Burgundy.x: The kingdom of Provence in the time of Louis the Blind, who was crowned emperor at Rome in 901 and blinded by Berengar I at Verona in 905. Count Hugh of Arles governed for him and later made himself king of Italy; Provence then passed to Rudolf II of Upper Burgundy.

Kingdom of Alba.x: The kingdom of the Scots and Picts north of the Forth, called Alba in Gaelic, which under Constantine II and Malcolm II took in Lothian and Strathclyde. The house of Canmore and David I brought Norman knights, burghs, and reformed monasteries, and Alexander III won the Western Isles from Norway; his death in 1286 opened the way to the wars of independence.

Kingdom of Germany.x: The East Frankish kingdom after the Carolingians, when the dukes of Franconia, Saxony, Bavaria, and Swabia chose Conrad of Franconia and then Henry the Fowler of Saxony as king. Henry and his son Otto I built a strong Saxon monarchy, broke the Magyars, and in 962 joined the German crown to the imperial dignity.

Kingdom of León.x: The successor of Asturias, whose kings moved their seat south to León in the tenth century and styled themselves emperors of all Spain. Ramiro II won at Simancas, Alfonso VI took Toledo, and Alfonso IX summoned the first Cortes with townsmen in 1188; in 1230 León was joined for good to Castile.

Kingdom of Galicia.x: The northwestern corner of Spain, home of the shrine of Santiago, repeatedly set apart as a kingdom for younger sons of the Asturian and Leonese kings: Ordoño II before he took León, García II in the eleventh century, and the boy Alfonso VII, crowned at Santiago in 1111.
Kingdom of Galicia.gov: Monarchy, often a sub-kingdom of León

(Kingdom of Germany).x: The German kingdom of the Saxon house with its subject duchies and marches: Saxony, Franconia, Swabia, Bavaria, Lotharingia, and the frontier marches against the Slavs and Magyars. Henry the Fowler and Otto the Great bound the dukes to the crown and the Church to the king, laying the base of the medieval Empire.

Upper Burgundy and Italy.x: The brief union of Upper Burgundy with the Italian crown under Rudolf II, called in by Italian lords against Berengar I, whom he defeated at Fiorenzuola in 923. The Italians soon turned to Hugh of Arles, and Rudolf withdrew beyond the Alps.

Duchy of Normandy.x: The duchy won by Rollo's Vikings on the lower Seine in 911, whose Norse settlers within a few generations became French-speaking Christian knights. Its dukes built the strongest feudal state of France, and in 1066 Duke William conquered England, binding the duchy to the English crown until 1204.

Kingdom of Croatia.x: The Croatian kingdom of Tomislav and the Trpimirović kings on the Adriatic coast and its hinterland. Peter Krešimir IV ruled the Dalmatian towns, and Zvonimir was crowned with papal blessing in 1076; after the native line died out, the crown passed in 1102 to Coloman of Hungary.

(Kingdom of England).x: The realm of the English crown with its lands beyond England: Normandy and the Angevin inheritance in France, the lordship and later kingdom of Ireland, Wales, and the Channel Islands. Its kings lost their French empire by 1453 save Calais, broke with Rome under Henry VIII, and in 1603 shared their king with Scotland.
(Kingdom of England).faith: Catholic Christianity, then the Church of England from 1534

Kingdom of England.x: The English kingdom united under the house of Wessex, conquered by the Danes in 1016 and the Normans in 1066, which grew into one of the strongest monarchies of Europe, with its common law and its Parliament. It fought France for a century, broke with Rome, beheaded a king in civil war, and in 1707 joined Scotland as Great Britain.
Kingdom of England.faith: Catholic Christianity, then the Church of England from 1534

Kingdom of Denmark.x: The Danish kingdom of the Jelling dynasty, made Christian by Harald Bluetooth, which under Sweyn and Cnut ruled England and Norway, under the Valdemars dominated the Baltic, and under Margaret led the Kalmar Union. With Iceland and Greenland as dependencies, it lost the lands east of the Sound to Sweden in 1658 and Schleswig-Holstein to Prussia and Austria in 1864.
Kingdom of Denmark.faith: Norse paganism, then Catholic, then Lutheran Christianity from 1536

(Kingdom of Denmark).x: The Danish realm with its dependencies: Scania and the lands across the Sound, the duchy of Schleswig, and at times Estonia, Norway, and the Wendish coast. Under the Valdemars it was the great power of the Baltic; Valdemar IV Atterdag rebuilt it after collapse, and his daughter Margaret joined it to Norway and Sweden.

Kingdom of Arles.x: The united kingdom of the two Burgundies, from Basel to the Mediterranean, formed under Rudolf II and Conrad the Peaceful. When the childless Rudolf III died in 1032 it passed to the emperor Conrad II, and the emperors kept the title of king of Arles while Provence, Dauphiné, and Savoy slipped from their grasp.
Kingdom of Arles.gov: Monarchy, then a nominal crown of the emperors

Icelandic Commonwealth.x: The commonwealth of free Norse farmers in Iceland, without king or executive, governed by chieftains, the godar, who met each summer at the Althing. It produced the sagas and the Eddas, accepted Christianity by vote of the assembly about 1000, and sank into the feuds of the Sturlung age before submitting to the King of Norway in 1262 to 1264.
Icelandic Commonwealth.gov: Commonwealth of chieftains under the Althing
Icelandic Commonwealth.faith: Norse paganism, then Catholic Christianity from 1000

Duchy of Brittany.x: The Breton duchy restored by Alan Barbetorte after he drove out the Vikings in 937, a great fief of France that balanced between the French and English crowns through the Hundred Years' War. The marriage of its heiress Anne to Charles VIII in 1491 bound it to France, with which it was formally united in 1532.

Jämtland.x: A land of free farmers in the mountains between Norway and Sweden, governed by its own assembly at Frösön and Christianized, its runestone says, by a man named Austmadr. King Sverre of Norway subdued it about 1178, and it remained Norwegian until ceded to Sweden in 1645.
Jämtland.gov: Farmers' commonwealth under its own assembly

County of Castile.x: The frontier county of the castles on the upper Ebro and Duero, carved from León's eastern march. Fernán González made it hereditary and all but independent; on the murder of the last count, García Sánchez, in 1029 it passed to Sancho the Great of Navarre, whose son Ferdinand made it a kingdom.

(Holy Roman Empire).x: The empire of the German kings, revived by Otto I in 962 and later styled Holy and Roman, embracing Germany, Bohemia, the Low Countries, Burgundy, and northern Italy. Its emperors contended with the popes and then with their own princes, until by 1648 it was a loose federation of hundreds of states; Francis II dissolved it in 1806.
(Holy Roman Empire).faith: Catholic Christianity; Lutheran and Calvinist states recognized in 1555 and 1648

Holy Roman Empire.x: The Empire of the Ottonian, Salian, and Staufer emperors, crowned in Rome and ruling Germany, Burgundy, and the Italian kingdom. Henry IV's quarrel with Gregory VII over the investiture of bishops, and the long war of Barbarossa and Frederick II with the popes and the Lombard cities, wore down its power; after 1250 it sank into the Great Interregnum.

(Kingdom of Poland).x: The Polish realm of the Piasts, baptized under Mieszko I in 966 and crowned under Bolesław the Brave, which broke into duchies after 1138 and was made whole again by Władysław the Elbow-high and Casimir the Great. Joined with Lithuania under the Jagiellonians in 1386, it broke the Teutonic Order at Grunwald.

Duchy of Poland.x: The Piast duchy of the Polans between the Oder and the Vistula, made Christian by Mieszko I in 966 and placed under the protection of the Holy See. His son Bolesław the Brave won an archbishopric at Gniezno in 1000, fought the emperor Henry II for fifteen years, and was crowned king in 1025.

Kingdom of Sweden.x: The kingdom of the Swedes and Götar about Lake Mälaren and the lakes of the south, Christianized from the eleventh century, which conquered Finland and then joined the Kalmar Union. Gustav Vasa freed it in 1523; under Gustavus Adolphus and his heirs it became the great power of the North, and after 1721 it sank back to a lesser rank under the rule of its estates.
Kingdom of Sweden.faith: Norse paganism, then Catholic, then Lutheran Christianity from 1527

(Kingdom of France).x: The realm of the French crown with its great fiefs, from the small Capetian domain about Paris to the kingdom of Louis XIV. Its kings absorbed Normandy, Toulouse, Burgundy, and Brittany, fought England for a century, and made France the most populous and powerful state of Europe and the model of absolute monarchy.
(Kingdom of France).faith: Catholic Christianity; Huguenots tolerated from 1598 to 1685

Kingdom of France.x: The kingdom of the Capetians and their Valois and Bourbon heirs, which grew from the royal domain of the Île-de-France by conquest, marriage, and law. It drove out the English under Joan of Arc and Charles VII, survived the Wars of Religion, and under Richelieu and Louis XIV became the first power of Europe, until the Revolution of 1789.
Kingdom of France.faith: Catholic Christianity; Huguenots tolerated from 1598 to 1685

Duchy of Aquitaine.x: The great duchy of southwestern France, held from the tenth century by the counts of Poitou, whose court under William IX, the first troubadour, was a cradle of the poetry of courtly love. Through Eleanor of Aquitaine it passed to the English kings, who held Gascony as dukes until the French took Bordeaux in 1453.

County of Toulouse.x: The county of the house of Saint-Gilles, lords of Languedoc from the Garonne to the Rhône, whose Raymond IV led the Provençals on the First Crusade. Raymond VI and VII, protectors of a land full of Cathars, lost the Albigensian Crusade, and by the Treaty of Paris in 1229 the county was bound to pass to the French crown.
County of Toulouse.faith: Catholic Christianity, with a strong Cathar church

County of Blois.x: The county of the house of Blois on the middle Loire, whose ambitious counts Odo II and Theobald the Great also held Champagne and rivaled the Capetian kings. Stephen of Blois, grandson of the Conqueror, became king of England; the last count sold Blois in 1391 to Louis of Orléans, and it came to the crown with Louis XII.

County of Flanders.x: The county of the Flemish coast and the cloth towns of Bruges, Ghent, and Ypres, the most thickly peopled land north of the Alps. Its counts, vassals of both France and the Empire, led crusades, and Baldwin IX became the first Latin emperor of Constantinople; in 1384 it passed to the dukes of Burgundy.

County of Champagne.x: The county of the plains east of Paris, whose fairs at Troyes, Provins, Lagny, and Bar drew the merchants of Italy and Flanders in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. Its court under Henry the Liberal and Marie of France fostered Chrétien de Troyes; through the heiress Joan it passed to Philip IV of France in 1284.

County of Anjou.x: The county on the lower Loire of the warlike counts of Anjou, Fulk Nerra the castle builder and Geoffrey Martel, whose descendants became kings of Jerusalem and, through Geoffrey Plantagenet and Henry II, of England. Philip Augustus took it in 1204, and Louis IX gave it to his brother Charles, founder of the second Angevin house.

County of Rouergue.x: A county of the Massif Central about Rodez, held by a branch of the house of Toulouse. When the countess Bertha died without heirs in 1065, it passed to her cousins, the counts of Toulouse.

Kingdom of Hungary.x: The Christian kingdom of the Magyars founded by St. Stephen in 1000, ruling the Carpathian basin, Croatia, and Transylvania, a bulwark of Latin Christendom against the steppe and the Turks. After Mohács in 1526 it was split among Habsburgs, Ottomans, and Transylvania, then won back by the Habsburgs and joined with Austria in the Dual Monarchy of 1867.
Kingdom of Hungary.gov: Monarchy (elective in practice, hereditary in the Habsburg house from 1687)
Kingdom of Hungary.faith: Catholic Christianity, with a large Protestant minority from the sixteenth century

Duchy of Burgundy.x: The French duchy about Dijon, held by a cadet line of the Capetians from 1032 and from 1363 by the Valois dukes, Philip the Bold, John the Fearless, Philip the Good, and Charles the Bold. Adding Flanders, Brabant, and Holland, they kept the richest court in Europe, until Charles fell at Nancy in 1477 and Louis XI seized the duchy.

(Taifas of Iberia).x: The petty Muslim kingdoms into which al-Andalus broke after civil war destroyed the Caliphate of Córdoba between 1009 and 1031: Seville, Toledo, Zaragoza, Badajoz, Granada, Valencia, Dénia, and others, brilliant in poetry and learning but paying tribute to the Christian kings. The Almoravids swept most away after 1086, and later crops of taifas rose and fell.

Taifa of Badajoz.x: The taifa of the lower Guadiana and the old province of Lusitania, ruled from Badajoz by the Aftasid house, patrons of poets and scholars. Its last king, al-Mutawakkil, sought Christian help against the Almoravids and was put to death by them in 1094.

Taifa of Toledo.x: The taifa of the old Visigothic capital and the central plateau, ruled by the Berber house of Dhu'l-Nun. Under al-Mamun it flourished and took Valencia and Córdoba, but his grandson al-Qadir, a tributary of Alfonso VI, surrendered Toledo to him in 1085 and was given Valencia in its place.
Taifa of Toledo.faith: Islam; Mozarabic Christian and Jewish subjects

Taifa of Valencia.x: The taifa of the eastern coast, founded by two freedmen of the house of Almanzor and later ruled by his grandson Abd al-Aziz. It passed to Toledo and then to the deposed al-Qadir, whose murder the Cid avenged by taking the city in 1094; James I of Aragon conquered the last Muslim kingdom of Valencia in 1238.

Taifa of Dénia.x: The sea taifa of Dénia and the Balearic Isles, founded by Mujahid, a freedman of the house of Almanzor, who in 1015 launched a great raid on Sardinia. His corsair fleets made it a naval power of the western Mediterranean until Zaragoza annexed it in 1076.

Republic of Genoa.x: The merchant republic of the Ligurian coast, which with Pisa drove the Saracens from Corsica and Sardinia and grew rich on the crusades, with colonies from Caffa on the Black Sea to Chios. Riven by faction, it chose doges for life from 1339, was refounded as an aristocratic republic by Andrea Doria in 1528, and fell to Bonaparte in 1797.

Republic of Pisa.x: The maritime republic at the mouth of the Arno, which led the attacks on Saracen Sardinia, Palermo, and Mahdia and built its cathedral from the spoils. Broken as a sea power by Genoa at Meloria in 1284, it was sold to Milan in 1399 and conquered by Florence in 1406.

Kingdom of Aragon.x: The small mountain kingdom of the upper Aragon valley, made a kingdom for Ramiro I, son of Sancho the Great.
