Alfonso the Battler conquered Zaragoza and the Ebro valley in 1118, and his brother Ramiro the Monk betrothed his heiress to the Count of Barcelona, forming the Crown of Aragon.

Taifa of Murcia.x: The taifa of the Segura valley about Murcia, which in the twelfth century under Ibn Mardanish, the Wolf King, defied the Almohads with Christian mercenaries and allies for a quarter of a century. After a last revival under Ibn Hud it became a vassal of Castile in 1243 and was annexed after the revolt of 1264 to 1266.

Taifa of Zaragoza.x: The taifa of the upper Ebro, the northern march of al-Andalus, ruled by the Tujibids and from 1039 by the Banu Hud. Al-Muqtadir built the Aljafería palace and with his son took the exiled Cid into his service; the Almoravids took the city in 1110, eight years before Alfonso the Battler won it for Aragon.

North Sea Empire.x: The realm of Cnut the Great, king of England from 1016, of Denmark from 1018, and of Norway from 1028, with lordship over the Scots and parts of Sweden. Governed through English and Danish earls, it was the greatest power of the northern seas, but fell apart within a few years of Cnut's death in 1035.

Kingdom of Poland.x: The Polish kingdom crowned under Bolesław the Brave in 1025, eclipsed by the division into duchies, and restored by the coronation of Władysław the Elbow-high in 1320. Casimir the Great found it built of wood and left it built of stone; Jadwiga and Jagiełło joined it to Lithuania and won at Grunwald.

Norman Italy.x: The lordships carved out of southern Italy and Sicily by Norman adventurers from 1030, above all the sons of Tancred of Hauteville. Robert Guiscard won Apulia and Calabria and drove out the Byzantines, his brother Roger conquered Muslim Sicily, and Roger's son Roger II united all in the Kingdom of Sicily in 1130.

Kingdom of Castile.x: The kingdom that grew out of the frontier county of Castile, raised to royal rank for Ferdinand I in 1035. Alfonso VI took Toledo, Alfonso VIII won at Las Navas de Tolosa, and in 1230 Ferdinand III inherited León as well, joining the two crowns forever.

Denmark-England.x: The last union of the Danish and English crowns, under Harthacnut, son of Cnut, king of Denmark from 1035 and of England from 1040. When he died at a wedding feast in 1042, England recalled the old line in Edward the Confessor, and Denmark passed to Magnus of Norway.

Norway-Denmark.x: The union of Norway and Denmark under Magnus the Good, son of St. Olaf, who by a pact with Harthacnut inherited Denmark in 1042. After his death in 1047 Harald Hardrada kept Norway and warred for years with Sweyn Estridsen for Denmark, until a peace in 1064 left each crown to its own king.

Principality of Novgorod.x: Novgorod the Great in the age of the Kievan princes, when it was the second city of Rus' and the seat of a son of the grand prince, who ruled with the townsmen's veche and its own posadnik. Its stone cathedral of St. Sophia rose from 1045, and its merchants traded with Gotland and the Baltic.
Principality of Novgorod.gov: Principality with a strong town assembly

Cumania.x: The Cuman-Kipchak confederation of Turkic nomads, the Polovtsy of the Russian chronicles, who drove out the Pechenegs and ruled the steppe from the Danube to the Volga after 1050. Raiders and allies by turns of Rus', Byzantium, Hungary, and Georgia, they were scattered by the Mongols between 1237 and 1241, and many fled into Hungary under Köten.

Principality of Chernigov.x: The principality on the Desna, east of the Dnieper, held by the heirs of Sviatoslav II, the Olgovichi, who fought endlessly for the throne of Kiev. Prince Igor's ill-fated raid on the Cumans in 1185 inspired the Lay of Igor's Campaign; the Mongols sacked Chernigov in 1239, and Prince Michael was martyred at the Horde in 1246.

Principality of Rostov-Suzdal.x: The forest principality of the northeast, between the upper Volga and the Oka, settled by Slav colonists among Finnic tribes. Yuri Dolgoruky founded Moscow, his son Andrei Bogolyubsky moved the seat to Vladimir and sacked Kiev in 1169, and under Vsevolod the Big Nest it became the strongest realm of Rus', until Batu burned its towns in 1238.

Principality of Smolensk.x: The principality on the upper Dnieper, a crossroads of the river roads, ruled by the Rostislavichi from 1125 and rich in its trade with Riga and Gotland. Spared by Batu, it fell under Lithuanian pressure and was annexed by Vytautas in 1404; Moscow won it in 1514.

Principality of Kiev.x: The principality of Kiev itself, the senior throne of Rus', after the death of Yaroslav the Wise. Its grand princes, chosen by seniority and the sword among Yaroslav's heirs, held a fading primacy over the other principalities; sacked by Andrei Bogolyubsky in 1169 and by rival princes in 1203, Kiev was destroyed by the Mongols in 1240.

Principality of Polotsk.x: The principality of the western Dvina, held by a branch of the Rurikids descended from Vladimir's son Iziaslav and his mother Rogneda, daughter of the Varangian lord of Polotsk. Its prince Vseslav the Sorcerer briefly seized Kiev in 1068; in the thirteenth century Polotsk fell under the sway of Lithuania.

Principality of Pereyaslavl.x: The frontier principality southeast of Kiev, guarding Rus' against the steppe, held by Vsevolod son of Yaroslav and his heirs. From Pereyaslavl Vladimir Monomakh led the campaigns that broke the Cumans in 1103 and 1111; the Mongols destroyed the town in 1239.

Principality of Volhynia.x: The principality of the western Bug about Vladimir-Volynsky, held after 1146 by Iziaslav Mstislavich and his heirs. Roman the Great joined it to Galicia in 1199, creating the principality of Galicia-Volhynia.

Principality of Peremyshl.x: One of the Red Ruthenian principalities on the San, held from the 1080s by the sons of Rostislav, grandson of Yaroslav the Wise. Volodar of Peremyshl defended it against Poles and Hungarians, and his son Vladimirko joined it with Terebovlia into the principality of Galicia, ruled from Halych from 1141.

Great Principality of Duklja.x: The Serbian principality of Duklja, the old Roman Dioclea on the coast of Montenegro, whose prince Stefan Vojislav threw off Byzantine rule by a victory about 1042. His son Mihailo won a royal crown from Pope Gregory VII in 1077.

Norman England.x: England under the Norman kings after the Conquest, when a French-speaking aristocracy of barons and bishops held their lands from the crown, stone castles and great Romanesque cathedrals rose across the country, and the Domesday survey recorded every manor. After the anarchy of Stephen and Matilda it passed in 1154 to the Angevin Henry II.

Kingdom of Duklja.x: The kingdom of Duklja on the Adriatic, whose prince Mihailo received a crown from Pope Gregory VII in 1077. His son Constantine Bodin, once proclaimed tsar by rebel Bulgarians, ruled Raška and Bosnia as well, but after his death the realm sank into civil war and passed under Raška.

Principality of Terebovlia.x: A principality of Red Ruthenia on the Seret, held by Vasilko Rostislavich, whose blinding by Sviatopolk II and David of Volhynia in 1097, just after the congress of Liubech had sworn peace among the princes, scandalized all Rus'. His heirs' lands passed into Galicia.

Principality of Ryazan.x: The principality of the middle Oka on the edge of the steppe, ruled by a branch of the Chernigov house. Its capital was the first Russian town stormed by Batu, in December 1237, when Prince Yuri and its people perished; the later principality, ruled from Pereyaslavl-Ryazansky, was annexed by Moscow in 1521.

Grand Principality of Serbia.x: The Serbian grand principality of Raška, in the upland valleys about the Ibar and Ras, which under Vukan and his heirs resisted the Komnenian emperors. Stefan Nemanja founded the dynasty that would rule Serbia for two centuries, built the monastery of Studenica, and died a monk on Mount Athos.

Principality of Minsk.x: A principality of the Polotsk lands on the Svislach, first named in the chronicle in 1067, when the sons of Yaroslav sacked it in their war with Vseslav. Its prince Gleb Vseslavich warred with Kiev until Vladimir Monomakh took him captive; in the fourteenth century Minsk passed to Lithuania.

Principality of Vitebsk.x: A principality of the Polotsk branch on the western Dvina, a trading town on the road between Smolensk and the Baltic. Its princes, descendants of Vseslav of Polotsk, were drawn into the orbit of Smolensk and later of Lithuania, which absorbed Vitebsk in the fourteenth century.

Principality of Jersika.x: A small Orthodox principality of the Latgalians on the Daugava in present Latvia, tributary to Polotsk. Its prince Visvaldis, allied with the Lithuanians, was forced to submit to Bishop Albert of Riga after the crusaders stormed his town in 1209, and received part of his lands back as a fief.

Angevins.x: The house of the counts of Anjou in the generation that made it a great power: Fulk V, who left in 1129 to become King of Jerusalem, and his son Geoffrey Plantagenet, who married the Empress Matilda, heiress of England, and conquered Normandy by 1144.

Novgorod Republic.x: Lord Novgorod the Great, the merchant republic of the Russian north, which chose and dismissed its princes, elected its posadniks and archbishop in the veche, and ruled a fur empire reaching to the White Sea and the Urals. Partner of the Hanseatic League and spared by the Mongols, it fell to Ivan III of Moscow in 1478.
Novgorod Republic.gov: Republic under the veche, with elected posadniks and invited princes

(Duchies of Poland).x: The Polish lands in the age of division after Bolesław Wrymouth split them among his sons in 1138: Silesia, Greater Poland, Masovia, Sandomierz, and the senior duchy of Kraków. Rival Piast dukes fought for the seniorate while the Mongols and the Teutonic Knights struck at the land, until Władysław the Elbow-high made it whole again.
(Duchies of Poland).gov: Duchies under a senior duke at Kraków

Duchy of Masovia.x: The duchy of the middle Vistula about Płock and later Warsaw, ruled by a Piast line descended from Konrad I, who in 1226 invited the Teutonic Knights to fight the pagan Prussians on his border. It stayed apart from the Polish crown until its last dukes died out in 1526.

Duchy of Sandomierz.x: The duchy of Little Poland east of Kraków on the Vistula, set aside for Henry, son of Bolesław Wrymouth, who died crusading against the Prussians in 1166. Later joined to Kraków under Casimir the Just and his heirs, it was ravaged by the Mongols in 1241, 1259, and 1287.

Kingdom of Sicily.x: The Norman kingdom of Roger II, which passed to the Hohenstaufen under Henry VI and Frederick II, and after the Vespers of 1282 to the house of Aragon. Thereafter Sicily was ruled by Aragonese and Spanish kings through viceroys, then by Savoy, Austria, and the Bourbons of Naples, until it was merged into the Two Sicilies in 1816.

Duchy of Silesia.x: The duchy of the upper and middle Oder, ruled by the senior Piast line of Władysław the Exile, which welcomed German settlers, towns, and monasteries. Henry the Bearded and Henry the Pious nearly reunited Poland before the Mongol disaster at Liegnitz in 1241; afterward the duchy split among many dukes and passed in the fourteenth century under the Bohemian crown.

Duchy of Greater Poland.x: The duchy of the old Polish heartland about Poznań and Gniezno, held by the line of Mieszko the Old. Przemysł II, its last duke, was crowned king of Poland at Gniezno in 1295, the first coronation in two centuries, and was murdered the next year.

Kingdom of Navarre.x: The Pyrenean kingdom restored in 1134 after a union with Aragon, which took the name of Navarre under Sancho the Wise. Sancho the Strong broke the Almohad guard at Las Navas; thereafter it passed to French houses, Champagne, Évreux, and Foix, until Ferdinand of Aragon conquered its lands south of the Pyrenees in 1512.

County of Portugal.x: The county of Portucale between the Minho and the Mondego, granted by Alfonso VI to his son-in-law Henry of Burgundy. Henry's son Afonso Henriques defeated his mother Teresa at São Mamede in 1128, and after his victory at Ourique in 1139 called himself king of Portugal.

Pomerania.x: The duchy of the Slavic Pomeranians on the Baltic coast about the mouth of the Oder, converted by Bishop Otto of Bamberg under Duke Wartislaw I between 1124 and 1128. Its dukes of the Griffin house paid homage to Poland, Saxony, and Denmark by turns, and Bogislaw I became a prince of the Empire in 1181.

Angevin Empire.x: The lands of Henry II and his sons, from the Scottish border to the Pyrenees: England, Normandy, Anjou, Maine, Touraine, and, through Eleanor, the great duchy of Aquitaine, with lordship over Brittany, Wales, and Ireland. Richard held it together by war, but John lost Normandy and Anjou to Philip Augustus in 1204.

Principality of Halych.x: The principality of the upper Dniester, formed from Peremyshl and Terebovlia by Vladimirko in 1141 and grown rich on the salt trade. Yaroslav Osmomysl, the eight-minded, praised in the Lay of Igor, ruled it from his castle on the river; in 1199 Roman of Volhynia took it and founded Galicia-Volhynia.

Crown of Aragon.x: The union of the kingdom of Aragon and the county of Barcelona under one dynasty, each keeping its own laws and Cortes. Its kings conquered Majorca, Valencia, Sicily, Sardinia, and Naples, and its Catalan merchants rivaled Genoa and Venice; Ferdinand II's marriage with Isabella of Castile joined it to the Spanish monarchy.

Duchy of Opole.x: A Silesian duchy on the upper Oder, held by the line of Mieszko Tanglefoot, which brought German settlers into Upper Silesia. Split into ever smaller duchies, it passed under Bohemian suzerainty in 1327, and its last Piast duke died in 1532.

Second Bulgarian Empire.x: The Bulgarian state restored by the brothers Peter and Asen in their revolt of 1185, ruled from Tarnovo. Kaloyan captured a Latin emperor, and Ivan Asen II made it the leading power of the Balkans; after Mongol raids and civil wars it fell apart and was conquered by the Ottomans in 1393 and 1396.

Principality of Turov and Pinsk.x: The principality of the Pripet marshes about Turov and Pinsk, a quiet corner of Rus' ruled by its own princes from the twelfth century and remembered for its bishop Cyril of Turov, a preacher and writer of prayers. It passed under Lithuanian rule in the fourteenth century.

Banate of Bosnia.x: The Bosnian banate in the mountains of the upper Bosna, under Hungarian overlordship, whose Ban Kulin's reign was remembered as a golden age. Accused of harboring heretics of the Bosnian Church, it outlasted Hungarian crusades; Stephen II Kotromanić won Hum, and his nephew Tvrtko I was crowned king in 1377.
Banate of Bosnia.faith: Catholic and Orthodox Christianity, and the Bosnian Church

(Kingdom of Bohemia).x: The lands of the Bohemian crown, Bohemia, Moravia, and later Silesia and Lusatia, whose king was the first lay elector of the Empire. Under Ottokar II and Charles IV it was the center of the Empire; the Hussite wars made it a land of two faiths, and in 1526 it passed to the Habsburgs.
(Kingdom of Bohemia).faith: Catholic, then Hussite and Catholic Christianity

Kingdom of Bohemia.x: The Czech kingdom of the Přemyslids, crowned for good under Ottokar I in 1198, which grew rich on the silver of Kutná Hora and the German colonists of its towns. Charles IV made Prague a great capital; the burning of Hus raised the Hussites, and George of Poděbrady, a Hussite king, defied the pope.
Kingdom of Bohemia.faith: Catholic, then Hussite and Catholic Christianity

Principality of Galicia-Volhynia.x: The union of Galicia and Volhynia formed by Roman the Great in 1199, the strongest realm of southwestern Rus'. After Roman's death in 1205, Hungarians, Poles, and rival princes fought over it for thirty years until his son Daniel won it back, just before the Mongol storm.

Livonian Brothers of the Sword.x: The crusading order founded by Bishop Albert of Riga in 1202 to conquer the pagan Livs, Letts, and Estonians, its knights marked with a red sword and cross on white. It subdued Livonia, but at Saule in 1236 the Lithuanians destroyed its army and slew its master, and the survivors were merged into the Teutonic Order in 1237.

Despotate of Epirus.x: The Greek successor state founded in the mountains of northwestern Greece by Michael Komnenos Doukas after the fall of Constantinople in 1204. Theodore took Thessalonica and claimed the empire, but Nicaea won the race; after Greek, Serbian, and Italian rulers, the Turks took Ioannina in 1430 and Arta in 1449.

County of Armagnac.x: A Gascon county about Auch and Lectoure whose count Bernard VII led the party of Orléans in the civil war against Burgundy, so that its men were called the Armagnacs. Its count John V, rebel and outlaw, was killed when Louis XI's army took Lectoure in 1473.

Kingdom of Thessalonica.x: The Latin kingdom of Macedonia and Thessaly carved out after the Fourth Crusade for Boniface of Montferrat, its leader. Boniface fell fighting the Bulgarians in 1207, and in 1224 Theodore of Epirus took Thessalonica from his son Demetrius.

County of Auvergne.x: The mountain land of the Massif Central about Clermont and Riom, divided among counts, dauphins, and bishops after Philip Augustus seized the chief county between 1209 and 1213. It passed as a royal appanage to Alfonse of Poitiers and then to the Duke of Berry, and later to the Bourbons, before reverting to the crown in 1527.

County of Poitou.x: The county about Poitiers, heart of the old domain of the dukes of Aquitaine, conquered from King John by Philip Augustus and Louis VIII. Louis IX gave it to his brother Alfonse in 1241; the revolt of the Lusignans, backed by Henry III of England, was crushed at Taillebourg and Saintes in 1242.

Kingdom of Serbia.x: The medieval Serbian kingdom of the Nemanjić house, crowned in 1217, which grew rich on silver mines and conquered Macedonia under Milutin and Dušan, its monasteries painted by Byzantine masters. The name returned when the modern principality became a kingdom under Milan Obrenović in 1882.

Grand Duchy of Lithuania.x: The last pagan realm of Europe, forged by Mindaugas in the forests of the Neman and enlarged by Gediminas and Algirdas over the Ruthenian lands from Polotsk to Kiev. Its grand dukes fought the Teutonic Order for two centuries; Jogaila accepted baptism and the Polish crown in 1386, and under Vytautas it reached from the Baltic to the Black Sea.
Grand Duchy of Lithuania.faith: Baltic paganism, then Catholic Christianity from 1387; Orthodox Ruthenian majority

Crown of Castile.x: The union of Castile and León under Ferdinand III, who conquered Córdoba and Seville and left only Granada to Islam. Its kings, Alfonso the Wise, Peter the Cruel, and the Trastámaras, ruled the largest Christian state of the peninsula, until Isabella I and Ferdinand took Granada, sent Columbus west, and founded the Spanish monarchy.

Teutonic Order.x: The German crusading order of St. Mary, founded at Acre, which from 1230 conquered the pagan Prussians and built a monastic state of brick castles on the Baltic. At its height it ruled Prussia and Livonia; broken at Grunwald in 1410, it became Poland's vassal in 1466, and its last Grand Master turned Lutheran duke in 1525.
Teutonic Order.gov: State of a military order under its Grand Master

County of Foix.x: The Pyrenean county of the Ariège, whose counts sheltered the Cathars and later won Béarn. Gaston Fébus, hunter, poet, and warrior, praised by Froissart, ruled from Orthez as a sovereign prince; through Catherine of Foix the county passed to the Albret kings of Navarre and so to Henry IV.

Empire of Thessalonica.x: The Epirote empire of Thessalonica, proclaimed by Theodore Komnenos Doukas, who was crowned emperor in the city and captured by Ivan Asen II at Klokotnitsa in 1230. His brother Manuel and his sons John and Demetrios held Thessalonica, at last as despots, until John III Vatatzes of Nicaea took it in 1246.

Principality of Vladimir-Suzdal.x: The grand principality of Vladimir under the Golden Horde, whose patent, the yarlyk, the khans gave to the Russian prince they favored. Alexander Nevsky held it by submission; Tver and Moscow fought for it until Ivan Kalita won it for Moscow, and it merged into Muscovy.

Galicia-Volhynia.x: The kingdom of Rus' in the southwest after the Mongol storm, whose prince Daniel received a royal crown from a papal legate at Dorohychyn in 1253 and founded Lviv for his son Leo. When the last ruler, the Piast Yuri II Boleslav, was poisoned in 1340, Poland and Lithuania divided it between them.

Capetian House of Anjou.x: The house of Charles of Anjou, brother of St. Louis, who conquered Sicily and Naples from the Hohenstaufen in 1266, and whose descendants ruled Naples, Provence, Hungary, and Poland. Its kings Robert the Wise and Louis the Great of Hungary were among the leading princes of fourteenth-century Europe.

Holy Roman Empire Minor States.x: The hundreds of lesser principalities, free imperial cities, prince-bishoprics, abbeys, and knightly lordships of the Holy Roman Empire, from Württemberg, Hesse, and the Palatinate to Mainz, Nuremberg, and Hamburg, each with its own court and laws but bound together under the emperor and the Imperial Diet, until Napoleon swept most of them away between 1803 and 1806.
Holy Roman Empire Minor States.gov: Patchwork of principalities, church states, and free cities under the emperor
Holy Roman Empire Minor States.faith: Catholic, Lutheran, or Reformed by the choice of each ruler

House of Habsburg.x: The house of the counts of Habsburg in Aargau, which won Austria and Styria when Rudolf I defeated Ottokar on the Marchfeld in 1278. Its dukes added Carinthia, Tyrol, and Carniola, Rudolf IV forged the privilege that made them archdukes, and Frederick III and Maximilian I, through marriage, laid the foundations of a world monarchy.
House of Habsburg.gov: Hereditary duchies of the Habsburg house

Duchy of Bavaria.x: The duchy of the Wittelsbach house from 1180, long divided among quarreling branches at Munich, Landshut, Ingolstadt, and Straubing until Albert IV reunited it and decreed primogeniture in 1506. Its dukes led the Catholic cause in Germany, and Maximilian I, head of the Catholic League, won the electoral dignity in 1623.

Margraviate of Brandenburg.x: The march on the Elbe and the Havel won from the Slavs by Albert the Bear, who took Brandenburg in 1157, and pushed east by his Ascanian heirs to the Oder and beyond. After the Ascanians died out in 1320 it passed to Wittelsbachs and Luxembourgs, who neglected it, until Sigismund granted it to Frederick of Hohenzollern in 1415.

House of Ascania.x: The lands of the Ascanian princes, descendants of Albert the Bear: the duchy of Saxe-Wittenberg on the middle Elbe, which won the Saxon electoral vote by the Golden Bull of 1356, and the principalities of Anhalt. When the Wittenberg line died out in 1422, the emperor gave Saxony to the Wettin margraves of Meissen.

County of Savoy.x: The Alpine county astride the passes between France and Italy, held since the eleventh century by the heirs of Humbert White-Hands. Peter II, the little Charlemagne, won Vaud; the Green Count, Amadeus VI, crusaded against the Turks and took Gallipoli in 1366; and in 1416 the emperor made Amadeus VIII a duke.

House of Hohenstaufen.x: The last of the Staufer, the Swabian house of the emperors Frederick Barbarossa and Frederick II, whose German lands dissolved after Conrad IV's death in 1254. Manfred, king of Sicily, fell at Benevento in 1266, and Conradin, the last legitimate heir, was beheaded at Naples in 1268.

Duchy of Brabant.x: The rich duchy of the Low Countries about Brussels, Leuven, and Antwerp, whose dukes won Limburg at Worringen in 1288 and swore to respect the liberties of their towns in the Joyous Entry of 1356. After the death of Duchess Joanna it passed to a younger branch of Burgundy, and in 1430 to Philip the Good.

House of Anjou-Sicily.x: The Angevin kingdom of Naples, which after the Sicilian Vespers of 1282 held the mainland south of the Papal States while Aragon kept the island. Robert the Wise made Naples a seat of learning and a patron of Petrarch and Giotto; the murder of Joanna I by Charles of Durazzo in 1382 began a long dynastic war.

Duchies of Poland.x: The Polish duchies in the last decades of division, when Leszek the Black, Henry Probus, and Przemysł II strove in turn for Kraków and a crown, and Wenceslaus II of Bohemia made himself king of Poland in 1300, before Władysław the Elbow-high reunited the land.

Grand Duchy of Kraków.x: The senior duchy of Kraków, seat of the princeps among the Polish dukes, held by Leszek the Black and then by Henry IV Probus of Silesia. In 1291 it fell to Wenceslaus II of Bohemia.

Kingdom of Naples.x: The kingdom of the Italian south, ruled from Naples by the Angevins after the Vespers, by the house of Aragon from 1442, and by Spanish viceroys for two centuries after 1504. Charles of Bourbon made it independent again in 1734 and began the palace of Caserta; French armies drove out his son Ferdinand in 1806.

Pskov Republic.x: The city republic of Pskov on the Velikaya, once Novgorod's younger brother, which won its own freedom from Novgorod in 1348 and governed itself by veche and posadniks. Its Lithuanian-born prince Dovmont made it a fortress against the Livonian knights; Vasily III annexed it in 1510 and carried off its veche bell.

Kingdom of Syrmia.x: The realm of Stefan Dragutin, who yielded the Serbian throne to his brother Milutin in 1282 and ruled Belgrade, Mačva, and Syrmia as a vassal of Hungary, his wife's homeland. Dragutin warred with Milutin for years; after his death in 1316 his lands were divided between Serbia and Hungary.

Grand Principality of Moscow.x: The principality of Moscow, a small appanage of Vladimir under Daniel, which by craft, service to the khans, and the favor of the Church rose to rule all northeastern Rus'. Dmitry Donskoy beat the Tatars at Kulikovo, Ivan III annexed Novgorod and threw off the yoke in 1480, and Vasily III gathered the last Russian lands.

Kingdom of Scotland.x: The kingdom of the Scots in the age of the wars of independence, won by Wallace and Bruce, and of the house of Stewart. Allied to France against England, it was struck down at Flodden, turned Protestant under Knox, and gave England its king in 1603, before joining it in the Union of 1707.
Kingdom of Scotland.faith: Catholic Christianity, then the Reformed Church of Scotland from 1560

Swiss Confederation.x: The league of free Alpine valleys and cities that grew from the oath of Uri, Schwyz, and Unterwalden in 1291, whose pikemen beat Habsburg and Burgundy and were the best infantry in Europe. Thirteen cantons by 1513, split by the Reformation yet held together, independent of the Empire in 1648, it became a federal state in 1848.
Swiss Confederation.gov: Confederation of cantons; federal republic from 1848

Principality of Pinsk.x: A small principality of the Pripet marshes, split off from Turov and ruled by its own Rurikid princes, until Gediminas of Lithuania brought it under his rule early in the fourteenth century.

Principality of Turov.x: The old principality of Turov on the Pripet, seat of a bishopric since the eleventh century, which fell under Lithuanian rule in the time of Gediminas.

Principality of Wallachia.x: The principality of the Romanians between the Carpathians and the Danube, founded by Basarab I after his victory over Charles Robert of Hungary in 1330. Its princes Mircea the Elder, Vlad the Impaler, and Michael the Brave fought the Turks, but from the fifteenth century it paid tribute to the sultan, and after 1716 it was ruled by Phanariot Greeks.
Principality of Wallachia.gov: Principality, elective within the princely house; Ottoman vassal

House of Bourbon.x: The duchy of the Bourbonnais and the lands of the house of Bourbon, a branch of the Capetians descended from St. Louis's son Robert. Its dukes were among the greatest princes of France until the Constable Charles betrayed Francis I in 1523; the cadet Vendôme line inherited the claim and in 1589 gave France Henry IV.
rulers: Henry of Navarre, later Henry IV

Earldom of Desmond.x: The palatine earldom of the Geraldines in Munster, created for Maurice FitzThomas FitzGerald in 1329, whose Anglo-Norman earls took on Gaelic speech and custom and kept bards. Gerald the Poet wrote verse in Irish; the Desmond Rebellion ended in the earl's death in 1583 and the confiscation of his lands.
Earldom of Desmond.gov: Palatine earldom under the English crown

Free County of Burgundy.x: The county of Burgundy east of the Saône, about Dole and Besançon, an imperial fief distinct from the French duchy. It passed by inheritance through queens and countesses of France and Flanders, and in 1384 to Philip the Bold, joining it to the Burgundian state; later Habsburg, it was conquered by Louis XIV in 1674.

Serbian Empire.x: The empire proclaimed by Stefan Dušan at Skopje in 1346, stretching from the Danube to the Gulf of Corinth and from the Adriatic to the Aegean, with its own patriarch at Peć and its own law code. Under his weak son Uroš it fell apart among its great lords, and the Ottomans struck it down on the Maritsa in 1371.

Blue Horde.x: The Golden Horde of the Russian chronicles in its decline: the Jochid khanate of the Volga steppe, torn after 1359 by the Great Troubles among rival khans and warlords such as Mamai. Tokhtamysh restored it and burned Moscow in 1382, but Timur broke it in 1395, and it split into the khanates of Kazan, the Crimea, and the Great Horde.
Blue Horde.gov: Khanate under Chinggisid khans and powerful beylerbeys

Principality of Moldavia.x: The principality between the eastern Carpathians and the Dniester, founded when Bogdan of Maramureș threw off Hungarian rule in the 1360s. Stephen the Great held it against Turks, Hungarians, and Poles in a reign of forty-seven years, but from the sixteenth century it paid tribute to the sultan, and its princes were Phanariot Greeks after 1711.

House of Valois-Anjou.x: The second house of Anjou, founded by Louis, son of John II of France, who was adopted as heir by Joanna I of Naples. Louis and his heirs held Anjou and Provence and fought in vain for Naples; René the Good, poet, painter, and titular king of Naples and Jerusalem, kept a brilliant court at Angers and Aix.

Electorate of Saxony.x: The electorate of Saxony on the middle Elbe, held after 1423 by the Wettins, lords of the silver mines of the Erzgebirge. Frederick the Wise sheltered Luther, Maurice won the electorate for the Albertine line in 1547, and Augustus the Strong, King of Poland, made Dresden the Florence of the Elbe.
Electorate of Saxony.faith: Catholic, then Lutheran; its electors Catholic from 1697

Despotate of Dobruja.x: A Bulgarian principality on the Black Sea coast between the Danube delta and Varna, whose despot Dobrotitsa, ruling from Kaliakra, fought the Genoese and meddled in Byzantine quarrels with his own fleet. His son Ivanko lost it to the Ottomans in the 1390s; the land still bears Dobrotitsa's name.

Moravian Serbia.x: The Serbian principality of Prince Lazar Hrebeljanović in the valley of the Morava, the strongest of the realms that rose from the ruins of Dušan's empire. Lazar fell at Kosovo in 1389; his son Stefan Lazarević served the sultan as a vassal and fought at Nicopolis and Ankara before he became despot.

Albanian Principalities.x: The lordships of the Albanian highlands and coast after the Serbian empire fell, held by noble houses such as the Thopia of Durazzo, the Balšić, the Dukagjini, and the Kastrioti. Karl Thopia styled himself prince of Albania; Balša II fell to the Ottomans at Savra in 1385, and the lords became Ottoman vassals.

Serbian Despots.x: Zeta, on the coast and in the mountains of present Montenegro and northern Albania, held after the fall of Dušan's empire by the Balšić lords, who warred with Venice over Scutari and the coast. When Balša III died in 1421 he left it to his uncle, the Serbian despot Stefan Lazarević.

Kingdom of Bosnia.x: The Bosnian kingdom of Tvrtko I, crowned in 1377 king of the Serbs and Bosnia, who added the Dalmatian towns and the coast. After him the great nobles made and unmade kings in a land divided among Catholic, Orthodox, and Bosnian churches; Mehmed II conquered it in 1463 and beheaded its last king.
Kingdom of Bosnia.faith: Catholic and Orthodox Christianity, and the Bosnian Church

Margraviate of Moravia.x: The margraviate of Moravia under the Luxembourg margraves Jobst and Prokop, nephews of Charles IV, who fought each other and their cousins Wenceslaus and Sigismund. Jobst, the richest prince of his house, was elected King of the Romans in 1410 but died within months.

(Polish-Lithuania Kingdom).x: The union of the Polish crown and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania under Jagiełło after 1386, the largest realm of Latin Christendom, whose joint armies broke the Teutonic Order at Grunwald in 1410. Lithuania kept its own grand dukes, Vytautas above all, and the bond between the two remained a personal one until 1569.
(Polish-Lithuania Kingdom).gov: Personal union of the Polish kingdom and the Lithuanian grand duchy
(Polish-Lithuania Kingdom).faith: Catholic Christianity, with Orthodox Ruthenian subjects

(Kalmar Union).x: The union of Denmark, Norway, and Sweden under one king, sealed at Kalmar in 1397 by Queen Margaret, which with Finland, Iceland, and the Atlantic isles stretched from Greenland to the Gulf of Finland. Danish kings ruled it from Copenhagen; Sweden rose again and again under its regents, and broke away for good under Gustav Vasa in 1523.
rulers: Sten Sture the Elder (regent of Sweden)
Sten Sture the Younger (regent of Sweden)

Kalmar Union.x: The joint kingdom of the three Scandinavian crowns from Queen Margaret to Christian II, held together by Danish power and the fear of the Hanseatic towns and the German princes. The Swedish nobility and peasants resented its Danish governors and taxes, and the Stockholm Bloodbath of 1520 provoked the revolt that ended it.
rulers: Sten Sture the Elder (regent of Sweden)
Sten Sture the Younger (regent of Sweden)

Serbian Despotate.x: The Serbian state of the despots, a title granted by the Byzantine emperor to Stefan Lazarević in 1402, which revived in the shadow of the Ottomans. Stefan made Belgrade his capital and a center of letters; Đurađ Branković built the great fortress of Smederevo on the Danube, which fell to Mehmed II in 1459.

Duchy of Milan.x: The duchy created for Gian Galeazzo Visconti in 1395, the strongest state of northern Italy, ruled from Milan by the Visconti and from 1450 by the condottiere Francesco Sforza and his heirs. Ludovico il Moro, patron of Leonardo, welcomed the French into Italy and lost his duchy to them; after 1535 it passed to Spain.

Duchy of Savoy.x: The Alpine duchy raised from the county in 1416, holding Savoy, Piedmont, and Nice astride the Alps. Overrun by France in 1536, it was restored by Emmanuel Philibert, victor of Saint-Quentin, who moved the capital to Turin; Victor Amadeus II won a royal crown by the Peace of Utrecht in 1713.

Livonian Confederation.x: The loose confederation of medieval Livonia: the lands of the Livonian Order, the archbishopric of Riga, the bishoprics of Dorpat, Ösel-Wiek, and Courland, and the free towns, bound by common diets. Master Wolter von Plettenberg beat back the Russians in 1502, but the Livonian War from 1558 destroyed it, and its last master became Duke of Courland.
Livonian Confederation.gov: Confederation of the Order, bishoprics, and towns

Electorate of Brandenburg.x: The march of Brandenburg under the Hohenzollern electors, granted to Frederick of Nuremberg in 1415 and ruled from Berlin, a sandy, poor land of nobles and serfs. Joachim II turned Lutheran in 1539, and John Sigismund, who became a Calvinist, inherited the Duchy of Prussia in 1618, laying the base of the Prussian state.

Khanate of Kazan.x: The Tatar khanate of the middle Volga founded about 1438 by Ulugh Muhammad, an exiled khan of the Golden Horde, on the lands of the old Volga Bulgars. Its raids filled its slave markets with Russian captives, and Moscow and the Crimea fought to set their own khans on its throne, until Ivan IV stormed Kazan in 1552.

Poland-Lithuania.x: The Jagiellonian realm of Poland and Lithuania in its golden age, when Casimir IV won Royal Prussia from the Teutonic Order, the nobility gained its Sejm and liberties, and Kraków under the two Sigismunds became a Renaissance capital. Wars with Muscovy over the Ruthenian lands drove the two states into the Union of Lublin in 1569.
Poland-Lithuania.faith: Catholic Christianity, with Orthodox and Protestant subjects

House of Oldenburg.x: The Danish realm under the first Oldenburg king, Christian I, elected king of Denmark in 1448 and of Norway in 1450, who won the Swedish crown in 1457 and Schleswig and Holstein in 1460. His house reigned in Denmark until 1863, and its branches gave kings to Norway, Sweden, Greece, and Russia.

Crimean Khanate.x: The Tatar khanate of the Crimea and the steppe north of it, founded by Hacı Giray about 1441 and an Ottoman vassal from 1475. For three centuries its horsemen raided Muscovy, Poland, and Ukraine, carrying off hundreds of thousands of Christian captives to the slave market of Kaffa; Catherine the Great annexed it in 1783.

Ambrosian Republic.x: The short-lived republic proclaimed by the citizens of Milan on the death of the last Visconti duke in 1447, named for the city's patron, St. Ambrose. Besieged by its own condottiere Francesco Sforza and torn by faction and famine, it surrendered to him in 1450.

Qasim Khanate.x: A Tatar khanate on the Oka about the town of Kasimov, granted by Vasily II of Moscow about 1452 to Qasim, son of Ulugh Muhammad, as a vassal state. Its khans, Chinggisid princes in Muscovite service, gave Moscow cavalry and candidates for the throne of Kazan; it endured in name until 1681.

(Habsburg Monarchy).x: The lands of the Austrian Habsburgs: the archduchies and duchies of Austria, the crowns of Bohemia and Hungary, and later the southern Netherlands, Milan, and Naples, held together by one dynasty and the Catholic faith. Twice it stopped the Turks at Vienna, and under Prince Eugene, Maria Theresa, and Joseph II it became a great power of Europe.

Astrakhan Khanate.x: The Tatar khanate of the Volga delta, founded about 1466 by a Chinggisid prince of the Great Horde on the trade road from Persia and the Caspian. Torn among Nogai, Crimean, and Muscovite factions, it was taken by Ivan IV's troops in 1556, giving Russia the whole course of the Volga.

Habsburg Monarchy.x: The realm of the Austrian Habsburgs, which won Bohemia and royal Hungary after Mohács in 1526 and held the Ottoman tide at Vienna in 1529 and 1683. Reconquering Hungary under Eugene of Savoy, defended by Maria Theresa against Frederick the Great, and reformed by Joseph II, it became the Austrian Empire in 1804.

Kingdom of Spain.x: The monarchy of the united crowns of Castile and Aragon, which under Charles V and Philip II ruled the Netherlands, half of Italy, and the Americas, and was the great Catholic power of Europe. It lost its primacy to France in the seventeenth century, passed to the Bourbons in 1700, and endured through Napoleon, republics, and civil war.
Kingdom of Spain.gov: Monarchy (absolute, then constitutional); republics in 1873 and from 1931 to 1939

Denmark-Norway.x: The union of Denmark and Norway, with Iceland, the Faroes, Greenland, and Schleswig-Holstein, under the Oldenburg kings in Copenhagen. Christian III made it Lutheran, Christian IV rebuilt Copenhagen and lost wars to Sweden, Frederick III made the crown absolute in 1660, and the union was broken in 1814 when Norway passed to Sweden.

Duchy of Prussia.x: The secular duchy made from the lands of the Teutonic Order in 1525, when the last Grand Master, Albert of Brandenburg-Ansbach, turned Lutheran and did homage to his uncle Sigismund of Poland at Kraków. Albert founded the University of Königsberg; on the death of his mad son in 1618 the duchy passed to the electors of Brandenburg.

Eastern Hungarian Kingdom.x: The realm of John Zápolya, elected king of Hungary after Mohács against Ferdinand of Habsburg, and of his son John Sigismund, under Ottoman protection. After Buda fell to the Turks in 1541 it was confined to Transylvania and the lands east of the Tisza, and in 1570 John Sigismund gave up the royal title to become Prince of Transylvania.
Eastern Hungarian Kingdom.faith: Catholic, Lutheran, Calvinist, and Unitarian Christianity

Duchy of Florence.x: The Medici duchy set up by Charles V and Pope Clement VII after the siege of 1530 ended the last Florentine republic. Duke Alessandro was murdered by his cousin Lorenzino in 1537; Cosimo I ruled with an iron hand, conquered Siena in 1555, and was raised to Grand Duke of Tuscany in 1569.

Kingdom of Ireland.x: The kingdom proclaimed by the Irish Parliament for Henry VIII in 1542, by which the English crown held Ireland in its own right rather than as a papal grant. Tudor conquest, the plantations of Ulster and Munster, Cromwell's confiscations, and the penal laws made it a Protestant ascendancy over a Catholic people, until the Act of Union of 1800.
Kingdom of Ireland.gov: Monarchy under the English, later British, crown, with its own Parliament
Kingdom of Ireland.faith: Church of Ireland established; Catholic majority

Tsardom of Russia.x: The Muscovite tsardom proclaimed by Ivan IV in 1547, which conquered Kazan, Astrakhan, and Siberia, survived the Time of Troubles, and under the Romanovs annexed eastern Ukraine and reached the Pacific. Peter the Great forced it toward the West, built a navy, and moved the capital to St. Petersburg.

Don Cossacks.x: The free Cossack host of the lower Don, formed of runaway serfs, adventurers, and frontiersmen who governed themselves in a circle under elected atamans. They raided Turks and Tatars, seized Azov in 1637, served the tsar for pay, and twice set Russia aflame under Stenka Razin and Kondraty Bulavin.

Grand Duchy of Tuscany.x: The Medici grand duchy created by Pope Pius V for Cosimo I in 1569, joining Florence and Siena. Its grand dukes patronized Galileo and the Uffizi and made Livorno a free port; when the Medici died out in 1737 it passed to the house of Lorraine, and Leopold I abolished the death penalty there in 1786.

Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.x: The Commonwealth of Both Nations formed at Lublin in 1569, an elective monarchy in which the nobility, a tenth of the people, chose its kings and wielded the liberum veto in its Sejm. It humbled Muscovy and saved Vienna, but wars, Cossack risings, and anarchy left it prey to its neighbors, who partitioned it away between 1772 and 1795.
Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.faith: Catholic Christianity, with Orthodox, Protestant, and Jewish subjects

Principality of Transylvania.x: The principality of the eastern Hungarian lands under Ottoman suzerainty, ruled by elected princes and three privileged nations, the Hungarian nobles, the Saxons, and the Székelys, with four received faiths. Under Gabriel Bethlen and the Rákóczis it was a Protestant power in the Thirty Years' War, before passing to the Habsburgs in 1690.
Principality of Transylvania.faith: Catholic, Lutheran, Calvinist, and Unitarian Christianity; Orthodox Romanians tolerated

Union of Utrecht.x: The alliance of the northern provinces of the Netherlands sealed at Utrecht in January 1579 against Philip II of Spain, under the leadership of William of Orange. By the Act of Abjuration of 1581 its states renounced the king altogether, and the union became the Dutch Republic.
Union of Utrecht.gov: Union of provinces under a stadtholder

Iberian Union.x: The union of the crowns of Spain and Portugal under the Habsburg kings Philip II, III, and IV, which joined the two great colonial empires, from Brazil and Goa to Mexico and Manila. Portugal kept its own laws and Cortes, but its colonies suffered from Spain's enemies, and in 1640 it rose and crowned John IV of Braganza.
Iberian Union.gov: Personal union of the Spanish and Portuguese crowns

Nalyvaiko Uprising.x: The Cossack and peasant rising led by Severyn Nalyvaiko in Ukraine and Belarus against the Polish lords and their stewards, which spread from the Dnieper to Mogilev. Surrounded by the hetman Stanisław Żółkiewski at Solonytsia in 1596, the rebels were betrayed, and Nalyvaiko was executed in Warsaw in 1597.

Swedish Empire.x: Sweden in its age as a great power, from Gustavus Adolphus to Charles XII, when it ruled Finland, Estonia, Livonia, Ingria, western Pomerania, and Bremen and made the Baltic a Swedish lake. Its armies won at Breitenfeld and Narva, but Poltava in 1709 broke it, and at Nystad in 1721 it yielded the eastern Baltic to Russia.

Brandenburg-Prussia.x: The lands of the Hohenzollern electors after Brandenburg and the Duchy of Prussia were joined in 1618, scattered from the Rhine to the Niemen. Ravaged in the Thirty Years' War, they were made a state by the Great Elector, who built a standing army and an excise, won full sovereignty in Prussia from Poland in 1657, and welcomed the Huguenots.
Brandenburg-Prussia.gov: Electorate and duchy in personal union

Bohemian Confederation.x: The confederation of the estates of Bohemia, Moravia, Silesia, and the Lusatias formed in 1619 after the Defenestration of Prague, which deposed Ferdinand II and elected the Calvinist Frederick V of the Palatinate king. It was destroyed at the White Mountain in November 1620.
Bohemian Confederation.gov: Confederation of estates under an elected king
Bohemian Confederation.faith: Protestant Christianity (Utraquist, Lutheran, Brethren, and Calvinist)

Electorate of Bavaria.x: The Wittelsbach duchy of Bavaria raised to an electorate in 1623 for Maximilian I, head of the Catholic League, who also won the Upper Palatinate. Max Emanuel stormed Belgrade and fought for France at Blenheim, Charles Albert was briefly emperor, and in 1806 Napoleon made the elector a king.

Kalmyk Khanate.x: The khanate of Oirat Mongols who migrated from Dzungaria to the lower Volga steppe in the 1630s under Kho Orluk, Buddhist herdsmen who served the tsars as light cavalry against Tatars and Turks. Ayuka Khan made it a power; in 1771 most of the Kalmyks fled east toward China, and Catherine II abolished the khanate.

Catalonia.x: The Catalan Republic proclaimed in January 1641 by Pau Claris, president of the Generalitat, during the Reapers' War against Philip IV. Within days Catalonia placed itself under Louis XIII of France, and French viceroys ruled it until Barcelona fell to Spain in 1652.

Irish Catholic Confederation.x: The Confederate Catholics of Ireland, who after the rising of 1641 governed most of the island from Kilkenny through a General Assembly and Supreme Council, professing loyalty to Charles I. Divided between Old English and Gaelic Irish and over terms with the king, they were overwhelmed by Cromwell's conquest from 1649.
Irish Catholic Confederation.gov: Confederation under a General Assembly and Supreme Council

Parliamentarian England.x: England under the Long Parliament in the Civil War, when Parliament ruled through its committees and the New Model Army of Fairfax and Cromwell defeated Charles I. The quarrels of Parliament and army led to Pride's Purge in December 1648 and the king's trial.
Parliamentarian England.gov: Parliamentary government in arms against the king

Commonwealth of England.x: The republic declared after the execution of Charles I in 1649, governed by the Rump Parliament and its Council of State, which conquered Ireland and Scotland and fought the Dutch at sea. Cromwell dissolved the Rump in 1653 and ruled as Lord Protector; after him the republic collapsed, and Charles II was restored in 1660.

The Protectorate.x: The rule of Oliver Cromwell as Lord Protector under the Instrument of Government of 1653, a written constitution, with a Council of State and Parliaments he purged or dissolved when they crossed him. It tolerated most Protestant sects, readmitted the Jews, and fought Spain, but it did not long survive his death in 1658.

Zaporozhian Cossacks.x: The free Cossack brotherhood of the Sich below the Dnieper rapids, a fortified camp of warriors under an elected koshovy otaman, who raided Tatar and Turkish shores and fought for and against Poland, Russia, and the Crimea. Catherine II's army destroyed the Sich in 1775.
Zaporozhian Cossacks.gov: Cossack brotherhood under an elected otaman

Sloboda Ukraine.x: The frontier land about Kharkov settled from the 1650s by Cossacks and peasants fleeing the wars west of the Dnieper, organized in five Cossack regiments under the tsar. Catherine II abolished the regiments in 1765 and made it a Russian province.

Principality of Upper Hungary.x: The principality granted by the sultan in 1682 to the rebel Imre Thököly, leader of the Protestant kuruc insurgents against Leopold I, in the Habsburg lands of northern Hungary. Thököly marched with the Turks toward Vienna in 1683; after their defeat the imperial armies overran his lands, and he ended his days in exile in Turkey.

Kingdom of Prussia.x: The Hohenzollern kingdom created in 1701, which Frederick William I, the soldier king, gave an army out of all proportion to its size, and Frederick the Great made a great power by seizing Silesia and surviving the Seven Years' War. Crushed by Napoleon at Jena, it rose again and became the core of the German Empire in 1871.

Pro-Habsburg Spain.x: The lands of Spain that recognized the Austrian claimant, Archduke Charles, as King Charles III in the War of the Spanish Succession, chiefly Catalonia, Valencia, and Aragon, which feared Bourbon centralism. Charles held court at Barcelona; after he became emperor in 1711 his allies abandoned him, and Barcelona fell in 1714.

Pro-Swedish Poland.x: The Poland of Stanisław Leszczyński, set on the throne by Charles XII of Sweden in 1704 in place of Augustus the Strong, who was forced to give up the crown at Altranstädt in 1706. After Poltava the Swedish cause collapsed and Augustus returned in 1709; Stanisław later became Duke of Lorraine and father-in-law of Louis XV.

Kingdom of Great Britain.x: The united kingdom of England and Scotland formed in 1707, ruled by Queen Anne and the Hanoverian Georges through ministers answerable to Parliament. It won Canada and India in the Seven Years' War, lost thirteen American colonies, led the world into the age of machines, and fought revolutionary France, before joining with Ireland in 1801.
Kingdom of Great Britain.faith: Church of England and Church of Scotland

Electorate of Hanover.x: The electorate of Brunswick-Lüneburg, raised in 1692 for Ernest Augustus, whose wife Sophia was a granddaughter of James I. Her son George became king of Great Britain in 1714, and Hanover was ruled from London in personal union, its interests a recurring entanglement of British policy, until Napoleon's armies occupied it in 1803.
Electorate of Hanover.gov: Electorate in personal union with Great Britain

Russian Empire.x: The empire proclaimed by Peter the Great in 1721 after his victory over Sweden, which under Catherine the Great took the Crimea and much of Poland, and under Alexander I drove Napoleon from Moscow to Paris. Stretching from the Baltic to the Pacific and from the Arctic to Persia, it fell to revolution in 1917.

Kingdom of Sardinia.x: The realm of the House of Savoy, which exchanged Sicily for Sardinia in 1720 and took its royal title from the island while ruling Piedmont, Savoy, and Nice from Turin. Under Charles Albert and Victor Emmanuel II, with Cavour as minister, it led the unification of Italy and became the Kingdom of Italy in 1861.

Duchy of Courland.x: The duchy of Courland and Semigallia, formed in 1561 for the last Livonian master, Gotthard Kettler, as a fief of Poland. Duke Jacob won it colonies in Tobago and on the Gambia; later it fell under Russian sway, and Empress Anna's favorite Biron ruled it before Russia annexed it in 1795.

(French First Republic).x: France and the lands its armies won under the First Republic, proclaimed in September 1792 after the fall of the monarchy: Belgium, Savoy, Nice, and the Rhineland. It fought a coalition of Europe with mass levies, executed Louis XVI, and governed through the Committee of Public Safety and the Terror, until the Directory took its place in 1795.
(French First Republic).faith: Catholicism persecuted; the cults of Reason and the Supreme Being

French First Republic.x: The French Republic of the National Convention, proclaimed in September 1792, which tried and beheaded the king, crushed the Vendée, and raised the levée en masse that drove the invaders from France. The Committee of Public Safety ruled by terror until Robespierre's fall in July 1794; the Constitution of the Year III handed power to the Directory.
French First Republic.faith: Catholicism persecuted; the cults of Reason and the Supreme Being

(French Directory).x: France under the Directory of five, set up by the Constitution of the Year III in 1795, with the sister republics its armies planted in the Netherlands, Italy, and Switzerland. Its generals, Bonaparte above all, conquered while the government at home lurched from coup to coup, until Bonaparte overthrew it in the coup of Brumaire in 1799.
(French Directory).gov: Republic under a Directory of five
(French Directory).faith: Catholic Christianity, restricted by the state

French Directory.x: The French Republic governed by five directors and two councils from 1795, a regime of war profiteers, purges, and paper money, saved more than once by its generals. It sent Bonaparte to conquer Italy and Egypt, made peace with Austria at Campo Formio, and fell to him and Sieyès in the coup of 18 Brumaire.
French Directory.gov: Republic under a Directory of five
French Directory.faith: Catholic Christianity, restricted by the state

(Batavian Republic).x: The Dutch republic proclaimed in 1795 when French armies crossed the frozen rivers and the stadtholder William V fled to England. A sister republic of France, it gained a unitary constitution in 1798, lost Ceylon, the Cape, and its fleet to Britain, and in 1806 was turned into the Kingdom of Holland for Louis Bonaparte.
(Batavian Republic).faith: Reformed Christianity; all faiths equal from 1796
rulers: Pieter Paulus (president of the National Assembly)

Batavian Republic.x: The republic of the Dutch patriots, founded with French help in 1795 on the ruins of the old United Provinces. It abolished the stadtholderate and the privileges of the provinces, separated church and state, and gave the Dutch their first written constitution in 1798, while paying heavily for its alliance with France.
Batavian Republic.faith: Reformed Christianity; all faiths equal from 1796
rulers: Pieter Paulus (president of the National Assembly)

Cisalpine Republic.x: The sister republic created by Bonaparte in 1797 in Lombardy, Emilia, and the Romagna, with Milan as capital and a constitution on the French model. Overrun by the Austrians and Russians in 1799, it was restored after Marengo and in 1802 renamed the Italian Republic, with Bonaparte as president.

Helvetic Republic.x: The unitary republic imposed on the Swiss by the French invasion of 1798, which abolished the old cantons and their subject lands and gave equal rights to all citizens. Torn between unitarists and federalists and fought over by French, Austrian, and Russian armies, it gave way in 1803 to Napoleon's Act of Mediation.
Helvetic Republic.gov: Unitary republic, a client of France

Revolutionary Roman Republic.x: The Roman Republic proclaimed in February 1798 under French bayonets, after the pope was deposed as temporal ruler and carried into exile, with consuls and tribunes in imitation of antiquity. Neapolitan and Austrian forces overthrew it in the autumn of 1799.

(British Empire).x: The British Crown with its dominions, colonies, protectorates, and mandates, built by trade, settlement, and the Royal Navy; at its height after 1919 the largest empire in history, ruling a quarter of the world's land and people, it gave way after 1945 to independent states, most of which joined the Commonwealth.
(British Empire).gov: Constitutional monarchy with parliamentary government; dominions, colonies, and protectorates
(British Empire).faith: Protestant Christianity (Church of England) at home; many faiths across the empire
rulers: William Pitt the Elder (secretary of state)

British Colonial Empire.x: Britain's overseas colonies and dependencies outside India: the West Indian sugar islands, Canada, the Australian colonies, the Cape, and later most of tropical Africa and the Pacific, governed through the Colonial Office from 1854; independence came to most after 1957, and the return of Hong Kong in 1997 closed the imperial age.
British Colonial Empire.gov: Crown colonies, protectorates, and self-governing dominions under the Crown and Parliament
British Colonial Empire.faith: Protestant Christianity among settlers; many faiths among subject peoples
rulers: William Pitt the Elder (secretary of state)

British Empire.x: The rule of the British East India Company in India, won at Plassey in 1757 and extended by war and treaty from Bengal across the subcontinent; governed from Calcutta under parliamentary control from 1773, it ended when the Mutiny of 1857 moved Parliament to transfer the Company's powers to the Crown in 1858.
British Empire.gov: Chartered company rule under parliamentary supervision (Governor-General in Council)
British Empire.faith: Company officially neutral; subjects Hindu, Muslim, Sikh, and others

(French Consulate).x: The French Republic under the Consulate with its overseas possessions, the sugar islands of the Antilles and the Mascarenes; Bonaparte restored slavery there in 1802, and the attempt to retake Saint-Domingue ended in the loss of that colony and the sale of Louisiana.
(French Consulate).gov: Republic under the Consulate, in effect the rule of the First Consul
(French Consulate).faith: Roman Catholicism, restored by the Concordat of 1801; Protestants and Jews tolerated

French Consulate.x: The government set up by Bonaparte's coup of 18 Brumaire in November 1799, with three consuls of whom the First held all real power; it made peace with Austria and Britain, signed the Concordat, centralized France under prefects, drew up the Civil Code, and was transformed into the Empire in May 1804.
French Consulate.gov: Republic under the Consulate, in effect the rule of the First Consul
French Consulate.faith: Roman Catholicism, restored by the Concordat of 1801; Protestants and Jews tolerated

Italian Republic.x: The Cisalpine Republic renamed at the Lyon consulta of January 1802, with Bonaparte as its president and Francesco Melzi d'Eril governing at Milan as vice-president; in 1805 it became the Kingdom of Italy, with Napoleon as its king.
Italian Republic.gov: Republic under French protection, presided over by Bonaparte

Kingdom of Etruria.x: A Bourbon kingdom made by Bonaparte in 1801 from the Grand Duchy of Tuscany for Louis of Parma, as the price of Spain's cession of Louisiana; after Louis died in 1803 his queen Maria Luisa ruled as regent for their son until Napoleon dissolved the kingdom in December 1807 and annexed Tuscany to France.
rulers: Charles Louis (under the regency of Maria Luisa)

(First French Empire).x: Napoleon's empire with its remaining colonies, the Antilles, Guiana, and the Mascarenes, nearly all taken by the Royal Navy and its allies between 1809 and 1811; the empire's true dependencies were the satellite kingdoms of Europe ruled by the Emperor's family.

First French Empire.x: The empire of Napoleon I, proclaimed in May 1804: at its height in 1811 it stretched in 130 departments from Hamburg to Rome and dominated Europe through satellite kingdoms and alliances, until the disaster in Russia, the defeat at Leipzig, and the allied invasion of 1814 forced the Emperor's abdication.

Kingdom of Italy (Napoleonic).x: The kingdom made by Napoleon in 1805 from the Italian Republic, with himself crowned king in Milan Cathedral with the Iron Crown of Lombardy and his stepson Eugène de Beauharnais as viceroy; enlarged by Venetia and the Marches, it sent tens of thousands of soldiers to the Grande Armée and fell in April 1814.
Kingdom of Italy (Napoleonic).gov: Monarchy in personal union with the French Empire, governed by a viceroy

Revolutionary Serbia.x: The Serbian state of the First Uprising, which rose against the janissaries in 1804 under Karađorđe and then fought the Ottoman Porte itself, governing through a council and assembly from Smederevo and Belgrade; left alone when Russia made peace with Turkey in 1812, it was crushed by Ottoman armies in 1813.
Revolutionary Serbia.gov: Insurgent principality under a supreme leader and a Governing Council
rulers: Mateja Nenadović (president of the Governing Council)

Austrian Empire.x: The empire proclaimed by Francis I in 1804 for the Habsburg hereditary lands and Hungary, the conservative pillar of Metternich's Europe after 1815; it survived the revolutions of 1848 with Russian help, lost Lombardy in 1859 and its German primacy at Königgrätz in 1866, and was remade as Austria-Hungary in 1867.
Austrian Empire.gov: Absolute monarchy; constitutional experiments in 1848 to 1849 and from 1860
rulers: Klemens von Metternich (foreign minister, then state chancellor)

Kingdom of Bavaria.x: Raised to a kingdom by Napoleon on 1 January 1806 as the price of alliance, Bavaria doubled its lands, gained a constitution in 1818, and was adorned with the Munich of Ludwig I; it sided with Austria in 1866 and entered the German Empire in 1871 as its second state, keeping in peacetime its own army, posts, and railways.

Kingdom of Naples (Napoleonic).x: Southern Italy under French rule after the Bourbons fled to Sicily in 1806: Joseph Bonaparte and then Joachim Murat abolished feudalism and reformed the laws, until Murat, who turned against Napoleon and then back to him, was beaten by the Austrians at Tolentino in May 1815 and shot in Calabria that October.

Kingdom of Saxony.x: Made a kingdom by Napoleon in December 1806, Saxony stayed loyal to him too long and lost three fifths of its land to Prussia in 1815; industrious and densely peopled, it gained a constitution in 1831, fought beside Austria in 1866, and became a state of the German Empire in 1871.
Kingdom of Saxony.faith: Lutheran people under a Roman Catholic dynasty

Kingdom of Holland.x: The kingdom Napoleon made of the Batavian Republic in 1806 for his brother Louis, who learned Dutch, tried to rule in the interest of his subjects, and let the Continental System leak; Napoleon forced him to abdicate in July 1810 and annexed Holland to France.
Kingdom of Holland.faith: Dutch Reformed Protestantism, with a large Roman Catholic minority

Grand Duchy of Hesse.x: The former landgraviate of Hesse-Darmstadt, raised to a grand duchy in the Confederation of the Rhine in 1806 and enlarged in 1816 by Rhenish Hesse with Mainz; it fought beside Austria in 1866, lost Hesse-Homburg, saw its northern province enter the North German Confederation, and joined the German Empire in 1871.
Grand Duchy of Hesse.faith: Lutheran Protestantism, with a Roman Catholic minority

Grand Duchy of Berg.x: A Rhineland state made by Napoleon in 1806 for his brother-in-law Joachim Murat from the duchies of Berg and Cleves, with Düsseldorf as capital; when Murat went to Naples in 1808 it passed to Napoleon, and then to his small nephew Napoleon Louis under imperial regency, until the allies dissolved it in 1813.

Duchy of Warsaw.x: Created by Napoleon at Tilsit in 1807 from Prussia's share of the partitions and given to the King of Saxony, it gave the Poles a constitution, the Code Napoléon, and an army under Prince Józef Poniatowski that fought for France to the end; the Congress of Vienna gave most of it to Russia as the Kingdom of Poland.
Duchy of Warsaw.gov: Constitutional monarchy under the King of Saxony, a French client state

Kingdom of Westphalia.x: A model kingdom made by Napoleon in 1807 for his youngest brother Jérôme from Hesse-Kassel, Brunswick, and Prussia's lands west of the Elbe, given one of the first written constitutions in Germany; taxed and conscripted for the Emperor's wars, it collapsed after Leipzig in 1813.
Kingdom of Westphalia.faith: Lutheran and Reformed Protestantism, with Roman Catholic and Jewish minorities

(Netherlands).x: The Kingdom of the Netherlands with its overseas empire: the East Indies, ruled from Batavia, Surinam, and the Antilles. The Indies passed to Indonesia in 1949 and western New Guinea in 1962; Surinam became independent in 1975, while Aruba, Curaçao, and Sint Maarten remain countries within the kingdom.
(Netherlands).gov: Constitutional monarchy with colonies; parliamentary from 1848
(Netherlands).faith: Dutch Reformed Protestantism and Roman Catholicism at home; Islam in the Indies

Kingdom of Norway.x: Norway, ceded by Denmark to Sweden in 1814, gave itself the Eidsvoll constitution that May and entered a personal union under the Swedish king; it dissolved the union in 1905 and chose Haakon VII, endured German occupation from 1940 to 1945, and became a founder of NATO and, through North Sea oil, one of the richest nations on earth.
rulers: Charles XIV John (Charles III John of Norway)

Sovereign Principality of the United Net.x: The Dutch state of 1813 to 1815, formed when the French withdrew and William Frederick of Orange accepted sovereignty; a constitution was adopted in March 1814, and in March 1815 he proclaimed himself king of a United Netherlands that took in the former Austrian provinces of Belgium.
Sovereign Principality of the United Net.faith: Dutch Reformed Protestantism, with a large Roman Catholic minority
rulers: Gijsbert Karel van Hogendorp (leader of the provisional government)

United Kingdoms of Sweden and Norway.x: The personal union of Sweden and Norway under one king, from the Convention of Moss in 1814 to the Storting's dissolution of the union in June 1905; each kingdom kept its own laws, parliament, army, and church, and quarrels over Norway's foreign and consular service finally broke it.
United Kingdoms of Sweden and Norway.gov: Personal union of two constitutional monarchies
United Kingdoms of Sweden and Norway.faith: Lutheran Christianity (Churches of Sweden and Norway)
rulers: Louis De Geer (prime minister of Sweden)
Erik Gustaf Boström (prime minister of Sweden)

Bourbon Kingdom of France.x: The restored monarchy of Louis XVIII and Charles X after Napoleon's fall, governing under the Charter of 1814 with a chamber elected by the wealthy few; it paid off the war indemnity, sent an army to restore Ferdinand VII in Spain in 1823, and fell when Charles X tried to rule by ordinance in July 1830.
Bourbon Kingdom of France.gov: Constitutional monarchy under the Charter of 1814
rulers: Duc de Richelieu (president of the council)
Duc de Richelieu (president of the council)
Joseph de Villèle (president of the council)
Vicomte de Martignac (head of the ministry)
Jules de Polignac (president of the council)

(Bourbon Kingdom of France).x: Restoration France with its remaining colonies, the Antilles, Guiana, Réunion, Senegal, and the Indian trading posts, and from 1830 the conquest of Algiers, which the July Monarchy inherited and extended across northern Algeria.
rulers: Duc de Richelieu (president of the council)
Duc de Richelieu (president of the council)
Joseph de Villèle (president of the council)
Vicomte de Martignac (head of the ministry)
Jules de Polignac (president of the council)

Kingdom of the Two Sicilies.x: The union of Naples and Sicily under the Bourbon Ferdinand I in 1816, ruled from Naples with Austrian backing; it put down the revolutions of 1820 and 1848, Ferdinand II earning the name King Bomba for shelling Messina, and fell to Garibaldi's Thousand in 1860, its last king holding out at Gaeta until February 1861.

Netherlands.x: The kingdom of the House of Orange-Nassau, governed from The Hague, which held Belgium until 1830 and became a parliamentary monarchy under Thorbecke's constitution of 1848; neutral in 1914, overrun by Germany in May 1940, it was a founder of NATO and the European Communities.
Netherlands.faith: Dutch Reformed Protestantism and Roman Catholicism

July Monarchy.x: The reign of Louis Philippe, King of the French, set up by the July Revolution of 1830: a bourgeois monarchy of a narrow electorate in which Guizot bade Frenchmen grow rich; it conquered Algeria and kept the peace in Europe, but refused electoral reform and fell to the February Revolution of 1848.
July Monarchy.gov: Constitutional monarchy under the revised Charter of 1830
rulers: Duc de Bassano (president of the council)
Duc de Broglie (president of the council)
Marshal Soult (president of the council, with Guizot leading)

French Algeria.x: The conquest begun with the capture of Algiers in July 1830: a slow, hard war of columns and razzias against the tribes and the emir Abd al-Qadir, waged under governors-general from Clauzel to Bugeaud, until the emir's surrender in December 1847; in 1848 Algeria was declared French territory and divided into departments.
French Algeria.faith: Sunni Islam among the Algerians; Roman Catholicism among the settlers

Kingdom of Poland (November Uprising).x: The Congress Kingdom of Poland in revolt, from the cadets' rising in Warsaw on 29 November 1830 until the fall of the city to Paskevich in September 1831; the Sejm dethroned Nicholas I as king in January 1831 and governed through a National Government under Prince Adam Czartoryski.
Kingdom of Poland (November Uprising).gov: Insurgent constitutional state under the Sejm and a National Government
rulers: Adam Jerzy Czartoryski (president of the National Government)
Jan Krukowiecki (president of the National Government)

Kingdom of Belgium.x: Born of the Brussels revolt of 1830 and guaranteed neutral by the powers in 1839, Belgium was a constitutional monarchy of the Saxe-Coburg line and the first industrial nation of the Continent; overrun by Germany in both world wars, it ruled the Congo until 1960 and became the seat of the European institutions.

Kingdom of Greece.x: The kingdom created by the powers in 1832 for the Bavarian prince Otto and given in 1863 to the Danish George I; it grew by the Ionian Islands, Thessaly, Crete, and Macedonia, was riven by the quarrel of Constantine I and Venizelos, and was a republic from 1924 to 1935 before the crown returned.
Kingdom of Greece.gov: Constitutional monarchy; dictatorship under Metaxas 1936 to 1941

Kingdom of Hanover.x: Raised from electorate to kingdom at Vienna in 1814 and ruled by the British kings until 1837, when the Salic law gave it to the Duke of Cumberland, Ernest Augustus, who tore up its constitution; its blind king George V sided with Austria in 1866 and lost his kingdom to Prussia days after his army's victory at Langensalza.

French Africa.x: France's African empire: Algeria from 1830, Senegal and the vast federations of West and Equatorial Africa, the protectorates of Tunisia and Morocco, and Madagascar, ruled from Paris through governors-general at Algiers, Dakar, and Brazzaville; Equatorial Africa rallied to de Gaulle in 1940, and nearly all of it became independent between 1956 and 1962.
French Africa.gov: Colonies, protectorates, and the French departments of Algeria under governors-general
French Africa.faith: Islam, traditional religions, and Christian missions; Roman Catholicism among settlers
rulers: Jacques-Charles Dupont de l'Eure (head of the provisional government)
François Arago (president of the executive commission)
Louis-Jules Trochu (president of the Government of National Defense)
Philippe Pétain (Chief of the French State)
Charles de Gaulle (Free France, then provisional government)
Félix Gouin (head of the provisional government)
Georges Bidault (head of the provisional government)
Léon Blum (head of the provisional government)

(French Second Republic).x: The Second Republic with Algeria, declared French territory and divided into three departments by the constitution of 1848, and the old colonies of the Antilles, Guiana, Réunion, and Senegal, where slavery was abolished by Victor Schoelcher's decree of April 1848.
(French Second Republic).gov: Republic; presidential under the constitution of November 1848
rulers: Jacques-Charles Dupont de l'Eure (head of the provisional government)
François Arago (president of the executive commission)

French Second Republic.x: The republic proclaimed in Paris in February 1848; it decreed universal manhood suffrage and abolished slavery in the colonies, shot down the Paris workers in the June Days, elected Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte president by a landslide that December, and was overthrown by him in the coup of 2 December 1851.
French Second Republic.gov: Republic; presidential under the constitution of November 1848
rulers: Jacques-Charles Dupont de l'Eure (head of the provisional government)
François Arago (president of the executive commission)

Italian Nationalists.x: The revolutionary government of Sicily, which rose at Palermo on 12 January 1848, deposed the Bourbons, and offered the crown to the Duke of Genoa, a son of Charles Albert, who would not take it; Ferdinand II's troops bombarded Messina that autumn and retook the island by May 1849.
Italian Nationalists.gov: Revolutionary constitutional kingdom without a king

Duchy of Holstein.x: The duchies of Schleswig and Holstein in revolt against Denmark from March 1848 under a provisional government at Kiel, backed by Prussia and the German Confederation; abandoned by Prussia, the Schleswig-Holstein army was beaten at Idstedt in 1850, and Holstein returned to the Danish king as its duke.
rulers: Frederick VII (King of Denmark, Duke of Holstein)
Wilhelm Hartwig Beseler (provisional government, then stadtholder)
Count Friedrich von Reventlou (provisional government, then stadtholder)

Hungarian State.x: Hungary in its war of independence: after Francis Joseph imposed a new constitution and his armies invaded, the Diet at Debrecen dethroned the Habsburgs on 14 April 1849 and made Lajos Kossuth governor-president; Russian intervention doomed the state, and Görgei surrendered at Világos that August.
Hungarian State.gov: Revolutionary independent state under a governor-president
rulers: Lajos Kossuth (head of the Defense Committee, then governor-president)

Hungarian Nationalists.x: The Hungarian national cause after the defeat of 1849: the kingdom lay under martial law and Bach's centralizing absolutism, governed by Archduke Albrecht, while Kossuth, freed from Ottoman internment in 1851, toured Britain and America to raise support for independence. Reconciliation came only with the Compromise of 1867.
Hungarian Nationalists.gov: Habsburg military and absolutist rule; a national movement in exile

(Second French Empire).x: The empire of Napoleon III with its colonies: Algeria, pushed to the edge of the Sahara; Senegal under Faidherbe; Cochinchina, taken from 1859; New Caledonia, annexed in 1853; and a protectorate over Cambodia from 1863.
rulers: Count of Palikao (head of the ministry)

Second French Empire.x: The empire of Napoleon III, proclaimed in December 1852 after his coup: an authoritarian regime that rebuilt Paris under Haussmann, built railways and banks, fought Russia in the Crimea and Austria in Italy, ventured into Mexico, and liberalized in the 1860s, until the surrender at Sedan in September 1870 brought it down.
Second French Empire.gov: Hereditary empire; authoritarian, then liberal from 1860 to 1870
rulers: Count of Palikao (head of the ministry)

French colonial empire.x: The first French foothold in Cochinchina, won by the Franco-Spanish expedition of Admiral Rigault de Genouilly, which attacked Tourane in 1858 and took Saigon in February 1859; the Treaty of Saigon of 1862 ceded three eastern provinces to France, the nucleus of French Indochina.
French colonial empire.faith: Buddhism and ancestral rites; Roman Catholic missions

United Principalities of Moldavia and Wa.x: Moldavia and Wallachia, which defeated the powers' plan to keep them apart by electing the same prince, Alexandru Ioan Cuza, in both early in 1859; Cuza united their governments in 1862 as Romania, freed the peasants, seized the monastic lands, and was deposed by a palace coup in February 1866.
United Principalities of Moldavia and Wa.gov: Personal union of two principalities, united in 1862, under Ottoman suzerainty

French Indochina.x: The French dominion in Southeast Asia, conquered from Cochinchina in 1859 to Laos in 1893 and federated as the Indochinese Union in 1887; it produced rice, rubber, and coal for France, was occupied by Japan in the Second World War, and was lost in the war against the Viet Minh that ended at Dien Bien Phu in 1954.
French Indochina.gov: Colony and protectorates federated under a governor-general
French Indochina.faith: Buddhism, ancestral rites, and Confucian tradition; Roman Catholic missions
rulers: Louis-Jules Trochu (president of the Government of National Defense)
Philippe Pétain (Chief of the French State)
Charles de Gaulle (head of the provisional government)
Félix Gouin (head of the provisional government)
Georges Bidault (head of the provisional government)
Léon Blum (head of the provisional government)
Jean de Lattre de Tassigny (high commissioner)

Principality of Romania.x: The united principality under Prince Carol of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen from 1866; it proclaimed its independence from the Ottomans in May 1877, won it beside Russia at Plevna, saw it recognized at Berlin in 1878 at the cost of southern Bessarabia, and became a kingdom in 1881.
Principality of Romania.gov: Constitutional principality under the constitution of 1866

Austria-Hungary.x: The Dual Monarchy of the Habsburgs created by the Compromise of 1867: an Austrian empire and a Hungarian kingdom under one emperor-king, with a joint army, diplomacy, and finance, ruling a dozen peoples from the Alps to the Carpathians; its ultimatum to Serbia in July 1914 began the First World War, which destroyed it in 1918.
Austria-Hungary.gov: Dual monarchy of two constitutional states under one emperor-king
Austria-Hungary.faith: Roman Catholicism, with Orthodox, Protestant, Jewish, and Muslim subjects
rulers: Gyula Andrássy (Hungarian prime minister, then foreign minister)

North German Confederation.x: The federal state under Prussian presidency formed in 1867 by the twenty-two German states north of the Main after Königgrätz; with Bismarck as chancellor and a Reichstag elected by universal manhood suffrage, it was the German Empire in embryo and became it in 1871.
North German Confederation.gov: Federal monarchy under the presidency of the Prussian crown

(French Third Republic).x: The French Republic together with its colonial empire, which grew under the Third Republic from Algeria and Cochinchina to West and Equatorial Africa, Tunisia, Madagascar, Indochina, Morocco, and the Levant mandates, nearly five million square miles ruled from Paris through governors-general and residents.
(French Third Republic).gov: Parliamentary republic with colonies, protectorates, and mandates
(French Third Republic).faith: Roman Catholicism at home, secular state from 1905; many faiths overseas
rulers: Louis-Jules Trochu (president of the Government of National Defense)
