German Empire.x: The federal empire of twenty-five German states under the King of Prussia, proclaimed at Versailles in 1871 after Bismarck's wars; the leading industrial and military power of the Continent, it built a navy to rival Britain's, went to war in 1914 beside Austria-Hungary, and fell in the revolution of November 1918.
German Empire.gov: Federal constitutional monarchy under the King of Prussia as German Emperor
German Empire.faith: Protestant majority (Lutheran and Reformed), large Roman Catholic minority
rulers: Paul von Hindenburg (chief of the General Staff)

French Third Republic.x: The French republic born of defeat at Sedan in 1870 and confirmed by the constitutional laws of 1875; it survived Boulanger, Panama, and the Dreyfus Affair, separated church and state, won the Great War at terrible cost, and built an empire second only to Britain's, until it voted full powers to Pétain in July 1940.
French Third Republic.gov: Parliamentary republic under the constitutional laws of 1875
French Third Republic.faith: Roman Catholicism; church and state separated in 1905
rulers: Louis-Jules Trochu (president of the Government of National Defense)

German-occupied France.x: The French departments held by a German army of occupation under the Treaty of Frankfurt of May 1871 as surety for the indemnity of five billion francs; Thiers' government paid early with two great loans, and the last German troops marched out of Verdun in September 1873.
rulers: Edwin von Manteuffel (commander of the army of occupation)

First Spanish Republic.x: The republic proclaimed by the Cortes on Amadeo I's abdication in February 1873; it ran through four presidents in eleven months amid the cantonal risings and the Third Carlist War, fell to General Pavía's coup in January 1874, and gave way to the restored Bourbon Alfonso XII at the end of that year.
First Spanish Republic.gov: Republic (federal in intent), then the Serrano dictatorship
rulers: Estanislao Figueras (president of the executive power)
Francisco Pi y Margall (president of the executive power)
Nicolás Salmerón (president of the executive power)
Emilio Castelar (president of the executive power)

Principality of Bulgaria.x: Created by the Treaty of Berlin in 1878 as an autonomous principality under Ottoman suzerainty, with the liberal Tarnovo Constitution; it absorbed Eastern Rumelia in 1885, defeated Serbia at Slivnitsa, and proclaimed full independence as a tsardom in October 1908.
Principality of Bulgaria.faith: Bulgarian Orthodox Christianity (Exarchate), with a Muslim minority

Kingdom of Romania.x: Romania as a kingdom of the Hohenzollern kings from 1881; it joined the Entente in 1916 and won Transylvania, Bessarabia, and Bukovina as Greater Romania in 1918, fell under the dictatorship of Carol II and then Marshal Antonescu, fought beside Germany from 1941, changed sides in August 1944, and saw King Michael forced to abdicate in December 1947.
Kingdom of Romania.gov: Constitutional monarchy; royal dictatorship 1938 to 1940; military dictatorship 1940 to 1944

Tsardom of Bulgaria.x: Bulgaria as an independent tsardom from Ferdinand's proclamation at Tarnovo in October 1908; it won and lost Macedonia in the Balkan Wars, joined the Central Powers in 1915 and the Axis in 1941, and fell to a Fatherland Front coup as the Red Army arrived in September 1944.

Albania.x: The state proclaimed at Valona in 1912 and recognized by the powers in 1913; fought over through the Great War, it found a ruler in Ahmet Zogu, president from 1925 and King Zog from 1928, and was seized by Mussolini on Good Friday 1939 and joined to the Italian crown.
Albania.gov: Principality, then republic, then kingdom from 1928; under Italian rule from 1939
Albania.faith: Sunni and Bektashi Islam, with Orthodox and Roman Catholic minorities
rulers: Ismail Qemali (head of the provisional government)
Ahmet Zogu (president, then King Zog I)
Enver Hoxha (head of the provisional government)

Russian Republic.x: Russia under the Provisional Government, between the abdication of Nicholas II in March 1917 and the Bolshevik seizure of Petrograd in November; Kerensky proclaimed it a republic in September, and the Constituent Assembly that was to settle its form met once in January 1918 before the Bolsheviks dispersed it.
Russian Republic.faith: Russian Orthodox Christianity (patriarchate restored in November 1917)
rulers: Georgy Lvov (chairman of the Provisional Government)
Alexander Kerensky (chairman of the Provisional Government)

Russian SFSR.x: Soviet Russia from the Bolshevik revolution to the founding of the Union: the state of Lenin and of Trotsky's Red Army, which won the Civil War against the Whites, the allied interventions, and the peasant risings, through Red Terror and grain requisitioning, and in 1922 became the largest republic of the Soviet Union.
Russian SFSR.gov: Soviet socialist republic under the one-party rule of the Bolsheviks
Russian SFSR.faith: State atheism; the Orthodox Church persecuted
rulers: Vladimir Lenin (chairman of the Council of People's Commissars)
Lev Kamenev (chairman of the Central Executive Committee)
Yakov Sverdlov (chairman of the Central Executive Committee)
Mikhail Kalinin (chairman of the Central Executive Committee)

Republic of Finland.x: The Finnish state independent from 6 December 1917; after a civil war won by Mannerheim's Whites it became a republic in 1919, defended itself against Soviet invasion in the Winter War and the Continuation War, kept its democracy and independence under a careful neutrality, and joined the European Union in 1995 and NATO in 2023.

British Mandates.x: The lands of the old Ottoman Empire placed under British administration after 1918 and held as League of Nations mandates: Mesopotamia, which became the Kingdom of Iraq and independent in 1932, Transjordan until 1946, and Palestine, torn between Arab and Jewish claims, until 1948.
British Mandates.gov: League of Nations mandates under British high commissioners
British Mandates.faith: Sunni and Shia Islam, with Christian and Jewish communities

Kingdom of Iceland.x: Iceland as a sovereign state in personal union with Denmark under the Act of Union of 1 December 1918, sharing only the king and leaving foreign affairs to Copenhagen; after Germany occupied Denmark and Britain occupied Iceland in 1940, it became a republic on 17 June 1944.
Kingdom of Iceland.gov: Constitutional monarchy in personal union with Denmark

Polish Armed Forces.x: The Polish I Corps in Russia under General Józef Dowbor-Muśnicki, formed from Poles of the old Russian army in 1917; it fought the Bolsheviks early in 1918, held the fortress of Bobruisk and a district of Belorussia, and disbanded under German terms in May 1918, many of its men later serving in the army of independent Poland.

Weimar Republic.x: The German republic of 1918 to 1933, named for the town where its constitution was written; burdened by defeat, Versailles, the hyperinflation of 1923, and enemies on left and right, it found a few good years under Stresemann before the Depression, when government by presidential decree opened the way for Hitler.
Weimar Republic.gov: Federal parliamentary republic; rule by presidential decree from 1930
Weimar Republic.faith: Protestant majority, large Roman Catholic minority

Second Polish Republic.x: Poland restored in November 1918, its frontiers won by war against Ukrainians, Lithuanians, and the Bolsheviks; a parliamentary republic until Piłsudski's May Coup of 1926 and the Sanacja regime that followed, it was invaded by Germany and the Soviet Union in September 1939, its government continuing in exile.
Second Polish Republic.gov: Parliamentary republic; authoritarian Sanacja regime after 1926
Second Polish Republic.faith: Roman Catholicism, with large Orthodox, Greek Catholic, and Jewish minorities
rulers: Józef Piłsudski (marshal, ruler of the state)

Ukrainian People's Republic.x: The Ukrainian state proclaimed by the Central Rada at Kiev in 1917 and declared independent in January 1918; overthrown by the German-backed Hetman Skoropadsky, restored under the Directorate in December 1918, it was driven from Kiev by Bolsheviks and Whites in turn and survived in 1919 as Petliura's army in Podolia.
Ukrainian People's Republic.gov: Republic under the Central Rada, then the Directorate
rulers: Mykhailo Hrushevsky (chairman of the Central Rada)

Yugoslavia.x: The Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes proclaimed under the Serbian dynasty on 1 December 1918 and renamed Yugoslavia when Alexander I took dictatorial power in 1929; dominated by Serbs and resented by Croats, it was invaded by the Axis in April 1941 and partitioned, the young King Peter II ruling in exile.
Yugoslavia.faith: Serbian Orthodox, Roman Catholic, and Muslim

Czechoslovakia.x: The republic of Czechs and Slovaks founded by Masaryk in October 1918, the one lasting democracy of interwar central Europe; dismembered after Munich, restored in 1945, seized by the Communists in 1948, invaded in 1968, freed by the Velvet Revolution of 1989, and peacefully divided into two states on 1 January 1993.

Republic of Lithuania.x: The republic declared at Vilnius on 16 February 1918, which lost its historic capital to Poland in 1920 and governed from Kaunas, under Antanas Smetona's authoritarian rule from 1926; annexed by the Soviet Union in 1940, it was the first Soviet republic to declare independence, on 11 March 1990, and joined NATO and the European Union in 2004.
Republic of Lithuania.gov: Parliamentary republic; authoritarian 1926 to 1940; parliamentary again from 1990
rulers: Vytautas Landsbergis (chairman of the Supreme Council)

Republic of Austria.x: The German-speaking rump left by the fall of the Habsburgs, forbidden to join Germany by the peace of Saint-Germain; torn between Socialist Vienna and the Catholic provinces, it became under Dollfuss in 1934 an authoritarian corporative state, and was annexed by Hitler in March 1938.
Republic of Austria.gov: Federal parliamentary republic; authoritarian Federal State from 1934
rulers: Karl Seitz (president of the Constituent Assembly)

Hungarian Republic.x: Hungary in its revolutionary year: the People's Republic of Count Mihály Károlyi, proclaimed in November 1918, gave way in March 1919 to Béla Kun's Soviet Republic, which fell to the Romanian army in August; Admiral Horthy's National Army entered Budapest in November.
rulers: Béla Kun (leader of the Soviet Republic)

Estonia.x: The republic proclaimed at Tallinn on 24 February 1918 and won in the War of Independence against the Red Army and the German Landeswehr; parliamentary until Konstantin Päts's coup of 1934, it was occupied and annexed by the Soviet Union in 1940.
Estonia.faith: Lutheran Christianity, with an Orthodox minority
rulers: Konstantin Päts (head of the provisional government)

Allied-occupied Rhineland.x: The German lands west of the Rhine, with bridgeheads at Cologne, Koblenz, and Mainz, held by Belgian, British, French, and American troops under the Treaty of Versailles and governed by an Inter-Allied High Commission at Koblenz; the zones were evacuated in stages, the last French troops leaving on 30 June 1930.
Allied-occupied Rhineland.gov: Military occupation under an inter-allied commission
rulers: Paul Tirard (president of the High Commission)
Jean Degoutte (commander of the French Army of the Rhine)

French Mandate for Syria and Lebanon.x: The Levant states placed under French mandate by the League of Nations in 1920 after Gouraud's army drove King Faisal from Damascus; France carved out Greater Lebanon, crushed the Druze revolt of 1925 to 1927, and lost the territories to British and Free French arms in 1941, leaving in 1946.
French Mandate for Syria and Lebanon.gov: League of Nations mandate under a French high commissioner
French Mandate for Syria and Lebanon.faith: Sunni Islam, with Maronite, Orthodox, Druze, Alawite, and Shia communities

Republic of Latvia.x: The republic proclaimed at Riga on 18 November 1918 and secured in 1920 after war against the Bolsheviks and the German Freikorps; ruled by Kārlis Ulmanis as dictator from 1934, annexed by the Soviet Union in 1940, it regained independence in August 1991 and joined NATO and the European Union in 2004.
Republic of Latvia.gov: Parliamentary republic; authoritarian 1934 to 1940; parliamentary again from 1991
rulers: Jānis Čakste (head of state, then president)
Anatolijs Gorbunovs (chairman of the Supreme Council)

Union of Soviet Socialist Republics.x: The Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, founded in December 1922 from the Bolshevik lands of the old Russian Empire and ruled by the Communist Party; under Stalin it was industrialized and terrorized, it bore the heaviest burden in the defeat of Nazi Germany, became the rival superpower of the Cold War, and dissolved in December 1991.
Union of Soviet Socialist Republics.gov: Federal one-party socialist state under the Communist Party
Union of Soviet Socialist Republics.faith: State atheism; Orthodox, Muslim, and other believers restricted and persecuted
rulers: Vladimir Lenin (chairman of the Council of People's Commissars)
Joseph Stalin (general secretary, leader of the Soviet Union)
Konstantin Chernenko (general secretary and head of state)
Mikhail Gorbachev (head of state, president from 1990)

Irish Free State.x: The self-governing dominion of twenty-six Irish counties established in December 1922 under the treaty with Britain; it won the civil war against the anti-treaty republicans, and under de Valera from 1932 dismantled the oath and the Crown's role, replacing the Free State in 1937 with the constitution of Éire.
Irish Free State.gov: Dominion under the Crown with parliamentary government
rulers: Michael Collins (chairman of the Provisional Government)
W. T. Cosgrave (president of the Executive Council)
Éamon de Valera (president of the Executive Council)

Second Hellenic Republic.x: The Greek republic proclaimed in March 1924 after the disaster in Asia Minor and the exile of the king, unsettled by the dictatorship of General Pangalos and repeated coups; Venizelos governed steadily from 1928 to 1932, and General Kondylis restored the monarchy by a rigged plebiscite in November 1935.
Second Hellenic Republic.gov: Parliamentary republic, interrupted by military dictatorship

Second Spanish Republic.x: The republic proclaimed when Alfonso XIII left Spain in April 1931; torn between left and right from the first, it was rent by the military rising of July 1936 and destroyed in the Civil War, its last government leaving Spain as Franco's armies took Madrid in March 1939.

Chinese Soviet Republic.x: The Communist state proclaimed at Ruijin in Jiangxi on 7 November 1931 with Mao Zedong as chairman; Chiang Kai-shek's fifth encirclement campaign drove the Red Army out on the Long March in October 1934, and the republic was dissolved into the northwestern base and the united front against Japan in 1937.
Chinese Soviet Republic.gov: Soviet republic under the Chinese Communist Party
Chinese Soviet Republic.faith: Communist and atheist rule over Chinese popular religion, Buddhism, and Taoism
rulers: Mao Zedong (chairman of the Central Executive Committee)

Nazi Germany.x: The Third Reich of Adolf Hitler and the National Socialist party from 1933 to 1945: a totalitarian state that rearmed, annexed Austria and the Czech lands, launched the Second World War in Europe, and murdered six million Jews and millions of others before its total defeat and unconditional surrender in May 1945.
Nazi Germany.faith: Protestant and Roman Catholic churches subordinated and persecuted; Jews persecuted and murdered

Spanish Nationalists.x: The rebel zone of the Spanish Civil War, ruled from Burgos by a junta of generals and from October 1936 by Francisco Franco as Generalissimo and head of state; backed by Germany and Italy, it fused the Falangists and Carlists into a single party in 1937 and conquered the Republic by April 1939.
rulers: Miguel Cabanellas (president of the National Defense Junta)
Emilio Mola (commander of the Army of the North)
Francisco Franco (Generalissimo and head of state)

British Burma.x: Burma as a British colony governed separately from India from April 1937, with a partly elected ministry; overrun by Japan in 1942 and reconquered by Slim's Fourteenth Army in 1945, it was led toward independence by Aung San, who was murdered in July 1947, and became an independent republic on 4 January 1948.
British Burma.gov: Crown colony with a partly elected ministry under a governor
rulers: Ba Maw (head of the Japanese-sponsored State of Burma)
Aung San (deputy chairman of the Executive Council)

Éire.x: The Irish state under de Valera's constitution of 1937, which named it Éire and gave it an elected president while the King kept a role in foreign affairs; neutral through the Second World War, which it called the Emergency, it declared itself the Republic of Ireland in 1949.
Éire.gov: Parliamentary state with an elected president, a republic in all but name

German-occupied territory.x: The lands of Europe under German military or civil occupation in the Second World War, from the General Government of Poland and the Reich Commissariats of the Ostland and Ukraine to the Low Countries, northern France, Norway, Serbia, and Greece; ruled by plunder, forced labor, and terror, they were the ground of the Holocaust.
German-occupied territory.gov: Military and civil occupation under the German Reich
German-occupied territory.faith: Roman Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant populations; Jews deported and murdered
rulers: Konstantin von Neurath (Reich protector of Bohemia and Moravia)
Arthur Seyss-Inquart (Reich commissioner for the Netherlands)
Alexander von Falkenhausen (military governor of Belgium)
Otto von Stülpnagel (military commander in France)
Alfred Rosenberg (minister for the occupied eastern territories)
Hinrich Lohse (Reich commissioner for the Ostland)
Carl-Heinrich von Stülpnagel (military commander in France)

Francoist Spain.x: Spain under General Francisco Franco after his victory in the Civil War: a Catholic, nationalist dictatorship that stayed out of the Second World War, emerged from isolation through its pact of 1953 with the United States, grew rich in the economic miracle of the 1960s, and, declared a kingdom in 1947, received in Juan Carlos the successor Franco named in 1969.
Francoist Spain.gov: Personal dictatorship of Franco; a kingdom without a king from 1947
rulers: Francisco Franco (head of state and, to 1973, of government)

Italian-occupied territory.x: The lands occupied or annexed by Fascist Italy in the Second World War: Albania from April 1939, then after the Axis conquests of 1941 the province of Ljubljana, Dalmatia, Montenegro, most of Greece, and a strip of southeastern France; all passed to German occupation or partisan control after the armistice of September 1943.
Italian-occupied territory.gov: Military occupation and annexation by the Kingdom of Italy
Italian-occupied territory.faith: Orthodox Christianity, Islam, and Roman Catholicism

Slovak Republic.x: The client state proclaimed under German pressure on 14 March 1939 by Monsignor Jozef Tiso, a priest who became its president; ruled by Hlinka's Slovak People's Party, it fought beside Germany against Poland and the Soviet Union and deported most of its Jews, until the Slovak National Uprising of 1944 and the Red Army ended it.
Slovak Republic.gov: One-party clerical-nationalist state under German protection

Vichy France.x: The French State of Marshal Pétain, governing from the spa town of Vichy the unoccupied south after the armistice of June 1940; it replaced the Republic's motto with Work, Family, Fatherland, collaborated with Germany, and handed over Jews for deportation, and lost even its nominal independence when the Germans occupied the south in November 1942.
Vichy France.gov: Authoritarian French State under Marshal Pétain, collaborating with Germany
Vichy France.faith: Roman Catholicism; Jews persecuted under the statutes of 1940 and 1941
rulers: Philippe Pétain (Chief of the French State)

(Vichy France).x: The French State of Marshal Pétain together with the colonies that held to it after June 1940: North and West Africa, Indochina, the Levant until 1941, and Madagascar until 1942; Equatorial Africa rallied to de Gaulle, and after the allied landings of November 1942 the African empire passed to the Free French side.
(Vichy France).gov: Authoritarian French State under Marshal Pétain, collaborating with Germany
(Vichy France).faith: Roman Catholicism; Jews persecuted under the statutes of 1940 and 1941
rulers: Philippe Pétain (Chief of the French State)

Independent State of Croatia.x: The Axis puppet state proclaimed in Zagreb on 10 April 1941 and given to Ante Pavelić's Ustaše, taking in Bosnia and Herzegovina; it murdered hundreds of thousands of Serbs, Jews, and Roma, many in the Jasenovac camp, and collapsed in May 1945 as Tito's partisans advanced.
Independent State of Croatia.gov: Ustaše one-party state under German and Italian protection
Independent State of Croatia.faith: Roman Catholicism and Islam; Orthodox Serbs persecuted
rulers: Prince Aimone of Savoy (designated King Tomislav II)
Slavko Kvaternik (marshal and minister of the armed forces)

Soviet-occupied Iran.x: Northern Iran under Soviet occupation after the Anglo-Soviet invasion of August 1941; Moscow sponsored the Azerbaijan People's Government of Ja'far Pishevari and the Kurdish republic of Mahabad in 1945 and 1946, and withdrew in May 1946 after Iran appealed to the new United Nations.
Soviet-occupied Iran.gov: Soviet military occupation, with client governments in Azerbaijan and Kurdistan
rulers: Ja'far Pishevari (head of the Azerbaijan People's Government)
Qazi Muhammad (president of the Republic of Mahabad)

British-occupied Iran.x: Southern and western Iran under British occupation after the Anglo-Soviet invasion of August 1941, which deposed Reza Shah for his German sympathies; the Persian Corridor carried American lend-lease supplies from the Gulf to the Soviet Union, and the British withdrew by March 1946.
British-occupied Iran.gov: Allied military occupation over the Shah's government

Yugoslav Partisans.x: The Communist-led National Liberation Army of Josip Broz Tito, which fought the Germans, Italians, Ustaše, and royalist Chetniks across the mountains of Bosnia and Montenegro from 1941; backed by the allies from late 1943, it governed liberated territory through the AVNOJ council and entered Belgrade with the Red Army in October 1944.
Yugoslav Partisans.gov: Communist-led liberation movement under the AVNOJ council
Yugoslav Partisans.faith: Communist movement among Orthodox, Catholic, and Muslim peoples

(French Fourth Republic).x: The French Republic of 1946 to 1958 with its overseas territories, reorganized as the French Union: the departments of Algeria, the federations of West and Equatorial Africa, Madagascar, and the Associated States of Indochina, lost in 1954, while Morocco and Tunisia became independent in 1956.
(French Fourth Republic).gov: Parliamentary republic with the French Union overseas
(French Fourth Republic).faith: Roman Catholicism (secular state); Islam in North and West Africa
rulers: Charles de Gaulle (head of the provisional government)
Félix Gouin (head of the provisional government)
Georges Bidault (head of the provisional government)
Léon Blum (head of the provisional government)

French Fourth Republic.x: The French republic of the constitution of 1946, which rebuilt the country with the Monnet Plan and helped found the European Communities, but with weak coalitions and a new cabinet almost every six months lost Indochina, sank into the war in Algeria, and fell when the army rose in Algiers in May 1958.
French Fourth Republic.gov: Parliamentary republic under the constitution of 1946
rulers: Charles de Gaulle (head of the provisional government)
Félix Gouin (head of the provisional government)
Georges Bidault (head of the provisional government)
Léon Blum (head of the provisional government)

Republic of Poland.x: Poland moved west by the victors of 1945, losing its eastern lands to the Soviet Union and gaining German Silesia and Pomerania; under Communist rule as a people's republic until 1989, it was then the first Soviet satellite to win free government, and joined NATO in 1999 and the European Union in 2004.
Republic of Poland.gov: Communist-led people's democracy to 1952; parliamentary republic from 1989
rulers: Bolesław Bierut (chairman of the State National Council, then president)

Allied-occupied Germany.x: Germany after its unconditional surrender, divided into American, British, French, and Soviet zones under an Allied Control Council in Berlin, itself split into four sectors; the Council broke down in March 1948, and in 1949 the western zones became the Federal Republic and the Soviet zone the German Democratic Republic.
Allied-occupied Germany.gov: Four-power military occupation under the Allied Control Council

Hungary.x: Hungary after its conquest and occupation by the Red Army in 1945: a short-lived coalition republic swallowed by Rákosi's Communists by 1949, then from 1956 Kádár's goulash communism, and from 1989 a parliamentary republic that joined NATO in 1999 and the European Union in 2004, governed since 2010 by Viktor Orbán.
Hungary.gov: Republic; communist people's republic 1949 to 1989; parliamentary republic from 1989

Second Republic of Austria.x: The Austrian republic restored in April 1945 under Karl Renner, occupied in four zones until the State Treaty of 1955 and permanently neutral thereafter; long governed by grand coalitions of Socialists and the People's Party, it prospered as a bridge between the blocs and joined the European Union in 1995.

Kingdom of Bulgaria.x: Bulgaria in the last years of its monarchy, after the Fatherland Front coup of September 1944: the boy Tsar Simeon II reigned under a regency while Communist People's Courts executed the old political class, and a referendum in September 1946 abolished the crown.
Kingdom of Bulgaria.gov: Monarchy under a Communist-dominated Fatherland Front government

Republic of Italy.x: The Italian republic chosen by referendum on 2 June 1946 over the House of Savoy; governed for half a century by the Christian Democrats, it was a founder of NATO and the European Communities, enjoyed an economic miracle, survived the terrorism of the 1970s, and after the corruption scandals of the 1990s remade its party system.
Republic of Italy.faith: Roman Catholicism (religion of the state until 1984)
rulers: Enrico De Nicola (provisional head of state, then president)

Federal People's Republic of Yugoslavia.x: Tito's Yugoslavia under its first constitution of 1946, a federation of six republics on the Soviet model; expelled from the Cominform in 1948, it devised workers' self-management, accepted Western aid, and with Nehru and Nasser led the Non-Aligned Movement, whose first conference met at Belgrade in 1961.
Federal People's Republic of Yugoslavia.faith: Serbian Orthodox, Roman Catholic, and Muslim, under a communist state

Republic of Iceland.x: The republic proclaimed at Þingvellir on 17 June 1944, ending the union with Denmark; a NATO founder without an army, it fought three Cod Wars with Britain over its fishing limits, chose in Vigdís Finnbogadóttir the first woman elected a head of state by popular vote, and weathered the collapse of its banks in 2008.

People's Republic of Bulgaria.x: The Communist people's republic proclaimed in September 1946 under Georgi Dimitrov, the most loyal of the Soviet satellites; Todor Zhivkov led it for thirty-five years from 1954, and from 1984 tried to force its Turkish minority to take Slavic names, driving some 300,000 to flee in 1989. He was deposed that November.
People's Republic of Bulgaria.faith: Bulgarian Orthodox Christianity, under state atheism
rulers: Valko Chervenkov (party leader and prime minister)
Todor Zhivkov (party leader, then head of state)
Petar Mladenov (party leader and head of state)

Soviet-occupied Korea.x: Korea north of the 38th parallel, occupied by the Soviet 25th Army in August 1945; Moscow installed Kim Il Sung, who led the Provisional People's Committee from February 1946 and became premier of the Democratic People's Republic proclaimed in September 1948.
Soviet-occupied Korea.gov: Soviet military occupation with a Korean Communist administration
Soviet-occupied Korea.faith: Confucian tradition, Buddhism, and Christianity, under Communist hostility
rulers: Kim Il Sung (chairman of the People's Committee)

People's Republic of Albania.x: Enver Hoxha's Albania, the most closed state in Europe: it broke with Tito in 1948 and with Khrushchev in 1961, binding itself to Mao's China, and in 1967 closed every church and mosque, proclaiming itself the first atheist state in the world, while concrete bunkers studded its hills.
People's Republic of Albania.faith: State atheism from 1967; Islam, Orthodoxy, and Catholicism suppressed

People's Republic of Romania.x: The Communist people's republic proclaimed on 30 December 1947 when King Michael was forced to abdicate; under Gheorghe Gheorghiu-Dej it collectivized the land, filled the prisons of Pitești and Sighet and the labor camps of the Danube canal, and after Soviet troops left in 1958 edged toward independence from Moscow.
People's Republic of Romania.faith: Romanian Orthodox Christianity under state pressure; the Greek Catholic Church suppressed in 1948
rulers: Ion Gheorghe Maurer (head of state, then prime minister)

German Democratic Republic.x: The German state founded in the Soviet zone on 7 October 1949 and ruled by the Socialist Unity Party; it crushed the rising of June 1953, walled in its people in 1961, and kept them watched by the Stasi, until mass flight and demonstrations broke it in 1989 and it joined the Federal Republic on 3 October 1990.
rulers: Willi Stoph (prime minister, then head of state)
Erich Honecker (party leader and head of state)

Republic of Ireland.x: The Irish state as a republic from Easter Monday 1949, outside the Commonwealth; long a land of emigration, it joined the European Communities in 1973, grew rich as the Celtic Tiger in the 1990s, and helped make the Good Friday Agreement of 1998.

Federal Republic of Germany.x: West Germany, founded in 1949 from the American, British, and French zones with its capital at Bonn; under Adenauer it was bound into NATO and the European Communities and rebuilt by the economic miracle, and on 3 October 1990 it absorbed the German Democratic Republic to become united Germany, governed from Berlin.

Netherlands New Guinea.x: Western New Guinea, kept by the Netherlands when it gave up the Indies in 1949 and governed from Hollandia as a separate colony being prepared for Papuan self-rule; under American pressure it was handed to a United Nations authority in October 1962 and to Indonesia in May 1963.
Netherlands New Guinea.faith: Papuan traditional religions, with Protestant and Catholic missions

Hungarian People's Republic.x: Communist Hungary under the constitution of August 1949: Rákosi's terror and show trials, the revolution of October 1956 crushed by Soviet tanks, then three decades of János Kádár's goulash communism; in 1989 the party negotiated away its monopoly, and the republic was proclaimed on 23 October.
Hungarian People's Republic.faith: Roman Catholicism and Reformed Protestantism, under state control

Polish People's Republic.x: Communist Poland under the constitution of 1952: Bierut's Stalinist years, Gomułka's Polish October of 1956, Gierek's borrowed prosperity, and the rise of Solidarity in 1980, crushed by Jaruzelski's martial law in December 1981; the Round Table talks of 1989 ended the party's monopoly.
Polish People's Republic.gov: Communist one-party state (Polish United Workers' Party)
rulers: Aleksander Zawadzki (chairman of the Council of State)
Edward Ochab (chairman of the Council of State)
Marian Spychalski (chairman of the Council of State)
Józef Cyrankiewicz (chairman of the Council of State)
Henryk Jabłoński (chairman of the Council of State)
Wojciech Jaruzelski (prime minister, first secretary, then head of state)
Mieczysław Rakowski (prime minister, then first secretary)

French Fifth Republic.x: The French republic of de Gaulle's constitution of 1958, with a president elected by the people from 1962; it ended the Algerian War, granted independence to the African colonies of the French Community in 1960, built a nuclear deterrent, and with Germany led the building of the European Union, keeping overseas departments from the Caribbean to the Indian Ocean.
French Fifth Republic.faith: Secular state; Roman Catholic majority, large Muslim minority

Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.x: Tito's Yugoslavia under the constitution of 1963 and the decentralizing constitution of 1974, which gave the republics and the provinces of Kosovo and Vojvodina near-sovereign powers; after Tito's death in 1980 its collective presidency could not master debt and nationalism, and the federation broke apart in war in 1991.
Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.gov: Communist federal republic; collective presidency after 1980
Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.faith: Serbian Orthodox, Roman Catholic, and Muslim, under a communist state

Socialist Republic of Romania.x: Romania under Nicolae Ceaușescu, who renamed the state in 1965, won Western favor by condemning the invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968, and then built a personal tyranny with his wife Elena, starving the country to pay off its foreign debt and razing old Bucharest for his palace; it ended with their execution in December 1989.
Socialist Republic of Romania.gov: Communist one-party state under personal rule
Socialist Republic of Romania.faith: Romanian Orthodox Christianity, under state control

Greek junta.x: The military dictatorship of the colonels who seized power on 21 April 1967 under Georgios Papadopoulos; King Constantine II failed in a counter-coup and fled in December 1967, the monarchy was abolished in 1973, and after Ioannidis's coup in Cyprus brought a Turkish invasion, the regime collapsed in July 1974.
rulers: Georgios Papadopoulos (prime minister, regent, then president)

Third Hellenic Republic.x: The Greek democracy restored by Konstantinos Karamanlis in July 1974 and made a republic by the referendum of December that year; it joined the European Community in 1981, alternated between Karamanlis's New Democracy and Andreas Papandreou's PASOK, and endured a debt crisis from 2010 that cost a quarter of its output.

People's Socialist Republic of Albania.x: Albania under its constitution of 1976 in the last years of Enver Hoxha, who broke with China in 1978 and forbade foreign loans; under his successor Ramiz Alia the regime gave way before student protests and mass flight by sea, and multi-party elections were held in 1991.
People's Socialist Republic of Albania.faith: State atheism; Islam, Orthodoxy, and Catholicism suppressed
rulers: Ramiz Alia (head of state, then party leader)

Romania.x: Romania after the revolution of 1989: governed at first by Ion Iliescu's National Salvation Front, which brought miners to Bucharest to beat protesters in 1990, it slowly became a parliamentary democracy and joined NATO in 2004 and the European Union in 2007.

Republic of Bulgaria.x: Bulgaria after the fall of Zhivkov, a parliamentary republic under the constitution of 1991; it suffered hyperinflation in 1996 and 1997, elected its former boy-tsar Simeon Saxe-Coburg-Gotha prime minister in 2001, and joined NATO in 2004 and the European Union in 2007.
Republic of Bulgaria.faith: Bulgarian Orthodox Christianity, with a Muslim minority

Republic of Albania.x: Albania as a pluralist republic from 1991: the collapse of fraudulent pyramid schemes threw it into anarchy in 1997, but it recovered under the long rivalry of Sali Berisha and Edi Rama, joined NATO in 2009, and became a candidate for the European Union.
Republic of Albania.faith: Islam, with Orthodox and Roman Catholic minorities

(Russian Federation).x: The Russian Federation together with the lands it holds beyond its recognized borders: the Crimea and the occupied provinces of Ukraine, and garrisons in Georgia's South Ossetia and Abkhazia and in Moldova's Transnistria. Its land spans eleven time zones from the Baltic to the Pacific.
(Russian Federation).faith: Russian Orthodox Christianity, with Muslim, Buddhist, and Jewish minorities

Russian Federation.x: The largest successor of the Soviet Union, independent from December 1991: a federal republic that passed through the shock reforms, the first Chechen war, and the default of Yeltsin's decade into the long rule of Vladimir Putin, who restored central power, crushed Chechnya in a second war, seized the Crimea in 2014, and invaded Ukraine in 2022.
Russian Federation.faith: Russian Orthodox Christianity, with Muslim, Buddhist, and Jewish minorities

Ukraine.x: The second republic of the Soviet Union, independent since August 1991; it gave up its nuclear arsenal in 1994, turned toward Europe in the Orange Revolution of 2004 and the Revolution of Dignity of 2014, lost the Crimea and part of the Donbas to Russia, and since February 2022 has fought a full-scale Russian invasion.
Ukraine.faith: Eastern Orthodox Christianity, with Greek Catholic and other minorities

Republic of Belarus.x: The former Soviet republic, independent from 1991, which since 1994 has been ruled by Alexander Lukashenko, who kept the collective farms, the KGB, and Soviet symbols, bound his country ever closer to Russia, crushed the protests of 2020, and let Russian armies attack Ukraine from Belarusian soil in February 2022.
Republic of Belarus.faith: Orthodox Christianity, with a Roman Catholic minority
rulers: Stanislav Shushkevich (chairman of the Supreme Soviet)

Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.x: The rump federation of Serbia and Montenegro proclaimed in April 1992 as Yugoslavia broke apart; under Slobodan Milošević it armed the Serbs of Croatia and Bosnia, bore United Nations sanctions and hyperinflation, and was bombed by NATO over Kosovo in 1999, until Milošević fell in October 2000.

Czech Republic.x: The Czech state that emerged from the peaceful division of Czechoslovakia on 1 January 1993, with Václav Havel as its first president; prosperous and stable, it joined NATO in 1999 and the European Union in 2004.
Czech Republic.faith: Largely irreligious, with a Roman Catholic minority

Republic of Croatia.x: The republic that declared independence from Yugoslavia on 25 June 1991 under Franjo Tuđman and won its Homeland War against the Yugoslav army and the Krajina Serbs, retaking the Krajina in Operation Storm in 1995; it joined NATO in 2009 and the European Union in 2013.

Bosnia and Herzegovina.x: The republic of Bosniaks, Serbs, and Croats that declared independence in March 1992 and was torn by three and a half years of war, with the siege of Sarajevo and the massacre at Srebrenica; the Dayton agreement of 1995 divided it into a Bosniak-Croat Federation and a Serb Republic under an international High Representative.
Bosnia and Herzegovina.gov: Federal state of two entities with a three-member presidency and an international High Representative
Bosnia and Herzegovina.faith: Islam, Serbian Orthodoxy, and Roman Catholicism

Slovakia.x: The Slovak state independent since 1 January 1993; under Vladimír Mečiar's governments it lagged in the 1990s, then reformed, joined NATO and the European Union in 2004, and adopted the euro in 2009. Its prime minister Robert Fico survived an assassin's bullets in May 2024.

Republic of Estonia.x: Estonia restored to independence in August 1991 on the legal basis of the republic of 1918; under Mart Laar's reforms it built one of the freest economies and most digital governments in Europe, joined NATO and the European Union in 2004, and adopted the euro in 2011.
Republic of Estonia.faith: Lutheran Christianity, largely secular, with an Orthodox minority
rulers: Arnold Rüütel (chairman of the Supreme Council)

Republic of Moldova.x: The former Soviet Moldavian republic, mostly Romanian-speaking, independent from August 1991; a short war in 1992 left the Transnistria strip beyond the Dniester under a Russian-backed separatist regime guarded by Russian troops, and Moldova, among the poorest countries of Europe, became a candidate for the European Union in 2022.

Former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia.x: The former Yugoslav republic of Macedonia, independent from September 1991, admitted to the United Nations under this provisional name because Greece objected to the name Macedonia; it escaped the Yugoslav wars, survived an Albanian insurgency in 2001, and settled the dispute with Greece by the Prespa Agreement of 2018.
Former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia.faith: Macedonian Orthodox Christianity; Islam among the Albanians

(Commonwealth of Nations).x: The free association of states that grew out of the British Empire, given its modern form by the London Declaration of 1949, under which republics could belong with the Crown as symbol of their association; it counted fifty-six members by 2024, most of them former British possessions.
(Commonwealth of Nations).gov: Voluntary association of sovereign states under the Head of the Commonwealth
(Commonwealth of Nations).faith: Many faiths: Christianity, Hinduism, Islam, and others

Serbia-Montenegro.x: The loose State Union of Serbia and Montenegro, which replaced the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in February 2003, a month before the Serbian prime minister Zoran Đinđić was shot dead in Belgrade; Montenegro voted for independence on 21 May 2006, and the union dissolved that June.
Serbia-Montenegro.gov: Loose state union of two republics

Republic of Serbia.x: Serbia as a sovereign state from June 2006 after Montenegro's departure; it rejected Kosovo's declaration of independence of February 2008, opened talks to join the European Union in 2014, and under Aleksandar Vučić balanced between Brussels, Moscow, and Beijing.

Russian-occupied Ukraine.x: The Ukrainian lands held by Russia: the Crimea annexed in March 2014, the self-styled people's republics of Donetsk and Luhansk set up by Russian-backed forces that spring, and the territory seized in the invasion of 2022, four provinces of which Moscow declared annexed in September 2022 in violation of international law.
Russian-occupied Ukraine.gov: Military occupation and annexation by the Russian Federation, through installed administrations
rulers: Sergei Aksyonov (Russian-installed head of the Crimea)
Igor Plotnitsky (head of the Luhansk People's Republic)
Alexander Zakharchenko (head of the Donetsk People's Republic)
Leonid Pasechnik (head of the Luhansk People's Republic)
Denis Pushilin (head of the Donetsk People's Republic)

North Macedonia.x: The Republic of North Macedonia, so named from February 2019 under the Prespa Agreement with Greece, which opened its way into NATO in March 2020; Bulgarian objections over history and language delayed its talks to join the European Union.
North Macedonia.faith: Macedonian Orthodox Christianity; Islam among the Albanians

Rashidun Caliphate.x: The first caliphate, ruled from Medina and then Kufa by four companions of Muhammad. In under thirty years its Arab armies overthrew Sasanian Persia and tore Syria, Egypt, and Libya from Rome, before civil war over the succession split Islam into Sunni and Shi'a.

Balasagan.x: A lowland district by the Caspian between the lower Kura and the Araxes, on the marches of Caucasian Albania and Persian Azerbaijan. It passed from Sasanian to Arab rule in the 640s and was soon absorbed into the caliphate's northern provinces.
Balasagan.gov: Local principality under Sasanian, then Arab, suzerainty

Principality of Armenia.x: Armenia under the presiding princes who governed it for the emperors and then for the caliphs after the Arab invasions of the 640s. Its nakharar nobility kept the Armenian Church and tongue alive through two centuries of tribute, revolt, and reprisal, until the Bagratids restored the crown in 885.
Principality of Armenia.gov: Principality under Byzantine and Arab suzerainty

Principality of Iberia.x: The presiding princes of Kartli in eastern Georgia, who governed the land after the Sasanian kings abolished its crown in 580. Caught between Byzantium, Persia, and then the Arabs, who planted an emirate at Tbilisi, the princes of the Guaramid and Chosroid houses kept Christian Iberia alive.
Principality of Iberia.gov: Principality under Byzantine, Persian, and Arab suzerainty

Kingdom of Lazica.x: The ancient Colchis on the eastern shore of the Black Sea, home of the Laz, a Christian client of Byzantium fought over by Rome and Persia in the sixth century. In the seventh and eighth centuries it was governed by patricians under imperial suzerainty, until its lands were absorbed into the rising Kingdom of Abkhazia.

Dabuyid Dynasty.x: A Zoroastrian dynasty of Persian princes who ruled Tabaristan, the forested Caspian shore below the Elburz, as ispahbads for over a century after the fall of the Sasanians. Shielded by its mountains, it paid tribute to the caliphs and struck coins in the Sasanian style, until the Abbasids conquered it in 760.

Umayyad Caliphate.x: The first hereditary caliphate, ruled by the Meccan clan of Umayya from Damascus. Its armies carried Islam from the Atlantic and Spain to the Indus and Transoxiana, its caliphs built the Dome of the Rock and made Arabic the tongue of empire, and it fell to the Abbasid revolution in 750.
rulers: Abdallah ibn al-Zubayr (rival caliph at Mecca)

Turks.x: The Western Turks, the On Oq or Ten Arrows, whose khaganate ruled the steppe from the Altai to the Oxus until Tang China broke it in 657. For a generation their tribes lived under khagans appointed by the Chinese, broken by risings, until the Türgesh rose among them and the Arabs pressed in from the south.

Volga Bulgaria.x: The state of the Bulgars on the middle Volga and Kama, whose king Almış embraced Islam in 922, making it the northernmost land of Islam. Rich from the fur trade between the Russian forests and the caliphate, it endured as a rival of the Rus until the Mongols destroyed its cities in 1236.

Türgesh.x: A Turkic confederation of the Ten Arrows that rose in the Seven Rivers country about 699 and became the chief foe of the Arabs in Transoxiana. Under its khagan Suluk, whom the Arabs called Abu Muzahim, the Butting One, it fought the Umayyad armies for twenty years, until his murder in 738 broke it apart.

Abbasid Caliphate.x: The caliphate of the house of al-Abbas, the Prophet's uncle, which overthrew the Umayyads in 750 and ruled from its new capital of Baghdad. Under Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma'mun it was the center of the world's learning; from 945 its caliphs were wards of Buyid and Seljuk lords, until the Mongols sacked Baghdad in 1258.

Kimek-Kipchak confederation.x: The Turkic nomads of the steppe north of the Aral Sea and the Caspian: first the Kimek confederation of the Irtysh, then its Kipchak tribes, who spread west to the Danube as the Cumans. Divided among many khans whose names are scarcely recorded and never a single state, they were conquered by the Mongols in the 1220s and 1230s.

Oghuz Turks.x: The Oghuz Turks of the steppe between the Aral Sea, the Syr Darya, and the Caspian, led by a yabgu from their winter town of Yangikent. From their clans came the Seljuks, who broke away in the late tenth century, and the Turkmen who later conquered Persia and Anatolia.

Fihrids.x: The rule of Abd al-Rahman ibn Habib al-Fihri, great-grandson of the conqueror Uqba ibn Nafi, who seized Ifriqiya in 745 as the Umayyad caliphate collapsed. He ruled Kairouan as an independent emir until his brothers murdered him in 755; his son Habib held on until the Kharijite Berbers overran the province.

Kharijites.x: The Kharijite Berber regimes that seized Ifriqiya after the fall of the Fihrids: first the Sufri Warfajuma, who took Kairouan in 757 and stabled their horses in its mosque, then the Ibadi imam Abu'l-Khattab al-Ma'afiri, who drove them out and ruled from Tripoli to Kairouan until an Abbasid army slew him in 761.

Rustamid dynasty.x: An Ibadi imamate founded by Abd al-Rahman ibn Rustam, of Persian descent, at Tahert in the hills of western Algeria. Its imams ruled a tolerant merchant city on the Saharan trade routes for over a century, until the Fatimid missionary Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i destroyed it in 909; its people fled to the oases of the desert.

Kingdom of Abkhazia.x: A Christian kingdom on the eastern Black Sea shore, which threw off Byzantine overlordship under Leon II in the late eighth century, absorbed Lazica, and ruled western Georgia from Kutaisi. Its heir Bagrat III, a Bagratid of Tao, united it with Kartli in 1008 to form the Kingdom of Georgia.

Idrisids.x: The first Muslim dynasty of Morocco, founded by Idris I, a descendant of the Prophet through Hasan who fled the Abbasids to the Berbers of Volubilis. His son Idris II made Fez its capital. Divided among brothers and squeezed between the Fatimids and the Umayyads of Córdoba, it dwindled to the Rif before its end in 985.

Barghawata Confederation.x: A confederation of Masmuda Berbers on the Atlantic plains of Morocco, whose king Salih ibn Tarif proclaimed himself a prophet in the eighth century and gave his people a Quran in Berber with laws of their own. They held out for three centuries against Idrisids, Umayyads, and Fatimids, and slew the Almoravid founder Abdallah ibn Yasin in 1059, before the Almoravids destroyed them.
Barghawata Confederation.faith: Barghawata religion, a heterodox Berber faith

Aghlabid Dynasty.x: An Arab dynasty of emirs who governed Ifriqiya from Kairouan for the Abbasids, in practice independently, from 800 to 909. They rebuilt the Great Mosque of Kairouan, ringed the coast with ribats, and from 827 conquered Sicily from Byzantium, until the Fatimid missionary's Kutama Berbers overthrew them.
Aghlabid Dynasty.gov: Hereditary emirate under nominal Abbasid suzerainty

Kingdom of the Iberians.x: The realm of the Bagratid princes of Tao-Klarjeti in the upper valleys of the Chorokhi and Kura, who bore the Byzantine title of curopalates and from 888 styled themselves kings of the Iberians. Their monasteries were the cradle of Georgian letters, and their heir Bagrat III united the Georgian lands in 1008.

Shirvan.x: The land of the Shirvanshahs on the western shore of the Caspian, between the Kura and the Caucasus. Ruled from the ninth century by Arab and then Persianized dynasties from Shamakhi and later Baku, it outlived Seljuks, Mongols, and Timur as a vassal state, until Shah Ismail killed its ruler in 1500 and Tahmasp annexed it in 1538.

Zaydi Alid dynasties.x: The Zaydi Shi'ite imams of the line of Hasan who ruled Tabaristan and Daylam on the Caspian shore from 864, converting the mountain Daylamites to Islam. Their converts later filled the armies of the Buyids and Ziyarids. Driven out by the Samanids and more than once restored, their power faded in the 920s.

Tulunids.x: The first independent dynasty of Muslim Egypt, founded by Ahmad ibn Tulun, a Turkish officer sent from Samarra as governor in 868. He built a new capital, al-Qata'i, raised a slave army, and seized Syria; his son Khumarawayh squandered the treasury, and an Abbasid army restored direct rule in 905.
Tulunids.gov: Hereditary emirate under nominal Abbasid suzerainty

Samanid Empire.x: A Persian dynasty descended from a Zoroastrian landowner of Balkh, which ruled Transoxiana and Khorasan from Bukhara as Abbasid governors in name and sovereigns in fact. Under it Persian rose again as a language of letters, with the poets Rudaki and Daqiqi and the young Avicenna; Turkish generals and Karakhanid invaders brought it down in 999.
Samanid Empire.gov: Hereditary emirate under nominal Abbasid suzerainty

Bagratid Armenia.x: The restored kingdom of Armenia under the Bagratid house, recognized by caliph and emperor alike in the 880s. From Ani, its capital from 961 and the city of a thousand and one churches, its kings ruled a land of trade and building, until Byzantium annexed it in 1045 on the eve of the Seljuk conquest.

Sajid Dynasty.x: A dynasty of Abbasid governors from Ushrusana in Central Asia who ruled Azerbaijan and Armenia in the late ninth and early tenth centuries, nominally for the caliph. Yusuf ibn Abi'l-Saj put King Smbat I of Armenia to death and fell fighting the Qarmatians in 928, and the line soon gave way to Daylamite adventurers.

Qarmatians.x: An Isma'ili sect that founded a state in Bahrain, the eastern coast of Arabia, under Abu Sa'id al-Jannabi about 899. Ruled by a council at al-Ahsa, its raiders terrorized Iraq and the pilgrim roads, sacked Mecca and carried off the Black Stone in 930, and fought the Fatimids for Syria, before the Uyunids overthrew them in the 1070s.
Qarmatians.gov: Republic under a council of elders and the Jannabi family

Fatimid Caliphate.x: The Isma'ili Shi'ite caliphate founded in Ifriqiya in 909 by Ubayd Allah al-Mahdi, descended by its own reckoning from Fatima, which ruled from Cairo, its own foundation, from 973. At its height it held Egypt, Syria, the Hijaz, and Sicily and rivaled Baghdad; worn by famine, schism, and the Crusades, it was ended by Saladin in 1171.

Kingdom of Vaspurakan.x: The Armenian kingdom of the Artsruni house about Lake Van, whose prince Gagik was crowned king in 908. His palace church of the Holy Cross on the island of Aghtamar is a jewel of Armenian art. Pressed by the Turks, King Senekerim ceded his realm to Basil II in 1021 in exchange for lands in Cappadocia.

Buyid Dynasty.x: A Shi'ite dynasty of Daylamite soldiers, the three sons of the fisherman Buya, who conquered western Persia and in 945 Baghdad itself, keeping the Abbasid caliphs as pensioners. Divided among branches at Shiraz, Rayy, and Baghdad, it reached its height under Adud al-Dawla and fell to Mahmud of Ghazni and the Seljuks.

Caliphate of Córdoba.x: The Umayyad caliphate of al-Andalus, proclaimed by Abd al-Rahman III in 929 against the Fatimids. Córdoba was the greatest city of the West, and the armies of the chamberlain Almanzor raided the Christian kingdoms almost yearly. After his son's death in 1008 it dissolved in civil war and was abolished in 1031, leaving the taifa kingdoms.

Hamdanid Emirates.x: An Arab dynasty of the Taghlib tribe that ruled Mosul and the Jazira and, under the famous Sayf al-Dawla, Aleppo and northern Syria in the tenth century. Sayf al-Dawla's court sheltered the poet al-Mutanabbi and the philosopher al-Farabi, and his raids into Byzantine Anatolia were sung in verse, though Nikephoros Phokas sacked Aleppo in 962.

Ziyarid dynasty.x: A dynasty founded by Mardavij ibn Ziyar, a Gilite soldier of fortune who dreamed of restoring the Persian empire and conquered western Persia before his Turkish slaves murdered him in 935. His heirs held Gorgan and Tabaristan; Qabus was a famed stylist, and his grandson Kay Kavus wrote the Qabus-nama, a mirror for princes.

Abbasid Caliphate/Buyid Dynasty.x: The Abbasid caliphs of Baghdad in the age of Buyid mastery, when the successor of the Prophet kept his title, his palace, and his name in the Friday prayer, while the Daylamite amir ruled Iraq, collected its revenues, and commanded its armies.

Seljuk Dynasty.x: The Oghuz clan of Seljuk, who led their Turkmen herdsmen from the lower Syr Darya into Transoxiana and Khorasan in the early eleventh century, serving and fighting the Karakhanids and Ghaznavids by turns. Under the brothers Tughril and Chaghri they took Merv and Nishapur and in 1040 broke the Ghaznavids at Dandanaqan.

Kingdom of Georgia.x: The united Christian kingdom of the Georgians under the Bagratid house, formed when Bagrat III joined Abkhazia and Kartli in 1008. David the Builder and Queen Tamar made it the strongest power of the Caucasus in the twelfth century; Mongol and Timurid invasions broke it, and in the late fifteenth century it split into Kartli, Kakheti, and Imereti.

Taifa of Almería.x: A Muslim kingdom on the coast of southeastern Spain, founded in 1013 by Khayran, a Slav freedman of the Córdoban court. Under the Banu Sumadih it was a rich port of silk weavers and a court of poets, until the Almoravids took it in 1091; Castile and Genoa held Almería from 1147 to 1157, and it later passed to Granada.

Taifa of Granada.x: The Berber kingdom of the Zirids of Granada, founded in 1013 by Zawi ibn Ziri. Its Jewish vizier Samuel ha-Nagid led its armies and wrote Hebrew poetry, and the murder of his son Joseph in 1066 brought a massacre of the Jews. Its last king, Abd Allah, deposed by the Almoravids in 1090, wrote a memoir of his reign in exile.

Hammadid Dynasty.x: A Sanhaja Berber dynasty, a branch of the Zirids, founded by Hammad ibn Buluggin in central Algeria in 1015. Its first capital, the Qal'a of the Banu Hammad, is famed for its minaret and palaces; pressed by the Banu Hilal it moved to the port of Bougie, a center of trade and learning, until the Almohads conquered it in 1152.

Taifa of Seville.x: The most powerful of the taifa kingdoms of al-Andalus, ruled by the Arab house of the Abbadids, who swallowed their neighbors from the Algarve to Murcia. Its last king, the poet al-Mu'tamid, called in the Almoravids against Castile in 1086 and was deposed by them in 1091, dying a captive at Aghmat.

Great Seljuk Empire.x: The empire of the Seljuk Turks, who conquered Persia, entered Baghdad as champions of the Sunni caliph in 1055, and under Alp Arslan broke Byzantium at Manzikert. Governed by Persian viziers such as Nizam al-Mulk, it reached from the Oxus to the Aegean; after Malik Shah it split among princes and atabegs, and its last sultan fell in 1194.
Great Seljuk Empire.gov: Sultanate under the nominal authority of the Abbasid caliph

Western Karakhanid Khanate.x: The western half of the Turkish Karakhanid realm, which split from the eastern khanate about 1040 and ruled Transoxiana from Samarkand and Bukhara. Its khans raised mosques and minarets, among them the Kalyan minaret of Bukhara, and were vassals in turn of the Seljuks and the Kara-Khitai, until the Khwarazm-shah ended them in 1212.

Almoravid Dynasty.x: A movement of veiled Sanhaja Berbers of the Sahara, fired by the preacher Abdallah ibn Yasin, that conquered Morocco, founded Marrakesh, and under Yusuf ibn Tashfin crossed to Spain, beat Castile at Sagrajas, and absorbed the taifa kingdoms. Strictly Maliki, it fell to the Almohads in 1147, though its Banu Ghaniya kin held the Balearics until 1203.
Almoravid Dynasty.gov: Emirate (Amir al-Muslimin) under nominal Abbasid suzerainty

Zirid dynasty.x: A Sanhaja Berber dynasty that governed Ifriqiya for the Fatimids after they moved to Cairo and broke with them in the 1040s. In revenge the Fatimids loosed the Banu Hilal upon it; driven from Kairouan to the coast at Mahdia, the Zirids lost their last stronghold to Roger II of Sicily in 1148.

Uyunid Emirate.x: An Arab dynasty of the Abd al-Qays tribe that overthrew the Qarmatians of eastern Arabia with Seljuk help in the 1070s and ruled al-Ahsa, Qatif, and the Bahrain islands for nearly two centuries. The poet Ibn al-Muqarrab sang of its princes and their quarrels.

Khwarezmian Empire.x: The empire of the Anushteginid shahs of Khwarazm, descended from a Turkish slave in Seljuk service, who threw off Seljuk and Kara-Khitai overlordship and under Muhammad II ruled from the Syr Darya to the Zagros. The murder of Genghis Khan's merchants at Otrar in 1218 brought the Mongols, who destroyed it; Jalal al-Din fought on until 1231.

Sultanate of Rum.x: The Seljuk sultanate of Anatolia, founded by Suleiman ibn Qutulmish after Manzikert, with its capital first at Nicaea and, after the First Crusade, at Konya. Under Kayqubad I its caravanserais and mosques made it rich and splendid; after the Mongol victory at Köse Dağ in 1243 it sank into a Mongol protectorate and vanished in the early fourteenth century.

Danishmendids.x: A Turkmen dynasty founded by Danishmend Gazi, a warrior of the Manzikert generation, which ruled north-central Anatolia from Sivas, Niksar, and Malatya. Its emirs captured Bohemond of Antioch in 1100 and rivaled the Seljuks of Rum, who absorbed their lands between 1175 and 1178.

Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia.x: An Armenian state founded by refugees from the Seljuk conquest of Armenia in the Taurus mountains and the Cilician plain, ally of the Crusaders and later of the Mongols. Its prince Leo was crowned king in 1198, and its port of Ayas carried the trade of the East, until the Mamluks took Sis and King Leo V in 1375.

Kingdom of Jerusalem.x: The Latin kingdom founded by the First Crusade after the taking of Jerusalem in 1099, ruled by French and later Cypriot dynasties and defended by the military orders. Saladin's victory at Hattin in 1187 cost it the Holy City; restored as a coastal realm with its capital at Acre, it ended when the Mamluks stormed Acre in 1291.

County of Edessa.x: The first of the Crusader states, founded in 1098 when Baldwin of Boulogne left the main army, was adopted by the Armenian lord of Edessa, and took the city on his death. Straddling the Euphrates among Armenian and Syriac Christians, it fell to Zengi in 1144, and its western remnant was sold to Byzantium in 1150.
County of Edessa.faith: Latin Christianity, over Armenian and Syriac Christians

Zengid dynasty.x: A Turkish dynasty founded by Imad al-Din Zengi, atabeg of Mosul, who took Edessa from the Franks in 1144. His son Nur al-Din united Muslim Syria, preached the holy war, and sent Shirkuh and Saladin to Egypt; after his death Saladin took Syria, and Zengid princes lingered at Mosul until 1234 and in Sinjar and the Jazira.
rulers: Badr al-Din Lu'lu' (atabeg, then lord of Mosul)

Almohad Caliphate.x: A Berber reform movement founded by Ibn Tumart, who preached the strict unity of God among the Masmuda of the High Atlas and proclaimed himself the Mahdi. His successor Abd al-Mu'min took the title of caliph and conquered the Maghreb and al-Andalus; beaten at Las Navas in 1212, the Almohads lost Spain and fell to the Marinids in 1269.

Kingdom of Africa.x: The Norman dominion on the coast of Ifriqiya won by King Roger II of Sicily and his admiral George of Antioch, who took Tripoli in 1146 and Mahdia, Sousse, and Sfax in 1148. Ruled through Muslim governors, it was lost to the Almohad caliph Abd al-Mu'min, who took Mahdia in 1160.
Kingdom of Africa.gov: Dependency of the Norman Kingdom of Sicily
Kingdom of Africa.faith: Latin Christian rulers over Muslim subjects

Nabhani dynasty.x: A dynasty of Arab kings who ruled inner Oman from the twelfth century into the seventeenth, setting aside the elected Ibadi imamate and governing from Bahla. Its great mud-brick fortress at Bahla was among the mightiest of Arabia; the Ya'rubi imams overthrew the last Nabhanis in the 1620s.

Ayyubid Sultanate.x: The Kurdish dynasty of Saladin, son of Ayyub, who ended the Fatimid caliphate in 1171, united Egypt and Syria, and retook Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 1187. His heirs divided his empire into family principalities at Cairo, Damascus, Aleppo, and elsewhere, until the Mamluk guards of the last sultan seized Egypt in 1250.
Ayyubid Sultanate.gov: Sultanate and family confederation of principalities

Nicaean Empire.x: The Byzantine successor state founded in Bithynia by Theodore Laskaris after the Fourth Crusade took Constantinople in 1204. Under John III Vatatzes it became the strongest of the Greek states, winning back much of Thrace and Macedonia, and in 1261 Michael VIII Palaiologos recovered Constantinople.

Latin Empire.x: The empire set up in Constantinople by the knights of the Fourth Crusade and the Venetians after they stormed and sacked the city in 1204. Poor, quarrelsome, and hemmed in by Bulgarians and Greeks, it shrank to the city and its environs, until a Nicaean force entered it almost unopposed in 1261.

Empire of Trebizond.x: A Greek empire on the southern shore of the Black Sea founded in 1204 by Alexios and David Komnenos, grandsons of Emperor Andronikos I. Rich from the silk and spice trade of Tabriz, it survived Seljuks, Mongols, and Turkmen by tribute and marriage alliance, and was the last Byzantine state to fall to the Ottomans, in 1461.

Principality of Achaea.x: A Frankish principality in the Morea founded after the Fourth Crusade by William of Champlitte and Geoffrey of Villehardouin. Under the Villehardouins it was the most brilliant of the Latin states of Greece, and William II built the castle of Mistra; it passed to the Angevins of Naples and others, and the Byzantine despots of the Morea absorbed it about 1430.

Mamluk Dynasty.x: The first dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate, called the Slave Dynasty because its founder Qutb ud-Din Aibak and the great sultans Iltutmish and Balban were Turkish slave soldiers, Aibak himself a slave of the Ghurid sultan Muhammad of Ghor. It held northern India against the Mongols, raised the Qutb Minar, and was overthrown by the Khaljis in 1290.

Rasulid Dynasty.x: A dynasty founded by Nur al-Din Umar ibn Rasul, the Ayyubid deputy in Yemen, who made himself independent in 1229. From Ta'izz and Zabid the Rasulids ruled Yemen and the Red Sea trade through Aden for over two centuries, patrons of learning whose sultans wrote on farming, astronomy, and medicine.

Hafsid Dynasty.x: A Berber dynasty descended from Abu Hafs Umar, a companion of the Almohad Mahdi, which governed Ifriqiya for the Almohads and broke away in 1229. From Tunis its sultans took the caliph's title in 1253, withstood Louis IX's crusade, and traded with Italy and Aragon; in the sixteenth century they became pawns of Spain and the Ottomans, who ended them in 1574.

Zayyanid dynasty.x: A dynasty of the Zenata Berbers of the Banu Abd al-Wad, founded by Yaghmurasen ibn Zyan, which ruled western Algeria from Tlemcen from 1236. Twice conquered by the Marinids of Fez, Tlemcen flourished as a market of the Saharan gold trade, until the Ottomans of Algiers absorbed the kingdom in 1556.

Mamluk Sultanate.x: The state of the Mamluks, Turkish and later Circassian slave soldiers bought as boys and trained to arms, who seized Egypt in 1250. They turned back the Mongols at Ain Jalut, drove the last Crusaders from Syria, and ruled Egypt, Syria, and the Hijaz from Cairo with shadow Abbasid caliphs, until the Ottomans conquered them in 1517.
Mamluk Sultanate.gov: Military oligarchy under an elective sultan

Emirate of Granada.x: The last Muslim state of Spain, founded by Muhammad I ibn Nasr in 1238 and ruled by his Nasrid house from the Alhambra for two and a half centuries. A tributary of Castile, crowded with refugees, and famed for its silks and gardens, it was conquered by Ferdinand and Isabella, to whom Muhammad XII surrendered the city in January 1492.

Marinid Sultanate.x: A dynasty of Zenata Berber nomads, the Banu Marin, who rose as the Almohads declined, took Fez in 1248 and Marrakesh in 1269, and ruled Morocco from Fez, which they adorned with madrasas. Under Abu al-Hasan and Abu Inan they briefly held Tlemcen and Tunis; power ebbed to their Wattasid viziers, and the last sultan was killed in 1465.

Bahrani Dynasty.x: The Arab dynasties that ruled eastern Arabia and the Bahrain islands after the Uyunids: the Usfurids, then the Shi'ite Jarwanids, and from the fifteenth century the Jabrids of al-Ahsa, Bedouin lords who mastered the coast and the pearl islands until the Portuguese and the Ottomans came in the sixteenth century.

Golden Horde.x: The western realm of the Mongols, the ulus of Genghis Khan's eldest son Jochi, founded by Batu after the conquest of the Rus and the Kipchak steppe. From Sarai on the Volga its khans, Muslims from Özbeg's time, took tribute from the Rus princes for two centuries; Timur ruined it, and it broke into the khanates of Kazan, Crimea, and Astrakhan.

Ilkhanate.x: The Mongol khanate of Persia founded by Hulagu, grandson of Genghis Khan, who destroyed the Assassins and the Abbasid caliphate between 1256 and 1258. Its khans warred with the Mamluks and the Golden Horde; Ghazan made Islam its faith in 1295, and it left great works of history and building before dissolving after 1335.
Ilkhanate.gov: Khanate under the nominal suzerainty of the Great Khan
Ilkhanate.faith: Tengrism and Buddhism, then Islam from 1295

Ottoman Empire.x: The empire of the house of Osman, which rose from a frontier beylik in Bithynia about 1300, took Constantinople in 1453, and under Selim I and Suleiman ruled from Hungary to Mesopotamia and the Maghreb as master of the holy cities of Islam. Long in retreat before Austria and Russia and reformed in the nineteenth century, it perished in the Great War.
Ottoman Empire.gov: Absolute monarchy (sultanate and caliphate), constitutional from 1876 and 1908

Germiyanids.x: A Turkmen beylik that arose in western Anatolia about 1300 as the Seljuk sultanate decayed, ruling from Kütahya and taking tribute from Byzantine Philadelphia. Its beys married their daughters into the Ottoman house, and the last, Yakub II, bequeathed his lands to Murad II, who took them at his death in 1429.

Beylik of Karaman.x: The strongest and most stubborn of the Turkmen beyliks of Anatolia, founded by Karaman Bey in the Taurus about 1250 and ruling from Larende, Ermenek, and Konya. Heir to the Seljuks in its own eyes and the Ottomans' great rival, it allied with Venice and the Aq Qoyunlu, until Mehmed II and Bayezid II annexed it between 1468 and 1487.

Beylik of Isfendiyar.x: The beylik of the Candarid or Isfendiyarid house on the Black Sea coast of Paphlagonia, ruling from Kastamonu and the port of Sinop. Rich from copper mines and the sea trade, it rode out the Ottoman and Timurid storms by shifting allegiances, until Mehmed II took Sinop and annexed it in 1461.

Beylik of Hamid.x: A Turkmen beylik of the Lakes Region of southwestern Anatolia, founded about 1300 by Felekeddin Dündar Bey, who ruled from Eğirdir until the Mongol governor Timurtash put him to death in 1324. A branch held Antalya as the Beylik of Teke; the main line yielded most of its lands to Murad I in 1374.

Kastamonu.x: The beylik seated at Kastamonu in Paphlagonia, held after the Seljuk decline by the frontier lords of the Çobanoğulları and, from the early fourteenth century, by the Candarid house, which later took the name of Isfendiyar. Its hill country of forests and copper mines faced the Byzantine ports of the Black Sea.

Beylik of Karasi.x: A Turkmen beylik on the Aegean shore of Mysia, ruling from Balıkesir and Pergamon, whose seamen raided the Aegean and served in the Byzantine civil wars. Orhan annexed it in the 1340s amid a quarrel of its princes, and its warriors and mariners helped carry the Ottomans across the Dardanelles into Europe.

Beylik of Teke.x: A branch of the Hamidid house that ruled the Pamphylian coast from Antalya in the fourteenth century. King Peter I of Cyprus took Antalya in 1361 and held it for a dozen years; the Ottomans absorbed the beylik under Bayezid I and, after the Timurid interlude, for good in the 1420s.

Jalayirid Sultanate.x: A Mongol dynasty of the Jalayir tribe founded by Hasan Buzurg amid the breakup of the Ilkhanate, which ruled Iraq and Azerbaijan from Baghdad and Tabriz. Shaikh Uvais was a patron of painting and poetry; Sultan Ahmad was twice driven from Baghdad by Timur, and the Qara Qoyunlu took the last of their lands by 1432.

Sarbadars.x: Rebels of western Khorasan who rose against Mongol tax-collectors in 1337, crying that they would rather see their heads on the gallows, sar-be-dar, than submit. Allied with Shi'ite dervishes, they ruled Sabzevar under a succession of short-lived leaders, most of them murdered, until the last submitted to Timur in 1381.
Sarbadars.gov: Republic of military chiefs and dervishes

Muzaffarids.x: An Arab-descended dynasty that served the Ilkhans as governors of Yazd and rose after their fall to rule Kerman, Fars, and Isfahan from Shiraz. Its prince Shah Shuja was the patron of the poet Hafiz; the house was riven by blindings and parricide, and Timur put its princes to death in 1393.

Chobanids.x: The heirs of the emir Chupan, all-powerful commander of the Ilkhan Abu Sa'id, who after the Ilkhanate's collapse ruled Azerbaijan from Tabriz through puppet khans. The tyranny of Malek Ashraf drove the people of Tabriz to call in Jani Beg of the Golden Horde, who killed him in 1357.
Chobanids.gov: Military emirate ruling through puppet khans

Injuids.x: A dynasty of stewards of the Ilkhans' crown estates, the inju, who became masters of Fars after the Ilkhanate fell. Its last prince, Abu Ishaq, made Shiraz a court of poets where the young Hafiz sang, until the Muzaffarid Mubariz al-Din took the city in 1353 and put him to death in 1357.

Beylik of Dulkadir.x: A Turkmen beylik of the upper Ceyhan and Euphrates, ruling from Elbistan and Maraş as a buffer between Mamluks and Ottomans, both of whom married its princesses. Its last great bey, Alaüddevle Bozkurt, was slain by Selim I's army in 1515, and his lands passed to the Ottomans.

White Horde.x: The eastern wing of the Golden Horde, the ulus of Jochi's son Orda, in the steppe of the lower Syr Darya and the Kazakh lands. In the 1370s its khan Urus fought for the Horde's throne at Sarai; his rival Tokhtamysh, with Timur's backing, overcame his sons and in 1380 reunited the eastern and western Horde.

Timurid Empire.x: The empire of Timur, the lame Barlas emir who from Samarkand conquered Persia, Iraq, the Golden Horde, and Delhi with unexampled slaughter. His heirs Shah Rukh and Ulugh Beg ruled a smaller realm from Herat and Samarkand, a golden age of Persian painting, poetry, and astronomy, until the Uzbeks took Transoxiana and Herat between 1500 and 1507.

Qara Qoyunlu.x: The Turkmen confederation of the Black Sheep, which rose about Lake Van in the late fourteenth century and under Qara Yusuf and Jahan Shah ruled Azerbaijan, Iraq, and western Persia from Tabriz. Jahan Shah was killed by the Aq Qoyunlu leader Uzun Hasan in 1467, and the confederation fell apart.

Ramadanid Emirate.x: A Turkmen dynasty that held Adana from the 1350s as vassals of the Mamluks and inherited the Cilician plain from the fallen Armenian kingdom. After 1517 its beys served the Ottomans as hereditary governors of Adana, until the province was taken under direct rule in 1608.
Ramadanid Emirate.gov: Beylik under Mamluk, then Ottoman, suzerainty

Aq Qoyunlu.x: The Turkmen confederation of the White Sheep, which ruled Diyarbakır and then, after Uzun Hasan's defeat of the Qara Qoyunlu in 1467, Azerbaijan, Iraq, and Persia from Tabriz. Uzun Hasan treated with Venice against the Ottomans and lost at Otlukbeli; after Ya'qub's death in 1490 his heirs fought one another until Shah Ismail destroyed them.

Makuria Kingdom.x: The Christian kingdom of Nubia on the middle Nile, with its capital at Old Dongola, which halted the Arabs in 652 and for six centuries traded slaves for grain under the Baqt. Weakened by Mamluk interventions and Arab migration, it saw its throne hall made a mosque in 1317; a remnant kingdom, Dotawo, lingered in Lower Nubia into the fifteenth century.
Makuria Kingdom.faith: Coptic and Melkite Christianity, giving way to Islam

Uzbek Khanate.x: The nomad khanate of the Uzbeks, Jochid tribes of the steppe east of the Urals, united by Abu'l-Khayr Khan from 1428. He ruled from the Tobol to the Syr Darya and seized Urgench and Sighnaq, but was routed by the Oirats in 1457; after his death in 1468 his people scattered, until his grandson Muhammad Shaybani led them south into Transoxiana.

Nogai Horde.x: A horde of Turkic nomads, led by the descendants of the emir Edigu, which grazed the steppe between the Volga and the Ural river after the Golden Horde fell apart. Its biys, kingmakers rather than khans, sold horses to Moscow by the tens of thousands; it split in the 1550s, and its western part became the Lesser Nogai Horde.

Tahirid Sultanate.x: A dynasty of Yemeni sheikhs from the country about Rada'a that seized power from the last Rasulids in 1454 and ruled southern Yemen from Ta'izz, Zabid, and Aden. Its sultan Amir ibn Abd al-Wahhab built the Amiriya madrasa at Rada'a; he was killed in 1517 by the Mamluk expedition that opened Yemen to the Ottomans.

Kingdom of Kartli.x: The kingdom of eastern Georgia about Tbilisi, formed when the united Georgian realm broke apart in the late fifteenth century. Under Persian suzerainty for most of its history, its Bagratid kings often served the shahs as converts and governors, while Vakhtang VI gave Georgia its first printing press, until Heraclius II joined it to Kakheti in 1762.
Kingdom of Kartli.gov: Monarchy under Persian or Ottoman suzerainty

Kazakh Khanate.x: The khanate of the Kazakhs, Jochid nomads who broke away from the Uzbeks under Kerey and Janibek and spread over the steppe from the Caspian to the Altai. Divided into the Great, Middle, and Junior Hordes and ravaged by the Dzungars, its khans sought Russian protection from 1731; Russia abolished the khanships in the 1820s and crushed Kenesary's rising in 1847.

Wattasid dynasty.x: A Zenata Berber family that served the Marinids as viziers and regents and, after a sharifian interlude, ruled Morocco from Fez as sultans from 1472. Unable to stop the Portuguese seizing the Atlantic ports, they lost the south to the Saadi sharifs, who took Fez in 1549 and, after a brief Wattasid return, for good in 1554.

Samtskhe-Saatabago.x: The principality of the Jaqeli atabegs in Meskheti, southwestern Georgia, which broke away from the Georgian crown in the fifteenth century and ruled from Akhaltsikhe. Courted by Persians and Ottomans alike, its princes fell under Ottoman control in the late sixteenth century, and in the seventeenth it became an Ottoman province under rulers turned Muslim.

Kingdom of Kakheti.x: The kingdom of eastern Georgia beyond the Gombori range, in the vine-growing valley of the Alazani, independent from 1465. Its kings, notably Alexander II and Teimuraz I, struggled against the Persian shahs; Shah Abbas laid it waste in 1614 to 1616 and carried off tens of thousands of its people. Heraclius II united it with Kartli in 1762.

Tyumen Khanate.x: A Tatar khanate of western Siberia on the Tura and Tobol, ruled by Shaybanid khans from Chimgi-Tura, the later Tyumen. Its khan Ibak slew Ahmad, last great khan of the Golden Horde, in 1481; after Ibak was murdered in 1495, the Taibugid house moved the seat to Qashliq on the Irtysh, founding the Khanate of Sibir.

Khanate of Sibir.x: The Tatar khanate of western Siberia, ruled from Qashliq on the Irtysh by the Taibugid and then the Shaybanid houses, which took fur tribute from the forest peoples. Its khan Kuchum, a Shaybanid who seized it in 1563 and spread Islam among his people, lost his capital to Yermak's Cossacks in 1582 and was finally beaten in 1598.

Shaybanids.x: The Uzbek dynasty of Muhammad Shaybani, grandson of Abu'l-Khayr, who led the Uzbek tribes into Transoxiana, took Samarkand in 1500 and Herat in 1507, and drove out the Timurids, Babur among them. Shaybani was slain by Shah Ismail at Merv in 1510; his kin recovered Transoxiana and ruled it from Bukhara and Samarkand through the sixteenth century.

Safavid Dynasty.x: The Persian dynasty that grew from a Sufi order of Ardabil, crowned Ismail I at Tabriz in 1501, and made Twelver Shi'ism the faith of Iran. Under Abbas I it drove the Ottomans and Uzbeks from its lands and made Isfahan a jewel of Islamic architecture; weak shahs followed, and an Afghan army took Isfahan in 1722.
