Khanate of Khiva.x: The khanate of Khwarazm on the lower Amu Darya, founded in 1511 by the Arabshahid Uzbeks and ruled from Khiva from the seventeenth century. A land of oases and slave markets where Persian and Russian captives were sold, it was taken by Nader Shah in 1740, passed to the Qongrat dynasty in 1804, and was a Russian protectorate from 1873 until the Bolsheviks ended it in 1920.

Khanate of Bukhara.x: The Uzbek khanate of Transoxiana ruled from Bukhara, by the Shaybanids until 1599, then by the Janids, kinsmen of the khans of Astrakhan, and from the mid eighteenth century by the Manghit chiefs. Its madrasas made Bukhara the holy city of Central Asian Islam, and Turkmen raids on Persia fed its slave market; Nader Shah made it a vassal in 1740.

Saadi Sultanate.x: A dynasty of sharifs from the Draa valley who led the holy war against the Portuguese, took Marrakesh in 1525 and Fez in 1549, and ruled all Morocco. Ahmad al-Mansur, victor of the Three Kings in 1578, built the El Badi palace and sent an army across the Sahara to conquer Songhai in 1591; civil war among his sons followed, and the line ended in 1659.

Lesser Nogai Horde.x: The western Nogais who, after the Nogai Horde split in the 1550s, followed the mirza Kazy across the Volga to the Kuban and the steppes north of the Caucasus. Usually vassals of the Crimean khans and partners in their slave raids into Russia and Poland, they were driven, slain, or resettled by Russia in the eighteenth century.

Yarubid dynasty.x: The Ya'rubi imams of Oman, elected Ibadi rulers who united the tribes from 1624, expelled the Portuguese from Muscat in 1650, and built a sea empire reaching to Mombasa and Zanzibar. Their great forts at Nizwa, Rustaq, and Jabrin still stand; a civil war over the imamate in the 1720s brought in the Persians, and the Al Bu Said took power in the 1740s.

Qasimids.x: The line of Zaydi imams descended from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, who rose against the Ottomans in 1597 and whose son drove them out of Yemen by 1636. Ruling from the highlands, the Qasimid imams held all Yemen and grew rich on the coffee of Mocha, until tribal revolts and the loss of the coffee trade wore down their power in the eighteenth century.

Morocco.x: The sharifian sultanate and kingdom of the Alawite dynasty, which rose from Tafilalt in the 1660s and has ruled Morocco ever since. Moulay Ismail united it by force from Meknes; it kept its independence until France and Spain made it a protectorate in 1912, and under Muhammad V it regained its freedom in 1956 as a kingdom.

Regency of Algiers.x: The Ottoman province and corsair state of Algiers, founded by the Barbarossa brothers between 1516 and 1518. Ruled by pashas, then by aghas of the Janissaries, and from 1671 by deys chosen by the soldiery, it lived for three centuries on the plunder of Christian ships and coasts and the ransom of captives, until the French conquest of 1830.

Beylik of Tunis.x: The Ottoman province of Tunis under the Husainid beys, founded by Husayn ibn Ali in 1705, who owed the sultan little more than nominal allegiance. Ahmad Bey abolished slavery in 1846, and his successors issued the first constitution of the Arab world in 1861; ruinous debts brought the French protectorate in 1881.

Hotaki Dynasty.x: The Ghilzai Pashtun dynasty of Kandahar founded by Mirwais Hotak, who threw off Safavid rule in 1709. His son Mahmud took Isfahan in 1722 and made himself shah of Persia, but Afghan rule there, cruel and unstable, was broken by Nader in 1729, and Nader took Kandahar from the last Hotaki in 1738.

Khanate of Kokand.x: An Uzbek khanate of the Ferghana valley founded by Shahrukh Biy of the Ming tribe about 1709, with its capital at Kokand from the 1740s. At its height under Umar and Madali Khan it held Tashkent and the Kazakh and Kyrgyz steppes to the north; Russia took Tashkent in 1865 and annexed the khanate in 1876.

Karamanli Dynasty.x: A dynasty of Kouloughli officers, sons of Turkish soldiers and local women, founded by Ahmed Karamanli, who seized Tripoli in 1711 and ruled Tripolitania almost independently of the sultan. Its corsairs preyed on Christian shipping; Yusuf Karamanli fought the United States from 1801 to 1805, and debts and civil war led the Ottomans to restore direct rule in 1835.

Afsharid Iran.x: The empire of Nader Shah, the Afshar Turkmen who drove the Afghans from Persia and the Ottomans and Russians from its provinces, crowned himself in 1736, and sacked Delhi in 1739. Murdered by his officers in 1747, he left a realm that his heirs, blinded or slain in turn, kept only in Khorasan, until Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar took Mashhad in 1796.
Afsharid Iran.faith: Shi'a Islam, with Nader's attempt at a Sunni accommodation

Emirate of Diriyah.x: The first Saudi state, born of the pact of 1744 between Muhammad ibn Saud, emir of Diriyah, and the reformer Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab. Its warriors united Najd, sacked Karbala in 1802, and took Mecca and Medina; at the sultan's command Muhammad Ali's armies under Ibrahim Pasha destroyed it in 1818.

Sultanate of Oman.x: The Omani state of the Al Bu Said dynasty, founded by Ahmad ibn Said, who drove out the Persians in the 1740s. Under Said ibn Sultan it ruled Zanzibar and the Swahili coast as a merchant empire; divided between his sons in 1861, its Arabian half was long isolated, until Sultan Qaboos opened and modernized it after 1970.

Zand Dynasty.x: The dynasty of Karim Khan Zand, a Lak chief of the Zagros who emerged from the chaos after Nader Shah's death to rule nearly all Persia from Shiraz as vakil, regent, rather than shah. His mild reign was followed by fratricidal war among his kin; the last Zand, the brave Lotf Ali Khan, was captured and killed by Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar in 1794.

Khanates of the Caucasus.x: The Muslim khanates that sprang up in the eastern Caucasus after Nader Shah's death in 1747: Karabakh, Ganja, Erivan, Nakhichevan, Shaki, Shirvan, Quba, Baku, and others, ruled by local khans under loose Persian suzerainty. Russia annexed them one by one between 1805 and 1828.
Khanates of the Caucasus.gov: Hereditary khanates under nominal Persian suzerainty

Bahrain.x: The islands of Bahrain in the Gulf, held for Persia by Arab sheikhs until the Al Khalifa of Zubarah conquered them in 1783. Rich in pearls and fought over by Omanis, Persians, and Saudis, the sheikhdom bound itself to Britain by the truce treaties of 1820 and 1861.
Bahrain.faith: Islam, Sunni rulers over a largely Shi'a people

Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti.x: The united kingdom of eastern Georgia under Heraclius II, who joined Kartli to his Kakheti in 1762 and sought Russian protection by the Treaty of Georgievsk in 1783. Russia failed him when Agha Mohammad Khan sacked Tbilisi in 1795, and after the death of his son George XII it annexed the kingdom in 1801.

Qajar Dynasty.x: The Turkmen dynasty that reunited Persia under Agha Mohammad Khan and ruled it from Tehran until 1925. It lost the Caucasus to Russia in two wars, yielded concessions and spheres of influence to Russia and Britain, and saw the Constitutional Revolution of 1906; its last shah was deposed in favor of Reza Khan.

Emirate of Bukhara.x: The Manghit emirate of Bukhara, whose rulers took the title of emir from Shah Murad in 1785. Nasrullah, called the Butcher, beheaded the British officers Stoddart and Conolly in 1842; beaten by Russia, Bukhara became a protectorate in 1868, and its last emir, Alim Khan, fled the Red Army in 1920.

Muhammad Ali dynasty.x: The dynasty of Muhammad Ali, the Albanian soldier who became Ottoman pasha of Egypt in 1805, massacred the Mamluks, built a modern army and industry, and conquered Sudan and, for a time, Arabia and Syria. His grandson Isma'il took the title of khedive and opened the Suez Canal; the dynasty reigned until the revolution of 1952.
Muhammad Ali dynasty.gov: Hereditary governorship under Ottoman suzerainty (khedivate from 1867)

Sokoto Caliphate.x: The Fulani caliphate founded by Usman dan Fodio's holy war of 1804 against the Hausa kings, ruled from Sokoto by a Commander of the Faithful over some thirty emirates in what is now northern Nigeria. One of the largest states of nineteenth-century Africa and a great slaving power, it was conquered by the British in 1903.
Sokoto Caliphate.gov: Caliphate (Commander of the Faithful over emirates)

Trucial States.x: The sheikhdoms of the Pirate Coast of southeastern Arabia, among them Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Sharjah, Ajman, Umm al-Quwain, Ras al-Khaimah, and Fujairah, bound to Britain by maritime truces from 1820 and an exclusive agreement in 1892. Pearling villages until oil was struck from the late 1950s, they formed the United Arab Emirates in 1971.

Qatar Dynasty.x: The peninsula of Qatar under the Al Thani sheikhs of Doha, who rose in the mid nineteenth century; Britain recognized Mohammed bin Thani in 1868 against the claims of Bahrain. His son Jassim beat an Ottoman force at al-Wajbah in 1893 and steered between Ottomans and British until his death in 1913.

First Hellenic Republic.x: The provisional government of the Greeks in revolt against the Ottomans, constituted at Epidaurus in January 1822. Riven by civil wars between islanders and mainland chiefs and saved by the allied victory at Navarino, it was organized as a state by its first governor, Ioannis Kapodistrias, from 1828 until he was assassinated at Nafplio in 1831.

Emirate of Nejd.x: The second Saudi state, raised at Riyadh by Turki ibn Abdullah in 1824 after the fall of Diriyah, and revived by Ibn Saud's capture of Riyadh in 1902. In between, quarrels among Faisal's sons let the Rashidis of Ha'il conquer Najd in 1891. Ibn Saud took the Hejaz in 1925 and joined his realms as Saudi Arabia in 1932.

Emirate of Jabal Shammar.x: The emirate of the Al Rashid of the Shammar tribe, ruling from Ha'il in northern Arabia from 1836. Under Muhammad ibn Rashid it took Riyadh in 1887, crushed the Saudis at Mulayda in 1891, and became the greatest power of the peninsula, allied to the Ottomans; Ibn Saud wore it down and took Ha'il in 1921.

Caucasian Imamate.x: The holy-war state of the Muslim mountaineers of Daghestan and Chechnya, founded by Ghazi Muhammad in 1828 to resist Russia and impose the sharia in place of custom. Under Imam Shamil it held the eastern Caucasus for a quarter century with an administration and army of its own, until Shamil surrendered at Gunib in 1859.

(July Monarchy).x: The constitutional monarchy of the Orléanist king Louis Philippe, who came to the French throne by the revolution of July 1830 and reigned as King of the French until the revolution of February 1848. In its years France conquered Algeria, in a long war against the emir Abd al-Qadir that ended with his surrender in 1847.

Ottoman Tripolitania.x: The Ottoman province of Tripoli in Barbary, taken back under direct rule from the Karamanlis in 1835 and governed by pashas sent from Constantinople. The tribes of the interior long resisted, and the Sanusi order spread through Cyrenaica; Italy invaded in 1911, and the Ottomans ceded the province in 1912.

Sultanate of Muscat and Oman.x: The Al Bu Said sultanate of the coast, ruled from Muscat under British protection, which by the Treaty of Seeb in 1920 left the interior to the Ibadi imams. Sultan Said ibn Taimur reunited the country in the 1950s but kept it sealed against the modern world; his son Qaboos deposed him in 1970 and renamed it the Sultanate of Oman.

Imamate of Oman.x: The Ibadi imamate of interior Oman, restored in 1913 when the tribes elected Salim ibn Rashid al-Kharusi imam and rose against the sultan of Muscat. By the Treaty of Seeb of 1920 the imams ruled the interior from Nizwa, until Sultan Said ibn Taimur, with British help, ended the imamate in the Jebel Akhdar War of 1957 to 1959.

Sultanate of Egypt.x: Egypt as a British protectorate during and after the Great War, when Britain deposed the khedive Abbas II and gave his uncle Hussein Kamel the title of sultan in December 1914. The national rising of 1919 under Saad Zaghloul led Britain to declare Egypt independent in 1922, and Sultan Fuad became king.

Kingdom of Hejaz.x: The kingdom proclaimed by Sharif Hussein ibn Ali of Mecca in 1916 when he raised the Arab Revolt against the Ottomans. Disappointed by the postwar settlement and discredited when he took the title of caliph in 1924, Hussein abdicated as Ibn Saud's Ikhwan advanced; his son Ali surrendered Jeddah in December 1925.

Georgia.x: The Georgian state, independent as a democratic republic led by the Mensheviks from 1918 until the Red Army conquered it in 1921, then a Soviet republic, and again independent from 1991. It lost control of Abkhazia and South Ossetia in secessionist wars backed by Russia, and turned toward the West after the Rose Revolution of 2003.

Azerbaijan Democratic Republic.x: The first republic of the Muslim East, proclaimed at Tiflis on 28 May 1918 by the Musavat party as the Russian empire fell apart, with its capital first at Ganja and from September at Baku. It gave women the vote and founded Baku University, but the Red Army overthrew it in April 1920.

Armenia.x: The First Republic of Armenia, proclaimed in May 1918 after the stand at Sardarabad, a land of refugees from the genocide wasted by famine and typhus. It fought Georgia, Azerbaijan, and the Turks over its borders; beaten by the Kemalists in 1920, it passed to the Bolsheviks that December.

United Kingdom.x: The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, which in the Middle East held Aden as a colony and the sheikhdoms and sultanates of South Arabia as protectorates. Britain withdrew from Aden in 1967 under insurgent fire and from its remaining Gulf protectorates in 1971.

Kingdom of Egypt.x: Egypt as a nominally independent monarchy from 1922, when Britain ended its protectorate while keeping troops on the Suez Canal. King Fuad and his son Farouk contended with the nationalist Wafd party and the British; defeat in the Palestine war of 1948 and corruption at court brought the Free Officers' coup of 1952.

Pahlavi Dynasty.x: The dynasty founded by Reza Shah, a Cossack officer who took the Persian throne in 1925 and drove the country toward secular modernity. The Allies deposed him in 1941; his son Mohammad Reza Shah, restored to power by the coup of 1953, pressed land reform and oil-fed growth with a heavy hand, until the revolution of 1979 overthrew him.

Republic of Turkey.x: The republic founded by Mustafa Kemal Atatürk in 1923 from the Anatolian core of the Ottoman Empire, with its capital at Ankara. Secular, nationalist, and Western in its founder's design, it became a multiparty democracy in 1950 and a NATO ally in 1952, and passed through military coups in 1960, 1971, and 1980 before the long ascendancy of Recep Tayyip Erdoğan.
rulers: Recep Tayyip Erdoğan (prime minister, then president)

Kingdom of Hejaz and Nejd.x: The dual kingdom of Abdulaziz ibn Saud, who was proclaimed King of the Hejaz at Mecca in January 1926 after conquering the Hashemite realm and took the title King of Nejd in 1927. He broke the rebellious Ikhwan at Sabilla in 1929 and in 1932 joined the two crowns as the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.

Kingdom of Iraq.x: The Hashemite monarchy created by Britain under its Mandate, which crowned Faisal, son of Sharif Hussein, king in 1921. Independent from 1932 but bound to Britain by treaty and oil, it was governed by a narrow circle about Nuri al-Said, until the revolution of 14 July 1958 slaughtered the royal family.

Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.x: The kingdom created in 1932 when Abdulaziz ibn Saud united Najd, the Hejaz, and al-Ahsa, ruled by him and then by his sons in turn. Guardian of Mecca and Medina and holder of vast oil reserves, it allied itself with the United States from 1945 and grew from a poor desert realm into one of the richest states on earth.

Second Syrian Republic.x: Syria from the departure of the French in 1946 to its union with Egypt in 1958, a parliamentary republic shaken by defeat in Palestine and by repeated military coups, three in 1949 alone. Adib Shishakli ruled as dictator from 1951 to 1954; restored civilian government drifted leftward until its leaders sought union with Nasser.
Second Syrian Republic.gov: Parliamentary republic interrupted by military rule
Second Syrian Republic.faith: Sunni Islam majority, with Alawite, Druze, and Christian minorities

Kingdom of Jordan.x: The Hashemite kingdom east of the Jordan, carved by Britain from the Palestine Mandate as the emirate of Transjordan for Abdullah, son of Sharif Hussein, in 1921 and independent from 1946. It annexed the West Bank in 1950 and lost it to Israel in 1967; under King Hussein it survived wars, Palestinian insurgency, and floods of refugees, and made peace with Israel in 1994.

State of Israel.x: The Jewish state proclaimed in 1948 as the British Mandate over Palestine ended, which fought its Arab neighbors in the wars of 1948, 1956, 1967, and 1973 and gathered in Jews from Europe and the Muslim world. It made peace with Egypt in 1979 and Jordan in 1994, while the conflict with the Palestinians endured.
State of Israel.faith: Judaism, with Muslim, Christian, and Druze minorities

Kingdom of Libya.x: The kingdom of Idris al-Sanusi, head of the Sanusi order, under whom Tripolitania, Cyrenaica, and the Fezzan became independent in 1951 as the first state created through the United Nations. Oil found in 1959 made it rich; federal until 1963, it was overthrown by Muammar Gaddafi's officers in September 1969.

Republic of Egypt.x: Egypt as a republic under the Revolutionary Command Council of the Free Officers from June 1953, when the monarchy was abolished. Gamal Abdel Nasser displaced General Naguib in 1954, became president in 1956, nationalized the Suez Canal, and in 1958 merged Egypt with Syria in the United Arab Republic.

Republic of Tunisia.x: Tunisia as an independent state from 1956 and a republic from 1957 under Habib Bourguiba, whose secular law code gave women rights unmatched in the Arab world. Zine El Abidine Ben Ali deposed him in 1987; Ben Ali's fall in January 2011 began the Arab Spring, and Tunisia's democracy lasted a decade before President Kais Saied gathered power to himself in 2021.

United Arab Republic.x: The union of Egypt and Syria proclaimed in February 1958 under Gamal Abdel Nasser, the first step, as its founders hoped, toward a single Arab state. Syria seceded after a coup in September 1961, but Egypt kept the name until Anwar Sadat renamed it the Arab Republic of Egypt in 1971.

Arab Federation.x: The short-lived union of the two Hashemite kingdoms of Iraq and Jordan, formed in February 1958 in answer to the United Arab Republic, with King Faisal II of Iraq at its head and his cousin King Hussein as deputy. It perished in July 1958, when Faisal was murdered in the Iraqi revolution.

Mali Federation.x: The federation of Senegal and the French Sudan formed in 1959 to win independence together, which it did on 20 June 1960. It broke apart within two months when Senegal seceded in August, and the Sudanese half took the name of the medieval empire of Mali.
rulers: Léopold Sédar Senghor (president of the assembly)

Iraqi Republic.x: Iraq from the overthrow of the monarchy in 1958 until the American conquest of 2003: first under Abd al-Karim Qasim, then the Arif brothers, and from 1968 the Ba'ath party, dominated after 1979 by Saddam Hussein. Oil wealth paid for his wars on Iran and Kuwait and his Anfal campaign against the Kurds; he was overthrown in 2003 and hanged in 2006.
Iraqi Republic.gov: Military republic, then one-party Ba'athist state
Iraqi Republic.faith: Islam (Shi'a majority, Sunni ruling elite), secular state

Republic of Mali.x: The West African republic of the middle Niger, independent in 1960 after the breakup of the Mali Federation. Ruled by the socialist Modibo Keïta and then for twenty-three years by the soldier Moussa Traoré, it became a democracy in 1991; since the Tuareg and jihadist risings of 2012 it has been torn by insurgency, and juntas have ruled it from 2020.
Republic of Mali.gov: Presidential republic, under military rule from 2020

Republic of the Niger.x: The Saharan and Sahelian republic of the middle Niger and the Aïr mountains, independent from France in 1960, whose uranium mines long fed French reactors. Ruled by Hamani Diori and then by a succession of soldiers and elected presidents, it was the West's partner against the jihadists of the Sahel until the coup of July 2023.
Republic of the Niger.gov: Presidential republic, often under military rule

Mauritania.x: The Islamic Republic of Mauritania, a land of Moorish nomads and black farmers of the Senegal valley between the Maghreb and West Africa, independent from France in 1960. It shared in partitioning the Western Sahara in 1976 and withdrew in 1979; ruled mostly by soldiers, it was the last country to abolish slavery, in 1981.
Mauritania.gov: Presidential republic, often under military rule

Republic of Syria.x: Syria after its secession from the United Arab Republic in September 1961, a conservative parliamentary republic under President Nazim al-Kudsi, troubled by the plots of rival officers. The Ba'ath party's coup of 8 March 1963 ended it.

People's Democratic Republic of Algeria.x: The republic born of the war of independence against France, ruled from 1962 by the National Liberation Front and the army. Houari Boumédiène built a socialist state on oil and gas; the cancelled elections of 1992 brought a decade of civil war with the Islamists, and Abdelaziz Bouteflika ruled for twenty years until the Hirak protests forced him out in 2019.
People's Democratic Republic of Algeria.gov: Presidential republic dominated by the army, one-party until 1989

Ba'athist Syria.x: Syria under the first Ba'athist regime, which seized power in the coup of March 1963 and ruled through a military committee in which Alawite officers, among them Salah Jadid and Hafez al-Assad, rose to the fore. Amin al-Hafiz presided until the radical faction's coup of February 1966.
Ba'athist Syria.gov: One-party Ba'athist state under military rule

Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party.x: Syria under the neo-Ba'athist regime of the party's military wing, which seized power in February 1966 under Salah Jadid with Nureddin al-Atassi as head of state. It lost the Golan Heights in 1967, and in November 1970 the defense minister Hafez al-Assad overthrew his comrades in what he called the Corrective Movement.

Israeli-occupied territory.x: The lands taken by Israel in the Six-Day War of 1967: Sinai and the Gaza Strip from Egypt, the West Bank and East Jerusalem from Jordan, and the Golan Heights from Syria. Sinai was returned to Egypt by 1982; Israel annexed East Jerusalem and the Golan, acts most nations do not recognize, left Gaza in 2005, and holds the West Bank under military rule.
Israeli-occupied territory.gov: Military administration, with Palestinian self-rule in parts from 1994

Libyan Arab Republic.x: Libya under the Revolutionary Command Council of Muammar Gaddafi, who overthrew King Idris in September 1969. The new regime closed the British and American bases, expelled the Italian settlers, and nationalized the oil, and in 1977 Gaddafi proclaimed the Jamahiriya, the state of the masses.

United Arab Emirates.x: The federation of seven emirates of the former Trucial Coast, formed in December 1971 under Sheikh Zayed of Abu Dhabi as Britain withdrew from the Gulf; Ras al-Khaimah joined in February 1972. Oil made Abu Dhabi one of the richest places on earth, and Dubai grew into a world city of trade, finance, and air travel.

Arab Republic of Egypt.x: Egypt under the name Anwar Sadat gave it in 1971. Sadat expelled the Soviet advisers in 1972, crossed the Suez Canal in 1973, and made peace with Israel in 1979; Hosni Mubarak ruled for thirty years until the rising of 2011, and after the Muslim Brotherhood's year in power the army under Abdel Fattah el-Sisi took over in 2013.
Arab Republic of Egypt.gov: Presidential republic dominated by the army
Arab Republic of Egypt.faith: Sunni Islam, with a Coptic Christian minority

Syria.x: Syria under Hafez al-Assad, who seized power in 1970, and from 2000 his son Bashar: a Ba'athist state resting on the army, the security services, and the Alawite minority. It fought Israel in 1973, occupied Lebanon from 1976 to 2005, and crushed the Brotherhood at Hama; the rising of 2011 became a civil war, and Bashar fled in December 2024.
Syria.faith: Sunni Islam majority, with Alawite, Christian, and Druze minorities; secular state

Western Sahara.x: The former Spanish colony on the Atlantic shore of the Sahara, disputed since Spain's withdrawal in 1975 and 1976. Morocco administers most of it behind a fortified sand wall; the Polisario Front's Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic, proclaimed in 1976 and based in the Tindouf camps in Algeria, holds the eastern desert. A ceasefire held from 1991 to 2020.
Western Sahara.gov: Disputed territory: Moroccan administration and the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic

Libyan Arab Jamahiriya.x: The state of the masses that Muammar Gaddafi proclaimed in 1977, governed in theory by people's congresses and in fact by the Guide of the Revolution, his family, and his security men. It sponsored terror abroad, suffered American bombing in 1986 and sanctions after Lockerbie, made peace with the West in 2003, and fell to the rising of 2011.

Islamic Republic of Iran.x: The Shi'ite theocracy founded by the revolution of 1979 under Ayatollah Khomeini, in which an elected president and parliament stand beneath the Supreme Leader, the guardian jurist. It fought Iraq for eight years, built a network of allied militias across the Arab world, and has defied the West over its nuclear program.

Kazakhstan.x: The largest of the Central Asian republics, stretching from the Caspian to the Altai, independent since the Soviet collapse in December 1991. Nursultan Nazarbayev ruled it for nearly three decades, built a new capital at Astana on the northern steppe, and grew rich on oil; his successor Kassym-Jomart Tokayev broke his clan's hold after the riots of January 2022.
Kazakhstan.faith: Sunni Islam, with an Orthodox Christian minority

Turkmenistan.x: The desert republic between the Caspian and the Amu Darya, independent since 1991 and holding some of the world's greatest reserves of natural gas. Its first president, Saparmurat Niyazov, styled Turkmenbashi, built a cult of personality to rival any of the century; his successors, the Berdimuhamedows, father and son, have kept the country closed.

Republic of Uzbekistan.x: The most populous Central Asian republic, heir to the cities of Samarkand, Bukhara, and Khiva, independent since 1991. Islam Karimov ruled it harshly for twenty-five years, crushing Islamist and other opposition, as at Andijan in 2005; Shavkat Mirziyoyev, president from 2016, has opened it to trade and travel.

Republic of Tajikistan.x: The mountain republic of the Persian-speaking Tajiks in the Pamirs and the upper valleys of the Oxus, independent since 1991 and torn by civil war from 1992 to 1997. Emomali Rahmon, who came to power during the war, has ruled it since in close alliance with Russia; it remains the poorest of the former Soviet republics.
Republic of Tajikistan.faith: Sunni Islam (Hanafi), with Isma'ilis in the Pamirs

Republic of Azerbaijan.x: The Caspian republic of the Azerbaijani Turks, independent since 1991 and rich in oil and gas from the fields off Baku. It lost Nagorno-Karabakh to the Armenians in the war of 1988 to 1994, and under Ilham Aliyev, son of Heydar Aliyev and president from 2003, recovered it by force in 2020 and 2023.

Republic of Armenia.x: The Armenian republic in the highlands about Yerevan and Lake Sevan, independent since 1991, a remnant of historic Armenia between Turkey and Azerbaijan. It won the first war for Nagorno-Karabakh but lost the region to Azerbaijan in 2020 and 2023, when its Armenians fled; the Velvet Revolution of 2018 brought Nikol Pashinyan to power.

State of Libya.x: Libya after the fall of Gaddafi in 2011, divided from 2014 between rival governments in Tripoli and the east, where Khalifa Haftar's Libyan National Army held Benghazi and the oil fields. Haftar's assault on Tripoli in 2019 and 2020 failed, Turkish and Russian forces backed the rival sides, and a nominal unity government took office in 2021.
State of Libya.gov: Divided transitional state with rival governments

Republic of Iraq.x: The federal republic of Iraq under the constitution of 2005, governed by Shi'ite-led coalitions with a Kurdish president, a Sunni speaker, and an autonomous Kurdistan in the north. It lost a third of its land to the Islamic State in 2014 and won it back by 2017 with American air power and Iranian-backed militias.
Republic of Iraq.faith: Shi'a Islam majority, with Sunni and Christian minorities

Non-government-held Syria.x: The parts of Syria beyond the Assad regime's control during the civil war: the rebel and Islamist enclaves of the north and about Idlib, the Kurdish-led autonomous administration east of the Euphrates, and from 2014 to 2019 the lands of the Islamic State. From Idlib, Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham launched the offensive that toppled Assad in December 2024.
Non-government-held Syria.gov: Rival rebel, Kurdish, and jihadist administrations
Non-government-held Syria.faith: Sunni Islam, with Kurdish, Christian, and Yazidi minorities
rulers: Ahmed al-Sharaa (al-Nusra Front, then Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham)

Shang Dynasty.x: The first Chinese dynasty attested by its own writing, ruling the middle Yellow River plain from a succession of capitals and finally from Yin near Anyang. Its kings divined on oracle bones, sacrificed captives to their ancestors, and commanded the finest bronze casting of the ancient world.
Shang Dynasty.faith: Ancestor worship and divination; the high god Di

Zhou Dynasty.x: The house of Zhou overthrew the Shang at Muye and ruled the Yellow River lands through kinsmen enfeoffed as lords, justifying its rule by the Mandate of Heaven. Its classic age of rites and bronze inscriptions ended when the Quanrong sacked Haojing in 771 B.C. and the court fled east.
Zhou Dynasty.faith: Worship of Heaven and the royal ancestors

Qin.x: The westernmost of the Zhou states, granted the old Zhou homeland in 770 B.C. and hardened by long wars with the Rong. Remade by the laws of Shang Yang into a machine of farming and war, it conquered the other six Warring States and united China in 221 B.C.
Qin.gov: Feudal duchy, kingdom from 325 B.C.; centralized Legalist state
Qin.faith: Worship of Heaven, the Five Emperors, and the ancestors

(Spring and Autumn States).x: The many states of the Eastern Zhou world, from 770 to the early fifth century B.C., which owed nominal homage to the Zhou kings at Luoyi while Qi, Jin, Chu, Qin, Wu, and Yue fought for primacy. Hegemons kept order in the king's name, and Confucius lived at the end of the age.
(Spring and Autumn States).gov: Feudal states under the nominal Zhou king
(Spring and Autumn States).faith: Worship of Heaven and the ancestors

Chu.x: The great southern state of the middle Yangtze, half outside the Zhou world, whose rulers called themselves kings in defiance of Zhou. Chu swallowed dozens of neighbours, gave China the shamanic poetry of Qu Yuan, and was the last great rival of Qin, which destroyed it in 223 B.C.

Qi.x: The rich state of the Shandong peninsula, mistress of salt and iron, whose Duke Huan was the first hegemon. In the fourth century B.C. the Tian family took its throne, and under the Tian kings Linzi was the greatest city of the age. Qi was the last state to fall to Qin, and revived briefly after Qin's collapse.
Qi.faith: Worship of Heaven and the ancestors; the Eight Spirits of Qi
rulers: Tian He (Duke Tai of Tian Qi)

Jin.x: The name of two states in Shanxi. The Zhou state of Jin, made hegemon by Duke Wen, was the strongest power of the north until its ministers divided it into Han, Zhao, and Wei. Centuries later the Shatuo Turk Li Keyong and his son Li Cunxu ruled a Jin from Taiyuan, which became the Later Tang in 923.
Jin.gov: Feudal duchy; later a military principality
Jin.faith: Ancestor worship; later Buddhism and Chinese popular religion

Wu.x: A state of the lower Yangtze whose rulers traced their line to an uncle of the Zhou founders. Little heard of until the sixth century B.C., it rose under King Helü and Wu Zixu to sack the Chu capital, then fell to its southern rival Yue in 473 B.C.

Yan.x: The northeastern Zhou state around later Beijing, guarding the frontier against the Donghu and the peoples of Liaodong. Its King Zhao gathered talent from all the states and nearly destroyed Qi in 284 B.C., and its Prince Dan sent Jing Ke against the King of Qin. Qin conquered it in 222 B.C.

Song.x: The state of the heirs of the Shang royal house, at Shangqiu on the eastern plain, which kept the rites of the old dynasty. Its Duke Xiang sought the hegemony and was beaten by Chu at the Hong River for refusing to strike an enemy in mid-crossing; its last king, Yan, was destroyed by Qi in 286 B.C.

Wey.x: A Zhou state founded for a brother of King Wu in the old Shang heartland near Chaoge. Overrun by the Di in 660 B.C., it was restored by Qi and dwindled into a small principality, which Qin spared as a vassal until 209 B.C., the last of the Zhou states to perish.

Eastern Zhou.x: The royal domain of the Zhou kings at Luoyi after the flight from the west in 770 B.C. Its kings kept the rites of the Son of Heaven and the nine sacred cauldrons, but ruled only a shrinking territory along the Luo River, until Qin extinguished the house in 256 B.C.
Eastern Zhou.gov: Monarchy with nominal suzerainty over the feudal lords
Eastern Zhou.faith: Worship of Heaven and the royal ancestors

Chen.x: A small Zhou state on the Huai plain, said to have been granted to descendants of the sage emperor Shun. Caught between Jin and Chu, it was once annexed by Chu and restored, and was finally extinguished by King Hui of Chu in 479 B.C.

Zheng.x: A Zhou state founded in 806 B.C. for a brother of King Xuan, which moved east to the plain of Xinzheng. Under Duke Zhuang it was for a time the strongest state of the age, and under the minister Zichan it published the first written laws in China. Han conquered it in 375 B.C.

Yue.x: A kingdom of the tattooed Yue peoples around Kuaiji in later Zhejiang. Its King Goujian, after years of humiliation, destroyed Wu in 473 B.C. and was hailed as hegemon. Yue later moved its seat north to Langya, and after Chu killed its king Wujiang it broke into lordships along the southern coast.
Yue.faith: Yue spirit worship and ancestor rites

Zhongshan.x: A state founded by the Xianyu, a people of the Di, in the hills of western Hebei, whose kings adopted Chinese ways. Their royal tombs at Pingshan held bronzes inlaid with gold and silver and the plan of a mausoleum cast in bronze. Zhao conquered it in 296 B.C.

(Warring States China).x: The seven great kingdoms of Qin, Chu, Qi, Yan, Zhao, Wei, and Han, with lesser states between them, which fought for mastery of China from the partition of Jin to the Qin conquest of 221 B.C. It was the age of mass infantry armies, iron, and the crossbow, and of the Hundred Schools of thought.
(Warring States China).gov: Rival kingdoms under the nominal Zhou king
(Warring States China).faith: Ancestor worship; Confucian, Mohist, Daoist, and Legalist schools

Wei.x: One of the three states carved from Jin, ruled from Anyi and then from Daliang, the later Kaifeng, which made it known also as Liang. Under Marquis Wen and his minister Li Kui it was the first great power of the Warring States, until Qi broke it at Guiling and Maling. Qin flooded Daliang and destroyed it in 225 B.C.
rulers: Wei Bao, King of Western Wei

Yuezhi.x: An Indo-European pastoral people of the grasslands of Gansu, masters of the jade trade, until the Xiongnu broke them in the second century B.C. and killed their king. The Great Yuezhi fled west to Bactria, where Zhang Qian found them, and one of their five tribes founded the Kushan Empire.
Yuezhi.faith: Steppe religion; later Buddhism and Iranian cults in Bactria

Han.x: The smallest of the three states carved from Jin, wedged between Qin and the central plain, which annexed Zheng in 375 B.C. and was governed for a time by the Legalist Shen Buhai. Qin destroyed it first of all, in 230 B.C.; Liu Bang's Han of 206 B.C. took its name, written with another character, from the Han River.

Zhao.x: A state carved from Jin and ruled from Handan, with a long northern frontier on the steppe. King Wuling's mounted archers made it a great military power, but Qin broke it at Changping in 260 B.C. and took Handan in 228 B.C.; a remnant held out as Dai until 222 B.C.

Minyue.x: A kingdom of the Yue peoples in the mountains of Fujian, ruled by a line that traced itself to King Goujian of Yue. Its king Wuzhu fought for Han against Xiang Yu and was recognized in 202 B.C.; when his successors defied the court, Emperor Wu destroyed the kingdom in 110 B.C. and moved its people north of the Yangtze.

Qin Dynasty.x: The first imperial dynasty, founded when King Zheng of Qin conquered the last of the Warring States and took the title First Emperor. It standardized script, coinage, weights, and axles, ruled through commanderies, and built roads and walls, but its harsh laws provoked revolt, and it fell within four years of his death.
Qin Dynasty.faith: State cults of Heaven and the Five Emperors; Legalist doctrine

Xiongnu.x: The first great empire of the Mongolian steppe, forged by the chanyu Modu from about 209 B.C. and stretching from Manchuria to the Tarim. For two centuries its horse archers fought the Han and drew tribute from them, until civil war split it in two; the northern chanyus were driven west after A.D. 91.
Xiongnu.faith: Worship of Heaven, earth, and the ancestors

(Eighteen Kingdoms).x: The eighteen kingdoms into which Xiang Yu, Hegemon-King of Western Chu, divided the fallen Qin empire in 206 B.C., rewarding rebel generals and heirs of the old royal houses. Their quarrels began at once, and within four years Liu Bang, King of Han, had overcome Xiang Yu and his rivals and refounded the empire.
(Eighteen Kingdoms).gov: Kingdoms under the Hegemon-King of Western Chu
rulers: Xiang Yu, Hegemon-King of Western Chu

Western Chu.x: The realm Xiang Yu kept for himself in 206 B.C., nine commanderies of the old Chu and Wei lands ruled from Pengcheng. As Hegemon-King he was overlord of the other kingdoms, but he lost the war with Liu Bang and died at the Wu River in 202 B.C.

Jibei.x: One of the Eighteen Kingdoms, north of the Ji River in Shandong, given to Tian An, a grandson of the last King of Qi. Within months Tian Rong, who had been left without a kingdom, killed him and reunited the lands of Qi.

Dai.x: A northern kingdom of the Eighteen, in the old Zhao lands of northern Shanxi and Hebei, given by Xiang Yu to Zhao Xie, the restored King of Zhao. Chen Yu soon put Zhao Xie back on the throne of Zhao and took Dai for himself, until Han Xin destroyed him at Jingxing.

Linjiang.x: A kingdom of the Eighteen on the middle Yangtze, ruled from Jiangling by Gong Ao, a former officer of King Huai of Chu. His son Gong Wei refused to submit to Han and was taken captive in 202 B.C.

Jiujiang.x: A kingdom of the Eighteen between the Huai and the Yangtze, given to Ying Bu, the branded convict who had become Xiang Yu's fiercest general. In 204 B.C. he went over to Liu Bang, and he later ruled as King of Huainan until his revolt and death in 195 B.C.

Hán.x: The kingdom of the Eighteen in the Yingchuan country that Xiang Yu left to Han Cheng, heir of the old royal house of Han. Xiang Yu soon had him killed and set up Zheng Chang, who was overthrown by Han Xin, a scion of the old kings and ally of Liu Bang, not the great general of that name.

Liaodong.x: A kingdom of the Eighteen beyond the Liao River, to which Xiang Yu moved Han Guang, the former King of Yan, to make room for Zang Tu. Han Guang would not go quietly, and Zang Tu killed him at Wuzhong and took his kingdom within the year.

Yong.x: One of three kingdoms carved from the Qin homeland for surrendered Qin generals, given to Zhang Han, who had led the last armies of Qin. Liu Bang burst out of Hanzhong in 206 B.C. and overran it; besieged in Feiqiu, Zhang Han killed himself in 205 B.C.

Jiaodong.x: A kingdom of the Eighteen on the eastern Shandong peninsula, to which Xiang Yu moved Tian Fu, the former King of Qi. Tian Rong, his uncle and the real power in Qi, killed him at Jimo in 206 B.C. and took his lands.

Henan.x: A kingdom of the Eighteen around Luoyang, given to Shen Yang, an officer of Zhao who had taken the city for the rebels. He surrendered to Liu Bang in 205 B.C., and his kingdom became the Han commandery of Henan.

Chang-shan.x: The kingdom of the Eighteen in the old Zhao lands of central Hebei, given to Zhang Er, a famous patron and statesman of Zhao. Driven out by his former friend Chen Yu, he fled to Liu Bang and was later made King of Zhao by the Han.

Zhai.x: One of three kingdoms carved from the Qin homeland, in the north of Shaanxi, given to Dong Yi, a surrendered Qin general. He submitted to Liu Bang in 206 B.C., then went back over to Xiang Yu, and died by his own hand when the Han took Chenggao.

Nanyue.x: A kingdom founded by the Qin officer Zhao Tuo in the far south, with its capital at Panyu, the later Canton, ruling Guangdong, Guangxi, and northern Vietnam. Its kings blended Chinese and Yue ways; the tomb of the second king, found in 1983, held a burial suit of jade. Han conquered it in 111 B.C.
Nanyue.faith: Yue spirit worship and Chinese ancestral rites

Han Dynasty.x: The dynasty founded by Liu Bang in 202 B.C., which ruled China, with the interruption of Wang Mang, for four centuries. It made Confucianism the creed of the state, drove back the Xiongnu, opened the Silk Road, and saw the making of paper; the Chinese still call themselves the people of Han.
Han Dynasty.gov: Imperial monarchy with a Confucian bureaucracy
Han Dynasty.faith: Confucian state cults and Daoism; Buddhism from the first century A.D.

Korean Jin.x: The Jin state of the southern Korean peninsula named in the Chinese histories, a league of chiefdoms south of Gojoseon that sought trade and tribute relations with Han. In the last centuries B.C. it gave way to the three Han confederacies of Mahan, Jinhan, and Byeonhan.

Gojoseon.x: The first Korean kingdom, by legend founded by Dangun in 2333 B.C., which by the fourth century B.C. held Liaodong and northwestern Korea. In 194 B.C. the refugee captain Wiman seized its throne at Wanggeom; the Han conquered his grandson Ugeo in 108 B.C. and set up the Lelang commandery.

Wusun.x: A nomad people of the Ili valley and Issyk Kul, tall and fair by Chinese report, who moved west after the Yuezhi and became allies of the Han against the Xiongnu. Han princesses were married to their kunmi, and one of them, Liu Xijun, wrote a famous lament for her lost home.

Mahan.x: The largest of the three Han confederacies of southern Korea, some fifty small states in the southwest of the peninsula. One of them, Baekje, gradually absorbed the rest, a conquest completed in the fourth century under King Geunchogo.

Dongye.x: The Eastern Ye, a people of the east coast of northern Korea, known to the Chinese histories for their fine bows and small horses, their taboos of clan and village, and their worship of the tiger. Subject in turn to Han commanderies and to Goguryeo, they were absorbed by Goguryeo and Silla.
Dongye.faith: Worship of Heaven and of the tiger

Jinhan.x: One of the three Han confederacies of southern Korea, twelve small states in the southeast whose people, the Chinese chronicles said, included refugees from Qin. One of them, Saro, grew into the kingdom of Silla and absorbed the others.

Goguryeo.x: The northern Korean kingdom founded by Jumong, which grew from the mountains of the middle Yalu to rule Manchuria and the northern peninsula. Its horsemen and mountain fortresses beat back the armies of Sui and Tang, until Tang and Silla together destroyed it in 668.
Goguryeo.faith: Shamanism, Buddhism from 372, and Confucian learning

Dong-okjeo.x: The Eastern Okjeo, a people of the northeastern coast of Korea, farmers and fishers who paid tribute of cloth, fish, and salt to Goguryeo. They laid the bones of a whole family together in a single great wooden coffin, and they were absorbed into Goguryeo.

Xin Dynasty.x: The short dynasty of Wang Mang, the regent who took the Han throne in A.D. 9 and tried to rebuild the state on the model of the Zhou classics. His reforms of land, slavery, and coinage, together with floods and famine, brought on the rebellions that killed him in 23.

Southern Xiongnu.x: The Xiongnu tribes who followed Bi, grandson of Huhanye, into submission to the Han in A.D. 48 and settled inside the frontier in the Ordos and Shanxi. They fought for Han against the Northern Xiongnu, and their descendant Liu Yuan founded the Han Zhao state in 304.

Xianbei.x: A people of the eastern steppe and the Manchurian forests, kin to the Wuhuan, who filled the grasslands after the Xiongnu were driven west. Tanshihuai united them in a vast confederacy in the second century, and later Xianbei clans, the Murong and the Tuoba, founded kingdoms in northern China.

Protectorate of the Western Regions.x: The Chinese protectorate over the oasis states of the Tarim Basin, set up by the Western Han in 60 B.C. and restored by Ban Chao and his son Ban Yong. Under Wei and Jin a Chief Clerk at Loulan kept the Chinese garrisons and farm colonies until the north fell into chaos.
Protectorate of the Western Regions.faith: Buddhism in the oases; Chinese rites among the garrisons

Han Dynasty (Cao Cao).x: The Han court under the control of Cao Cao, who brought the boy Emperor Xian to Xu in 196 and ruled northern China in his name as chancellor and, from 216, as King of Wei, with his own seat at Ye. On Cao Cao's death in 220 his son Cao Pi took the throne and founded the Wei.
Han Dynasty (Cao Cao).gov: Han imperial monarchy under a military chancellor
rulers: Cao Cao (chancellor from 208, King of Wei from 216)

Eastern Wu.x: The southern kingdom of the Three Kingdoms, built by the Sun family on the lands of the lower and middle Yangtze. Sun Quan held the river against Cao Cao at the Red Cliffs and took the imperial title in 229; Wu opened the south to settlement and the sea trade until Jin conquered it in 280.
Eastern Wu.faith: Chinese popular religion, Daoism, and early Buddhism

Cao Wei.x: The northern kingdom of the Three Kingdoms, founded when Cao Pi made the last Han emperor abdicate in 220. Ruling the old heartland of China from Luoyang, it conquered Shu in 263, but its generals of the Sima family had already taken the real power, and in 266 Sima Yan replaced it with the Jin.

Shu Han.x: The kingdom founded at Chengdu by Liu Bei, a distant kinsman of the Han house, who proclaimed himself emperor in 221 to carry on the Han. Governed by the chancellor Zhuge Liang, it sent expedition after expedition north against Wei, but fell to Wei's general Deng Ai in 263.

Eastern Kushans.x: The later Kushan kings who held the Punjab and the lands around Taxila and Mathura after the Sasanian Persians took Bactria in the third century A.D. They paid homage to the Sasanians, and in the fourth century their lands passed to the Kidarites and to the Gupta emperors.

Western Jin.x: The dynasty founded by Sima Yan, who took the Wei throne in 266 and conquered Wu in 280, reuniting China for a single generation. The War of the Eight Princes among his kinsmen opened the way to the risings of the Xiongnu and other peoples, who sacked Luoyang in 311 and took Chang'an in 316.
Western Jin.faith: Confucian state cults, Daoism, and Buddhism

Tuyuhun.x: A kingdom founded by a branch of the Murong Xianbei who migrated to the Kokonor country, ruling Qiang tribes and the caravan routes south of the Gansu corridor. Its kings took the title of khagan; Sui and Tang fought it, and in 663 the Tibetan Empire conquered it.

Former Zhao.x: The first of the Sixteen Kingdoms, founded in 304 by Liu Yuan, a Chinese-educated Xiongnu noble who named his state Han in memory of the dynasty that had married princesses to his forefathers. Its armies sacked Luoyang and Chang'an and ended the Western Jin; renamed Zhao in 319, it fell to its former general Shi Le in 329.

Cheng Han.x: A kingdom of Sichuan founded by Li Xiong, leader of the Di refugees of the Ba country, who took Chengdu in 304 and named his state Cheng; his cousin Li Shou renamed it Han. It was a time of light taxes and quiet in Sichuan, until the Jin general Huan Wen conquered it in 347.

Yaudheya Republic.x: An ancient warrior republic of the eastern Punjab and Haryana, governed by an assembly of its clans, whose coins bear the war god Karttikeya. It threw off Kushan rule in the third century and became a tributary of the Gupta emperor Samudragupta in the fourth.

Eastern Jin.x: The Jin dynasty restored south of the Yangtze by Sima Rui after the north was lost. Ruled in fact by the great émigré families, the Wang, the Xie, and the Huan, it turned back Former Qin at the Fei River in 383 and was the age of Wang Xizhi and Tao Yuanming, until Liu Yu seized the throne in 420.
Eastern Jin.gov: Imperial monarchy dominated by aristocratic clans

Former Liang.x: A state of the Chinese Zhang family in the Gansu corridor, governors who ruled from Guzang in the name of the vanished Jin, sheltering refugees from the north and keeping the road to the Western Regions open. Former Qin conquered it in 376.
Former Liang.gov: Monarchy (nominally Jin governors, later dukes and kings)

Former Yan.x: A kingdom of the Murong Xianbei, founded in Liaoxi by Murong Huang, which seized the northeastern plain after the fall of Later Zhao and moved its capital to Ye. Weakened by the jealousy that drove its best general, Murong Chui, into exile, it was conquered by Former Qin in 370.

Later Zhao.x: The state of Shi Le, a Jie slave who rose to be a general of Han Zhao and destroyed it in 329, ruling all northern China from Xiangguo and Ye. His nephew Shi Hu built palaces of legendary cruelty and splendour; after his death the general Ran Min massacred the Jie, and the state collapsed in 351.
Later Zhao.faith: Buddhism, patronized through the monk Fotudeng

Baekje.x: The southwestern kingdom of Korea, founded by tradition by Onjo in 18 B.C. near later Seoul. Driven south by Goguryeo in 475, it moved to Ungjin and then to Sabi, and was famed for its graceful Buddhist art and for carrying Buddhism and letters to Japan. Tang and Silla destroyed it in 660.
Baekje.faith: Buddhism, Confucian learning, and ancestor worship

Former Qin.x: The state of the Di chieftains of the Fu family, founded at Chang'an in 351. Under Fu Jian and his Chinese minister Wang Meng it conquered Former Yan, Former Liang, and Dai and united all northern China by 376; Fu Jian's defeat at the Fei River in 383 shattered it into a dozen successor kingdoms.

Silla.x: The kingdom of the southeastern Korean peninsula, ruled from Gyeongju, which rose from a small Jinhan state to conquer Gaya, take the Han River valley, and with Tang help destroy Baekje and Goguryeo. Its hwarang youth, its bone-rank aristocracy, and its golden crowns are its memorials.

Northern Wei.x: The empire of the Tuoba Xianbei, founded by Tuoba Gui in 386, which united northern China in 439 and ruled it for a century. It raised Buddhist cave temples on a colossal scale at Yungang and Longmen, devised the equal-field system, and under Emperor Xiaowen took up Chinese dress and speech, before splitting into Eastern and Western Wei in 534.

Tarim Basin city-states.x: The oasis kingdoms ringing the Taklamakan desert, Kucha, Karashahr, Turfan, Kashgar, Khotan, and Shanshan among them, which lived by irrigation and the Silk Road caravans. They spoke Tocharian and Saka tongues, wrote in Indian scripts, were centres of Buddhist learning, and paid tribute in turn to Chinese, Rouran, and Turkic overlords.

Later Qin.x: The kingdom of the Qiang chieftains of the Yao family, founded by Yao Chang, who strangled his former master Fu Jian of Former Qin in 385. Yao Xing made Chang'an a centre of Buddhist learning and brought the translator Kumarajiva there. The Eastern Jin general Liu Yu destroyed it in 417.

Later Yan.x: A kingdom revived by Murong Chui of the Murong Xianbei after the collapse of Former Qin, ruling the northeastern plain from Zhongshan. Northern Wei crushed it at Canhe Slope in 395 and drove it back to its old seat at Longcheng in Liaoxi, where it was overthrown in 407.

Western Qin.x: A kingdom of the Qifu clan of the Xianbei in southern Gansu around Lanzhou, founded in 385 amid the ruin of Former Qin. It swallowed Southern Liang in 414 but was destroyed by the Xia in 431.

Later Liang.x: The kingdom of the Di general Lü Guang, who had conquered Kucha for Former Qin and brought the monk Kumarajiva back with him, then made himself master of Guzang in the Gansu corridor when Former Qin collapsed. Beset by rebels and rivals, it surrendered to Later Qin in 403.

Western Yan.x: A short-lived Murong Xianbei state, founded by princes of Former Yan who rose against Former Qin in 384 and later settled at Changzi in Shanxi. Torn by murders among its rulers, it was conquered by its kinsman Murong Chui of Later Yan in 394.

Northern Liang.x: A kingdom of the Gansu corridor ruled by the Juqu clan of the Lushui Hu, a people of Xiongnu stock, from Zhangye and then Guzang. Juqu Mengxun was a great patron of Buddhist translation and cave temples; Northern Wei conquered the kingdom in 439, and a remnant fled to rule Turfan.

Southern Liang.x: A kingdom of the Tufa branch of the Xianbei in the Huangshui valley around Xining and Ledu, founded in 397. Its last king, Tufa Rutan, was overthrown by Western Qin in 414.

Rouran Khaganate.x: The steppe empire that ruled Mongolia between the Xianbei and the Türks, whose rulers first made khagan the title of a steppe emperor. They fought the Northern Wei for a century and a half; in 552 their Türk ironsmiths rose against them, and the last Rouran fled west, perhaps to become the Avars of Europe.

Southern Yan.x: The last of the Murong kingdoms, founded by Murong De in Shandong in 398 after the fall of Later Yan's southern lands. His nephew Murong Chao provoked the Eastern Jin, and Liu Yu took his capital Guanggu and extinguished the state in 410.

Western Liang.x: A small state of the far western Gansu corridor, founded in 400 by Li Gao, of the Chinese Li family of Longxi, at Dunhuang and later at Jiuquan. Northern Liang conquered it in 421; the Tang emperors counted Li Gao among their ancestors.

Xia.x: The state of Helian Bobo, a Xiongnu warlord of the Tiefu clan, who built the white-walled fortress city of Tongwan on the edge of the Ordos, its walls tested, the story goes, by driving in an awl and killing the builders wherever it went in. He took Chang'an in 418; Northern Wei destroyed his state by 431.

Northern Yan.x: The last of the Sixteen Kingdoms in the northeast, founded in 407 when Gao Yun, of Goguryeo descent, and the Chinese general Feng Ba overthrew Later Yan at Longcheng. Northern Wei conquered it in 436, and its last ruler fled to Goguryeo, where he was put to death.

Liu Song Dynasty.x: The first of the Southern Dynasties, founded when the general Liu Yu, conqueror of Southern Yan and Later Qin, took the Jin throne in 420. The long reign of Emperor Wen was a golden age, but the dynasty sank into fratricide and was overthrown by its general Xiao Daocheng in 479.

Southern Qi.x: The second of the Southern Dynasties, founded by the general Xiao Daocheng in 479. After the peaceful reign of Emperor Wu it descended into purges and the murders of the boy tyrant Xiao Baojuan, until his kinsman Xiao Yan took Jiankang and founded the Liang in 502.

Liang Dynasty.x: The southern dynasty of Xiao Yan, Emperor Wu, whose reign of nearly half a century was the high summer of southern Buddhism and letters. The rebellion of Hou Jing in 548 wrecked Jiankang and starved the old emperor; the dynasty lingered at Jiangling and Jiankang until Chen Baxian took the throne in 557.
Liang Dynasty.faith: Buddhism, with Emperor Wu as its royal devotee

Western Wei.x: The western half of the divided Northern Wei, ruled from Chang'an by the general Yuwen Tai through puppet emperors of the Yuan house. Yuwen Tai's militia and the alliance of Xianbei and Chinese nobles he forged laid the foundations of Sui and Tang; his son replaced the dynasty with the Northern Zhou in 557.
Western Wei.gov: Imperial monarchy under a military regent

Eastern Wei.x: The eastern half of the divided Northern Wei, ruled from Ye by the general Gao Huan through the boy emperor Yuan Shanjian. Gao Huan's son Gao Yang set the emperor aside and founded the Northern Qi in 550.
Eastern Wei.gov: Imperial monarchy under a military regent

Asuka Japan.x: The Yamato state of the Asuka age, when the court sat in the Asuka valley and Buddhism, writing, and Chinese law arrived by way of Korea. Under the Soga ministers, Prince Shōtoku, and the Taika reformers, the great clans were drawn into a centralized monarchy whose rulers took the title of tennō.
Asuka Japan.gov: Monarchy of the Great Kings, later the tennō
Asuka Japan.faith: Shinto and, from the sixth century, Buddhism

Göktürk Khaganate.x: The empire of the Ashina Türks, who overthrew the Rouran in 552 and within a generation ruled the steppe from Manchuria to the Black Sea, trading silk with Persia and Byzantium through their Sogdian merchants. Rival khagans split it into eastern and western halves after 581.
Göktürk Khaganate.faith: Worship of Tengri, with Buddhist and Zoroastrian influence

Northern Qi.x: The dynasty of the Gao family, founded by Gao Yang in 550 on the ruins of Eastern Wei and ruling the rich northeastern plain from Ye. Its court was notorious for the madness and cruelty of its emperors and famous for the Buddhist caves of Xiangtangshan; Northern Zhou conquered it in 577.

Yenisei Kyrgyz.x: A people of the upper Yenisei and the Minusinsk basin, farmers, herders, and ironworkers, described by the Chinese as red-haired and green-eyed. Long subject to the Türks and the Uyghurs, they destroyed the Uyghur Khaganate in 840 and ruled Mongolia for a time, then withdrew to their valleys; they submitted to the Mongols in 1207.

Northern Zhou.x: The dynasty of the Yuwen family, founded in 557 on the ruins of Western Wei and ruling from Chang'an. Emperor Wu threw off his overbearing cousin Yuwen Hu, suppressed Buddhism and Daoism, and conquered Northern Qi in 577; four years later Yang Jian, father-in-law of his son, took the throne and founded the Sui.
Northern Zhou.faith: Buddhism, proscribed from 574 to 578; Confucian rites

Later Western Liang.x: A remnant of the Liang dynasty at Jiangling on the middle Yangtze, set up by Western Wei for the prince Xiao Cha after it sacked the city in 554. For three decades its emperors reigned as vassals of Western Wei, Northern Zhou, and Sui, until Emperor Wen of Sui abolished it in 587.
rulers: Emperor Xuan of Western Liang (Xiao Cha)
Emperor Ming of Western Liang (Xiao Kui)

Chen Dynasty.x: The last of the Southern Dynasties, founded by the general Chen Baxian in 557 on the ruins of Liang, ruling only the lands south of the Yangtze. Its last emperor, Chen Shubao, gave his days to poetry and his consorts, and the Sui conquered the dynasty in 589, reuniting China.

Western Göktürks.x: The western half of the Türk empire, ruled by khagans of Istämi's line from the Ili and Chu valleys, master of the Silk Road through Sogdiana and ally of Byzantium against Persia. Torn by the feud of its two tribal wings, it fell to the Tang general Su Dingfang in 657.
Western Göktürks.faith: Worship of Tengri, with Buddhist influence

Sui Dynasty.x: The dynasty of Yang Jian, Emperor Wen, who seized the Northern Zhou throne in 581 and reunited China in 589 after nearly three centuries of division. His son Emperor Yang dug the Grand Canal and rebuilt Luoyang, but three disastrous wars against Goguryeo brought revolt, and the dynasty fell in 618.

Eastern Göktürks.x: The eastern half of the Türk empire, ruled from the Ötüken highlands of Mongolia, which raided Sui and early Tang China and in 626 camped on the Wei River within sight of Chang'an. In 630 the Tang general Li Jing captured its khagan, and the Türks lived for half a century under Tang rule.

Tang Dynasty.x: The dynasty of the Li family, founded in 618, under which China reached the height of its power and cosmopolitan splendour, ruling from Korea to the Pamirs from Chang'an, then the greatest city on earth. The rebellion of An Lushan broke its strength in 755, and it ended in the hands of its generals in 907.
Tang Dynasty.gov: Imperial monarchy with examinations and an equal-field system
Tang Dynasty.faith: Buddhism, Daoism, and Confucianism; foreign faiths tolerated until 845

Tibetan Empire.x: The empire of the Yarlung kings, united by Songtsen Gampo in the seventh century, which became the great military power of inner Asia, conquering the Tuyuhun, holding the Tarim and Gansu, and briefly taking Chang'an in 763. Its kings made Buddhism the faith of the state; after Langdarma's murder in 842 the empire broke apart.
Tibetan Empire.gov: Monarchy of the tsenpo with a council of great nobles
Tibetan Empire.faith: Bon and Buddhism, the latter the faith of the state from 779

Gao Kaidao.x: The state of Gao Kaidao, a salt worker turned rebel who in the chaos at the end of Sui proclaimed himself King of Yan in northern Hebei, with his seat at Huairong and the Eastern Türks as his allies. Deserted by his officers as the Tang closed in, he killed his family and himself in 624.

Kashmir.x: The Himalayan kingdom of the Vale of Kashmir, ruled from Srinagar by the Karkota, Utpala, and Lohara dynasties, a seat of Sanskrit learning and Shaiva philosophy. Its greatest king, Lalitaditya Muktapida, raised the sun temple of Martand; the chronicle of its kings, Kalhana's Rajatarangini, is the finest history written in Sanskrit.
Kashmir.faith: Shaivism and Buddhism; Islam from the fourteenth century

Unified Silla.x: Silla after its conquest of Baekje and Goguryeo and its expulsion of the Tang, ruling the peninsula south of the Taedong from Gyeongju, then one of the great cities of Asia. Its golden age of Buddhist art, of Bulguksa and Seokguram, gave way in the ninth century to rebellion, and in 935 its last king yielded to Goryeo.

Second Turkic Khaganate.x: The Türk empire restored in 682 by Ilterish Qaghan after half a century under Tang rule, centred on the Ötüken highlands of the Orkhon. Under Qapaghan and Bilge Qaghan, with the counsellor Tonyukuk, it ruled the eastern steppe and left the Orkhon inscriptions, until the Uyghurs and their allies overthrew it in 744.

Balhae.x: The kingdom of Goguryeo exiles and Mohe tribes founded by Dae Joyeong in 698, which ruled Manchuria and northern Korea from five capitals laid out on the model of Chang'an. The Tang called it the Flourishing Land in the East; the Khitan destroyed it in 926.

Nara Japan.x: Japan of the Nara age, when the court sat at Heijō-kyō, a capital modelled on Chang'an, and governed by the ritsuryō codes of law. It was the age of the Kojiki and the Man'yōshū and of the Great Buddha of Tōdai-ji, and of monasteries grown so mighty that the court moved away in 784.
Nara Japan.gov: Imperial monarchy under the ritsuryō codes

Kannauj-Varman Dynasty.x: The kingdom of Yashovarman of Kannauj, who in the early eighth century revived the power of Harsha's old capital on the Ganges, kept the poets Bhavabhuti and Vakpati at his court, and sent an embassy to the Tang. He was beaten by Lalitaditya of Kashmir, and his line faded before the rise of the Pratiharas.

Nanzhao.x: A kingdom of the Erhai lake country in Yunnan, formed when Piluoge, chief of the southernmost of six chiefdoms, united the others with Tang help in 738. Turning on Tang, it destroyed two Chinese armies, allied in turn with Tibet and Tang, and raided Chengdu and Hanoi, until its minister Zheng Maisi overthrew the royal line in 902.

Uyghur Khaganate.x: The steppe empire of the Uyghurs, who overthrew the Second Turkic Khaganate in 744 and ruled Mongolia from their walled capital Ordu-Baliq on the Orkhon. They saved the Tang from An Lushan's rebels, took Manichaeism as the religion of their court, and grew rich on the horse and silk trade, until the Kyrgyz destroyed them in 840.

Qarlugs.x: The Karluks, a Turkic people of the Altai and later of the Ili and Chu valleys, whose defection decided the battle of the Talas in 751 and who took the old Türk lands around Suyab. Their yabgus ruled the Seven Rivers country until the rise of the Kara-Khanids, whose royal house many count among them.
Qarlugs.faith: Worship of Tengri, Buddhism, and Manichaeism; Islam from the tenth century

Heian Japan.x: Japan of the Heian age, when the imperial court at Kyoto, ruled in fact by the Fujiwara regents and later by retired emperors, created the kana scripts, the Pillow Book, and the Tale of Genji. In the provinces the warrior bands grew strong, and the Genpei War between the Taira and the Minamoto ended the age.
Heian Japan.gov: Imperial monarchy under Fujiwara regents and cloistered emperors
Heian Japan.faith: Buddhism of the Tendai, Shingon, and Pure Land schools, and Shinto

Tibetans.x: Tibet in the age of fragmentation after the fall of its empire, divided between the lines of Langdarma's sons Ösung and Yumtän, lords of the great clans, and rising monasteries. King Yeshe-Ö of Guge and the masters Atisha, Marpa, and Milarepa brought the second spreading of Buddhism; in 1247 the Sakya abbots made terms for Tibet with the Mongols.

Kara-Khanids.x: A Turkic dynasty, probably of Karluk stock, ruling the Seven Rivers country and Kashgar, which became the first Turkic royal house to embrace Islam under Satuq Bughra Khan. It overthrew the Samanids of Bukhara in 999, conquered Buddhist Khotan in 1006, and divided into eastern and western khanates about 1041.
Kara-Khanids.gov: Dual khaganate of a senior and a junior khan
Kara-Khanids.faith: Worship of Tengri; Sunni Islam from the tenth century

Qocho Kingdom.x: The kingdom of the Uyghurs who fled to the Turfan oasis after 840, ruling from Qocho and their summer seat at Beshbalik. They turned from Manichaeism to Buddhism and painted the cave temples of Bezeklik; their idiqut Barchuq Art Tegin submitted to Genghis Khan in 1209, among the first rulers to do so of his own will.
Qocho Kingdom.faith: Manichaeism, then Buddhism; a Nestorian Christian minority

Ganzhou Kingdom.x: A kingdom of Uyghurs who settled in the Gansu corridor around Ganzhou, the later Zhangye, after the fall of their steppe empire in 840. They traded horses to the Five Dynasties and the Song and fought the Tanguts, who took Ganzhou in 1028.

Kingdom of Khotan.x: The ancient Saka kingdom of the Khotan oasis on the southern Silk Road, famed for its jade, its silk, and its Buddhist learning, whose kings traced their line to a son of the Indian emperor Ashoka. Its king Visa Sambhava took the Chinese name Li Shengtian; the Kara-Khanids conquered it after a long war in 1006.

Hubaekje.x: Later Baekje, the kingdom proclaimed in southwestern Korea by the Silla general Gyeon Hwon in the name of old Baekje. He sacked Gyeongju in 927 and forced the Silla king to kill himself, but was deposed by his own son and fled to Wang Geon, who destroyed Later Baekje in 936.

(Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms).x: The half century of division after the fall of Tang in 907, when five short-lived dynasties followed one another in the north at Kaifeng and Luoyang, while ten kingdoms ruled the south and Shanxi. Generals made and unmade emperors, the Khitan took the Sixteen Prefectures, and the Song gathered the pieces together between 960 and 979.
(Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms).faith: Buddhism, Daoism, and Chinese popular religion

Liao Dynasty.x: The empire of the Khitan, founded by Abaoji, which ruled Manchuria, Mongolia, and the Sixteen Prefectures of northern China from five capitals. It governed nomads and farmers by separate laws, drew a rich yearly tribute from the Song, and was destroyed by its Jurchen subjects in 1125; its name, Cathay, lived on in the West.
Liao Dynasty.gov: Imperial monarchy with dual northern and southern administrations

Later Liang Dynasty.x: The first of the Five Dynasties, founded by Zhu Wen, once a lieutenant of the rebel Huang Chao, who ended the Tang in 907. Its long war with the Shatuo Jin along the Yellow River ended in 923, when Li Cunxu took Kaifeng and the last Liang emperor had himself killed.
rulers: Emperor Taizu of Later Liang (Zhu Wen)

Former Shu.x: A kingdom of Sichuan founded by Wang Jian, a one-time robber who rose to be a Tang general, and who proclaimed himself emperor at Chengdu when the Tang fell. His rich and cultivated court was ruined under his pleasure-loving son Wang Yan, who surrendered to the Later Tang in 925.

Southern Wu.x: The kingdom of Wu between the Huai and the Yangtze, founded by the Tang governor Yang Xingmi and ruled from Yangzhou. Real power passed to the regent Xu Wen and his adopted son Xu Zhigao, who took the throne in 937 and founded the Southern Tang.

Wuyue.x: The kingdom of the Qian family around Hangzhou, founded by Qian Liu, once a salt smuggler, who built great sea walls against the tides of the Qiantang. Peaceful and prosperous, it paid homage to the northern dynasties, and its last king, Qian Chu, gave his land to the Song without a fight in 978.

Qi Kingdom.x: The principality of Li Maozhen, the Tang military governor of Fengxiang west of Chang'an, who had been made Prince of Qi by the Tang and refused to recognize the Later Liang. He held out among the passes of the Wei valley until he submitted to the Later Tang in 924.

Taebong.x: The kingdom proclaimed in central Korea by Gung Ye, a disowned Silla prince turned monk and rebel, first as Later Goguryeo in 901 and from 911 as Taebong, with its capital at Cheorwon. He called himself the living Maitreya and grew so cruel that his generals overthrew him in 918 and made Wang Geon king.

Yan Kingdom.x: The short-lived Great Yan proclaimed at Youzhou, the later Beijing, by Liu Shouguang, a cruel warlord who had imprisoned his own father, Liu Rengong. The Jin prince Li Cunxu captured him in 913 and later put father and son to death.

Southern Chu.x: The kingdom of Ma Yin, a carpenter turned soldier, who ruled Hunan from Changsha and grew rich on tea and silk sold to the north. His sons quarrelled after his death, and Southern Tang overran the kingdom in 951; the officers of Hunan then drove the Tang out and ruled the province themselves until the Song came.

Min.x: A kingdom of Fujian founded by Wang Shenzhi, a Tang general from Henan, who ruled from Fuzhou, built schools, and opened the port of Quanzhou to Arab and Persian merchants. His heirs took the imperial title and murdered one another, and Southern Tang and Wuyue divided the kingdom in 945.

Goryeo.x: The Korean kingdom founded by Wang Geon in 918, which united the peninsula in 936 and ruled it from Kaesong for nearly five centuries; from its name comes Korea. It beat back the Khitan, endured a century of military dictators and thirty years of Mongol invasion, carved the Tripitaka Koreana, and made celadon of unrivalled beauty.
Goryeo.gov: Monarchy; military rule 1170 to 1270; Mongol vassal from 1270

Former Jin.x: The Shatuo Turkic state of Jin in Shanxi under Li Keyong and his son Li Cunxu, called Former Jin by later historians, which never recognized the Later Liang. Li Cunxu conquered Yan in 913, won the long war on the Yellow River, and in 923 proclaimed himself emperor of the Later Tang.

Later Tang.x: The second of the Five Dynasties, proclaimed in 923 by the Shatuo prince Li Cunxu, who destroyed the Later Liang and conquered Former Shu. A lover of actors who was killed in a mutiny in 926, he was followed by the able Li Siyuan; the dynasty fell in 936 when Shi Jingtang brought in the Khitan.
rulers: Emperor Zhuangzong of Later Tang (Li Cunxu)
Emperor Mingzong of Later Tang (Li Siyuan)

Jingnan.x: Also called Nanping, the smallest of the Ten Kingdoms, ruled by the Gao family from Jiangling on the middle Yangtze, which survived by paying homage to every neighbour and taxing the traffic on the river. It surrendered to the Song in 963.

Later Jin.x: The third of the Five Dynasties, founded by the Shatuo general Shi Jingtang with Khitan help in 936, at the price of the Sixteen Prefectures and of calling himself the Khitan emperor's son. When his nephew Shi Chonggui defied the Khitan, Yelü Deguang took Kaifeng in 947 and carried him off.
rulers: Emperor Gaozu of Later Jin (Shi Jingtang)

Later Shu.x: A kingdom of Sichuan founded by Meng Zhixiang, a Later Tang governor, in 934. Under his son Meng Chang, Chengdu flourished in peace and luxury, cut the classics on wooden blocks, and gathered the lyric anthology Among the Flowers; the Song conquered it in 965.

Southern Tang.x: The richest of the Ten Kingdoms, founded at Jinling, the later Nanjing, by Li Bian, who took the Tang imperial surname and dynastic name. Its court was famed for painting, ink, and paper; its last ruler, Li Yu, was a great lyric poet, who surrendered to the Song in 975 and died a captive three years later.

Later Han.x: The fourth and briefest of the Five Dynasties, founded at Kaifeng in 947 by the Shatuo general Liu Zhiyuan after the Khitan withdrew. When his young son Liu Chengyou murdered his ministers and plotted against the general Guo Wei, Guo marched on the capital and founded the Later Zhou in 951.
rulers: Emperor Gaozu of Later Han (Liu Zhiyuan)

Kingdom of Dali.x: The kingdom of the Duan family in Yunnan, founded in 937 at Yangjumie, the later Dali, beside Lake Erhai. A land of Buddhist kings, many of whom gave up the throne to become monks, it sold horses to the Song and was ruled in fact by the Gao ministers in its last age, until Kublai conquered it in 1253.
Kingdom of Dali.faith: Buddhism, especially the esoteric Azhali school

Later Zhou.x: The last of the Five Dynasties, founded in 951 by the general Guo Wei. His adopted son Chai Rong, Emperor Shizong, one of the ablest rulers of the age, reformed the army, beat Northern Han and Southern Tang, and won back part of the Sixteen Prefectures, but died young; in 960 his general Zhao Kuangyin took the throne.
rulers: Emperor Taizu of Later Zhou (Guo Wei)
Emperor Shizong of Later Zhou (Chai Rong)

Utpala Dynasty.x: The dynasty of Kashmir founded by Avantivarman in 855, whose engineer Suyya drained the marshes of the valley and tamed the Jhelum, and under whom the Shaiva philosophers of Kashmir flourished. After a century of palace guards and intrigue, power passed to the strong-willed Didda, who ruled as regent and then as queen until 1003.

Northern Han.x: The last surviving Shatuo state, founded at Taiyuan by Liu Min, brother of the Later Han founder, when Guo Wei took the throne in 951. Kept alive by the Liao as a buffer, it held out in the Shanxi mountains until the Song emperor Taizong took Taiyuan in 979 and razed it.

Northern Song.x: The Song dynasty while it ruled from Kaifeng, from Zhao Kuangyin's accession in 960 to the Jurchen capture of the capital in 1127. It was an age of scholar-officials chosen by examination, of printing, paper money, gunpowder, and the compass, and of a commercial economy unmatched in the world, though it never won back the north from the Liao.
Northern Song.gov: Imperial monarchy with a civil bureaucracy

Western Xia.x: The empire of the Tangut people, proclaimed by Li Yuanhao in 1038 on the Ordos and the Gansu corridor and ruled from Xingqing. It had a script of its own, printed Buddhist books by the thousand, and fought the Song and the Liao to a standstill, until the Mongols destroyed it in 1227.
rulers: Emperor Jingzong of Western Xia (Li Yuanhao)

Lohara Dynasty.x: The dynasty of Kashmir founded by Sangramaraja, nephew of Queen Didda, which ruled the valley for three centuries. Its age saw Mahmud of Ghazni turned back from the mountain fortress of Lohkot, the brilliant and ruinous reign of King Harsha, and the writing of Kalhana's Rajatarangini under Jayasimha.

Eastern Kara-Khanids.x: The eastern half of the divided Kara-Khanid realm, ruling Kashgar, Balasagun, and the Seven Rivers country. At its court in Kashgar Yusuf Khass Hajib wrote the Kutadgu Bilig, and Mahmud al-Kashgari, a prince of its house, compiled his great dictionary of the Turkic tongues at Baghdad; in the 1130s its khans became vassals of the Kara-Khitai.

Northern Fujiwara.x: The Ōshū Fujiwara, a family who ruled the far northern province of Mutsu for four generations from Hiraizumi, rich in gold and horses, and raised there the Golden Hall of Chūson-ji. They sheltered the fugitive hero Minamoto no Yoshitsune until Yasuhira, under threat, had him killed; Yoritomo destroyed them all the same in 1189.

Kara-Khitans.x: The Western Liao, founded by the Khitan prince Yelü Dashi, who fled west from the Jurchen, made himself Gurkhan, ruled from Balasagun, and crushed the Seljuk sultan Sanjar at Qatwan in 1141. A Buddhist court of Chinese style ruling Muslim vassals, it fell to the Naiman prince Kuchlug in 1211 and to the Mongols in 1218.
Kara-Khitans.gov: Khanate under the Gurkhan with Chinese-style administration
Kara-Khitans.faith: Buddhism and Khitan shamanism, over Muslim vassals

Great Jin.x: The empire of the Jurchen, founded by Aguda in 1115, which destroyed the Liao, took Kaifeng from the Song in 1127, and ruled northern China for a century. Its emperors moved their capital to Zhongdu, the later Beijing, took up Chinese ways, and were destroyed by the Mongols, who took Caizhou in 1234.
Great Jin.gov: Imperial monarchy with Jurchen military households

Southern Song.x: The Song dynasty after the loss of the north, ruling from Lin'an, the later Hangzhou, which Marco Polo called the finest city in the world. It was an age of Neo-Confucian philosophy, of landscape painting, and of a thriving sea trade; it withstood the Jin and for forty years the Mongols, until the boy emperor perished at Yamen in 1279.
Southern Song.gov: Imperial monarchy with a civil bureaucracy

Kamakura Shogunate.x: The first warrior government of Japan, set up at Kamakura by Minamoto no Yoritomo and ruled, after his line died out, by the Hōjō family as regents for puppet shoguns. It turned back the Mongol invasions of 1274 and 1281, but the cost ruined its vassals, and the supporters of Emperor Go-Daigo overthrew it in 1333.
Kamakura Shogunate.faith: Buddhism of the Zen, Pure Land, and Nichiren schools, and Shinto

Mongol Empire.x: The empire founded by Genghis Khan in 1206, which under him, his sons, and his grandsons became the largest land empire in history, from Korea to Hungary and from Siberia to Persia. Its armies destroyed Khwarazm, the Jin, the Abbasid caliphate, and the Song; after 1260 it divided into the Yuan, the Golden Horde, the Ilkhanate, and the Chagatai Khanate.
Mongol Empire.gov: Steppe empire under the Great Khan and the kurultai
Mongol Empire.faith: Worship of Tengri, with tolerance of all faiths

Yuan Dynasty.x: The Mongol dynasty in China, proclaimed by Kublai in 1271, which conquered the Song and ruled all China from Khanbaliq and the summer capital of Shangdu. It ranked its subjects by people, leaned on Muslim and Central Asian officials, and wasted itself on failed invasions of Japan and Java, until the Ming drove it to the steppe in 1368.
