Yuan Dynasty.gov: Imperial monarchy of the Great Khans
Yuan Dynasty.faith: Tibetan Buddhism at court; Confucianism, Daoism, Islam, and Christianity tolerated

Chagatai Khanate.x: The khanate of the heirs of Chagatai, second son of Genghis Khan, ruling Transoxiana, the Seven Rivers country, and the Tarim. In the fourteenth century it split: Transoxiana fell to Turkic emirs and at last to Timur, while the eastern khans of Moghulistan, Muslims since Tughlugh Timur, ruled the steppe and the oases into the fifteenth century.
Chagatai Khanate.faith: Worship of Tengri, then Sunni Islam from the fourteenth century

Kenmu Restoration.x: The brief restoration of direct imperial rule by Emperor Go-Daigo after the fall of the Kamakura shogunate in 1333. His favour to courtiers over the warriors who had won his victory drove Ashikaga Takauji into revolt; Takauji took Kyoto in 1336, and Go-Daigo fled to Yoshino, where his line kept a Southern Court for half a century.

Ashikaga Shogunate.x: The second warrior government of Japan, founded by Ashikaga Takauji in 1338 and ruled from the Muromachi quarter of Kyoto. Under Yoshimitsu it ended the schism of the two courts, traded with Ming China, and raised the Golden Pavilion; after the Ōnin War its shoguns were the puppets of warring lords, until Oda Nobunaga drove out the last in 1573.
Ashikaga Shogunate.faith: Zen and Pure Land Buddhism, and Shinto

Kashmiri Sultanate.x: The Muslim sultanate of the Vale of Kashmir, founded by Shah Mir in 1339 after the death of the last Hindu queen, Kota Rani. Under Sultan Sikandar the temples were thrown down and Islam spread by force and by the preaching of Persian Sufis; his son Zain-ul-Abidin restored tolerance and the arts. Akbar annexed the valley in 1586.
Kashmiri Sultanate.faith: Sunni Islam; Shia Islam under the Chak sultans

Tibet.x: Tibet from the fall of Sakya rule to the coming of the Chinese army, governed in turn by the Phagmodrupa princes, the Rinpungpa and Tsangpa lords of Tsang, and from 1642 by the Dalai Lamas of the Gelug church under Mongol and later Qing protection. The Thirteenth Dalai Lama declared independence in 1913; Chinese troops entered in 1950.
Tibet.gov: Princely rule, then the theocracy of the Dalai Lamas (Ganden Phodrang)
rulers: Fifth Dalai Lama, Ngawang Lobsang Gyatso

Ming Dynasty.x: The Chinese dynasty founded by Zhu Yuanzhang in 1368 after the expulsion of the Mongols, ruling from Nanjing and from 1421 from Beijing. It rebuilt the Great Wall in stone, sent Zheng He's fleets to Africa, raised the Forbidden City, and drew in the silver of the New World, until rebellion and the Manchus brought it down in 1644.
Ming Dynasty.gov: Imperial autocracy with a civil bureaucracy

Northern Yuan.x: The Mongol court after its flight from China in 1368, which kept the style of the Yuan emperors on the steppe. Crushed by the Ming at Buir Nor in 1388, the line of Kublai fell into a long struggle with the Oirats of the west, who made and unmade its khans for half a century.
Northern Yuan.faith: Worship of Tengri and Tibetan Buddhism

Joseon.x: The Korean dynasty of the Yi family, founded by Yi Seong-gye in 1392 and ruling from Hanseong, the later Seoul, for five centuries. A model Neo-Confucian state, it gave Korea the Hangul alphabet under King Sejong, survived the Japanese invasions of the 1590s and two Manchu invasions, and kept its ports shut until Japan forced them open in 1876.
Joseon.gov: Neo-Confucian monarchy with a yangban aristocracy
Joseon.faith: Neo-Confucianism; Buddhism suppressed; Catholic converts persecuted

Four Oirats.x: The western Mongols, a league of four peoples of the Altai and the upper Yenisei, who rose against the khans of Kublai's line after 1400. Under Toghon and his son Esen they mastered the steppe, and in 1449 Esen captured the Ming emperor at Tumu and later took the title of khan, before his murder in 1454.

Lodi Dynasty.x: The Afghan dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate, founded by Bahlul Lodi in 1451, which revived the sultanate's power across the Ganges plain. Sikandar Lodi founded Agra; Ibrahim Lodi, quarrelling with his Afghan nobles, was killed by Babur at Panipat in 1526, and the Mughal Empire began.
Lodi Dynasty.gov: Sultanate with an Afghan tribal nobility

Eastern Moghulistan.x: The eastern realm of the Chagatai khans of Moghulistan, centred on Turfan and the Tarim oases, which parted from the steppe khanate under Ahmad Alaq and his son Mansur Khan and later passed to the khans of Yarkent. Its khans fought the Ming at Hami and the Oirats on the steppe, until the Dzungars ended their line in 1680.

Moghulistan.x: The Mongol khanate of the Chagatayids on the steppes north of the Tian Shan, from Lake Balkhash to the Tarim, whose khans had turned to Islam under Tughlugh Timur. Yunus Khan, schooled in Persian letters, won Tashkent and ruled the steppe; his heirs lost it to the Uzbeks, the Kazakhs, and the Kyrgyz.

Mongol Khanate.x: The eastern Mongols under khans of Kublai's line, reunited by Dayan Khan and Queen Mandukhai at the end of the fifteenth century and divided among his sons into six tümens. The senior Chahar khans lost power to princes such as Altan Khan; the last, Ligdan Khan, died fleeing the Manchus in 1634, and his son surrendered the next year.

Warring States Japan.x: Japan in the Sengoku age, from the Ōnin War to the unification, when the shogun's authority collapsed and daimyo fought for land from their castles, while armed leagues of Pure Land believers held whole provinces. Muskets and Christianity came from Portugal, and Oda Nobunaga and Toyotomi Hideyoshi brought the warring provinces to heel.
Warring States Japan.gov: Rival daimyo domains under a powerless shogunate

Eastern Chagatai Khanate.x: The Chagatai khanate of the Moghul steppes north of the Tian Shan under Sultan Mahmud Khan, son of Yunus, who ruled from Tashkent and the Issyk Kul country until the Uzbek Muhammad Shaybani beat him and put him to death in 1508.

Western Moghulistan.x: The steppe lands of Moghulistan around Issyk Kul and the Tian Shan after the Chagatai khans withdrew to the Tarim oases. Through the sixteenth century they were fought over by the last Moghul princes, the Kazakhs, and the Kyrgyz, whose tribes came to hold the mountains of the later Kyrgyzstan.

Sur Empire.x: The Afghan empire of Sher Shah Suri, who drove the Mughal Humayun out of India in 1540 and in five years reordered the north, rebuilding the Grand Trunk Road, minting the silver rupee, and measuring the land for taxation. His heirs quarrelled, and Humayun came back to take Delhi in 1555.

Tümed.x: The Tümed Mongols of the Yin Mountains and the Ordos borderlands, who under Altan Khan became the strongest power of the eastern steppe, burned the suburbs of Beijing in 1550, built Kökeqota, and brought the Gelug faith and the title of Dalai Lama to the Mongols. They submitted to the Manchus in the 1630s and became banners.

Khoshut Khanate.x: The khanate of the Khoshut, a western Mongol people led by Güshi Khan, who moved into the Kokonor country in the 1630s, destroyed the enemies of the Gelug church, and made the Fifth Dalai Lama master of Tibet in 1642. His heirs ruled Kokonor and bore the title King of Tibet until the Dzungars killed Lha-bzang Khan in 1717.

Gorkha Kingdom.x: A hill kingdom of central Nepal ruled by the Shah dynasty from its fortress-palace at Gorkha, founded by Drabya Shah in 1559. From there Prithvi Narayan Shah set out to conquer the Kathmandu valley, taking it in 1768 and founding the Kingdom of Nepal.

Toyotomi Japan.x: Japan under Toyotomi Hideyoshi, the low-born general who completed the unification begun by Oda Nobunaga, took the offices of regent and chancellor, surveyed the land, disarmed the peasants in his sword hunt, and fixed the classes. His invasions of Korea failed, and after his death in 1598 the guardians of his young son fell out, to Tokugawa Ieyasu's profit.
Toyotomi Japan.gov: Military hegemony exercised through the imperial regency
Toyotomi Japan.faith: Buddhism and Shinto; Christianity banned from 1587

Tokugawa Shogunate.x: The warrior government founded by Tokugawa Ieyasu after Sekigahara, which ruled Japan from Edo through two and a half centuries of peace. It bound the daimyo by enforced residence at Edo, crushed Christianity, and closed the country to all but the Dutch and Chinese at Nagasaki, until the American ships of 1853 set in motion its fall in 1868.
Tokugawa Shogunate.faith: Buddhism, Shinto, and Neo-Confucianism; Christianity proscribed

Dzungar Khanate.x: The last great steppe empire, built in the seventeenth century by the Choros and allied Oirat peoples of Dzungaria, which conquered the Tarim oases, overran the Khalkha, and in 1717 sacked Lhasa. It fought the Qing for seventy years, until the Qianlong Emperor destroyed it and the greater part of its people in the 1750s.

Oirat Confederation.x: The league of the western Mongol peoples, the Choros, Torghuts, Dörbets, and Khoshuts, who in 1640 joined the eastern Mongols in the great code of laws agreed in the Tarbagatai and gave birth to the Dzungar, Khoshut, and Kalmyk khanates. The Torghuts moved west to the Volga; the Choros of Dzungaria came to lead those who stayed.
Oirat Confederation.faith: Tibetan Buddhism; the Zaya Pandita devised the Clear Script in 1648

Later Jin Dynasty.x: The Jurchen state proclaimed by Nurhaci in 1616, named after the Jin of his forefathers and built on the banners that organized every family for war. It broke the Ming at Sarhū, took Liaodong, and moved its capital to Mukden; in 1636 his son Hong Taiji renamed it the Qing.
Later Jin Dynasty.gov: Khanate organized in the Eight Banners

Li Zicheng.x: The realm of Li Zicheng, a dismissed post-station attendant who became the greatest rebel of the late Ming, proclaimed the Shun dynasty at Xi'an early in 1644, and took Beijing in April. Routed by Wu Sangui and the Manchus at the Shanhai Pass, he fled west and was killed in Hubei in 1645.

Qing Dynasty.x: The Manchu dynasty proclaimed by Hong Taiji in 1636, which conquered China after 1644 and under the Kangxi, Yongzheng, and Qianlong emperors ruled the largest empire in Chinese history, from Mongolia and Tibet to Xinjiang and Taiwan. Weakened by the Opium Wars, the Taiping rebellion, and defeat by Japan, it fell in the revolution of 1911.
Qing Dynasty.gov: Imperial monarchy of the Manchu banners with a Chinese bureaucracy
Qing Dynasty.faith: Confucianism, Buddhism, Daoism, and Manchu shamanism

Southern Ming.x: The Ming loyalist courts of the south after the fall of Beijing in 1644, at Nanjing, Fuzhou, Zhaoqing, and at last Kunming, whose emperors the Qing took one by one. The last, the Yongli Emperor, was strangled at Kunming in 1662; Koxinga's house in Taiwan kept the Ming calendar until 1683.
Southern Ming.faith: Neo-Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism; Catholic converts at the Yongli court

Sikhs.x: The Sikh rising led by Banda Singh Bahadur, sent to the Punjab by the tenth Guru, Gobind Singh, which sacked Sirhind in 1710 to avenge the execution of the Guru's young sons, broke up the great estates, and struck coins in the Gurus' name at Lohgarh. The Mughals took Banda in 1715 and executed him at Delhi in 1716.

Sikh Confederacy.x: The twelve misls, warrior bands of the Sikh Khalsa that rose in the Punjab amid the wars of the Afghans and the decline of the Mughals. They met twice a year at Amritsar, drove out the armies of Ahmad Shah Durrani and his heirs, and were united by force under Ranjit Singh, who took Lahore in 1799.
Sikh Confederacy.gov: Confederacy of misls under the Sarbat Khalsa

Kingdom of Nepal.x: The kingdom founded by Prithvi Narayan Shah of Gorkha, who took the Kathmandu valley from the Malla kings in 1768 and made Kathmandu his capital. His heirs carried the conquest east and west along the Himalaya, until war with Tibet brought a Qing army over the mountains in 1792.

Rajput states.x: The Hindu princely states of Rajputana, Mewar, Marwar, Jaipur, Bikaner, and their neighbours, ruled by Rajput clans who traced their lines to the sun and the moon. Wasted by Maratha and Pindari raids, they accepted British paramountcy by the treaties of 1818 and kept their thrones until 1947.

Nepal.x: The Himalayan kingdom of the Shah dynasty, which lost its western conquests to the British in 1816 but kept its independence; from 1846 to 1951 the Rana family ruled as hereditary prime ministers. After a decade of Maoist insurgency and the massacre of the royal family in 2001, the monarchy was abolished in 2008.
Nepal.gov: Hindu monarchy; Rana premiership 1846 to 1951; federal republic from 2008

Sikh Empire.x: The empire built by Maharaja Ranjit Singh, the Lion of the Punjab, who took Lahore in 1799 and with an army drilled by French and Italian officers conquered Multan, Kashmir, and Peshawar. After his death in 1839 the court fell to murder and intrigue, and the British annexed the Punjab after two hard-fought wars in 1849.
Sikh Empire.faith: Sikhism, over Muslim and Hindu subjects

Kashmir and Jammu.x: The princely state formed when the British, after the First Anglo-Sikh War, sold the Vale of Kashmir to the Dogra raja Gulab Singh of Jammu for seventy-five lakh rupees by the Treaty of Amritsar. Its Hindu maharajas ruled a mostly Muslim people; in 1947 Hari Singh acceded to India, and the state was divided by war.
Kashmir and Jammu.faith: Hindu dynasty over a Muslim majority

Taiping Heavenly Kingdom.x: The rebel state of Hong Xiuquan, who after feverish visions proclaimed himself the younger brother of Jesus Christ, a heresy that horrified the missionaries, and led his God Worshippers from Guangxi to Nanjing, their Heavenly Capital, in 1853. It forbade opium, footbinding, and idols and held the lower Yangtze for eleven years, until Zeng Guofan's armies stormed Nanjing in 1864.
Taiping Heavenly Kingdom.gov: Theocratic monarchy of the Heavenly King
Taiping Heavenly Kingdom.faith: Hong Xiuquan's heretical sect, drawn from Protestant tracts

Dali Sultanate.x: The Muslim state set up at Dali in western Yunnan by Du Wenxiu, styled Sultan Suleiman, during the Panthay rebellion of the Hui against the Qing. It ruled half of Yunnan and sought help from Britain; when the Qing closed in, Du Wenxiu took poison and gave himself up in 1872, and the city was put to the sword.

Empire of Japan.x: The Japanese state from the Meiji Restoration to defeat in 1945, which in two generations made itself an industrial and military power, beat China and Russia, and ruled Taiwan, Korea, and Manchuria. Its army drove it into war with China in 1937 and with the United States and Britain in 1941, and the war ended in atomic ruin and surrender.
Empire of Japan.gov: Constitutional monarchy under a sacred emperor, dominated by the military from the 1930s

Korean Empire.x: The empire proclaimed by King Gojong in 1897 to assert Korea's equality with China and Japan, which built railways, telegraphs, and electric trams in Seoul. Japan, victorious over Russia, made it a protectorate in 1905, forced Gojong to abdicate in 1907, and annexed it in 1910.

Republic of China.x: The republic founded after the revolution of 1911, which ruled China through the warlord years from Beijing and from 1928 under the Nationalists from Nanjing. It fought Japan from 1937 to 1945 and lost the civil war to the Communists in 1949, withdrawing to Taiwan, where it became a prosperous democracy.
Republic of China.gov: Republic; Nationalist one-party rule 1928 to 1987; democracy from the 1990s
Republic of China.faith: Chinese popular religion, Buddhism, Daoism, and Christianity

Great Mongol State.x: The Bogd Khanate of Mongolia, proclaimed at Urga in 1911 under the Jebtsundamba Khutughtu as Holy Emperor when the Qing fell. Reduced to autonomy under China in 1915 and occupied by Chinese troops in 1919, it was restored by Ungern-Sternberg and then by the revolutionaries of 1921, and became a people's republic at the Bogd Khan's death.

Republic of Uryankhay.x: The Uryankhay country of the upper Yenisei, the later Tuva, whose Tuvan nobles broke from Qing rule as the dynasty fell. Its fate was disputed between Mongolia, China, and Russia, which declared a protectorate over it in 1914.

Empire of China.x: The short-lived monarchy of Yuan Shikai, president of the Republic, who accepted the throne in December 1915 as the Hongxian Emperor. Revolt in Yunnan and the southern provinces and the desertion of his own generals forced him to give it up after eighty-three days, and he died in June 1916.

Tuvan People's Republic.x: The People's Republic of Tannu Tuva on the upper Yenisei, set up under Soviet protection after the Russian civil war. Its communist party under Salchak Toka purged lamas and nomad princes on the Soviet model, and in 1944 the republic was quietly annexed by the Soviet Union.

Provisional Priamurye Government.x: The last White government of the Russian civil war, set up at Vladivostok in 1921 by the merchant brothers Spiridon and Nikolai Merkulov under the protection of the Japanese army. When the Japanese withdrew in 1922, the forces of General Mikhail Diterikhs were beaten, and the Red Army entered Vladivostok in October.

Mongolian People's Republic.x: The communist state proclaimed in Outer Mongolia in 1924, the second in the world after the Soviet Union, on which it depended. Under Choibalsan it destroyed the monasteries and killed tens of thousands of lamas and nobles in the purges of the 1930s; under Tsedenbal it was collectivized and settled, until the peaceful revolution of 1990.

Nationalist Government.x: The government of the Kuomintang at Canton, built by Sun Yat-sen with Soviet advisers and Communist allies and from 1925 constituted as the National Government under Wang Jingwei. Chiang Kai-shek's Northern Expedition carried it to Wuhan and Nanjing in 1926 and 1927, where it split between left and right before reuniting under Chiang.
Nationalist Government.faith: Chinese popular religion, Buddhism, and Christianity

Chinese Communists.x: The Communist base areas of the Jinggang Mountains and southern Jiangxi, where Mao Zedong and Zhu De built the Red Army among the peasants after the defeats of 1927, dividing the land and beating off the Nationalist encirclement campaigns. In 1931 they proclaimed the Chinese Soviet Republic at Ruijin.

Anti-Kuomintang Coalition.x: The alliance of the warlords Yan Xishan and Feng Yuxiang with the Guangxi generals Li Zongren and Bai Chongxi against Chiang Kai-shek in the Central Plains War of 1930, with a rival government at Beiping under Yan Xishan and Wang Jingwei. Beaten when Zhang Xueliang sided with Chiang, its southern remnant set up a rival government at Canton in 1931.

Manchukuo.x: The puppet state set up by Japan's Kwantung Army in Manchuria after the Mukden Incident, with the last Qing emperor, Puyi, as chief executive and from 1934 as the Kangde Emperor. Japan built mines, steel mills, and railways there and planted colonists, and the Soviet invasion of August 1945 destroyed it in days.
Manchukuo.gov: Puppet monarchy under the Kwantung Army

Japanese-occupied territory.x: The lands of China and Southeast Asia held by the Japanese army and navy between the Mukden Incident and the surrender of 1945, ruled by military governments and puppet regimes such as Wang Jingwei's at Nanjing, under the banner of the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere. Occupation brought forced labour, massacres, and famine.
Japanese-occupied territory.faith: State Shinto imposed beside local faiths

Communist-held China.x: The territory held by the Chinese Communist Party from the end of the Long March to its victory in the civil war, centred on Yan'an in the loess country of northern Shaanxi. Uneasily allied with the Nationalists against Japan, the Communists spread behind the Japanese lines, and after 1945 seized Manchuria and launched the campaigns that won the mainland.

Occupied Japan.x: Japan under Allied occupation after the surrender of 1945, governed through the Japanese state by General Douglas MacArthur as Supreme Commander. The occupation disarmed the country, purged militarists, broke up the great estates and the zaibatsu, and gave Japan the pacifist constitution of 1947, before the Treaty of San Francisco restored its sovereignty in 1952.
Occupied Japan.gov: Military occupation over a constitutional monarchy

East Turkestan Republic.x: The Second East Turkestan Republic, proclaimed at Ghulja in the Ili valley in 1944 by Uyghur and Kazakh rebels against Nationalist Chinese rule in Xinjiang, with Soviet arms and advisers. It joined a coalition government of Xinjiang in 1946, and in 1949 its leaders died in an air crash on the way to Beijing as the People's Liberation Army arrived.

US-occupied Korea.x: Korea south of the 38th parallel under the United States Army Military Government after the Japanese surrender, while the Soviet army held the north. Under General John R. Hodge it put down left-wing risings and prepared the elections of 1948, which made Syngman Rhee president of the Republic of Korea.

Democratic People's Republic of Korea.x: The communist state of northern Korea, founded in 1948 under Kim Il Sung with Soviet backing, which invaded the south in 1950. Ruled by three generations of the Kim family under the doctrine of Juche, it suffered famine in the 1990s while building nuclear weapons, and remains the most closed state on earth.
Democratic People's Republic of Korea.faith: State atheism and the cult of the Kims; religion persecuted

Republic of Korea.x: The state of southern Korea, founded in 1948 under Syngman Rhee and saved by the United Nations in the Korean War. Under the stern rule of Park Chung-hee it grew from poverty into an industrial power, and after the June Struggle of 1987 it became a democracy and one of the richest nations of Asia.

People's Republic of China.x: The communist state proclaimed by Mao Zedong in 1949, which unified the mainland, fought the United States in Korea, and passed through the famine of the Great Leap and the terror of the Cultural Revolution. From 1978 Deng Xiaoping's reforms opened it to markets and foreign capital, and it became the second economy of the world and a great power.
People's Republic of China.faith: State atheism; Buddhism, Daoism, Islam, and Christianity under state control

Japan.x: Postwar Japan, restored to sovereignty in 1952 under its pacifist constitution and allied to the United States, which rose from ruin to become the second economy of the world by 1968. After its asset bubble burst in 1990 it entered decades of slow growth; it remains a constitutional monarchy, governed mostly by the Liberal Democratic Party.

Mongolia.x: The democratic republic of Mongolia, which took a new constitution in 1992 after the peaceful revolution of 1990 and dropped the word People's from its name. Wedged between Russia and China, it lives by its herds and its great copper and coal mines, and honours Genghis Khan as the founder of the nation.

Kyrgyzstan.x: The mountain republic of the Kyrgyz in the Tian Shan, independent since the breakup of the Soviet Union in 1991. Its first president, Askar Akayev, and his successor, Kurmanbek Bakiyev, were driven out by popular revolts in 2005 and 2010, and in 2020 a third uprising brought Sadyr Japarov to power.

Indus Valley Civilization.x: The Bronze Age civilization of the Indus and Ghaggar-Hakra valleys, the most extensive of its age, with planned cities of baked brick such as Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, and Dholavira, covered drains, standard weights, and an undeciphered script. It traded with Mesopotamia, which knew it as Meluhha, and faded after about 1900 B.C.
Indus Valley Civilization.gov: Unknown; no kings or palaces identified
Indus Valley Civilization.faith: Unknown; ritual bathing and fire altars attested

(Mahajanapadas).x: The sixteen great realms of northern India named in Buddhist and Jain scripture, kingdoms such as Magadha, Kosala, Avanti, and Vatsa and clan republics such as the Vajji league, in the age of the second rise of cities, the first coins, and the Buddha and Mahavira. Magadha swallowed its rivals and became the core of the first Indian empire.
(Mahajanapadas).faith: Vedic religion; rise of Buddhism and Jainism

Magadha - Haryanka dynasty.x: The first imperial house of Magadha in the Ganges plain, founded by Bimbisara, patron of the Buddha. Bimbisara annexed Anga; his son Ajatashatru crushed the Vajji republics, fought Kosala, and fortified Pataligrama; Udayin made Pataliputra the capital. Buddhist tradition says every generation of the line was stained by parricide until the people deposed it.
Magadha - Haryanka dynasty.faith: Vedic religion; patrons of Buddhism and Jainism

Magadha - Shaishunaga dynasty.x: The dynasty that succeeded the Haryankas in Magadha, founded by Shishunaga, a minister raised to the throne by the people, who annexed the old rival kingdom of Avanti. Under his son Kalashoka the Second Buddhist Council met at Vaishali. The line was overthrown by Mahapadma Nanda about 345 B.C.

Nanda Empire.x: The first great empire of northern India, founded by Mahapadma Nanda, a ruler of low birth who overthrew the old warrior houses and ruled from Pataliputra over the Ganges plain and Kalinga. Famed for its treasure and its army, whose report helped turn Alexander's men back at the Hyphasis, it fell to Chandragupta Maurya about 321 B.C.

Maurya Empire.x: The first empire to unite almost the whole Indian subcontinent, founded by Chandragupta Maurya and ruled from Pataliputra. Its third emperor, Ashoka, turned to Buddhism after conquering Kalinga, carved his edicts of dhamma across the land, and sent envoys abroad. After him the empire shrank, and it ended when Pushyamitra Shunga slew Brihadratha.
Maurya Empire.faith: Vedic religion, Jainism, and Buddhism; Ashoka's dhamma

Kalinga.x: The kingdom of the eastern coast between the Mahanadi and the Godavari, which Megasthenes credited with an army of sixty thousand foot, a thousand horse, and seven hundred elephants. Its conquest by Ashoka about 261 B.C. turned him to the Buddha; it was then governed from Tosali until it rose again under the Mahameghavahana kings.

Anurādhapura.x: The first great Sinhalese kingdom of Lanka, ruled for some fourteen centuries from the sacred city of Anuradhapura, where Mahinda brought Buddhism in the third century B.C. Its kings raised colossal stupas and a vast web of irrigation tanks. Often invaded from South India, it fell to the Cholas, who took the city in 993 and the king in 1017.

Early Pandyas.x: The Pandya kings of the far south in the age of the Tamil Sangam poems, ruling from Madurai over the pearl fisheries of the Gulf of Mannar. Megasthenes knew their land, and Strabo records an embassy from a king Pandion to Augustus. Their power waned under the obscure Kalabhras from the fourth century A.D.

Early Cholas.x: The Chola kings of the Kaveri delta celebrated in the Sangam poems, ruling from Uraiyur and the port of Puhar, whose ships traded with the Roman world and Southeast Asia. Their most famous king, Karikala, won the battle of Venni and is remembered for the Kallanai weir on the Kaveri. They sank into obscurity after the third century.

Early Cheras.x: The Chera kings of the Malabar coast in the Sangam age, lords of the pepper country whose port of Muziris drew Roman shipping each monsoon. The epic Silappatikaram names the Chera prince Ilango as its author and makes King Senguttuvan the hero who carried a Himalayan stone south to carve an image of the faithful wife Kannagi.

Greco-Bactrian Kingdom.x: The Greek kingdom founded by the Seleucid satrap Diodotus between the Hindu Kush and the Oxus, rich in irrigated oases and caravan trade, with Greek cities such as Ai-Khanoum. Its kings Euthydemus and Demetrius carried Greek arms into India, and its coins are among the finest of antiquity. It fell to Saka and Yuezhi nomads about 130 B.C.
Greco-Bactrian Kingdom.faith: Greek religion; Zoroastrian and Buddhist subjects

Satavahana Dynasty.x: The Andhra kings who ruled the Deccan for some four centuries from Pratishthana and later Dhanyakataka, linking the trade of the western ports with the eastern coast. Patrons of Buddhist caves and of the stupas of Sanchi and Amaravati, they warred long with the Saka satraps; Gautamiputra Satakarni was the greatest of their line.

Shunga Empire.x: The dynasty founded by the Brahmin general Pushyamitra Shunga, who slew the last Maurya about 185 B.C. Ruling the Ganges heartland from Pataliputra and Vidisha, the Shungas fought the Indo-Greeks and Kalinga and revived the Vedic horse sacrifice, while the stupas of Bharhut and Sanchi were raised. The last king, Devabhuti, was murdered by his minister Vasudeva Kanva.

Mahameghavahana Dynasty.x: The Jain kings of Kalinga who rose after the fall of the Mauryas. Their great king Kharavela recorded in the Hathigumpha inscription at Udayagiri thirteen years of building, festivals, and campaigns against the Satavahanas, Magadha, and the Greeks of the north, and the recovery of a Jain image carried off by the Nandas.

Indo-Scythians.x: The Saka nomads who, driven south by the Yuezhi, entered India by way of Sistan and the Indus and won Gandhara, the Punjab, and Mathura under Maues and the Azes kings in the first century B.C. Their satraps ruled on in western India for centuries, and the era named for Azes dated the inscriptions of Gandhara.

Indo-Greeks.x: The Greek kingdoms south of the Hindu Kush founded when Demetrius invaded India about 180 B.C., ruled by some forty kings known chiefly from their coins in Greek and Kharoshthi. Menander, the Milinda of Buddhist tradition, ruling from Sagala, was the greatest. They yielded to Sakas, Parthians, and Kushans, the last fading in the eastern Punjab about A.D. 10.
Indo-Greeks.gov: Hellenistic monarchies, often several at once

Dayuan.x: The Chinese name for the Fergana valley and its people, whose walled towns, vineyards, and famous blood-sweating horses Zhang Qian described. When its king refused horses to the Han emperor Wu and slew his envoy, Han armies besieged its capital in 102 and 101 B.C. and set a compliant king on the throne.

Kanva Dynasty.x: The brief Brahmin dynasty founded when Vasudeva Kanva, minister of the last Shunga king Devabhuti, had his master murdered and took the throne. Four Kanva kings ruled a shrinking realm in Magadha for some forty-five years, until the last, Susharman, was overthrown, the Puranas say, by an Andhra king of the Satavahana house.

Indo-Parthians.x: The Parthian princes of Sistan who under Gondophares wrested Arachosia, Gandhara, and the Punjab from the Indo-Scythians early in the first century A.D. The Acts of Thomas set the Apostle's mission at the court of Gondophares. Their realm passed to the Kushans in the later first century.

Kushan Empire.x: The empire of the Kushan clan of the Yuezhi, founded by Kujula Kadphises and reaching at its height under Kanishka from the Oxus to the Ganges. Astride the Silk Road between Rome, Parthia, and China, it saw the art of Gandhara and Mathura, the first images of the Buddha, and the passage of Buddhism into Central Asia and China.

Western Satraps.x: The Saka satraps of western India, the Kshaharatas of Nahapana and the long line of Chashtana, who ruled Gujarat, Malwa, and Sind from Ujjain for some three centuries. Rudradaman left the first long Sanskrit inscription at Junagadh, and their dated silver coins give an unbroken chronology. Chandragupta II of the Guptas destroyed them about A.D. 400.

Western Kushans.x: The Kushan lands of Bactria and the Kabul valley in the third century, after the empire split, when Kushan kings still held the west before the Sasanian Persians annexed it as Kushanshahr under princes of their own house. The eastern Kushans lingered on in Gandhara and the Punjab.

Vakataka Kingdom.x: The Brahmin dynasty that ruled the Deccan between the Narmada and the Krishna from the third to the fifth century, in two branches seated at Nandivardhana and Vatsagulma. Allied by marriage to the Guptas, it was governed for years by the Gupta princess Prabhavatigupta as regent. Under Harishena its ministers carved and painted the great caves of Ajanta.
Vakataka Kingdom.faith: Hinduism (Shaiva and Vaishnava); patrons of Buddhism

Indo-Sasanian Empire.x: The Kushano-Sasanian kingdom, ruled by princes of the Persian royal house as Kushanshahs, kings of the Kushans, over Bactria, the Kabul valley, and at times Gandhara, after Ardashir I and Shapur I overthrew the Kushans in the west. Their coins in the Kushan manner show Shiva and his bull beside Iranian gods. The Kidarites overran it in the fourth century.

Late Pallava Empire.x: The Pallava kings of Kanchipuram, masters of the northern Tamil country and rivals of the Chalukyas and Pandyas. Mahendravarman I and Narasimhavarman I, conqueror of Vatapi, cut the first rock temples of the south and the reliefs and rathas of Mamallapuram, and their script carried Indian letters to Southeast Asia. The Cholas overthrew them about 897.
Late Pallava Empire.faith: Hinduism (Shaiva and Vaishnava); Jainism and Buddhism

Gupta Empire.x: The empire of India's classical age, founded by Chandragupta I and enlarged by Samudragupta and Chandragupta II from the Ganges to the Narmada and the Arabian Sea. Its centuries saw Kalidasa's poetry, Aryabhata's astronomy, the decimal numerals, Nalanda, and the shaping of Hindu temple art. Hun invasions and ambitious vassals broke it in the sixth century.
Gupta Empire.gov: Monarchy (King of Kings with vassal kings)

Kamarupa Kingdom.x: The kingdom of the Brahmaputra valley in Assam, ruled in turn by the Varman, Mlechchha, and Pala dynasties. Its king Bhaskaravarman, ally of Harsha, received Xuanzang about 643. Rich in elephants, silk, and aloe-wood, it was the first state of Assam known to history, and broke into local kingdoms in the twelfth century.

Kadamba Empire.x: The first native dynasty of Karnataka, founded at Banavasi about A.D. 345 by the Brahmin Mayurasharma after an insult at the Pallava court of Kanchi. Its kings ruled the western Deccan and the Konkan, were the first to use Kannada in their records, and fought the Pallavas and Gangas until the Chalukyas of Badami absorbed them in the sixth century.

Kalabhra Dynasty.x: An obscure dynasty that overran the Tamil country between the fourth and sixth centuries, ending the Sangam kingdoms of the Cholas, Pandyas, and Cheras. Later Hindu records call their rule an evil age, but Buddhist and Jain learning flourished under them. The Pandya Kadungon and the Pallava Simhavishnu overthrew them late in the sixth century.

Kidarites.x: A Hunnic people named for their king Kidara, who seized Bactria from the Kushano-Sasanians in the fourth century and then Gandhara and Kashmir, striking coins in the style of the Kushan kings. They fought the Sasanians and the Guptas, and were driven from Bactria by the Hephthalites and from Gandhara by the Alchon Huns in the fifth century.

Xionites.x: The Chionitae of the Roman historian Ammianus, a Hunnic people of the Oxus lands who warred with Shapur II of Persia and then, as his allies, besieged Amida in 359 under their king Grumbates, whose son fell before its walls. They were the forerunners of the Kidarites and Hephthalites.

White Huns.x: The Hephthalites and their kin the Alchon Huns, steppe peoples who mastered Bactria and Sogdia in the fifth century, slew Shah Peroz in 484, and under Toramana and Mihirakula invaded northern India and shattered the Gupta Empire. Persians and Turks destroyed the Hephthalites about 557; the Alchons, thrown back by Yashodharman, faded away.
White Huns.faith: Shaivism among the Alchon kings; Buddhist, Zoroastrian, and Hindu subjects

Maitraka Dynasty.x: The dynasty founded by the general Bhatarka, a Gupta officer, which ruled Saurashtra and Gujarat from Valabhi for three centuries. Valabhi was a seat of Buddhist learning that rivalled Nalanda and the city where the Jain canon was written down. Arab raiders from Sind are held to have destroyed it late in the eighth century.

Chalukya Dynasty.x: The Chalukyas of Badami, who ruled the Deccan from Vatapi in the sixth to eighth centuries. Pulakeshin II threw back Harsha on the Narmada, and its builders at Aihole, Badami, and Pattadakal set side by side the southern and northern temple styles. The Pallavas sacked Vatapi in 642, and the Rashtrakuta Dantidurga overthrew the line in 753.

Maukhari Dynasty.x: The Maukharis of Kannauj, once vassals of the Guptas, who ruled the middle Ganges plain in the sixth century and made Kannauj an imperial city. Their last king, Grahavarman, husband of Harsha's sister Rajyashri, was killed in 606 by the king of Malwa, and the kingdom passed to Harsha.

Turk Shahis.x: The Buddhist Turkic kings of Kabul and Kapisa in the seventh to ninth centuries, heirs of the Western Turks and the Hephthalites, who withstood the Arab advance from Sistan for two centuries and were honoured as allies by Tang China. Their Brahmin minister Kallar overthrew the last of them, Lagaturman, and founded the Hindu Shahi dynasty.

Karkota Dynasty.x: The kings of Kashmir in the seventh to ninth centuries, founded by Durlabhavardhana, in whose reign Xuanzang studied in the valley. Lalitaditya Muktapida made Kashmir a power reaching into the Punjab and Central Asia and built the Sun temple of Martand. Kalhana's chronicle preserves their deeds.

Pandya Dynasty.x: The first Pandya empire of the far south, revived about 590 by Kadungon after the Kalabhra interregnum and ruling from Madurai over the Tamil country between the Kaveri and Cape Comorin. Its kings fought the Pallavas and invaded Lanka. The Cholas under Parantaka I overthrew it early in the tenth century.

Gauda Kingdom.x: The kingdom of Bengal under Shashanka, the first known king of a united Bengal, who ruled from Karnasuvarna. He killed Harsha's brother Rajyavardhana in 606 and was remembered by the Buddhists, through Xuanzang, as a persecutor who cut down the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya.

Harsha's Empire.x: The empire of Harsha of the Pushyabhuti house, who came to the throne of Thanesar in 606 and ruled northern India from Kannauj, the last great native empire of the north before the Turks. Poet, playwright, and patron of Buddhism, he is known through Bana's Harshacharita and the memoirs of Xuanzang. It broke apart at his death in 647.

Khadga Dynasty.x: A Buddhist dynasty of the seventh century that ruled Samatata and Vanga in eastern Bengal from Karmanta, near modern Comilla. Known from its copper-plate grants and the reports of Chinese pilgrims, it was among the chief patrons of Buddhism in Bengal before the Palas.

Gurjara-Pratihara Dynasty.x: The Rajput imperial house that turned back the Arabs of Sind in the eighth century and from Kannauj ruled most of northern India in the ninth. The Arab Sulaiman judged its cavalry the finest in India and its king the sternest foe of the Arabs. Worn down by the Rashtrakutas, it was shattered by Mahmud of Ghazni in 1018.

Pala Empire.x: The Buddhist dynasty of Bengal and Bihar founded about 750 by Gopala, chosen king to end anarchy. Dharmapala and Devapala made it a great power contending for Kannauj, and the Palas endowed Nalanda, Vikramashila, and Somapura, whence Buddhism passed to Tibet. Ramapala revived it after the revolt of the Kaivartas; the Senas supplanted it in the twelfth century.
Pala Empire.faith: Mahayana and Vajrayana Buddhism; Hindu subjects

Rashtrakuta Dynasty.x: The Deccan empire founded by Dantidurga, who overthrew the Chalukyas of Badami in 753. Its kings raided to the Ganges and the Kaveri, carved the Kailasa temple at Ellora, and ruled from Manyakheta, and Arab travellers counted their king among the four great sovereigns of the world. The Chalukya Tailapa II overthrew the line in 973.

Chola Empire.x: The empire of the imperial Cholas of Thanjavur, founded by Vijayalaya about 848. Rajaraja I and Rajendra I conquered southern India and Lanka, sent armies to the Ganges and a fleet against Srivijaya, raised the great temples of Thanjavur and Gangaikonda Cholapuram, and governed through self-ruling village assemblies. The Pandyas and Hoysalas reduced it in the thirteenth century.

Saffarid Dynasty.x: The dynasty of Ya'qub ibn al-Layth, a coppersmith of Sistan who rose as a frontier warrior and made himself master of eastern Iran, Khurasan, and the marches of India, the first Persian ruler since the Arab conquest to defy the caliphs openly. He marched on Baghdad and was beaten in 876; his brother Amr fell to the Samanids in 900.

Sind-Habbari Dynasty.x: The Arab emirs of the Habbari family who ruled Sind from al-Mansura on the lower Indus from the mid-ninth century, nominally under the Abbasid caliphs, while a rival emirate held Multan. Al-Masudi visited their country in 915. Mahmud of Ghazni overthrew the last of them in 1026.

Chandra Dynasty.x: A Buddhist dynasty of eastern Bengal in the tenth and eleventh centuries, which rose from Harikela and the hills about Chittagong and ruled Vanga and Samatata from Vikramapura. Its kings issued copper-plate grants in Sanskrit, and Srichandra was the most powerful of them. The Varmans displaced them in the eleventh century.

Chaulukya Dynasty.x: The Solanki kings of Gujarat, who ruled from Anahilavada Patan from the tenth to the thirteenth century, rebuilt Somnath after Mahmud's sack, and raised the sun temple at Modhera. Under Siddharaja Jayasimha and Kumarapala, guided by the Jain scholar Hemachandra, Gujarat was rich and strong, and in 1178 their army routed Muhammad of Ghur at Kasahrada.

Chandela Kingdom.x: The Rajput kings of Jejakabhukti, modern Bundelkhand, who ruled from Khajuraho, Mahoba, and the fortress of Kalinjar between the tenth and thirteenth centuries and raised the temples of Khajuraho. Vidyadhara held out against Mahmud of Ghazni; Paramardi lost to Prithviraj Chauhan and then to Qutb al-Din Aibak, who took Kalinjar in 1203.

Ghaznavid Empire.x: The Turkish dynasty founded at Ghazni by the slave commanders Alp Tegin and Sabuktigin. Mahmud made it an empire from the Caspian to the Ganges, raiding India again and again for its temple treasure and its captives, and drew to his court Firdawsi and al-Biruni. The Seljuks took its west in 1040, the Ghurids the rest.

Western Chalukya Empire.x: The Chalukyas of Kalyani, who rose under Tailapa II on the ruin of the Rashtrakutas in 973 and ruled the western Deccan for two centuries, ever at war with the Cholas. Vikramaditya VI, founder of an era of 1076, brought it to its height; its ornate soapstone temples schooled the Hoysalas. Its vassals divided it after 1180.

Chauhan Dynasty.x: The Chahamanas of Shakambhari, Rajput kings of the Sambhar lake country who founded Ajmer early in the twelfth century and took Delhi from the Tomaras. Their most famous king, Prithviraj III, beat Muhammad of Ghur at Tarain in 1191 and lost to him on the same field in 1192, and his fall opened northern India to the Turks.

Paramara Dynasty.x: The Rajput kings of Malwa who ruled from Ujjain and then Dhar from the tenth to the fourteenth century. The scholar-king Bhoja made their court the most learned in India and his name a byword for royal patronage. Worn down by wars with the Chaulukyas and Chandelas, Malwa fell to Alauddin Khalji in 1305.

Soomra dynasty.x: A native dynasty of Sind that took power as the Arab emirates faded in the eleventh century and ruled the lower Indus valley for some three centuries, at first with Ismaili leanings. Its kings Dodo and Chanesar live on in Sindhi ballad. The Samma clan supplanted them in the fourteenth century.

Eastern Ganga Kingdom.x: The dynasty that ruled Kalinga and Orissa from the eleventh to the fifteenth century. Anantavarman Chodaganga united Orissa and began the temple of Jagannath at Puri, and Narasimhadeva I built the Sun temple of Konark and carried war into Muslim Bengal. They held out against the sultans of Delhi and Bengal until the Gajapatis replaced them in 1434.

Sena Dynasty.x: The house from the Karnataka country that supplanted the Palas in Bengal in the late eleventh and twelfth centuries. Vijaya Sena and Ballala Sena made Bengal a stronghold of Brahmin orthodoxy, and Jayadeva wrote the Gita Govinda at Lakshmana Sena's court. Bakhtiyar Khalji's raid on Nadia in 1204 drove them into eastern Bengal, where they lingered.

Kingdom of Polonnaruwa.x: The Sinhalese kingdom ruled from Polonnaruwa after Vijayabahu I drove out the Cholas in 1070. Under Parakramabahu I it built the vast Parakrama Samudra and other reservoirs, reunited the Buddhist order, and sent fleets abroad, and Nissanka Malla adorned the city. The invasion of Kalinga Magha in 1215 shattered it and ended the irrigation civilization of the north.

Gahadavala Dynasty.x: The Rajput dynasty that ruled the middle Ganges plain from Kannauj and Benares in the late eleventh and twelfth centuries, champions of Hindu orthodoxy who guarded the holy cities against the Ghaznavids. Govindachandra was their greatest king. Jayachandra fell to Muhammad of Ghur at Chandawar in 1194.

Hoysala Kingdom.x: The dynasty of the Malnad hills of Karnataka that rose under Vishnuvardhana in the early twelfth century and ruled the southern Deccan from Belur and Dwarasamudra. Its star-shaped temples of soapstone at Belur, Halebidu, and Somanathapura are masterpieces of carving. Malik Kafur sacked Dwarasamudra in 1311, and Veera Ballala III fell fighting the sultan of Madurai in 1343.

Ghurid Dynasty.x: The dynasty of the mountain land of Ghur in central Afghanistan. Ala al-Din Husayn burned Ghazni in 1150; his nephews Ghiyath al-Din and Mu'izz al-Din built an empire from Khurasan to Bengal, the younger winning northern India at Tarain in 1192. The minaret of Jam survives from their mountain seat. The Khwarazmshahs took their homeland by 1215.
rulers: Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad (at Ghazni; sole sultan from 1203)

Kakatiya Dynasty.x: The Telugu dynasty that ruled the eastern Deccan from Warangal in the twelfth to fourteenth centuries, building great irrigation tanks and the fortress of Orugallu. Queen Rudrama Devi ruled in her own right, praised by Marco Polo. Prataparudra II paid tribute to Alauddin Khalji and was carried off by the Tughlaq prince Ulugh Khan when Warangal fell in 1323.

Yadava Dynasty.x: The Seuna Yadavas, who ruled the western Deccan from the fortress city of Devagiri in the twelfth to fourteenth centuries. Simhana carried their power to its height, and the poet-saint Jnaneshwar wrote his Marathi commentary on the Gita in their realm. Alauddin Khalji plundered Devagiri in 1296, and Malik Kafur annexed the kingdom in 1313.

(Delhi Sultanate).x: The succession of Muslim sultanates that ruled northern India from Delhi between 1206 and 1526 under the Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid, and Lodi dynasties. It held off the Mongols, carried its arms to the far south, raised the Qutb Minar, and took Hindu captives into slavery in great numbers. Timur shattered it in 1398, and Babur ended it at Panipat.

Pandya Empire.x: The second Pandya empire, which rose from Madurai as the Cholas declined and under Jatavarman Sundara Pandya in the 1250s became the leading power of the south, from Lanka to Nellore. Marco Polo found it rich in pearls and horses. A war between two royal brothers opened the way to Malik Kafur's invasion in 1311.

Ceylon.x: The Sinhalese kingdoms of Lanka after the fall of Polonnaruwa, whose kings moved their seats southwest to Dambadeniya, Yapahuwa, Kurunegala, Gampola, and Kotte, carrying the Tooth Relic with them. Parakramabahu VI reunited the island from Kotte in the fifteenth century, and the Portuguese arrived in 1505.

Khalji Dynasty.x: The second dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate, founded by Jalal al-Din Firuz Khalji in 1290. His nephew Alauddin murdered him, beat back the Mongols, fixed market prices to pay a vast standing army, and through Malik Kafur carried his arms to the far south. The line ended in 1320 when Ghiyath al-Din Tughlaq overthrew the usurper Khusrau Khan.

Jaffna kingdom.x: The Tamil kingdom of northern Lanka ruled by the Aryacakravarti dynasty from Nallur, master of the pearl fishery of the Gulf of Mannar. Ibn Battuta was its king's guest in 1344. It warred with the Sinhalese kings of Kotte and resisted the Portuguese until they conquered it in 1619.

Tughlaq Dynasty.x: The third dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate, founded in 1320 by Ghiyath al-Din Tughlaq. Muhammad bin Tughlaq ruled the widest realm any sultan held but wrecked it with grand schemes; Firuz Shah built canals, towns, and mosques and carried Ashokan pillars to Delhi. Provinces broke away, and Timur's sack of Delhi in 1398 left the dynasty a shadow.

Vijayanagara Empire.x: The Hindu empire of the south founded on the Tungabhadra in 1336 by Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama family. For two centuries it held the line against the Deccan sultanates; under Krishnadevaraya it reached its height, and its capital amazed Portuguese visitors. After Talikota in 1565 the city was sacked and the Aravidu kings withdrew south to Penukonda.

Kartids.x: The Kart maliks of Herat, a Tajik dynasty who served the Mongols as vassals from the mid-thirteenth century and became independent masters of Herat and its province as the Ilkhanate collapsed. They rebuilt the city after the Mongol devastation and were extinguished by Timur, who took Herat in 1381.

Sultanate of Bengal.x: The independent sultanate founded when Shams al-Din Ilyas Shah united Bengal in 1352. Its rulers built at Pandua and Gaur the Adina mosque and brick mosques in a Bengali manner, patronised Bengali letters, and traded with Ming China. The Husain Shahi line brought it to its height, and Sher Shah Suri conquered it in 1538.

Sind-Samma Dynasty.x: The Samma dynasty of Sind, which supplanted the Soomras in the fourteenth century and ruled the lower Indus from Thatta, beside which grew the vast necropolis of Makli Hill. Jam Nizam al-Din II was its most celebrated king. The Arghuns from Kandahar overthrew it in the 1520s.

Bahmani Sultanate.x: The first independent Muslim kingdom of the Deccan, founded in 1347 by Ala al-Din Hasan Bahman Shah in revolt against Muhammad bin Tughlaq. Ruling from Gulbarga and then Bidar, it fought Vijayanagara for the Raichur doab; the vizier Mahmud Gawan built up its power and was put to death in 1481. It broke into five sultanates by 1518.

Jaunpur Sultanate.x: The Sharqi sultanate of the eastern Ganges plain, founded in 1394 by Malik Sarwar, a eunuch governor sent east by the Tughlaqs, whose heirs ruled independently after Timur's sack of Delhi. Its capital Jaunpur, adorned with the Atala and Jami mosques, was a seat of learning called the Shiraz of India. Bahlul Lodi annexed it in 1479.

Sayyid Dynasty.x: The fourth dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate, founded by Khizr Khan, Timur's governor of Multan, who took Delhi in 1414 and ruled as the deputy of Timur's son Shah Rukh. His successors held a shrunken realm about Delhi; the last, Alam Shah, withdrew to Badaun and yielded the throne to Bahlul Lodi in 1451.

Kingdom of Mrauk U.x: The Arakanese kingdom founded in 1430 by Min Saw Mon, who regained his throne with help from the sultan of Bengal. Its Buddhist kings took Muslim titles, held Chittagong for over a century, and with Portuguese freebooters raided Bengal for slaves. Mrauk U, its temple-studded capital, fell to the Burmese king Bodawpaya in 1785.

Bijapur Sultanate.x: The Adil Shahi sultanate of the western Deccan, founded by Yusuf Adil Shah, a Bahmani governor, in 1490. It joined the alliance that destroyed Vijayanagara at Talikota and adorned Bijapur with the Ibrahim Rauza and the Gol Gumbaz. Its long war with Shivaji drained it, and Aurangzeb took Bijapur in 1686.
Bijapur Sultanate.faith: Islam (Shia and Sunni rulers by turns)

Ahmadnagar Sultanate.x: The Nizam Shahi sultanate of the northwestern Deccan, founded in 1490 by Malik Ahmad, son of a Brahmin convert. The regent Chand Bibi defended its capital against Akbar's army in 1595 and 1596, and the Abyssinian minister Malik Ambar kept it alive by guerrilla war for a generation. Shah Jahan extinguished it in 1636.

Berar Sultanate.x: The Imad Shahi sultanate of Berar in the northern Deccan, founded in 1490 by Fathullah Imad-ul-Mulk, a Bahmani governor of Brahmin birth. One of the five successor states, it ruled from Ellichpur and the hill fort of Gawilgarh until Ahmadnagar annexed it in 1574.

Bidar Sultanate.x: The Barid Shahi sultanate, founded by Qasim Barid, the Bahmani minister who kept the last Bahmani sultans as puppets in their own capital of Bidar. His grandson Ali Barid took the royal title of shah in 1542. The smallest of the Deccan sultanates, it was annexed by Bijapur in 1619.

Portuguese Ceylon.x: The coastal lands of Ceylon held by the Portuguese, who arrived in 1505, built a fort at Colombo, made the kings of Kotte their clients, and inherited Kotte by the bequest of its Catholic king Dharmapala, who died in 1597. They conquered Jaffna in 1619 but never subdued Kandy, and the Dutch drove them out between 1638 and 1658.
Portuguese Ceylon.faith: Roman Catholicism; Buddhist and Hindu subjects

Golconda Sultanate.x: The Qutb Shahi sultanate of the eastern Deccan, founded by Sultan Quli, a Turkman of the Qara Qoyunlu house in Bahmani service. Its kings built Hyderabad and the Charminar, patronised Telugu and Deccani poetry, and grew rich on the diamonds of the Krishna valley. Aurangzeb took Golconda in 1687.

Mughal Empire.x: The empire founded by Babur at Panipat in 1526, which under Akbar, Jahangir, Shah Jahan, and Aurangzeb ruled nearly the whole subcontinent with a Persianate court, a ranked nobility, and a revenue system of great refinement, and left the Taj Mahal and the Red Fort. After 1707 it decayed, and the British deposed its last emperor in 1858.
Mughal Empire.faith: Sunni Islam, with Akbar's eclectic court; Hindu majority

Nayaks of Madurai.x: The Telugu governors of the Tamil south appointed by Vijayanagara, who after Talikota ruled as kings from Madurai and Tiruchirappalli. Thirumalai Nayak enlarged the Meenakshi temple and raised his own great palace, and Queen Mangammal governed long as regent. Chanda Sahib of the Carnatic ended the line in 1736.

Hussain Shahi Dynasty.x: The last great dynasty of the Bengal Sultanate, founded in 1494 by Alauddin Husain Shah, under whom Bengal reached its widest bounds and Bengali poetry and the devotional movement of Chaitanya flourished. Sher Shah Suri overran Bengal and took Gaur in 1538, ending the dynasty.

Karrani Sultanate.x: The Afghan dynasty of the Karrani clan that ruled Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa from Tanda after the fall of the Sur dynasty. Sulaiman Khan Karrani conquered Orissa in 1568; his son Daud Khan defied Akbar and was killed after the battle of Rajmahal in 1576, when Bengal passed to the Mughals.

Kingdom of Mysore.x: The kingdom of the Wodeyar dynasty in southern Karnataka, vassals of Vijayanagara who took Srirangapatna in 1610 and grew into a regional power. The soldier Haidar Ali seized real power in 1761, and he and his son Tipu Sultan fought four wars against the East India Company. After Tipu's death in 1799 the Wodeyars were restored under British protection.
Kingdom of Mysore.gov: Monarchy (Wodeyar, usurped by Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan from 1761 to 1799)

Bhutan.x: The Drukpa state of the eastern Himalaya founded by Ngawang Namgyal, the Zhabdrung, who came from Tibet in 1616 and united its valleys under a dual rule of religious and civil chiefs seated in fortress-monasteries. Torn by the feuds of its regional governors, it lost the Duars to Britain in 1865 and was united at last by Ugyen Wangchuck.
Bhutan.gov: Theocracy (dual system of Zhabdrung and Druk Desi)

Dutch Ceylon.x: The coastal provinces of Ceylon ruled by the Dutch East India Company after it drove out the Portuguese between 1638 and 1658. The Dutch built forts at Galle and Colombo, held the cinnamon trade as a monopoly, and brought in Roman-Dutch law, which still governs much of Sri Lankan civil law. The British took the colony in 1796.
Dutch Ceylon.gov: Colony of the Dutch East India Company
Dutch Ceylon.faith: Dutch Reformed Church; Buddhist, Hindu, and Catholic subjects

Maratha Empire.x: The Hindu power founded by Shivaji, crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad in 1674, which survived Aurangzeb's long war and under the Peshwas of Pune spread from the Deccan to the Punjab and Bengal, levying chauth on the Mughal provinces. Broken at Panipat in 1761, it revived as a confederacy of chiefs and fell to the British in 1818.
Maratha Empire.gov: Monarchy (Chhatrapati), later a confederacy under the Peshwas

Carnatic Sultanate.x: The nawabs of Arcot, Mughal governors of the Carnatic coast who became hereditary rulers in the eighteenth century. The war of succession between Chanda Sahib and Muhammad Ali, backed by France and Britain, drew the European companies into Indian politics; Muhammad Ali won, but sank into debt to the Company, which took over the Carnatic in 1801.

Nawabs of Bengal.x: The hereditary governors of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa who ruled from Murshidabad after Murshid Quli Khan, nominally for the Mughal emperor. Alivardi Khan fought off the Maratha raiders; his grandson Siraj ud-Daulah lost Plassey in 1757, and the later nawabs were puppets of the East India Company, which took the diwani in 1765.

Hyderabad State.x: The realm of the Nizams of Hyderabad, founded by the Mughal viceroy of the Deccan Asaf Jah I in 1724. The largest and richest of the princely states under the British, it kept its own army, coinage, and railways. When the seventh Nizam held out against joining India, the Indian army marched in in September 1948 and annexed it.
Hyderabad State.gov: Monarchy (nizam); princely state under British paramountcy
rulers: Nizam Ali Khan, Asaf Jah II
Mahbub Ali Khan, Asaf Jah VI
Osman Ali Khan, Asaf Jah VII

Nawab of Awadh.x: The Shia dynasty of Awadh founded by Saadat Khan, a Persian noble whom the Mughals made governor in 1722. From Faizabad and then Lucknow the nawabs, kings from 1819, ruled the rich middle Ganges plain and made Lucknow a centre of Urdu poetry, music, and courtly refinement. Lord Dalhousie annexed Awadh in 1856, feeding the anger of the Rebellion.

Durrani Empire.x: The empire founded in 1747 by Ahmad Shah Durrani, chosen king by the Afghan chiefs at Kandahar, which stretched from Khurasan to Kashmir, Sind, and the Punjab, and whose armies crushed the Marathas at Panipat in 1761. His heirs lost the Punjab to the Sikhs and their throne to the Barakzai family by 1826.

British Ceylon.x: The maritime provinces of Ceylon taken by Britain from the Dutch in 1796, governed at first by the East India Company from Madras and from 1802 as a Crown colony. In 1815 the Kandyan chiefs ceded their kingdom, and the whole island came under British rule.
British Ceylon.faith: Theravada Buddhism; Hindu, Muslim, and Christian subjects

Gwalior State.x: The realm of the Scindia family, Maratha generals who rose under the Peshwas and under Mahadji Scindia became masters of Delhi and the Mughal emperor in the 1780s. Beaten by Wellesley and Lake in 1803, the Scindias kept a large state in central India as princes under British paramountcy, ruling from Lashkar at Gwalior until 1948.
Gwalior State.gov: Monarchy; princely state under British paramountcy from 1818

Talpur Dynasty.x: The Baloch Talpur Mirs, who overthrew the Kalhora rulers of Sind in 1783 and shared the country among branches seated at Hyderabad, Khairpur, and Mirpur. Charles Napier beat them at Miani and Dubba in 1843 and annexed Sind; the Khairpur branch survived as a princely state until 1955.

Emirate of Afghanistan.x: The Afghan state under the Barakzai emirs, from Dost Mohammad, who took Kabul in 1826, to Amanullah, who made himself king in 1926. It fought two wars with British India, yielded its foreign policy to Britain in 1879, and was hammered into a centralized state by the Iron Amir, Abdur Rahman. Amanullah won full independence in 1919.

Durrani Dynasty.x: The restored kingdom of Shah Shuja Durrani, whom the British set on the throne of Kabul in 1839 in place of Dost Mohammad. Kept there by British bayonets, he was murdered in 1842 after the British retreat, and the brief reign of his son ended when Dost Mohammad returned in 1843.

British Raj.x: The rule of the British Crown over India from 1858, after the Rebellion ended the Company's government, until independence in 1947. Ruled by a viceroy through an elite civil service and a largely Indian army, it built railways, canals, and universities and was scourged by famines; the national movements of Congress and the Muslim League brought it to an end.
British Raj.gov: Crown rule under a viceroy; princely states under paramountcy
British Raj.faith: Hindu majority with Muslim, Sikh, Christian, and other subjects

Kingdom of Bhutan.x: The hereditary monarchy of the Wangchuck dynasty, founded when an assembly at Punakha chose Ugyen Wangchuck as king in 1907. Long closed to the world, Bhutan opened slowly under its third and fourth kings, made Thimphu its capital, joined the United Nations in 1971, and became a constitutional monarchy with an elected parliament in 2008.

Kingdom of Afghanistan.x: The Afghan monarchy from Amanullah's assumption of the royal title in 1926 to the overthrow of Zahir Shah in 1973. After Amanullah's fall the Musahiban kings Nadir Shah and Zahir Shah ruled a cautious, neutral state, and Zahir Shah's constitution of 1964 brought an elected parliament. His cousin Daoud ended the monarchy in a coup.

Dominion of India.x: The independent Dominion of India within the Commonwealth, from the transfer of power on 15 August 1947 to the inauguration of the Republic on 26 January 1950. In these years it absorbed more than five hundred princely states, fought the first war over Kashmir, mourned Gandhi, and adopted its constitution.

Dominion of Pakistan.x: The Dominion of Pakistan, created at partition on 14 August 1947 in two wings, west and east, a thousand miles apart, with Muhammad Ali Jinnah as its first governor-general. It took in millions of refugees, fought over Kashmir, lost Jinnah in 1948 and Liaquat Ali Khan to an assassin in 1951, and became an Islamic Republic in 1956.
Dominion of Pakistan.faith: Islam; Hindu minority in the east

Dominion of Ceylon.x: Ceylon as an independent dominion from 4 February 1948 until it became the Republic of Sri Lanka in 1972. Its first governments under the Senanayakes were conservative and Western in sympathy; S. W. R. D. Bandaranaike's Sinhala Only Act of 1956 embittered the Tamils, and in 1960 his widow Sirimavo became the first woman prime minister in the world.
Dominion of Ceylon.faith: Theravada Buddhism; Hindu, Muslim, and Christian minorities
rulers: S. W. R. D. Bandaranaike (prime minister)

Republic of India.x: The sovereign democratic republic proclaimed on 26 January 1950 under the constitution drafted by B. R. Ambedkar's committee. The largest democracy on earth, it fought wars with Pakistan and China, became a nuclear power, opened its economy in 1991, and by 2023 had become the most populous nation in the world.

Islamic Republic of Pakistan.x: Pakistan as an Islamic Republic from its first constitution of 1956. Ruled by turns by soldiers and elected civilians, it lost its eastern wing as Bangladesh in 1971, built an atomic bomb, and was the base of the war against the Soviets in Afghanistan. Its capital moved from Karachi to the new city of Islamabad.
Islamic Republic of Pakistan.gov: Federal parliamentary republic, often under military rule
rulers: Muhammad Zia ul-Haq (military ruler and president)

Sri Lanka.x: The republic proclaimed in 1972, when Ceylon took the name Sri Lanka; a presidential constitution followed in 1978. From 1983 the island was torn by war between the government and the Tamil Tigers, which ended in 2009, and an economic collapse in 2022 drove President Gotabaya Rajapaksa from office.
Sri Lanka.faith: Theravada Buddhism (given the foremost place); Hindu, Muslim, and Christian minorities
rulers: J. R. Jayewardene (prime minister, then president)

Republic of Afghanistan.x: The republic proclaimed by Mohammed Daoud Khan after he overthrew his cousin King Zahir Shah in 1973. Daoud ruled as president until communist officers killed him in the Saur Revolution of 1978. Najibullah revived the name Republic of Afghanistan in 1987 as he sought reconciliation with the mujahideen.

People's Republic of Bangladesh.x: The nation of the Bengalis of the former East Pakistan, independent after the war of 1971. Its founder Sheikh Mujibur Rahman was murdered in 1975, and soldiers ruled until 1990; thereafter Sheikh Hasina and Khaleda Zia took turns in power. Battered by cyclones and floods, it grew fast on garment exports, and a revolt drove Hasina out in 2024.

Afghanistan.x: Afghanistan in the years of the Soviet occupation under Babrak Karmal, from 1979 to 1986, when Soviet troops held Kabul, the cities, and the main roads, while the mountains and much of the countryside were held by the mujahideen resistance, divided among rival parties based in Peshawar and in Iran.
Afghanistan.gov: Soviet-backed single-party state contested by the mujahideen

Democratic Republic of Afghanistan.x: The communist state proclaimed after the Saur Revolution of 1978 by the People's Democratic Party of Afghanistan. Its purges and forced reforms provoked revolt, and Soviet troops invaded in December 1979 to save it. Under Najibullah it outlasted the Soviet withdrawal of 1989 until the mujahideen took Kabul in 1992.

Islamic State of Afghanistan.x: The government of the mujahideen parties that took Kabul in 1992, with Burhanuddin Rabbani as president. Its factions fought one another for the capital and shelled it to ruins; the Taliban drove it from Kabul in 1996, and under Ahmad Shah Massoud it held out in the northeast as the Northern Alliance until 2001.

Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan.x: The Taliban state, proclaimed under Mullah Mohammed Omar after the fall of Kabul in 1996, which imposed a rigid reading of Islamic law and harboured al-Qaeda until it was overthrown in 2001. Restored when the Taliban retook Kabul in August 2021, it is led by Hibatullah Akhundzada from Kandahar and bars girls from secondary school.

Islamic Republic of Afghanistan.x: The state founded after the fall of the Taliban under the Bonn agreement and the constitution of 2004, led by Hamid Karzai and then Ashraf Ghani and guarded by American and NATO troops. It held elections and reopened schools to girls, but never mastered the Taliban insurgency, and collapsed as the Americans withdrew in August 2021.

Âu Lạc.x: The kingdom founded about 257 B.C. by An Duong Vuong in the Red River delta after he overthrew the last of the Hung kings. Remembered for the spiral citadel of Co Loa and the legend of the magic crossbow, it fell to Zhao Tuo of Nanyue, in 179 B.C. by Chinese reckoning or 208 B.C. by the Vietnamese annals.
Âu Lạc.faith: Ancestral and spirit worship of the Lac peoples

Trưng sisters.x: The short-lived realm of the sisters Trung Trac and Trung Nhi, who in A.D. 40 led the Lac lords of the Red River delta in revolt against the Han, took sixty-five citadels, and reigned at Me Linh until the general Ma Yuan crushed them in 43.
Trưng sisters.gov: Monarchy (a queen reigning with her sister)

Funan.x: The first great state of mainland Southeast Asia, on the lower Mekong and its delta, known chiefly from Chinese envoys. Its port of Oc Eo traded with India, China, and Rome, and its kings, heirs of the Kaundinya legend, took Indian names, letters, and gods, until Chenla absorbed it in the sixth and seventh centuries.

Pyu City-States.x: The walled brick cities of the Pyu, Beikthano, Sri Ksetra, and Halin, which from about 200 B.C. ruled the dry zone of the Irrawaddy. Buddhist, writing a script of Indian origin, and burying the ashes of their kings in stone urns, they were broken by Nanzhao in 832 and absorbed by the rising Burmans of Pagan.

Champa.x: The Cham kingdoms of the central and southern coast of Vietnam, Austronesian in speech and Hindu in faith, which from the second century traded, raided, and fought Khmer and Vietnamese alike. Remembered for the brick sanctuaries of My Son and Po Nagar, they retreated south before the Vietnamese until the last principality was annexed in 1832.
Champa.faith: Hinduism (Shaivism) and Mahayana Buddhism; Islam among the later Cham

Tarumanagara.x: A Hindu kingdom of western Java, the oldest known on the island, whose king Purnavarman in the fifth century left Sanskrit inscriptions near Bogor and Jakarta, among them his carved footprints likened to Vishnu's. Chinese records of its embassies run from 528 to 669, after which Sunda and Srivijaya held the west of Java.

Early Lý Dynasty.x: The independent kingdom of Van Xuan proclaimed in 544 by Ly Bi, who expelled the Liang from Jiaozhou. Though Ly Bi was soon defeated, his successors Trieu Quang Phuc and Ly Phat Tu held the delta until the Sui reconquest of 602, a first, brief break in the long Chinese rule.

(Chenla).x: Chenla in its whole extent: the Khmer kingdom that rose on the middle Mekong in the sixth century, swallowed Funan, and under Ishanavarman I and Jayavarman I ruled from the Mun River to the delta, before breaking early in the eighth century into Land Chenla in the north and Water Chenla in the south.
(Chenla).gov: Monarchy, later divided among rival princes
(Chenla).faith: Hinduism (Shaivism and the cult of Harihara) and Buddhism

Chenla.x: The Khmer kingdom of the sixth and seventh centuries, named by the Chinese, whose kings Bhavavarman I and Chitrasena overran Funan and whose capital Ishanapura, now Sambor Prei Kuk, held more than a hundred brick temples. After Jayavarman I died in 681 the realm passed to his widow Jayadevi and fell apart into rival principalities.

Lavo Kingdom.x: The kingdom of Lavo, the modern Lopburi, on the lower Chao Phraya: a Mon city of the Dvaravati age that became the western bastion of the Khmer Empire, whose temple of Phra Prang Sam Yot still stands. It regained its freedom in the thirteenth century, sent embassies to the Yuan, and merged into Ayutthaya after 1350.
Lavo Kingdom.gov: Monarchy, at times a Khmer viceroyalty
Lavo Kingdom.faith: Theravada Buddhism, with Mahayana and Hindu cults under the Khmer

Haripuñjaya.x: The Mon kingdom of the upper Ping valley, ruled from Haripunjaya, now Lamphun, and founded by tradition under Queen Chamadevi, a princess of Lavo. A seat of Theravada learning with its relic stupa of Wat Phra That Haripunchai, it fell in 1292 to the Tai king Mangrai, who made its lands the core of Lan Na.

Srivijaya.x: The maritime empire of the Malays, centered at Palembang and later at Jambi, which from the seventh century commanded the Straits of Malacca and Sunda and the sea road between India and China. A great seat of Buddhist learning praised by Yijing, it was struck by the Cholas in 1025 and slowly dissolved into lesser states.
Srivijaya.gov: Monarchy (a maharaja over river chiefs bound by oath)

Sunda Kingdom.x: The Hindu kingdom of the Sundanese in western Java, which from its capital Pakuan Pajajaran, near Bogor, held the pepper port of Sunda Kalapa. It sought a Portuguese alliance in 1522 against the Muslim coastal states, lost its port to Demak in 1527, and fell to Banten in 1579.
Sunda Kingdom.faith: Hinduism and the Sundanese ancestral religion

Galuh Kingdom.x: The eastern Sundanese kingdom of the Citanduy valley in West Java, sister and frequent partner of Sunda, ruled in its later age from Kawali, where the inscriptions of Prabu Raja Wastu survive. Its crown was joined to Sunda's under Sri Baduga Maharaja about 1482, and its lands later passed to Cirebon and Mataram.
Galuh Kingdom.faith: Hinduism and the Sundanese ancestral religion

Water Chenla.x: The southern half of Chenla after its breakup early in the eighth century, a cluster of principalities in the Mekong delta and along the coast. Harried by raiders from Java, it was the land from which Jayavarman II emerged to reunite the Khmer and found the empire of Angkor in 802.

Land Chenla.x: The northern half of Chenla after its breakup early in the eighth century, called Wendan by the Chinese, stretching from the middle Mekong toward the Khorat plateau and the Lao country. It sent embassies to Tang China, one led by a royal son in 753, before its lands passed under the kings of Angkor.

Mataram Kingdom.x: The Javanese kingdom of Medang, or Mataram, on the plains of Central Java, where the Shaivite line of Sanjaya and the Buddhist Sailendras raised Borobudur and Prambanan in the eighth and ninth centuries. In 929 Mpu Sindok moved the court to East Java, where the realm ended in the catastrophe of 1016.

Khmer Empire.x: The empire of Angkor, founded by Jayavarman II in 802, which at its height under Suryavarman II and Jayavarman VII ruled from the Mekong delta to the Khorat plateau and the Malay isthmus. Remembered for Angkor Wat, the Bayon, and the great reservoirs that fed its rice fields, it declined after 1300 and lost Angkor to Ayutthaya in 1431.
Khmer Empire.faith: Hinduism (Shaivism and Vaishnavism) and Mahayana Buddhism, then Theravada Buddhism

Pagan Kingdom.x: The first empire of the Burmans, raised by Anawrahta from 1044 at Pagan on the Irrawaddy, uniting the valley and the Mon south under Theravada Buddhism. Its people built more than ten thousand temples; drained by gifts of land to the monks and struck by the Mongols, it broke apart after 1287. Its early reigns follow the chronicles.

Southern Han.x: One of the Ten Kingdoms of China's age of division, founded by Liu Yan at Guangzhou, which he called Xingwang, and proclaimed an empire in 917. Its rulers, notorious for cruelty and for their legions of eunuchs, tried to recover Jiaozhou and were beaten by Ngo Quyen at the Bach Dang River in 938; the Song conquered them in 971.

Ngô Dynasty.x: The first independent Vietnamese dynasty after a thousand years of Chinese rule, founded by Ngo Quyen after his victory at the Bach Dang in 938. At his death in 944 his brother-in-law Duong Tam Kha usurped the throne; Ngo Quyen's sons won it back, but their realm dissolved into the strife of the Twelve Warlords.

Đinh dynasty.x: The dynasty of Dinh Bo Linh, who ended the anarchy of the Twelve Warlords in 968 and proclaimed the empire of Dai Co Viet at Hoa Lu, ruling by harsh laws and winning the recognition of the Song. He and his eldest son were murdered in 979, and the throne passed to the general Le Hoan.

Early Lê dynasty.x: The dynasty of Le Hoan, the general who took the throne of Dai Co Viet in 980 with the support of the widowed queen, routed a Song invasion in 981, and sacked the Cham capital of Indrapura in 982. His sons fought over the throne after his death, and the cruel Le Long Dinh was the last of the line.

Lý dynasty.x: The first great Vietnamese dynasty, founded by Ly Cong Uan in 1009, which moved the capital to Thang Long, built the Temple of Literature, held the first civil examinations, and beat back the Song and the Cham. Devoutly Buddhist, it ended in 1225 when its last ruler, the girl empress Ly Chieu Hoang, yielded the throne to her Tran husband.

Kahuripan.x: The East Javanese kingdom rebuilt by Airlangga after the catastrophe of 1016, uniting the Brantas valley and the ports of the north coast, with a court that heard Mpu Kanwa's poem the Arjunawiwaha. Before his death in 1049 Airlangga divided it between two sons as Janggala and Kediri.

Kediri Kingdom.x: The western half of Airlangga's realm, ruled from Daha on the Brantas, which outgrew Janggala to dominate East Java and the spice trade of the eastern islands. Its court produced the classic kakawin poems, among them the Bharatayuddha of 1157; it fell in 1222 when Ken Arok defeated King Kertajaya at Ganter.

Kingdom of Janggala.x: The eastern half of Airlangga's kingdom, holding the Brantas delta and the ports near modern Surabaya after the division of about 1045. Overshadowed by Kediri, it was absorbed in the twelfth century, but its memory lived on in the Panji tales of Javanese and Malay romance, whose hero is a prince of Janggala.

Trần dynasty.x: The dynasty that took the throne of Dai Viet in 1226 through the marriage of Tran Canh to the last Ly empress. Its princes and its great general Tran Hung Dao defeated the Mongols in 1258, 1285, and 1288, and its retired emperors guided their sons from Buddhist retreats. It fell to Ho Quy Ly in 1400.
Trần dynasty.gov: Monarchy (emperor, guided by a senior retired emperor)
Trần dynasty.faith: Mahayana Buddhism (Truc Lam Zen) and Confucianism

Singhasari.x: The East Javanese kingdom founded by Ken Arok after his victory over Kediri in 1222, whose tale of murder and revenge fills the Pararaton. Under Kertanegara it sent the Pamalayu expedition to Sumatra and defied Kublai Khan, until Jayakatwang of Kediri slew him in 1292. Its temples of Singhasari and Jago survive.

Sukhothai Kingdom.x: The Tai kingdom of the upper Chao Phraya basin, founded about 1238 when Si Inthrathit threw off Khmer rule. Under Ram Khamhaeng it reached the Malay peninsula and the Mekong, and Thai tradition honors it as the cradle of Thai letters and of Sinhalese Theravada Buddhism in Siam. It became a vassal of Ayutthaya and was absorbed in 1438.

Majapahit.x: The greatest of the Javanese empires, founded by Raden Wijaya in 1293 after he outwitted the Mongols. Under King Hayam Wuruk and his minister Gajah Mada it claimed lordship over the islands from Sumatra to New Guinea, as Prapanca's poem of 1365 records. Torn by civil war after 1400, it was extinguished by Muslim Demak in the early sixteenth century.

Shan States.x: The principalities of the Tai-speaking Shan in the hills of upper Burma and the Yunnan frontier, ruled by hereditary lords called saophas. After the fall of Pagan they dominated the upper Irrawaddy; in 1527 a confederation led by Mohnyin sacked Ava and ruled it until Bayinnaung subdued the Shan States between 1557 and 1563.

Dharmasraya.x: The Malay kingdom of Malayu on the upper Batang Hari in central Sumatra, heir to the power of Srivijaya in the thirteenth century. Its ruler Tribhuwanaraja received from Kertanegara of Singhasari a statue of Amoghapasa in 1286, and the Majapahit prince Adityawarman later moved its court to the Minangkabau highlands at Pagaruyung.

Myinsaing Kingdom.x: The realm of the three brothers Athinkhaya, Yazathingyan, and Thihathu, sons of a Shan father, who rose from the Kyaukse granary after the fall of Pagan, withstood a Mongol siege of Myinsaing in 1301, and ruled jointly until Thihathu founded Pinya in 1313.

Malaya.x: The Malay Peninsula in the century between the decline of Srivijaya and the rise of Malacca, a patchwork of river states such as Kedah, Pahang, and Temasek, with Tambralinga at Ligor the strongest in the north. Sukhothai and then Ayutthaya claimed lordship over much of it, and Majapahit's fleets over the rest.
Malaya.gov: Petty Malay river states under Siamese or Javanese overlordship
Malaya.faith: Buddhism and Hinduism, with Islam spreading from the fourteenth century

Hanthawaddy Kingdom.x: The Mon kingdom of Lower Burma, founded by Wareru at Martaban in 1287 and later ruled from Pegu, rich from the trade of the Indian Ocean. Under Razadarit it withstood Ava in the Forty Years' War; under Queen Shin Sawbu and the monk-king Dhammazedi it enjoyed a golden age, until Toungoo conquered it in 1539.
