Lan Na Kingdom.x: The northern Tai kingdom of the million rice fields, founded by Mangrai, who took Haripunjaya in 1292 and built Chiang Mai in 1296. Under Tilokkarat it fought Ayutthaya and hosted a great Buddhist council in 1477; it fell to Bayinnaung of Burma in 1558.

Kingdom of Pinya.x: The Burman kingdom founded in 1313 by Thihathu, youngest of the Myinsaing brothers, at Pinya near the later Ava. It soon lost Sagaing to Thihathu's son Saw Yun, and the two rival courts wore each other down until raiders from the Shan state of Mong Mao sacked both in 1364.

Sagaing Kingdom.x: The Burman kingdom set up across the Irrawaddy from Pinya by Saw Yun, a son of Thihathu, in 1315. Rival of Pinya for half a century, it was sacked by the Shan of Mong Mao in 1364, after which Thado Minbya, a prince of Sagaing, united both halves in the new kingdom of Ava.

Ayutthaya Kingdom.x: The Siamese kingdom founded by U Thong in 1351 on an island in the Chao Phraya, heir to Khmer kingship and Thai custom. For four centuries it was among the great powers and ports of Southeast Asia, trading with China, Japan, Persia, and Europe and twice falling to Burma, until the Burmese destroyed the city in 1767.
Ayutthaya Kingdom.gov: Absolute monarchy with the sakdina hierarchy of ranks
Ayutthaya Kingdom.faith: Theravada Buddhism with Brahmanical court rites

Lan Xang.x: The Lao kingdom of the Million Elephants, founded by Fa Ngum in 1353 and stretching along the middle Mekong from the borders of Yunnan to Champasak. Its capitals of Luang Prabang and Vientiane were great Buddhist centers; it reached its height under Sourigna Vongsa in the seventeenth century, and after his death split into three kingdoms between 1707 and 1713.
Lan Xang.faith: Theravada Buddhism and the worship of spirits (phi)

Sultanate of Brunei.x: The Malay sultanate of Brunei Bay, whose rulers embraced Islam in the fourteenth or fifteenth century and under Sultan Bolkiah held sway along the coasts of Borneo to the Sulu Sea and Manila. Shorn of Sarawak and Sabah in the nineteenth century, it became a British protectorate in 1888, struck oil in 1929, and won independence in 1984.

Ava Kingdom.x: The Burman kingdom founded in 1364 by Thado Minbya at Ava, where the Myitnge meets the Irrawaddy, which reunited upper Burma after the fall of Pagan. It fought the Mon of Pegu in the Forty Years' War and was worn down by Shan raids until the Confederation of Shan States took it in 1527.

Hồ dynasty.x: The brief dynasty of Ho Quy Ly, the Tran minister who seized the throne in 1400, ruled from his stone citadel of Tay Do, issued paper money, and limited the estates of the great families. His reforms made him enemies, and the Ming conquered the country in 1407 on the pretext of restoring the Tran.

Lê Dynasty.x: The Later Le dynasty of Le Loi, who expelled the Ming in 1428. Under Le Thanh Tong it reached its height with the Hong Duc code, a Confucian bureaucracy, and the conquest of Vijaya in 1471. Deposed by the Mac in 1527, it was restored in name in 1533 by the Nguyen and Trinh, who ruled in its stead.
Lê Dynasty.gov: Monarchy (emperor), later nominal under the Trinh lords

Kingdom of Cambodia.x: The Khmer kingdom after the abandonment of Angkor, ruled from Phnom Penh, Longvek, and Oudong and squeezed for four centuries between Siam and Vietnam. A French protectorate from 1863, it won independence under Norodom Sihanouk in 1953, suffered war and the Khmer Rouge after 1970, and was restored as a constitutional monarchy in 1993.
Kingdom of Cambodia.gov: Monarchy (absolute, then constitutional from 1947 and again from 1993)

Sultanate of Sulu.x: The Muslim sultanate of the Sulu archipelago, founded in the fifteenth century by Sharif ul-Hashim, a scholar of Arab descent from Johor. Enriched by pearls, the China trade, and the slave raids of its Iranun and Samal allies on the Christian Philippines, it resisted Spain for three centuries and leased North Borneo to a British syndicate in 1878.

Demak Sultanate.x: The first Muslim sultanate of Java, founded about 1475 at Demak on the north coast by Raden Patah, by tradition a son of the last king of Majapahit. With the Wali Songo it spread Islam through Java; Pati Unus attacked Portuguese Malacca in 1513, and Trenggana conquered Sunda Kalapa and the Majapahit heartland before he fell on campaign in 1546.

Sultanate of Cirebon.x: The Muslim sultanate of Cirebon on the north coast of West Java, founded under Sunan Gunungjati, one of the Wali Songo, who with Demak took Banten and Sunda Kalapa from the Hindu Sundanese. In 1677 it was split among rival princes into the courts of Kasepuhan and Kanoman and passed under the Dutch Company.

First Toungoo Empire.x: The empire built by the kings of Toungoo, Tabinshwehti and his brother-in-law Bayinnaung, who from 1530 conquered the Mon south, upper Burma, the Shan States, Lan Na, Ayutthaya, and Lan Xang: the largest empire in the history of Southeast Asia. It fell apart under Nanda Bayin, whose capital Pegu was sacked in 1599.

Johor Sultanate.x: The successor of Malacca, founded by the sons of Sultan Mahmud Shah after the Portuguese took the city in 1511, and ruled from shifting capitals on the Johor River and in the Riau islands. Allied with the Dutch to take Malacca in 1641, it lost its royal line in 1699 and fell under Bugis warlords in the eighteenth century.
Johor Sultanate.gov: Sultanate with bendahara, temenggong, and later Bugis viceroys

Sultanate of Aceh.x: The Muslim sultanate of northern Sumatra, founded by Ali Mughayat Syah about 1514, which grew rich on pepper and fought the Portuguese of Malacca for a century with Ottoman guns and gunners. Its height came under Iskandar Muda; a line of four queens followed, and it resisted the Dutch from 1873 until 1903.

Blambangan Kingdom.x: The last Hindu kingdom of Java, in the island's eastern tip facing Bali, which outlived Majapahit by playing Bali against the Muslim powers of Mataram. It flourished under Tawang Alun in the seventeenth century; the Dutch Company conquered it between 1768 and 1772, and much of its people perished or were driven away.

Balinese Kingdom.x: The Hindu kingdom of Gelgel in Bali, heir to the court culture of Majapahit, which under Dalem Waturenggong in the sixteenth century ruled Bali and reached across the straits to Lombok, Sumbawa, and Blambangan. After a usurpation in 1651 the court moved to nearby Klungkung, and Bali split into rival kingdoms.

Sultanate of Maguindanao.x: The Muslim sultanate of the Pulangi valley in Mindanao, founded by tradition by Sharif Kabungsuwan of Johor early in the sixteenth century. Under Sultan Kudarat it united much of Mindanao, made war on Spain and its Christian subjects, and long held the Spaniards to the coast before declining in the nineteenth century.

Sultanate of Banjar.x: The Muslim sultanate of southern Borneo, founded when Prince Samudra, heir of the Hindu kingdom of Negara Daha, won his throne with help from Demak and took Islam as Sultan Suriansyah. Rich in pepper and diamonds, it fell under Dutch control, and the Banjarmasin War of 1859, led by Prince Antasari, ended in its abolition in 1860.

Sultanate of Johor.x: The Malay sultanate of the southern peninsula, descended from the royal house of Malacca and after 1699 from its bendaharas. In the nineteenth century real power passed to the temenggongs, who shared in the sale of Singapore and won Johor itself in 1855; Abu Bakar built Johor Bahru and was recognized as sultan in 1885.

Đại Việt.x: Dai Viet under the Mac dynasty, founded when the general Mac Dang Dung deposed the Le in 1527. The Mac held Thang Long and the north against the Le restoration based in Thanh Hoa until 1592, when the Trinh recaptured the capital; Mac princes clung to Cao Bang on the Chinese border, under Ming and Qing protection, until 1677.

Sultanate of Banten.x: The Muslim sultanate of western Java, founded when the forces of Demak and Cirebon took the port from Sunda, and made by Maulana Hasanuddin a great pepper emporium that drew Chinese, Gujarati, English, and Dutch merchants. It held Lampung across the strait; Sultan Ageng Tirtayasa defied the Dutch, but his son made Banten their vassal in 1682.

Sultanate of Perak.x: The Malay sultanate of the Perak River, founded about 1528 by Muzaffar Shah, eldest son of the last sultan of Malacca, whose line reigns there still. Its tin drew Chinese miners whose feuds, mixed with royal quarrels over the succession, brought the Pangkor Engagement of 1874, the killing of the British Resident in 1875, and British rule.

Portuguese Colonies.x: Portugal's possessions in the Lesser Sundas, centered on Timor and Solor, where Dominican friars built a fort on Solor in 1566 and the sandalwood trade drew Portuguese merchants and the mixed-blood Topasses. Governed from Lifau and, from 1769, from Dili, Portuguese Timor survived Dutch rivalry, its border fixed by treaty in 1859 and an award of 1914.
Portuguese Colonies.gov: Colonial governorship under the Portuguese crown
Portuguese Colonies.faith: Roman Catholicism among the colonists and converts; native religions

Trịnh lords.x: The house of Trinh, which ruled northern Vietnam in the name of the powerless Le emperors from the 1540s to 1786. From Thang Long the Trinh lords fought the Mac and then the Nguyen lords of the south in a fifty-year war; the Tay Son swept them away in 1786.
Trịnh lords.gov: Hereditary military regency under nominal Le emperors

Nguyễn lords.x: The house of Nguyen, which from 1558 ruled the southern provinces of Vietnam, nominally for the Le emperors, from Thuan Hoa and later Phu Xuan. Holding off the Trinh behind the walls of Dong Hoi, they pushed the frontier south through Champa and into the Khmer lands of the Mekong delta, until the Tay Son overthrew them in 1777.
Nguyễn lords.gov: Hereditary lordship under nominal Le suzerainty

Sultanate of Pajang.x: A short-lived Javanese sultanate of the interior, founded about 1568 by Hadiwijaya, known in legend as Jaka Tingkir, after his protege Sutawijaya slew the Demak usurper Arya Penangsang. Its power passed to Sutawijaya's Mataram, which absorbed Pajang in 1587.

Patani Kingdom.x: The Malay sultanate of Patani on the east coast of the isthmus, a busy port for Chinese, Japanese, and European traders, which reached its height under a line of queens from 1584, Ratu Hijau, Ratu Biru, Ratu Ungu, and Ratu Kuning. A tributary of Siam that often rebelled, it was annexed by Bangkok in 1902.

Dutch Republic.x: The East Indies dominion of the Dutch Republic, ruled from Batavia by the Dutch East India Company (VOC), chartered in 1602. The Company won a monopoly of the Moluccan spices by war and treaty, held the coasts of Java and the chief ports of the archipelago, and became overlord of Java's princes before its dissolution in 1799.
Dutch Republic.gov: Chartered company rule (VOC) under the States General
Dutch Republic.faith: Dutch Reformed Church among the Dutch; Islam and other faiths among their subjects

Mataram Sultanate.x: The Javanese sultanate of the interior founded by Panembahan Senopati about 1587, which under Sultan Agung conquered nearly all Java and twice besieged Dutch Batavia. His successors, beset by rebellion, leaned ever more on the Dutch Company, which in 1755 divided the realm into Surakarta and Yogyakarta.
Mataram Sultanate.faith: Sunni Islam blended with Javanese mysticism

Restored Toungoo dynasty.x: The Toungoo dynasty restored by Nyaungyan Min after the collapse of Bayinnaung's empire, which reunited Burma under Anaukpetlun and ruled from Pegu and, after 1635, from Ava. More inward-looking and agrarian than its forebear, it governed the Irrawaddy valley for a century and a half, until the Mon of Pegu took Ava in 1752.

Lan Na.x: Lan Na in its long subjection to Burma, from Bayinnaung's conquest of 1558 until Kawila and the armies of Taksin drove the Burmese out in 1774 and 1775. Ruled by Burmese governors and vassal princes, it rose in revolt in 1727, and Ong Kham then held Chiang Mai free of Burma for three decades.
rulers: Nawrahta Minsaw (Burmese king of Lan Na)

Sultanate of Palembang.x: The Malay sultanate of the Musi River in southern Sumatra, founded after the Dutch burned the old court in 1659, when a prince of Javanese descent took the title of sultan. Rich in pepper and the tin of Bangka, it was crushed after Sultan Mahmud Badaruddin II fought first the British and then the Dutch, who exiled him in 1821.

Sultanate of Jambi.x: The Malay sultanate of the Batang Hari River in central Sumatra, a pepper port contested by Palembang, Johor, and the Dutch. Its last great sultan, Thaha Saifuddin, deposed by the Dutch in 1858, led a resistance from the forests of the interior for nearly half a century until he was killed in 1904.

Cambodia.x: Cambodia in the eighteenth century, a shrinking kingdom ruled from Oudong by quarreling princes who sought Siamese or Vietnamese backing in turn. The Nguyen lords took the Mekong delta province by province, Siam seized Battambang and Siem Reap in 1794, and the young Ang Chan II was crowned under Siamese tutelage in 1806.
Cambodia.gov: Monarchy under Siamese and Vietnamese suzerainty

Kingdom of Luang Phrabang.x: The northern Lao kingdom formed when Lan Xang split in 1707, ruled from the old royal city of Luang Prabang. A vassal by turns of Burma, Siam, and Vietnam, it was sacked by Chinese Haw bandits in 1887, after which its king accepted French protection; his line became the royal house of Laos.

Vientiane.x: The central Lao kingdom of Vientiane, formed when Lan Xang split in 1707 and holding the old capital with its Emerald Buddha. Siam took the city in 1779 and carried the image to Thonburi; when Chao Anouvong rose against Bangkok in 1827, the Siamese razed Vientiane and deported its people across the Mekong.

Kingdom of Champasak.x: The southern Lao kingdom founded in 1713 by Nokasad, a grandson of Sourigna Vongsa, on the Mekong around Champasak and the Bassac plain, near the ancient temple of Wat Phu. A Siamese vassal from 1778, it lost its lands east of the Mekong to French Laos in 1893, and its crown in 1904.

Kingdom of Bulungan.x: A Muslim sultanate on the Kayan River in northeastern Borneo, founded in the early eighteenth century by a house of Kayan descent that embraced Islam, and living by the forest trade in birds' nests, rattan, and camphor. It passed under Sulu and then Dutch overlordship, and was abolished by Indonesia in 1964.

Restored Hanthawaddy Kingdom.x: The Mon kingdom revived at Pegu in 1740 by Smim Htaw Buddhaketi in revolt against the decaying Toungoo court. With French arms from Pondicherry its king Binnya Dala sacked Ava in 1752, but Alaungpaya rallied the Burmans, took Pegu in 1757, and gave it over to massacre.

Konbaung Dynasty.x: The last royal dynasty of Burma, founded by Alaungpaya in 1752. Its warrior kings destroyed Ayutthaya, defeated four Chinese invasions, and conquered Arakan, Manipur, and Assam, carrying Burma to its greatest extent and into collision with British India.

Thonburi Kingdom.x: The Siamese kingdom of Taksin, the general of Chinese descent who rallied the Thai after the fall of Ayutthaya in 1767, expelled the Burmese, and reunited Siam from his new capital at Thonburi. He extended his rule over Lan Na, Laos, and Cambodia, but was deposed and put to death in 1782 amid charges of madness.

Tây Sơn dynasty.x: The dynasty of the three brothers from Tay Son in Binh Dinh who rose in 1771, destroyed the Nguyen lords and the Trinh, routed a Siamese army in 1785 and a Qing army in 1789, and briefly ruled a united Vietnam. After the sudden death of Quang Trung in 1792 the realm fell to Nguyen Anh in 1802.

Chiangmai.x: The principality of Chiang Mai restored after Burmese rule by Kawila, a prince of Lampang, who with Siamese help won back the north and resettled the deserted city in 1796. Its princes, vassals of Bangkok, governed the old lands of Lan Na until Siam absorbed the principality in the reforms of the late nineteenth century.

Rattanakosin Kingdom.x: Siam under the Chakri dynasty from the founding of Bangkok in 1782, which fought off the Burmese, held Laos and Cambodia in vassalage, and under Mongkut and Chulalongkorn modernized the state, kept its independence by yielding outer provinces, and abolished slavery. The revolution of 1932 ended absolute monarchy.

Nguyễn dynasty.x: The last imperial dynasty of Vietnam, founded by Gia Long in 1802, which ruled from the Chinese border to the Gulf of Siam from its citadel at Hue. Confucian and wary of the West, it persecuted the Catholics and lost the south to France from 1859; after 1884 its emperors reigned under French protection until Bao Dai abdicated in 1945.

Dutch East Indies.x: The Dutch colonial empire in the Indonesian archipelago, which passed from the Company to the state in 1800 and, after British rule from 1811 to 1816, spread by war and treaty over the whole archipelago. It drew vast wealth from coffee, sugar, tin, rubber, and oil until Japan overran it in 1942; the Dutch yielded sovereignty in 1949.
Dutch East Indies.faith: Islam among most subjects; Christianity, Hinduism, and others
rulers: Ludolph Anne Jan Wilt Sloet van de Beele
Carel Herman Aart van der Wijck
Louis Beel (high representative of the Crown)
Tony Lovink (high representative of the Crown)

(Kingdom of Holland).x: The kingdom created by Napoleon in 1806 for his brother Louis Bonaparte out of the Batavian Republic, together with its colonies in the East Indies, where Louis sent Marshal Daendels to fortify Java against the British. Too mindful of Dutch interests for his brother's liking, Louis abdicated in 1810, and Holland was annexed to France.
(Kingdom of Holland).faith: Dutch Reformed Church and Catholicism; Islam in the Indies

Burma.x: Burma from the reign of Bagyidaw to 1989: the Konbaung kingdom, cut down in three wars with Britain until it was annexed in 1886; then a province of British India and from 1937 a separate colony; and from 1948 the independent Union of Burma, under U Nu and, after 1962, the army rule of Ne Win.
Burma.gov: Monarchy; British colony; parliamentary republic from 1948; military rule from 1962
rulers: Ba Maw (head of state under Japan)

Riau-Lingga Sultanate.x: The Malay sultanate of the Riau and Lingga islands, split from Johor by the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824, which left the peninsula to Britain and the islands to the Netherlands. Its sultans held court at Daik on Lingga, while the Bugis viceroys on Penyengat fostered a flowering of Malay letters, until the Dutch deposed the last sultan in 1911.

Kingdom of Sarawak.x: The realm of the White Rajahs, carved from Brunei's dominions by James Brooke in 1841 and enlarged by his nephew Charles to the bounds of modern Sarawak. Ruled paternally from Kuching with Iban levies and a small European service, it became a British protectorate in 1888 and was ceded to the Crown by the third rajah in 1946.
Kingdom of Sarawak.faith: Islam among the Malays; Christianity and native religions among the Dayaks; Chinese religions

Pahang Sultanate.x: The Malay state of the Pahang River on the east coast of the peninsula, ruled in the nineteenth century by bendaharas descended from the ministers of Johor. Wan Ahmad won it in the civil war of 1857 to 1863, took the title of sultan in 1882, and accepted a British Resident in 1888 after a British subject was murdered.

Kingdom of Fiji.x: The kingdom proclaimed at Levuka in 1871 under Ratu Seru Cakobau, chief of Bau, with a cabinet of European settlers, in an effort to bring order to the islands. Burdened by debt and by quarrels between planters and chiefs, it lasted three years before Cakobau ceded Fiji to Britain in 1874.

New Hebrides.x: The islands of modern Vanuatu, where British and French planters and missionaries competed until the two powers set up a joint naval commission in 1887 and in 1906 a Condominium, with two police forces, two currencies, and two school systems. It became independent as Vanuatu in 1980, amid the brief Santo rebellion.
New Hebrides.faith: Presbyterian, Anglican, and Catholic Christianity; kastom religions

Commonwealth of Australia.x: The federal dominion formed on 1 January 1901 from the six British colonies of Australia, with its seat of government at Melbourne and from 1927 at Canberra. It fought in both world wars, turned toward the United States after the fall of Singapore, abandoned the White Australia policy after 1966, and grew into a prosperous democracy of many peoples.
Commonwealth of Australia.faith: Christianity (Anglican and Catholic), with growing irreligion

New Zealand.x: The self-governing colony, from 1907 a dominion, of the islands of Aotearoa, where British settlers and the Maori lived under the Treaty of Waitangi. A pioneer of votes for women and of the welfare state, it fought at Gallipoli and in both world wars, and since the 1980s has been known for refusing nuclear arms and redressing Maori grievances.
New Zealand.faith: Christianity, with growing irreligion; the Maori Ratana and Ringatu churches

Kingdom of Thailand.x: Siam under constitutional monarchy from the revolution of 1932, renamed Thailand in 1939. Allied to Japan in the Second World War and to the United States in the Cold War, it has swung between elected governments and military coups, while King Bhumibol, reigning seventy years, made the crown the pivot of national life.
Kingdom of Thailand.gov: Constitutional monarchy, often under military rule

Republic of Indonesia.x: The republic proclaimed by Sukarno and Hatta on 17 August 1945 and recognized by the Netherlands in 1949, the largest Muslim nation on earth and the largest island state. Sukarno's Guided Democracy gave way after the killings of 1965 to Suharto's New Order; since 1998 it has been a democracy of some 280 million people.
Republic of Indonesia.faith: Sunni Islam, with Christian, Hindu, and Buddhist minorities

Territory of Papua and New Guinea.x: The Australian-administered union of the Territory of Papua and the United Nations trust territory of New Guinea, formed after the Second World War and ruled from Port Moresby. Australia built roads, schools, and a House of Assembly, and led the territory to self-government in 1973 and independence in 1975.

Republic of the Philippines.x: The republic that received its independence from the United States on 4 July 1946, the largest Catholic nation of Asia. It has passed through the Huk rebellion, the martial law of Ferdinand Marcos, the People Power revolt of 1986, and long wars with Muslim and Communist insurgents in Mindanao and the hills.
Republic of the Philippines.faith: Roman Catholicism, with Islam in the south

Kingdom of Laos.x: The Lao monarchy united under the king of Luang Prabang in 1946 and independent of France by 1953. Riven by the struggle of royalists, neutralists, and the Communist Pathet Lao, and drawn into the Vietnam War as the Ho Chi Minh Trail ran through its east, it fell to the Pathet Lao in 1975.

Democratic Republic of Vietnam.x: The Communist state proclaimed by Ho Chi Minh in Hanoi on 2 September 1945, which fought the French to victory at Dien Bien Phu, ruled the north after the division at Geneva in 1954, and waged the long war against the South and the United States until the fall of Saigon in 1975.
Democratic Republic of Vietnam.faith: State atheism; Buddhism and Catholicism among the people

Republic of Vietnam.x: The state of South Vietnam, proclaimed by Ngo Dinh Diem in 1955 after he ousted Bao Dai. Backed by the United States with money and, from 1965, with half a million troops, it fought the Viet Cong and the North for twenty years, passed through coups after Diem's murder in 1963, and fell on 30 April 1975.
Republic of Vietnam.gov: Presidential republic, often under military rule
Republic of Vietnam.faith: Buddhism, Catholicism, Cao Dai, and Hoa Hao

Federation of Malaya.x: The federation of nine Malay states with Penang and Malacca, formed under British rule in 1948 and independent on 31 August 1957 under Tunku Abdul Rahman, while the Emergency against the Communist guerrillas wound down. In 1963 it joined Singapore, Sarawak, and Sabah to form Malaysia.
Federation of Malaya.faith: Sunni Islam (official), with Buddhism, Hinduism, and Christianity
rulers: Tuanku Abdul Rahman of Negeri Sembilan (king)

Malaysia.x: The federation formed on 16 September 1963 from Malaya, Singapore, Sarawak, and Sabah; Singapore left in 1965. Under the long rule of the Barisan Nasional and of Mahathir Mohamad it grew from tin and rubber into an industrial nation, balancing its Malay, Chinese, and Indian peoples, until the ruling coalition first lost power in 2018.
Malaysia.faith: Sunni Islam (official), with Buddhism, Christianity, and Hinduism

Khmer Republic.x: The republic proclaimed in October 1970 after General Lon Nol and the National Assembly deposed Prince Sihanouk. Backed by the United States and drawn into the Vietnam War, it lost the countryside to the Khmer Rouge and the North Vietnamese and fell when Phnom Penh was taken on 17 April 1975.

Republic of Fiji.x: Fiji since its independence from Britain in 1970, a nation divided between indigenous Fijians and the descendants of Indian laborers. Its politics have been broken by four coups, two by Sitiveni Rabuka in 1987, which made it a republic, one by George Speight in 2000, and one by Frank Bainimarama in 2006.
Republic of Fiji.gov: Parliamentary republic (from 1987), often under military rule

Papua New Guinea.x: The independent state formed in 1975 from the eastern half of New Guinea and its islands, a land of more than eight hundred languages ruled by shifting parliamentary coalitions. It weathered the Bougainville civil war of 1988 to 1998 and the Sandline crisis of 1997, and lives largely on gold, copper, timber, and gas.

Socialist Republic of Vietnam.x: The united Communist state proclaimed in 1976 after the conquest of the South. It sent hundreds of thousands to re-education camps, drove out the boat people, overthrew the Khmer Rouge, and fought China in 1979; from 1986 the reforms of Doi Moi opened it to markets and made it one of the fastest-growing economies of Asia.
Socialist Republic of Vietnam.faith: Officially atheist; Buddhism, Catholicism, Cao Dai, and folk religion

Communist Laos.x: The Lao People's Democratic Republic, proclaimed by the Pathet Lao on 2 December 1975 after the abdication of King Savang Vatthana. A close ally of Vietnam, it sent thousands to re-education camps and drove much of the Hmong people into exile, and since 1986 has opened slowly to markets and to Chinese investment.

Democratic Kampuchea.x: The Khmer Rouge state of Pol Pot, which emptied the cities in April 1975, abolished money, markets, religion, and family life, and worked and starved the people in agrarian communes. Some 1.7 million died of execution, hunger, and disease before Vietnam overthrew it in January 1979.
Democratic Kampuchea.gov: Communist dictatorship of the party center (Angkar)

People's Republic of Kampuchea.x: The state set up by Vietnam after it overthrew the Khmer Rouge in January 1979, led by Heng Samrin and Hun Sen. Unrecognized by most of the world, which seated the Khmer Rouge coalition at the United Nations, it rebuilt the ruined country under Vietnamese occupation until 1989, when it became the State of Cambodia.

Solomon Islands.x: The archipelago of the old British Solomon Islands Protectorate, scene of the Guadalcanal campaign, independent within the Commonwealth since 1978. Strife between the peoples of Guadalcanal and Malaita from 1998 brought a coup in 2000 and an Australian-led regional mission from 2003 to 2017.

Vanuatu.x: The republic formed from the Anglo-French New Hebrides at independence on 30 July 1980 and led first by the Anglican priest Walter Lini. Papua New Guinean troops put down the secession of Espiritu Santo in its first weeks; it remains a parliamentary democracy of some three hundred thousand people speaking more than a hundred languages.
Vanuatu.faith: Christianity (Presbyterian, Anglican, and Catholic) and kastom religions

Union of Myanmar.x: Burma under the junta that crushed the rising of 1988 and renamed the country Myanmar in 1989. After decades of military rule, the constitution of 2008 allowed the partly civilian governments of Thein Sein and Aung San Suu Kyi, until the coup of 2021 plunged the country into civil war.
Union of Myanmar.gov: Military junta; partly civilian republic from 2011 to 2021
Union of Myanmar.faith: Theravada Buddhism, with Christian and Muslim minorities

Sabaeans.x: The kingdom of Saba in the highlands of Yemen, the Sheba of the Bible, which grew rich on the caravan trade in frankincense and myrrh and raised the great dam of Marib. Its mukarribs and kings ruled much of southern Arabia for centuries, until Himyar absorbed it late in the third century after Christ.

Hadhramaut.x: The incense kingdom of the Wadi Hadhramaut in southern Arabia, whose capital Shabwa gathered the frankincense of Dhofar for the caravans bound north. It long rivaled Saba and Qataban, and was conquered by Himyar early in the fourth century after Christ.

Olmec Civilization.x: The earliest great civilization of Mesoamerica, in the swampy Gulf lowlands of Veracruz and Tabasco, remembered for its colossal basalt heads, its carved jade, and its were-jaguar gods. From San Lorenzo and later La Venta its rulers spread an art and ritual, the rubber ball game among them, that shaped every later people of Mexico.

Zapotec Civilization.x: The civilization of the Valley of Oaxaca, whose kings ruled from Monte Albán, a capital built on a leveled mountaintop about 500 B.C. The Zapotecs devised one of the earliest scripts and calendars of the Americas; after Monte Albán declined their lords held smaller kingdoms, and they were never wholly subdued by the Aztecs.

Mayan City-States.x: The Classic Maya kingdoms of the lowland forests of Guatemala, Mexico, Belize, and Honduras, ruled by divine lords who recorded their deeds in hieroglyphic inscriptions dated by the Long Count. Tikal and Calakmul contended for mastery for two centuries, until the great cities of the south emptied in the ninth century.

Himyarite Kingdom.x: The last great kingdom of ancient southern Arabia, which from its capital Zafar had united all Yemen by about A.D. 300. Its kings turned from the old gods to monotheism, some of them to Judaism; the slaughter of the Christians of Najran by Dhu Nuwas brought an invasion from Axum in 525.
Himyarite Kingdom.faith: South Arabian polytheism, then monotheism and Judaism; Christianity under Axumite rule

Kingdom of Axum.x: The trading empire of the northern Ethiopian highlands and the Red Sea, whose granite stelae still stand at Aksum. It minted gold coins; under Ezana, about 330, it became one of the first Christian kingdoms; under Kaleb it conquered Himyar in 525. It sheltered the first Muslim refugees, then declined as the Arab conquests closed its sea trade.
Kingdom of Axum.faith: Polytheism, then Orthodox Christianity from the fourth century

Alodia.x: The southernmost of the three Christian kingdoms of Nubia, on the Blue and White Niles, with its capital at Soba near modern Khartoum. Converted by the missionary Longinus about 580, it outlived Makuria and fell to the Funj and the Arab Abdallab about 1504.
Alodia.faith: Miaphysite Christianity under the Patriarch of Alexandria

Classic Veracruz Culture.x: The civilization of the Gulf lowlands of Veracruz between the age of the Olmec and the Aztec conquest, whose chief city, El Tajín, raised the Pyramid of the Niches and some twenty ballcourts. Its sculptors excelled in the carved stone yokes, palmas, and hachas of the sacred ball game.

Sasanian Yemen.x: Yemen as a province of the Persian Sasanian empire, after the general Vahriz, sent by Khosrow I at the plea of the Himyarite prince Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan, drove out the Axumites about 570. Persian governors ruled from Sana'a until the last of them, Badhan, accepted Islam in 628.
Sasanian Yemen.gov: Province of the Sasanian Empire under Persian governors
Sasanian Yemen.faith: Zoroastrianism among the rulers; Christianity, Judaism, and polytheism among the people

Ghana Empire.x: The empire of the Soninke kings of Wagadu in the Sahel between the Senegal and Niger rivers, called by Arab writers the land of gold. Its kings commanded the meeting of southern gold with the salt caravans of the Sahara, until Almoravid pressure, drought, and the rise of Sosso and Mali broke it in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries.
Ghana Empire.faith: Soninke traditional religion; Islam among the merchants and later the court

Later Mayan City-States.x: The Postclassic Maya of Yucatán and the Guatemalan highlands after the southern collapse: Chichen Itza, then Mayapán under the Cocom lords, then some sixteen warring provinces in Yucatán, and the highland kingdoms of the K'iche' and Kaqchikel. The Spaniards subdued them between 1524 and 1546.

Puebloans - Chaco Regional System.x: The network of great houses and straight roads centered on Chaco Canyon in the San Juan basin of New Mexico, built by the Ancestral Pueblo people between about 850 and 1150. Pueblo Bonito and its neighbors were seats of ceremony and of trade in turquoise; drought in the twelfth century broke the system.
Puebloans - Chaco Regional System.gov: Ritual and trading confederacy of Pueblo towns

Ziyadid dynasty.x: An Arab dynasty that ruled the Tihama plain of Yemen from Zabid, the city founded by Muhammad ibn Ziyad, sent by the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun in 818 to subdue the region. Loyal in name to Baghdad, the Ziyadids made Zabid a seat of Sunni learning until their Abyssinian slave ministers took power.

Takrur.x: A kingdom of the middle Senegal valley, home of the people later called Tukulor, whose ruler War Jabi, who died in 1040 or 1041, was the first king of West Africa to embrace Islam and impose its law. Allied with the Almoravids, Takrur later fell under the sway of Mali.

Sulayhid Dynasty.x: An Ismaili dynasty of Yemen founded by Ali al-Sulayhi, a missionary of the Fatimid caliphs of Cairo, who conquered most of the country after 1047. Its most famous ruler was Queen Arwa, who governed from Dhu Jibla for half a century and is remembered as one of the great women of Islamic history.

Najahid Dynasty.x: A dynasty founded by Najah, an Abyssinian slave commander of the Ziyadids, which ruled Zabid and the Tihama coast of Yemen and warred with the Sulayhids of the highlands, whose founder Ali al-Sulayhi it slew. The Mahdids overthrew it in 1159.

Norse Greenland.x: The colony founded by Erik the Red about 985 in the fjords of southwest Greenland, with an Eastern and a Western Settlement, a bishop at Garðar, and some two thousand people at its height. It submitted to the king of Norway in 1261 and faded away in the fifteenth century as the climate cooled and the ships ceased to come.
Norse Greenland.gov: Commonwealth of chieftains; a dependency of the Norwegian crown from 1261
Norse Greenland.faith: Norse paganism, then Catholic Christianity from about 1000

Empire of Kanem.x: The empire of the Sayfawa kings northeast of Lake Chad, whose king Hummay embraced Islam about 1085 and whose successor Dunama Dibalemi carried its power north over the Fezzan trade routes in the thirteenth century. Pressed by the Bulala, the Sayfawa abandoned Kanem for Bornu, west of the lake, late in the fourteenth century.

Kingdom of Portugal.x: The Atlantic kingdom founded by Afonso Henriques, which won its independence from León, completed its reconquest in the Algarve in 1249, and under the house of Aviz opened the sea roads to Africa, India, and Brazil. Here it includes its African dominions, chief among them Angola and Mozambique; the monarchy fell to revolution in 1910.

Mahdids.x: A short-lived dynasty of Zabid in Yemen founded by Ali ibn Mahdi, a stern reforming preacher who overthrew the Najahids in 1159 and ruled the Tihama with puritan severity. His son Abd al-Nabi was overthrown in 1174 by the Ayyubid prince Turan-Shah, brother of Saladin.

Chimu Empire.x: The kingdom of Chimor on the north coast of Peru, heir of the Moche, whose capital Chan Chan was the largest adobe city of the Americas. Its kings ruled some six hundred miles of irrigated desert valleys and the finest goldsmiths of the Andes, until Topa Inca conquered it about 1470.
Chimu Empire.faith: Andean religion (worship of the moon, Si)

Sosso Empire.x: The kingdom of the Sosso of the Kaniaga country, whose smith-king Sumanguru Kante seized the remnants of Ghana early in the thirteenth century and oppressed the Malinke, until Sundiata Keita destroyed his power at Kirina about 1235.

Mali Empire.x: The empire of the Malinke mansas founded by Sundiata Keita about 1235, which under Mansa Musa and Mansa Sulayman ruled from the Atlantic to beyond the Niger bend, commanding the gold of Bambuk and Bure and the scholars of Timbuktu. Songhai stripped it of the Niger bend in the fifteenth century, and it shrank to its Manding heartland.
Mali Empire.gov: Monarchy (the mansa) with a council of clans
Mali Empire.faith: Islam at court, with traditional religion

Ethiopian Empire.x: The Christian empire of the Ethiopian highlands under the Solomonic dynasty, which traced its line to Solomon and the Queen of Sheba. It withstood the jihad of Ahmad Gragn, the Jesuit missions, and the Era of the Princes, and under Menelik II crushed Italy at Adwa in 1896, remaining free until Mussolini's invasion of 1935.

Ifat Sultanate.x: A Muslim sultanate on the eastern escarpment of Shewa, ruled by the Walashma dynasty from 1285, which commanded the trade road from Zeila into the highlands. Ever at war with the Christian emperors, it was crushed by Amda Seyon and finally by Dawit I and Yeshaq; its princes fled to Yemen and returned to found Adal.

Michoacán.x: The Tarascan or Purépecha state of western Mexico, founded by the war leader Tariacuri around Lake Pátzcuaro in the fourteenth century and ruled from Tzintzuntzan. Its warriors, armed with copper, routed the Aztecs about 1478; its last king, Tangaxuan II, submitted to the Spaniards in 1522 and was put to death by Nuño de Guzmán in 1530.

Bornu Empire.x: The Sayfawa kingdom west of Lake Chad, to which the dynasty withdrew from Kanem late in the fourteenth century. From Ngazargamu, founded by Ali Gaji, it dominated the central Sudan, and Idris Alooma armed it with Turkish musketeers; after 1808 the al-Kanemi family ruled from Kukawa, until Rabih az-Zubayr conquered it in 1893.
Bornu Empire.gov: Sacred monarchy (the mai); the shehus from 1846

Adal Sultanate.x: The Muslim sultanate of the Horn of Africa, heir of Ifat, centered on Dakkar and from 1520 on Harar, which commanded the trade of Zeila. Under Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi, called Gragn, its armies, with Ottoman matchlocks, overran most of Christian Ethiopia between 1529 and 1543, burning churches and forcing conversions.
Adal Sultanate.gov: Sultanate, with imams as war leaders

Aztec Triple Alliance.x: The alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco, and Tlacopan formed in 1428 to overthrow Azcapotzalco, which grew under the Mexica into the Aztec empire, drawing tribute from thirty-eight provinces between the two oceans and offering captives in sacrifice on a vast scale. It fell to Hernán Cortés and his Tlaxcalan allies in 1521.
Aztec Triple Alliance.gov: Tribute empire under the huey tlatoani of Tenochtitlan
Aztec Triple Alliance.faith: Mexica religion (Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc), with human sacrifice

Inca Empire.x: Tawantinsuyu, 'the four parts together,' the empire raised from Cusco by Pachacuti and Topa Inca, which within a century ruled some ten million people along 2,500 miles of the Andes, bound by roads, storehouses, and the knotted cords of the quipu. Pizarro's seizure of Atahualpa in 1532 broke it; the Inca of Vilcabamba held out until 1572.
Inca Empire.faith: Inca religion (Inti, the Sun, and Viracocha)

Kingdom of Kongo.x: The kingdom of the Bakongo south of the Congo estuary, ruled by the manikongo from Mbanza Kongo, which embraced Catholicism from 1491 and under Afonso I became a Christian kingdom with ties to Lisbon and Rome. Drained by the slave trade and broken at Mbwila in 1665, it lived on as a lesser kingdom until 1914.
Kingdom of Kongo.faith: Kongo religion, then Catholic Christianity from 1491

Haudenosaunee.x: The League of the Iroquois, the Five Nations of the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, and Seneca, joined by the Tuscarora about 1722, who kept their council fire at Onondaga. Armed with Dutch and English guns, they destroyed the Huron in 1649 and held the balance of power between France and Britain for a century.
Haudenosaunee.gov: Confederacy under a council of fifty chiefs
Haudenosaunee.faith: Iroquoian traditional religion; Catholic and Anglican missions among some

Songhai Empire.x: The empire of the Songhai of Gao on the Niger bend, raised by Sunni Ali, who took Timbuktu in 1468 and Djenné in 1473, and organized by Askia Muhammad into the largest state West Africa had known. Moroccan musketeers shattered it at Tondibi in 1591; its last kings held out in Dendi downriver.

(Portuguese Empire).x: Portugal's seaborne empire as a whole, the first of the European world empires and the last to end: forts and colonies from Brazil and the Gold Coast to Angola, Mozambique, Goa, Malacca, Macau, and Timor. Brazil, its richest part, became independent in 1822; the African colonies were held until 1975.
(Portuguese Empire).gov: Colonial empire of the Portuguese crown

Portuguese Empire.x: Portugal's American dominion, the colony of Brazil, reached by Cabral in 1500 and settled from 1532, which grew rich on sugar and then on gold and diamonds, worked by millions of African slaves. In 1808 it became the seat of the Portuguese monarchy and in 1815 a kingdom; it broke away as the Empire of Brazil in 1822.
Portuguese Empire.gov: Colony of the Portuguese crown under a governor-general, later a viceroy

Funj Sultanate.x: The sultanate of the Funj on the Blue Nile, founded by Amara Dunqas at Sennar about 1504 on the ruins of Christian Alodia, which ruled the Gezira and the middle Nile with the Abdallab as its vassals. Its schools spread Islam through the Sudan until the Egyptian army of Muhammad Ali ended it in 1821.

Portuguese Africa.x: Portugal's forts, islands, and trading posts along the African coast in the sixteenth century: São Jorge da Mina on the Gold Coast, the sugar island of São Tomé, the Cape Verde Islands, and the fortified posts of the east coast from Sofala to Mozambique Island. Through them passed gold, ivory, and the first great traffic in slaves.
Portuguese Africa.gov: Royal captaincies and forts of the Portuguese crown

(Spanish Empire).x: The worldwide monarchy of the Spanish crown from the accession of Charles I, embracing the Americas from California to Patagonia, the Philippines, and for a time Portugal, the Netherlands, and much of Italy, the first empire on which the sun never set. The American mainland was lost by 1825, and Cuba, Puerto Rico, and the Philippines in 1898.
rulers: First Republic (Figueras, Pi y Margall, Salmerón, Castelar)

Spanish Empire.x: Spain's empire of the Indies, won by the conquistadors from 1492 and governed through the viceroyalties of New Spain and Peru, later also New Granada and the Río de la Plata, whose silver from Potosí and Zacatecas paid for the wars of the Habsburgs. The mainland broke away between 1810 and 1825; Cuba and Puerto Rico remained.
Spanish Empire.gov: Viceroyalties under the Council of the Indies
rulers: First Republic (Figueras, Pi y Margall, Salmerón, Castelar)

Sultanate of Harar.x: The remnant of the Adal state after Gragn's fall, ruled from the walled city of Harar, whose Jugol wall was raised by the emir Nur ibn Mujahid, husband of Gragn's widow, who slew Emperor Gelawdewos in 1559. Worn down by the Oromo migrations, Adal's rulers withdrew to Aussa in 1577.

Itza Mayans.x: The Itza Maya kingdom of the Petén, ruled from the island city of Nojpetén in Lake Petén Itzá by kings bearing the title Kan Ek', which kept its independence, its books, and its gods for more than a century and a half after the fall of the Aztecs. Spanish forces under Martín de Urzúa stormed it in 1697.
Itza Mayans.gov: Monarchy (the Kan Ek' kings) with a council of lords

(Dutch Republic).x: The Republic of the Seven United Provinces, born of the revolt against Philip II and the Union of Utrecht of 1579, the greatest trading nation of seventeenth-century Europe, whose East and West India Companies held posts from New Amsterdam and Brazil to the Cape, Ceylon, and Batavia. It fell to the armies of revolutionary France in 1795.
(Dutch Republic).gov: Federal republic of provinces with a stadtholder
(Dutch Republic).faith: Dutch Reformed Christianity, with toleration of other faiths
cap: The Hague (seat of the States General)

Jesuit Reducciones.x: The missions founded from 1609 by the Society of Jesus among the Guaraní of the Paraná and Uruguay rivers, thirty towns at their height holding more than a hundred thousand Indians, governed by the fathers and native councils, armed against the slave raiders, and famed for their churches and music. The expulsion of the Jesuits in 1767 ruined them.
Jesuit Reducciones.gov: Mission towns under Jesuit fathers and Guaraní cabildos, subject to the Spanish crown

Sultanate of Darfur.x: The sultanate of the Keira dynasty of the Fur in the mountains of Jebel Marra and the plains of western Sudan, which grew rich on the Forty Days Road to Egypt, trading slaves, ivory, and ostrich feathers. Al-Zubayr Pasha conquered it for Egypt in 1874; restored under Ali Dinar in 1898, it was annexed by the British in 1916.

New France.x: France's empire in North America, founded at Quebec by Champlain in 1608, which spread along the St. Lawrence and the Great Lakes and down the Mississippi to Louisiana through the fur trade and the Jesuit missions. Never numbering more than some seventy thousand settlers, it fell to Britain in the Seven Years' War.
New France.gov: Royal colony under a governor-general and an intendant (from 1663)

English Colonial Empire.x: England's plantations overseas before the union with Scotland: Virginia and New England, Bermuda, Barbados and the Leeward Islands, Jamaica from 1655, and New York from 1664, colonies of tobacco, of sugar worked by African slaves, and of Puritan towns. In 1707 they passed to the new kingdom of Great Britain.
English Colonial Empire.gov: Royal, proprietary, and chartered colonies of the English crown

Oyo Empire.x: The empire of the Yoruba alaafins of Oyo-Ile, north of the forest, whose cavalry made it the greatest power between the Volta and the Niger in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, holding Dahomey tributary and selling captives through Porto-Novo and Badagry. Revolt at Ilorin from 1817 and the Fulani jihad destroyed it by about 1835.
Oyo Empire.gov: Monarchy (the alaafin) checked by the Oyo Mesi council and the Ogboni

New Netherland.x: The Dutch West India Company's colony on the Hudson, the Delaware, and the Connecticut, with Fort Orange at Albany and New Amsterdam on Manhattan, a fur-trading province of Dutch, Walloons, and many other nations. Peter Stuyvesant surrendered it to the English in 1664, and it became New York.
New Netherland.gov: Chartered colony of the Dutch West India Company under a director-general

Dutch Brazil.x: New Holland, the Dutch West India Company's conquest of the sugar coast of northeast Brazil, taken from Portugal with Recife and Olinda in 1630. Under Count Johan Maurits of Nassau-Siegen it flourished, with painters, naturalists, and toleration for Jews, but the Portuguese planters rose in 1645 and drove the Dutch out in 1654.
Dutch Brazil.faith: Dutch Reformed Christianity; Catholics and Jews tolerated

Wadai Empire.x: A sultanate east of Lake Chad founded by Abd al-Karim about 1635, which threw off the Tunjur and rose in the nineteenth century to dominate the central Sudan, raiding the south for slaves and trading across the desert to Benghazi. France conquered it between 1909 and 1912.
Wadai Empire.faith: Sunni Islam (Sanusi influence in the nineteenth century)

Dutch Cape Colony.x: The Dutch East India Company's settlement at the Cape of Good Hope, founded by Jan van Riebeeck in 1652 to refresh the Indies fleets. Its free burghers, Huguenot refugees, and slaves from Madagascar and the East were forebears of the Afrikaners and the Cape Coloured; its trekboers pushed east to the Great Fish River. Britain seized it in 1795.
Dutch Cape Colony.gov: Company colony under a governor and Council of Policy

Dutch Guiana.x: The Dutch plantation colonies of the Guiana coast: Suriname, taken from the English in 1667 and kept by the Treaty of Breda in exchange for New Netherland, and Essequibo, Demerara, and Berbice to the west. Their sugar estates rested on African slaves, many of whom escaped to found the Maroon nations of the interior.
Dutch Guiana.gov: Chartered colonies (Society of Suriname, West India Company)
Dutch Guiana.faith: Dutch Reformed Christianity; Judaism; Moravian missions

French India.x: The French East India Company's possessions in the Indian Ocean: the trading towns of India under Pondichéry, with Chandernagore, Mahé, Karikal, and Yanam, and the Mascarene islands of Bourbon and Île de France that served as their naval base. Dupleix nearly won southern India for France before Britain prevailed in the 1750s.
French India.gov: Company possessions under governors-general (crown rule from 1769)
French India.faith: Catholic Christianity; Hinduism and Islam among Indian subjects

Ashanti Empire.x: The empire of the Akan kingdom of Asante, founded by Osei Tutu and the priest Okomfo Anokye about 1701 and bound together by the Golden Stool, which ruled the forests of modern Ghana from Kumasi and traded gold and slaves to the coast. It fought the British in a series of wars until its annexation in 1901.
Ashanti Empire.gov: Confederate monarchy (the asantehene) with the Asanteman council

Kingdom of Lunda.x: The Lunda empire of the upper Kasai, founded in the seventeenth century, by tradition through the marriage of the Luba hunter Chibinda Ilunga to the Lunda queen Lueji. From their capital Musumba its rulers, the mwata yamvo, sent out conquering kinsmen to found tributary kingdoms as far as the Luapula, and traded slaves and ivory west to Angola.
Kingdom of Lunda.gov: Monarchy (the mwata yamvo) with tributary kingdoms

Bamana Empire.x: The Bambara kingdom of Ségou on the middle Niger, organized by Biton Coulibaly about 1712 around his warrior band, the tonjon, and consolidated by the Diarra dynasty of Ngolo Diarra. Its armies sold their captives to the Atlantic trade; it fell to El Hadj Umar Tall in 1861.

Greenland.x: Colonial Greenland, which Denmark-Norway resettled from 1721, when Hans Egede's Lutheran mission came in search of the lost Norse, and held under the royal trade monopoly of the Royal Greenland Trading Department from 1774. Denmark kept it when Norway was lost in 1814; in 1940, with Denmark occupied by Germany, the United States took it under its protection.
Greenland.gov: Colony of the Danish crown under a royal trade monopoly

French West Indies.x: France's sugar islands after the Seven Years' War: Saint-Domingue, the richest colony in the world, with Martinique, Guadeloupe, and their dependencies, where more than half a million African slaves produced much of Europe's sugar and coffee. The slave rising of 1791 in Saint-Domingue began the end of the system.
French West Indies.gov: Royal colonies under governors and intendants
French West Indies.faith: Catholic Christianity; Vodou among the slaves

United States of America.x: The federal republic born of the Declaration of Independence of 1776 and the Constitution of 1787, which spread across the continent by purchase, treaty, and war, survived the Civil War of 1861 to 1865 that ended slavery, and in the twentieth century became the foremost industrial, financial, and military power on earth.
United States of America.faith: Protestant Christianity predominant, with Catholic, Jewish, and other faiths; no established church

Vermont Republic.x: The independent state proclaimed in 1777 by the settlers of the New Hampshire Grants, claimed by both New Hampshire and New York, with Ethan Allen's Green Mountain Boys as its militia. Its constitution was the first in America to forbid adult slavery and to give the vote to men without property; it joined the Union in 1791.

Kingdom of Hawaï'i.x: The kingdom united by Kamehameha I, who conquered the islands with the help of European arms between 1795 and 1810, and ruled by his dynasty and its successors from Lahaina and Honolulu. Its kings embraced Christianity and a constitution, and sugar planters of American birth grew powerful, until they overthrew Queen Liliʻuokalani in 1893.
Kingdom of Hawaï'i.faith: Hawaiian religion until 1819; Protestant Christianity thereafter

French Colony of Guiana.x: The French colony on the northeast coast of South America, centered on the island town of Cayenne, a land of struggling plantations which the Revolution would make a place of exile for deported priests and political prisoners, and which later held the penal colony of Devil's Island.

Merina Kingdom.x: The kingdom of the Merina of the central highlands of Madagascar, united by Andrianampoinimerina and enlarged by Radama I, who, allied with Britain, made himself master of most of the island. Ranavalona I persecuted the Christians; her successors embraced Protestantism, until France conquered the island in 1895 and abolished the monarchy in 1897.
Merina Kingdom.gov: Monarchy (from 1864 governed by the prime minister Rainilaiarivony)
Merina Kingdom.faith: Malagasy ancestral religion; Protestant Christianity as the state faith from 1869

Haiti.x: Saint-Domingue in the years of revolution, from the slave rising of 1791 and the abolition of slavery by the French commissioners in 1793 to the rule of Toussaint Louverture, who expelled the Spanish and British invaders, overran Spanish Santo Domingo, and in 1801 gave the colony a constitution naming himself governor for life.
Haiti.gov: French colony under revolutionary commissioners, then Toussaint's governorship

British Cape Colony.x: The Cape of Good Hope under British rule, first from 1795 to 1803 and again from 1806, which abolished slavery in 1834, drove the Boers to trek inland, fought the Xhosa on its eastern frontier for most of the century, and won responsible government in 1872. Diamonds made it rich; it joined the Union of South Africa in 1910.

French Louisiana.x: Louisiana returned to France by Spain under the secret Treaty of San Ildefonso in 1800, the heart of Napoleon's dream of a new empire in America fed by the sugar of Saint-Domingue. When Leclerc's army perished in Saint-Domingue, Napoleon sold the whole territory to the United States in 1803, before French rule had truly begun.
French Louisiana.gov: French colony (held for twenty days in 1803)

United Kingdom of Great Britain and Irel.x: The kingdom formed by the union of Great Britain and Ireland in 1801, heart of the largest empire in history, the first industrial nation, and mistress of the seas for a century after Trafalgar. Its dominions included Aden, seized in 1839 to guard the road to India; the Irish Free State broke away in 1922.
United Kingdom of Great Britain and Irel.faith: Protestant Christianity (Church of England established; Church of Ireland until 1871)

Cape Colony (Batavian Republic).x: The Cape of Good Hope restored to the Dutch, now the Batavian Republic, by the Peace of Amiens of 1802, handed over in 1803, and governed by the reforming Commissioner-General Jacob de Mist and Governor Jan Willem Janssens, who promoted religious toleration and civil marriage. The British retook it after Blaauwberg in January 1806.
Cape Colony (Batavian Republic).faith: Dutch Reformed Christianity, with toleration of other faiths

Empire of Haiti.x: Haiti under its crowned rulers: Jean-Jacques Dessalines, who proclaimed himself emperor in 1804 and was murdered in 1806; Henri Christophe, king of the north from 1811 to 1820, who built the Citadelle Laferrière and the palace of Sans-Souci; and Faustin Soulouque, emperor from 1849 to 1859.
Empire of Haiti.gov: Monarchy (empire, then northern kingdom, then empire again)

Republic of Haiti.x: The republic founded by Alexandre Pétion in the south and west in 1806, which under Jean-Pierre Boyer ruled the whole island from 1822 to 1844. Torn by coups, occupied by the United States from 1915 to 1934, ruled by the Duvaliers from 1957 to 1986, and devastated by the earthquake of 2010, it is the poorest nation of the Americas.
Republic of Haiti.faith: Catholic Christianity and Vodou; growing Protestantism

Río de la Plata.x: The United Provinces of the Río de la Plata, born of the May Revolution of 1810 in Buenos Aires, which declared independence at Tucumán in 1816 and sent San Martín over the Andes. Its central government dissolved in 1820 into rival provinces, Buenos Aires foremost, which fought Brazil and lost Uruguay before Rosas rose to master them.
Río de la Plata.gov: Republic of juntas, triumvirates, and supreme directors; then a league of provinces
rulers: Juan Gregorio de Las Heras (governor of Buenos Aires)
Juan José Viamonte (governor of Buenos Aires)
Juan Manuel de Rosas (governor of Buenos Aires)
Juan Ramón Balcarce (governor of Buenos Aires)
Juan José Viamonte (governor of Buenos Aires)

New Granada.x: The United Provinces of New Granada, the federation of patriot provinces formed in 1811, whose quarrels with Antonio Nariño's centralist Cundinamarca earned the age the name of the Foolish Fatherland. Pablo Morillo's Spanish army reconquered it in 1815 and 1816 and shot its leaders, until Bolívar's victory at Boyacá in 1819 freed it for good.
rulers: Camilo Torres Tenorio (president of the United Provinces)

Paraguay.x: The landlocked republic of the upper Paraná, which threw off Spain and Buenos Aires in 1811 and was sealed off from the world by the dictator Dr. Francia. The López dictators made it a military power, but the war of 1864 to 1870 against Brazil, Argentina, and Uruguay destroyed perhaps half its people. It won the Chaco War.

Republic of Venezuela.x: The First and Second Republics of Venezuela: the first proclaimed at Caracas on 5 July 1811 and lost in 1812 after the great earthquake and Francisco de Miranda's surrender; the second won by Bolívar's Admirable Campaign of 1813 and destroyed in 1814 by the llanero cavalry of José Tomás Boves.

Mexicans.x: Insurgent Mexico in the war of independence: the rising of Miguel Hidalgo in 1810, then the cause of the priest José María Morelos, whose Congress of Chilpancingo declared independence in 1813 and whose Constitution of Apatzingán of 1814 proclaimed a republic. After Morelos was shot in 1815, guerrillas under Vicente Guerrero kept the cause alive in the south.

Republic of Chile.x: The republic of the long Pacific coast between the Andes and the sea, freed by O'Higgins and San Martín in 1817 and 1818. Ordered by the conservative constitution of 1833, it won the War of the Pacific and its nitrate provinces, and passed through Allende's socialism and Pinochet's military rule before democracy returned in 1990.

State of Quito.x: The short-lived state formed by the second junta of Quito, which in 1812 proclaimed the first constitution of the lands that became Ecuador. Royalist troops under Toribio Montes crushed it in November 1812.
rulers: José de Cuero y Caicedo (president of the junta)

Federal League.x: The League of the Free Peoples formed by José Gervasio Artigas, Protector of the Banda Oriental, Entre Ríos, Corrientes, Santa Fe, Córdoba, and the Misiones, who championed a federal republic against the centralism of Buenos Aires. A Portuguese invasion from Brazil in 1816 and the defection of his allies broke it; Artigas died in exile in Paraguay.
Federal League.gov: Confederation of provinces under a protector

Omani East Africa.x: The Swahili coast under the Al Bu Said sultans of Oman, who broke the rival Mazrui of Mombasa in 1837 and made Zanzibar, with its clove plantations and its slave market, the capital of an empire of the Indian Ocean. On the death of Sa'id bin Sultan in 1856 his African and Arabian lands were divided between his sons.

Cundinamarca.x: The Free State of Cundinamarca, the province of Bogotá, whose president Antonio Nariño, translator of the Rights of Man, upheld a strong central government against the federalist United Provinces of New Granada and declared full independence from Spain in 1813. It was forced into the United Provinces after Bolívar took Bogotá in December 1814.

Imamate of Yemen.x: The Zaydi imamate of the Qasimid line, which had expelled the Ottomans from Yemen in the seventeenth century and ruled the highlands from Sana'a. By the nineteenth century it had lost the coast and much of its authority to the tribes and to rival imams; the Ottomans retook Sana'a in 1872.

Dutch West Indies.x: The Dutch islands of the Caribbean: Curaçao, taken from Spain in 1634, with Aruba, Bonaire, Sint Eustatius, Saba, and Sint Maarten, entrepôts of the West India Company's trade, not least in slaves. After the Napoleonic wars the name took in Suriname as well. Slavery was abolished in 1863, and the Curaçao refineries of Venezuelan oil brought wealth in the twentieth century.
Dutch West Indies.gov: West India Company posts, then Dutch colonies under governors
Dutch West Indies.faith: Protestant and Catholic Christianity; Hinduism and Islam among Asian immigrants

Massina Empire.x: The Fulani caliphate of the inland delta of the Niger founded by Seku Amadu after his victory over the Bambara in 1818, ruled from Hamdullahi by a council of forty scholars under strict Islamic law. It fell in 1862 to El Hadj Umar Tall's Tukulor empire.

Zululand.x: The Zulu kingdom forged by Shaka from 1816 through the drill of his regiments and the conquest of his neighbors, which dominated the lands between the Phongolo and the Thukela. It beat the British at Isandlwana in 1879 but was broken at Ulundi, carved into thirteen chiefdoms, and annexed to Natal in 1897.

Empire of Brazil.x: The South American empire founded when Pedro, heir of Portugal, proclaimed Brazil's independence in 1822, the one lasting monarchy of the Americas. Under the long reign of the scholarly Pedro II it held together a country the size of a continent, won the Paraguayan War, and abolished slavery in 1888; a military coup proclaimed the republic in 1889.

Gran Colombia.x: The Republic of Colombia created by Bolívar at Angostura in 1819 and Cúcuta in 1821, uniting New Granada, Venezuela, Quito, and Panama in one great state. Rent by the rivalry of Venezuela's Páez and New Granada's Santander, it fell apart in 1830 as Bolívar lay dying, into Venezuela, Ecuador, and New Granada.
rulers: Francisco de Paula Santander (vice president, acting)

First Mexican Empire.x: The empire proclaimed after Mexican independence, which crowned its liberator Agustín de Iturbide as Agustín I in July 1822 and for a time took in all Central America, the largest state of the Americas. Iturbide dissolved the congress, was overthrown by Santa Anna and the republicans in March 1823, and was shot on his return from exile in 1824.
rulers: Agustín de Iturbide (president of the regency)

Republic of Peru.x: The republic proclaimed by San Martín at Lima in 1821 and secured at Ayacucho in 1824, the old heart of Spain's South American empire. Through decades of caudillos it lived on guano, lost its southern provinces to Chile in the War of the Pacific, and passed in the twentieth century between oligarchs, generals, and reformers.
rulers: Supreme Governing Junta (José de La Mar)

Liberia.x: The colony planted on the Grain Coast in 1822 by the American Colonization Society as a home for free black Americans and recaptured Africans, governed by white agents and then by Joseph Jenkins Roberts. Its settlers, the Americo-Liberians, ruled the coast and its native peoples, and declared independence in 1847.
Liberia.gov: Colony of the American Colonization Society

Federated Republic of Mexico.x: The United Mexican States under the federal constitutions of 1824 and 1857, a republic of states racked by pronunciamientos, from which Texas broke away in 1836 and which lost half its territory to the United States in 1848. The Reform of Benito Juárez stripped the Church of its estates and fought the War of the Reform before the French intervention.
Federated Republic of Mexico.faith: Catholic Christianity (the sole permitted religion until the Reform)
rulers: Triumvirate (Pedro Vélez, Lucas Alamán, and Luis Quintanar)
Manuel de la Peña y Peña

United Provinces of Central America.x: The Federal Republic of Central America, formed in 1823 by the five provinces of the old Captaincy-General of Guatemala, Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, and Costa Rica, after their brief union with Iturbide's Mexico. Its Liberal president Francisco Morazán fought for it until the conservative peasant leader Rafael Carrera broke it between 1838 and 1840.

Bolivia.x: The republic of Upper Peru, named for Bolívar in 1825, a land of high plateaus and of silver and tin. It lost its coast to Chile, the Acre to Brazil, and most of the Chaco to Paraguay; the revolution of 1952 gave land and votes to the Indian majority, and Evo Morales became its first indigenous president in 2006.

Oriental Republic of Uruguay.x: The old Banda Oriental between the River Plate and Brazil, made independent in 1828 as a buffer between its great neighbors. After the long strife of Blancos and Colorados it became, under José Batlle y Ordóñez, a model welfare state, the 'Switzerland of America,' interrupted by military rule from 1973 to 1985.
Oriental Republic of Uruguay.faith: Catholic Christianity; a secular state since 1918

Argentine Confederation.x: The league of Argentine provinces under the iron rule of Juan Manuel de Rosas, governor of Buenos Aires and master of their foreign affairs from 1835, whose Mazorca terrorized his Unitarian enemies. After Justo José de Urquiza beat him at Caseros in 1852, the Confederation adopted the constitution of 1853 with its capital at Paraná, while Buenos Aires stood apart.

Republic of New Granada.x: The republic formed in 1831 from the central part of Gran Colombia, with Panama, after the secession of Venezuela and Ecuador, and organized by Francisco de Paula Santander, 'the man of laws.' Its Liberal and Conservative parties, born in these years, fought their first civil wars; in 1858 it became the Granadine Confederation.

Venezuela.x: The republic that left Gran Colombia in 1830 under José Antonio Páez, ruled through the nineteenth century by caudillos from Páez and the Monagas brothers to Antonio Guzmán Blanco. Under the dictator Juan Vicente Gómez it became the world's foremost oil exporter; democracy came in 1958, and Hugo Chávez's Bolivarian revolution in 1999.

Republic of Ecuador.x: The republic of the old Audiencia of Quito, which left Gran Colombia in 1830 under the Venezuelan general Juan José Flores. Its politics swung between the Catholic conservatism of the highlands, embodied by Gabriel García Moreno, who consecrated the nation to the Sacred Heart, and the liberalism of the port of Guayaquil under Eloy Alfaro.

Peru-Bolivian Confederation.x: The confederation of North Peru, South Peru, and Bolivia created by the Bolivian marshal Andrés de Santa Cruz after his victories of 1835 and 1836, with himself as Supreme Protector. Chile and Argentina, alarmed at so great a power, made war on it, and a Chilean army under Manuel Bulnes broke it at Yungay in January 1839.
rulers: Luis José de Orbegoso (president of North Peru)
José de la Riva-Agüero (president of North Peru)
Pío de Tristán (president of South Peru)

Centralist Mexico.x: Mexico under the centralist Seven Laws of 1836, which abolished the states in favor of departments ruled from the capital, provoking the secession of Texas and of Yucatán and risings across the north. Its governments, made and unmade by Santa Anna, met the American invasion of 1846, when federalism was restored.

Republic of Texas.x: The republic won from Mexico by the American settlers of Texas at San Jacinto in 1836, which for nearly ten years kept its independence under Sam Houston and Mirabeau Lamar, with a navy and a lone-star flag, while Mexico refused to recognize it. The United States annexed it in 1845, which led to war with Mexico.

Riograndense Republic.x: The republic proclaimed in 1836 by the ranchers of Rio Grande do Sul in the Ragamuffin War against the Empire of Brazil, led by Bento Gonçalves, with the young Giuseppe Garibaldi and his Anita among its fighters. After ten years the Treaty of Ponche Verde of 1845 brought it back into the Empire on generous terms.

Republic of the Rio Grande.x: A breakaway republic proclaimed in January 1840 by federalists of Tamaulipas, Nuevo León, and Coahuila against the centralist government of Mexico, with Jesús de Cárdenas as president and Antonio Canales as commander. Its army was beaten, and Canales made his peace with the government in November 1840.

Republic of Nicaragua.x: The republic that left the Central American federation in 1838, long torn between Liberal León and Conservative Granada, invaded by the filibuster William Walker in 1855, occupied by American marines for most of the years from 1912 to 1933, and ruled by the Somoza family from 1936 to 1979, before the Sandinista revolution.

Honduras.x: The mountainous republic of the isthmus, independent since 1838 and birthplace of Francisco Morazán, whose banana coast fell in the twentieth century under the sway of the United Fruit and Standard Fruit companies, the original 'banana republic.' Tiburcio Carías ruled it from 1933 to 1949, and soldiers for much of the century after.

Guatemala.x: The most populous Central American republic, set up as a separate state by the conservative caudillo Rafael Carrera, who ruled it until 1865. Liberal dictators from Justo Rufino Barrios to Jorge Ubico followed; the reforming governments of 1944 to 1954 ended in a coup backed by the CIA, and a civil war of thirty-six years followed.
Guatemala.faith: Catholic Christianity, with Maya traditions; growing Protestantism

Republic of Costa Rica.x: The southernmost of the five republics of the old Central American federation, a land of small coffee farmers, which beat William Walker's filibusters in 1856 under Juan Rafael Mora and became the steadiest democracy of the isthmus. After the brief civil war of 1948 José Figueres abolished its army.

Republic of El Salvador.x: The smallest and most crowded of the Central American republics, ruled by its coffee oligarchy, whose dictator Maximiliano Hernández Martínez crushed the peasant rising of 1932 in the massacre called La Matanza. The civil war of 1980 to 1992 cost some 75,000 lives; since 2019 Nayib Bukele has governed with a strong hand.

Natalia Republic.x: The republic founded by the Voortrekkers south of the Thukela after their victory at Blood River in 1838, with its capital at Pietermaritzburg, named for the trek leaders Piet Retief and Gert Maritz. British troops seized Port Natal in 1842 and annexed the republic in 1843; most of its Boers trekked back over the Drakensberg.

Los Altos.x: The highland state of western Guatemala, centered on Quetzaltenango, which declared itself the sixth state of the Central American federation in 1838. Rafael Carrera's army reconquered it in 1840, and it rose again only briefly in 1848.
Los Altos.gov: Liberal state of the Central American federation

Colony of Natal.x: The British colony on the Indian Ocean coast between the Drakensberg and the sea, annexed in 1843, whose sugar planters brought indentured laborers from India from 1860; among the Indians of Natal Mohandas Gandhi worked from 1893. It absorbed Zululand in 1897 and joined the Union of South Africa in 1910.
Colony of Natal.faith: Protestant Christianity; Hinduism and Islam among Indians; Zulu traditional religion

Dominican Republic.x: The eastern two-thirds of Hispaniola, which won independence from Haiti in 1844 under Juan Pablo Duarte's Trinitarios, returned briefly to Spanish rule from 1861 to 1865, and was occupied by the United States from 1916 to 1924. Rafael Trujillo ruled it as his private estate from 1930 until his assassination in 1961.

Republic of Liberia.x: Africa's oldest republic, proclaimed in 1847 by the settlers of the American Colonization Society's colony, which kept its independence through the Scramble for Africa, though it yielded land to Britain and France. Ruled for over a century by the Americo-Liberian True Whig Party, it fell to Samuel Doe's coup in 1980 and to civil wars from 1989 to 2003.

State of Buenos Aires.x: The province of Buenos Aires as a separate state, after it refused in 1852 to join the Confederation led by Urquiza and kept for itself the customs revenues of the port. Beaten at Cepeda in 1859, it won at Pavón in 1861 under Bartolomé Mitre, who reunited Argentina on Buenos Aires's terms.

Republic of Baja California.x: The paper republic proclaimed in November 1853 by the American filibuster William Walker, who landed at La Paz with forty-five men and soon declared it part of a Republic of Sonora. Mexican resistance and hunger drove his band back across the border in May 1854.

Mosquito Kingdom.x: The kingdom of the Miskito people of the Caribbean coast of Nicaragua and Honduras, whose kings were crowned under British protection from the seventeenth century and whose warriors raided the Spanish frontier. Britain gave up its protectorate by the Treaty of Managua in 1860; Nicaragua annexed the Mosquito Reserve in 1894.

South African Republic.x: The Transvaal republic of the Boers north of the Vaal, recognized by Britain at the Sand River Convention of 1852, annexed by Britain in 1877, and restored after Majuba in 1881. The gold of the Witwatersrand made it rich and drew the uitlanders whose grievances, joined to British ambition, brought on the war of 1899 to 1902 that ended it.

Free Orange State.x: The Orange Free State, the Boer republic between the Orange and the Vaal, independent from 1854 by the Bloemfontein Convention and a model of orderly government under President Johannes Brand. Allied with the Transvaal, it went to war with Britain in 1899 and was annexed as the Orange River Colony in 1900.

Majeerteen Sultanate.x: The sultanate of the Majeerteen clan of northeastern Somalia, at the tip of the Horn, which grew rich on frankincense and on salvage from the ships wrecked on Cape Guardafui. Its sultan Osman Mahamuud accepted an Italian protectorate in 1889, and Italy suppressed the sultanate in 1927.

Sultanate of Zanzibar.x: The island sultanate left to Majid bin Said when his father's empire was divided in 1856, master of the clove plantations and of the East African trade in slaves and ivory. Britain made it a protectorate in 1890 and shelled the palace in the shortest war in history in 1896; independent in 1963, it fell to revolution a month later.

Granadine Confederation.x: The federal constitution of 1858 that turned New Granada into a confederation of sovereign states under the Conservative president Mariano Ospina Rodríguez. The Liberal general Tomás Cipriano de Mosquera rose against it and, after taking Bogotá in 1861, refounded the country as the United States of Colombia.

Argentine Republic.x: The Argentine nation reunited under Buenos Aires after Pavón in 1861, which by immigration from Italy and Spain, by railways, and by the wheat and beef of the pampas became one of the richest nations on earth by 1914. Its twentieth century brought coups, Peronism, the Dirty War of the military junta, and defeat in the Falklands in 1982.

Confederate States of America.x: The confederacy of eleven slaveholding Southern states that seceded after Lincoln's election, with Jefferson Davis as president, and fought four years for independence under generals such as Robert E. Lee and Stonewall Jackson. It collapsed in the spring of 1865 after the fall of Richmond and Lee's surrender at Appomattox.

United States of Colombia.x: The federal Colombia of the Liberal constitution of Rionegro of 1863, a union of nine sovereign states under a weak president serving two-year terms, which separated Church and state. Civil wars and stagnation led Rafael Núñez to replace it with the centralist Republic of Colombia in 1886.

Mexican Monarchists.x: The Mexican conservatives who, with the French army that took Mexico City in June 1863, set up a Regency under General Juan Nepomuceno Almonte and Archbishop Pelagio Antonio de Labastida and offered the throne to the Archduke Maximilian of Austria, who accepted it at Miramar in April 1864.

Second Mexican Empire.x: The empire of Maximilian of Habsburg, set on the throne of Mexico by Napoleon III's army in 1864 with his wife Carlota, a liberal-minded monarch who disappointed his conservative backers. When the French withdrew under American pressure, Juárez's republicans took him at Querétaro and shot him in June 1867.

Khedivate of Egypt.x: Egypt under the khedives of Muhammad Ali's line, nominally vassals of the Ottoman sultan, whose dominion stretched up the Nile through the Sudan toward the Great Lakes under Khedive Isma'il. Bankrupted by Isma'il's debts and the Suez Canal, it fell under British occupation in 1882 and lost the Sudan to the Mahdi in 1885.
Khedivate of Egypt.gov: Hereditary viceroyalty under Ottoman suzerainty (British occupation from 1882)

Dominion of Canada.x: The self-governing federation of British North America created in 1867, which bought the Hudson's Bay lands, spanned the continent with the Canadian Pacific Railway in 1885, and peopled its prairies with immigrants. Its sacrifices at Ypres and Vimy Ridge in the Great War won it a voice of its own, and the Statute of Westminster of 1931 made it sovereign.
Dominion of Canada.gov: Federal parliamentary monarchy under the British crown

Mexico.x: The Mexican republic restored by Benito Juárez after the fall of Maximilian, ruled for more than thirty years by Porfirio Díaz, convulsed by the Revolution of 1910 to 1920, and governed for seventy-one years by the party that became the Institutional Revolutionary Party, until Vicente Fox won in 2000. Lázaro Cárdenas nationalized its oil in 1938.

British Gold Coast.x: The British colony of the Gold Coast, proclaimed in 1874 after Wolseley's march on Kumasi, which joined the old forts bought from the Danes in 1850 and the Dutch in 1872 to the Fante coast under British protection. Its capital moved from Cape Coast to Accra in 1877; Asante was annexed in 1901 after Yaa Asantewaa's war.
British Gold Coast.faith: Akan traditional religion; Christianity on the coast; Islam in the north

Sultanate of Hobyo.x: The Somali sultanate founded about 1878 by Yusuf Ali Kenadid, a Majeerteen prince who, worsted by his kinsman Boqor Osman, carved out a new realm on the Indian Ocean coast at Hobyo. He accepted Italian protection in 1888, and Italy suppressed the sultanate in 1925.

German Africa.x: The German colonial empire in Africa, proclaimed in 1884 and 1885: Togoland, Kamerun, German South West Africa, and German East Africa, governed from Lomé, Buea and Duala, Windhoek, and Dar es Salaam. Marked by the Herero and Maji Maji wars, all of it was lost in the First World War, though Lettow-Vorbeck fought on in the east until the armistice.
German Africa.gov: Colonial empire of the German Reich
German Africa.faith: Traditional religions and Islam; Protestant and Catholic missions
