British Africa.x: Britain's African empire as a whole, from the Cape and the Rhodesias to Egypt's Sudan and from the Gold Coast and Nigeria to Kenya and Uganda, ruled by governors and, under Lugard's system of indirect rule, through native chiefs. The Sudan and Ghana led the way to independence in 1956 and 1957; Zimbabwe was the last, in 1980.
British Africa.gov: Colonial empire of the British crown (colonies, protectorates, and mandates)

Republic of Colombia.x: The centralist republic founded by Rafael Núñez's constitution of 1886, which lost Panama in 1903 after the Thousand Days' War. Bound to the coffee trade, it lived through La Violencia between Liberals and Conservatives after 1948 and half a century of war with Marxist guerrillas and drug cartels, ended in large part by the peace with the FARC in 2016.

United States of Brazil.x: The Brazilian republic proclaimed by Marshal Deodoro da Fonseca in 1889: the First Republic of the coffee planters of São Paulo and the cattlemen of Minas Gerais, Getúlio Vargas's revolution of 1930 and his Estado Novo, the democratic republic of Kubitschek, who built Brasília, and the military regime that seized power in 1964.
United States of Brazil.gov: Federal presidential republic (dictatorship 1937 to 1945; military rule from 1964)
United States of Brazil.faith: Catholic Christianity; a secular state from 1890
rulers: Military junta (Tasso Fragoso, Mena Barreto, and Isaías de Noronha)

Italian Africa.x: Italy's African empire: Eritrea from 1890, Italian Somaliland, Libya from 1912, and, after Mussolini's conquest of 1935 and 1936, Ethiopia, joined with Eritrea and Somalia as Italian East Africa. British and Commonwealth forces conquered East Africa in 1941, and the last of Libya fell to the Allies early in 1943.
Italian Africa.gov: Colonial empire of the Kingdom of Italy
Italian Africa.faith: Islam, Ethiopian Orthodox Christianity, and Catholicism

Congo Free State.x: The vast Congo basin held as the personal possession of Leopold II, King of the Belgians, under the sanction of the Berlin Conference, and worked for profit in ivory and wild rubber gathered by forced labor enforced with hostage-taking, flogging, and mutilation. International outcry forced its annexation by Belgium in 1908.
Congo Free State.gov: Personal absolute rule of Leopold II
Congo Free State.faith: Traditional religions; Catholic and Protestant missions

Mahdist State.x: The Islamic state of the Sudan founded by Muhammad Ahmad, the Mahdi, who drove out the Egyptians and took Khartoum in 1885, and ruled after his death that same year by the Khalifa Abdallahi from the new capital of Omdurman. Kitchener's Anglo-Egyptian army destroyed it at Omdurman in 1898.
Mahdist State.gov: Theocratic state (the Mahdi, then the Khalifa)

Cuban Nationalists.x: The Republic of Cuba in Arms, the insurgent government of the war of independence that José Martí launched in 1895 and that Máximo Gómez and Antonio Maceo waged across the island against some 200,000 Spanish soldiers. American intervention in 1898 ended Spanish rule, but the United States occupied the island until 1902.

Republic of Hawai'i.x: The republic proclaimed on 4 July 1894 by the men who had overthrown Queen Liliʻuokalani, with Sanford B. Dole as president and power reserved to the propertied. It crushed a royalist counter-rising in 1895 and won its aim of annexation by the United States in 1898.

British West Africa.x: Britain's four West African colonies: Nigeria, united by Lugard in 1914, the Gold Coast, Sierra Leone, and the Gambia, sharing a currency board from 1912 and ruled largely through native authorities. Ghana led the march to independence in 1957, followed by Nigeria in 1960, Sierra Leone in 1961, and the Gambia in 1965.
British West Africa.faith: Islam in the north; Christianity and traditional religions in the south

Republic of Cuba.x: The island republic born in 1902 under the American tutelage of the Platt Amendment, ruled by Gerardo Machado and then Fulgencio Batista, and turned by Fidel Castro's revolution of 1959 into a communist state allied with the Soviet Union, the scene of the missile crisis of 1962. The Castro brothers governed it for nearly sixty years.
Republic of Cuba.gov: Presidential republic; communist one-party state from 1961
Republic of Cuba.faith: Catholic Christianity and Santería; an officially atheist state from 1976 to 1992

Republic of Panama.x: The isthmian republic that seceded from Colombia in November 1903 with the backing of the United States, which at once took the Canal Zone in perpetuity. Ruled by the National Guard of Omar Torrijos and Manuel Noriega from 1968 until the American invasion of 1989, it received the canal itself on 31 December 1999.

Belgian Congo.x: The Congo annexed by Belgium from Leopold II in 1908 and ruled by the trinity of state, Catholic missions, and great mining companies such as the Union Minière of Katanga, whose copper, and whose uranium, used in the first atomic bombs, made it rich. Hastily granted independence in June 1960, it fell at once into mutiny and secession.
Belgian Congo.faith: Catholic and Protestant Christianity; traditional religions; Kimbanguism

Union of South Africa.x: The self-governing dominion that joined the Cape, Natal, the Transvaal, and the Orange River Colony in 1910, eight years after the Boer War, under the Boer generals Louis Botha and Jan Smuts. It fought for Britain in both world wars, built apartheid under the National Party from 1948, and in 1961 left the Commonwealth as a republic.
Union of South Africa.gov: Parliamentary dominion under the British crown
Union of South Africa.faith: Protestant Christianity (Dutch Reformed and Anglican); African churches and traditional religion

Portuguese Republic.x: The First Portuguese Republic proclaimed in October 1910, anticlerical and unstable, with forty-five governments in sixteen years, which sent troops to Flanders and Africa in the Great War. A military coup in May 1926 ended it, and in 1932 the finance minister António de Oliveira Salazar became prime minister.

Maderistas.x: The revolutionary forces of Francisco I. Madero, who proclaimed the Plan of San Luis Potosí against the dictatorship of Porfirio Díaz in 1910 and whose northern irregulars under Pascual Orozco and Pancho Villa took Ciudad Juárez in May 1911, driving Díaz into exile. Madero was elected president that autumn.

Asir.x: The Idrisid emirate of Asir on the Red Sea coast of Arabia, founded by Muhammad ibn Ali al-Idrisi, a Sufi leader who allied with Italy and then Britain against the Ottomans. After his death in 1923 it fell under the protection and then the rule of Ibn Saud.

North Yemen.x: Highland Yemen of the Zaydi imams, the Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Imam Yahya, independent upon the Ottoman collapse in 1918, which his son Ahmad ruled from Taiz. The army revolution of 1962 proclaimed the Yemen Arab Republic and began a civil war between royalists backed by Saudi Arabia and republicans backed by Egypt; it united with the south in 1990.
North Yemen.faith: Zaydi Shia and Shafi'i Sunni Islam

Canada.x: The sovereign Canadian federation after the Statute of Westminster, a founder of NATO, which took in Newfoundland in 1949, adopted the maple leaf flag in 1965, and brought its constitution home from London with a charter of rights in 1982. Quebec's sovereignty movement tested its unity, losing referendums in 1980 and, by a hair, in 1995.

Estado Novo.x: The authoritarian, corporative, and Catholic regime of António de Oliveira Salazar, the 'New State' of the constitution of 1933, which kept Portugal neutral in the Second World War and fought from 1961 to hold Angola, Mozambique, and Guinea against independence movements. The Carnation Revolution of 25 April 1974 overthrew Salazar's successor Marcelo Caetano.

Free French.x: Free France, the movement and government in exile of General Charles de Gaulle, who refused the armistice of 1940 from London; its first great territories were French Equatorial Africa and Cameroon, rallied by Félix Éboué and Leclerc, with Brazzaville as their capital. It merged with the forces of French North Africa in 1943 and returned to Paris in August 1944.
Free French.gov: Government in exile (National Committee, then Committee of National Liberation)
Free French.faith: Catholic Christianity; Islam and traditional religions in Africa

Ethiopia.x: Ethiopia restored in 1941, which absorbed Eritrea in 1952 and 1962, and whose aged emperor fell to the Marxist Derg in 1974. Mengistu's Red Terror, famine, and civil wars ended in 1991; the ethnic federal republic of Meles Zenawi followed, and Abiy Ahmed, prime minister from 2018, won the Nobel Peace Prize before the war in Tigray.
Ethiopia.gov: Monarchy; Marxist military regime 1974 to 1991; federal parliamentary republic
Ethiopia.faith: Ethiopian Orthodox Christianity; Islam; Protestant Christianity

Denmark.x: The Kingdom of Denmark after the German occupation, whose realm includes Greenland, a colony until 1953 and then a county, with home rule from 1979 and self-government from 2009, and the Faroe Islands. A founder of NATO, Denmark joined the European Community in 1973; Greenland withdrew from it in 1985.

Netherlands Antilles.x: The autonomous country of the Dutch Caribbean islands created by the Charter for the Kingdom of the Netherlands in 1954: Curaçao, Bonaire, Aruba, Sint Maarten, Saba, and Sint Eustatius, with its seat at Willemstad. Aruba left in 1986, and the country was dissolved on 10 October 2010.
Netherlands Antilles.gov: Autonomous country within the Kingdom of the Netherlands

Republic of Sudan.x: The largest country of Africa until 2011, independent of Anglo-Egyptian rule in 1956 and torn between its Arab and Muslim north and its African south by civil wars from 1955 to 1972 and 1983 to 2005. Omar al-Bashir's Islamist regime waged war in Darfur; the south seceded in 2011, and a new civil war broke out in 2023.
Republic of Sudan.faith: Sunni Islam; Christianity and traditional religions in the south

Ghana.x: The first of Britain's black African colonies to win independence, the Gold Coast renamed in 1957 for the medieval empire, led by Kwame Nkrumah into one-party rule and pan-African ambition until a coup in 1966. Years of coups ended with Jerry Rawlings, who ruled from 1981 and restored elections in 1992; since then power has passed peacefully between parties.

Democratic Republic of the Congo.x: The former Belgian Congo, independent in 1960, which passed through mutiny, the secession of Katanga, and Lumumba's murder to the thirty-two-year dictatorship of Mobutu Sese Seko, who renamed it Zaire. After his fall in 1997 the country, rich in copper, cobalt, and diamonds, was ravaged by the Congo wars, the deadliest conflict since the Second World War.
Democratic Republic of the Congo.faith: Catholic and Protestant Christianity; Kimbanguism; Islam

Federal Republic of Somalia.x: The republic formed in 1960 by the union of British Somaliland and Italian Somalia, which dreamed of gathering all Somalis into one nation and fought Ethiopia for the Ogaden. Siad Barre's dictatorship of 1969 to 1991 ended in clan war, famine, and the collapse of the state; since 2006 the federal government has fought the jihadists of al-Shabaab.

Madagascar.x: The great island, independent of France in 1960 under Philibert Tsiranana, which turned to Didier Ratsiraka's Marxist Second Republic in 1975 and back to multiparty rule in 1993. Its politics since have been a rivalry of strong men, among them Marc Ravalomanana and Andry Rajoelina, who seized power in 2009.
Madagascar.faith: Christianity (Catholic and Protestant); Malagasy ancestral religion

Republic of Cameroon.x: The republic formed from the French trust territory of Cameroun on its independence in 1960, joined in 1961 by the southern part of British Cameroons in a bilingual federation that Ahmadou Ahidjo made a unitary one-party state. Paul Biya has ruled it since 1982; the revolt of its English-speaking regions began in 2016.
Republic of Cameroon.faith: Christianity; Islam in the north; traditional religion

Guinea.x: The former French Guinea, which alone rejected de Gaulle's French Community in 1958 and became independent under Ahmed Sékou Touré, a pan-Africanist whose dictatorship filled the cells of Camp Boiro. Coups followed his death in 1984; Guinea holds what may be the world's largest reserves of bauxite.
Guinea.faith: Sunni Islam; Christianity and traditional religion

Togo.x: The former French trust territory of Togo, independent in 1960 under Sylvanus Olympio, who was murdered in 1963 in the first coup of independent black Africa. Gnassingbé Eyadéma, who said he had fired the shot, ruled from 1967 until his death in 2005, and his son Faure succeeded him.

Ruanda-Urundi.x: The former German territory east of the Congo, administered by Belgium under a League of Nations mandate from 1922 and a United Nations trusteeship from 1946, and ruled through the Tutsi monarchies of Rwanda and Burundi. The Hutu revolution of 1959 overthrew the Rwandan monarchy; in 1962 the territory became the separate states of Rwanda and Burundi.

South Africa.x: The Republic of South Africa proclaimed in 1961, which under the National Party drove apartheid to its extreme, with black homelands and the banning of the ANC, until isolation, sanctions, and township risings moved F. W. de Klerk to negotiate. The free elections of 1994 brought Nelson Mandela to power and ended white minority rule.
South Africa.faith: Christianity (Protestant majority); African traditional religion; Hindu, Muslim, and Jewish minorities
rulers: P. W. Botha (prime minister, then state president)

Republic of Chad.x: The vast land of the Sahara and the Sahel around Lake Chad, independent of France in 1960, whose Muslim north rose against the southern government of François Tombalbaye in 1966, beginning decades of civil war, Libyan invasion, and French intervention. Idriss Déby ruled from 1990 until he was killed fighting rebels in 2021.

Federal Republic of Nigeria.x: Africa's most populous nation, joined by Lugard in 1914 from the Muslim emirates of the north and the Yoruba and Igbo lands of the south, and independent in 1960. Coups and the Biafran war of 1967 to 1970 marked its first decades; enriched and troubled by oil, it returned to civilian rule in 1999.
Federal Republic of Nigeria.gov: Federal presidential republic (military rule 1966 to 1979 and 1983 to 1999)
Federal Republic of Nigeria.faith: Islam in the north; Christianity in the south; traditional religion

Central African Republic.x: The former French colony of Ubangi-Shari, independent in 1960, whose army commander Jean-Bédel Bokassa seized power in 1966 and in 1977 crowned himself emperor in a Napoleonic coronation, until French paratroopers deposed him in 1979. Coups and civil war have since kept it among the poorest lands on earth.

Tanganyika.x: The former German East Africa, held by Britain under mandate and trusteeship, which won its independence peacefully in December 1961 under Julius Nyerere, the schoolteacher called Mwalimu. In 1964 it joined Zanzibar to form Tanzania.

Republic of the Congo.x: The former French Middle Congo, independent in 1960 with its capital at Brazzaville, which in 1969 became under Marien Ngouabi the first avowedly Marxist-Leninist people's republic of Africa. Denis Sassou Nguesso has ruled it for most of the years since 1979, returning to power by civil war in 1997.

Republic of Côte d'Ivoire.x: The former French Ivory Coast, independent in 1960 under Félix Houphouët-Boigny, who made it by cocoa, coffee, and close ties with France the 'Ivorian miracle' of West Africa, and raised at his home town of Yamoussoukro a basilica to rival St. Peter's. After his death in 1993 it fell into coups and civil wars until 2011.

Gabon.x: The former French colony on the equator, independent in 1960, rich in oil, manganese, and timber, and ruled by the Bongo family, Omar Bongo from 1967 to 2009 and his son Ali until a military coup in 2023. Albert Schweitzer's hospital at Lambaréné made it known to the world.

Republic of Upper Volta.x: The landlocked former French colony of the Mossi and other peoples of the Volta basin, independent in 1960 under Maurice Yaméogo, overthrown by the army in 1966, and governed through a series of coups until Captain Thomas Sankara renamed it Burkina Faso in 1984.

Republic of Senegal.x: The former French colony whose capital Dakar had been the seat of French West Africa, independent in 1960 under the poet-president Léopold Sédar Senghor, apostle of négritude. Unlike most of its neighbors it has never suffered a successful coup, and its presidents have handed over power peacefully.

Republic of Dahomey.x: The former French colony on the Bight of Benin, independent in 1960, so unstable that it saw six coups in its first twelve years and a rotating presidency of its three regional chiefs, Maga, Apithy, and Ahomadégbé. Mathieu Kérékou's coup of 1972 ended it, and in 1975 he renamed the country Benin.

Sierra Leone.x: The former British colony founded for freed slaves at Freetown, independent in 1961, which fell under the one-party rule of Siaka Stevens and then, from 1991 to 2002, into a civil war over its diamond fields, notorious for the mutilations inflicted by the Revolutionary United Front. British troops helped end the war in 2000.

Republic of Kenya.x: The former British colony of the white highlands and the Mau Mau war, independent in 1963 under Jomo Kenyatta, a one-party state under Daniel arap Moi, and a multiparty republic since 1992, whose disputed election of 2007 brought killings and whose new constitution of 2010 devolved power to the counties.
Republic of Kenya.faith: Christianity; Islam on the coast; traditional religion

Republic of Uganda.x: The former British protectorate built around the kingdom of Buganda, independent in 1962, whose prime minister Milton Obote overthrew the kabaka in 1966 and was himself overthrown by Idi Amin, whose reign of terror ended when Tanzania invaded in 1979. Yoweri Museveni has ruled since 1986.

Republic of Rwanda.x: The small, crowded land of the Great Lakes hills, made a republic by the Hutu revolution of 1959 to 1962, which drove many Tutsi into exile. In 1994 Hutu extremists murdered some 800,000 Tutsi and moderate Hutu in a hundred days; Paul Kagame's Rwandan Patriotic Front ended the genocide and has ruled since.

Republic of Burundi.x: The Great Lakes kingdom of the Tutsi mwami, independent in 1962, which became a republic under Tutsi army officers in 1966. Massacres of Hutu in 1972, the murder of its first Hutu president, Melchior Ndadaye, in 1993, and the civil war that followed marked its history until the Arusha accords of 2000.

Tanzania.x: The United Republic formed in 1964 by the union of Tanganyika and Zanzibar under Julius Nyerere, whose African socialism of ujamaa villages failed economically but forged one nation of many peoples with Swahili as its tongue. Tanzania overthrew Idi Amin in 1979 and has been ruled throughout by Nyerere's party.

Federative Republic of Brazil.x: Brazil under the constitution of 1967, through the military presidencies of the 'economic miracle' and the slow opening that returned power to civilians in 1985, the democratic constitution of 1988, the stable currency of the Real Plan, and the alternating governments of Lula's Workers' Party and its rivals. It is the largest nation of Latin America.

Zambia.x: The former Northern Rhodesia, independent in 1964 under Kenneth Kaunda, whose copper mines made it one of the richer states of Africa until prices fell in the 1970s. Kaunda's one-party state yielded to multiparty elections in 1991, which Frederick Chiluba won.

Republic of Botswana.x: The former Bechuanaland Protectorate, independent in 1966 under Seretse Khama, chief of the Bamangwato, whose marriage to an Englishwoman had cost him years of exile. Diamonds found at Orapa in 1967 made it one of the fastest-growing economies in the world, and it has remained a stable democracy.

Rhodesia.x: The self-governing British colony of Southern Rhodesia, whose white minority government under Ian Smith declared independence unilaterally in 1965 rather than accept black majority rule, and proclaimed a republic in 1970. International sanctions and the guerrilla war of ZANU and ZAPU forced it to accept majority rule in 1979.
Rhodesia.gov: Parliamentary state under white minority rule (republic from 1970)

Guyana.x: The former British Guiana, independent in 1966, where the rivalry of the Indian party of Cheddi Jagan and the African party of Forbes Burnham shaped politics; Burnham ruled as a socialist strongman until his death in 1985. Oil found offshore in 2015 has made it the fastest-growing economy in the world.

Malawi.x: The former Nyasaland, land of Livingstone's missions on Lake Malawi, independent in 1964 under Hastings Kamuzu Banda, who ruled it as president for life with a puritan hand until a referendum restored multiparty politics in 1993.

Lesotho.x: The mountain kingdom of the Basotho, forged by Moshoeshoe I in the wars of the Mfecane and preserved as the British protectorate of Basutoland, which became independent in 1966. Wholly surrounded by South Africa, it has endured coups and royal quarrels under its constitutional monarchy.

People's Democratic Republic of Yemen.x: South Yemen, formed from the British colony of Aden and the sultanates of the protectorate when the British withdrew in 1967 under fire from the National Liberation Front, the only Marxist state of the Arab world. Its party factions fought a short, bloody civil war in Aden in 1986; it united with the north in 1990.

Equatorial Guinea.x: The former Spanish Guinea, the island of Fernando Po and the mainland of Río Muni, independent in 1968 under Francisco Macías Nguema, whose reign of terror killed or drove into exile perhaps a third of the people. His nephew Teodoro Obiang overthrew and executed him in 1979 and, enriched by offshore oil from the 1990s, rules still.

Zaire.x: The name Mobutu Sese Seko gave the Congo in 1971 in his campaign of 'authenticity,' which made his subjects drop their Christian names and Western dress, while the state became the instrument of his enrichment and he served the West as a bulwark against communism. Ruined by kleptocracy, Zaire collapsed before Kabila's rebellion in 1997.

Republic of Guinea-Bissau.x: The former Portuguese Guinea, where Amílcar Cabral's PAIGC waged the most successful guerrilla war of the Portuguese colonies and declared independence in the liberated hills in September 1973, eight months after Cabral's murder. Portugal recognized it in 1974; coups and military rivalries have dominated its politics since.

Portugal.x: The democratic Third Republic born of the Carnation Revolution of 1974, which gave independence to the African colonies in 1974 and 1975, weathered the revolutionary ferment of 1975, adopted its constitution in 1976, and joined the European Community in 1986. Macau, its last overseas possession, passed to China in 1999.
rulers: Diogo Freitas do Amaral (acting prime minister)

Republic of Benin.x: Dahomey renamed Benin in 1975 by Mathieu Kérékou, who made it a Marxist-Leninist people's republic until a national conference in 1990, the first of its kind in Africa, restored democracy. Kérékou lost the election of 1991, among the first African rulers unseated at the ballot box, and won again in 1996.

People's Republic of Angola.x: Angola under the Marxist MPLA of Agostinho Neto and José Eduardo dos Santos after independence in 1975, a one-party state upheld by Cuban troops and Soviet arms in its civil war against Jonas Savimbi's UNITA, which South Africa and the United States backed. The Bicesse accords of 1991 brought multiparty elections and a new name.

Mozambique.x: The former Portuguese East Africa, independent in 1975 under the Marxist FRELIMO of Samora Machel, who died in an air crash in 1986. Its civil war against RENAMO, backed by Rhodesia and South Africa, killed perhaps a million before the peace of Rome in 1992; FRELIMO has governed since, and jihadists have fought in Cabo Delgado since 2017.

Republic of Suriname.x: The former Dutch colony on the Guiana coast, independent in 1975, a land of Hindustani, Creole, Javanese, Maroon, and Amerindian peoples. Dési Bouterse seized power in 1980, had fifteen of his opponents shot in the December murders of 1982, and later returned as elected president from 2010 to 2020.

Zimbabwe Rhodesia.x: The short-lived state of 1979 born of the 'internal settlement' between Ian Smith and moderate black leaders, which gave Bishop Abel Muzorewa the premiership but left the army and civil service in white hands. Unrecognized abroad and still at war with Mugabe and Nkomo, it returned to British rule in December 1979 pending the elections of 1980.

Republic of Djibouti.x: The former French Territory of the Afars and the Issas on the strait of Bab-el-Mandeb, independent in 1977. Its port and the foreign military bases it hosts, French, American, and Chinese among them, are its fortune; it has been ruled by Hassan Gouled Aptidon and his nephew Ismaïl Omar Guelleh.

Republic of Zimbabwe.x: The former Rhodesia, independent under majority rule in 1980 and ruled by Robert Mugabe, whose Fifth Brigade massacred thousands of Ndebele in the Gukurahundi of the 1980s and whose seizure of white-owned farms from 2000 brought economic collapse and hyperinflation. The army removed him in 2017.

Belize.x: The former British Honduras on the Caribbean coast of Central America, settled by British logwood cutters and their slaves from the seventeenth century and independent in 1981, despite Guatemala's claim to it. Its capital moved inland to Belmopan after a hurricane wrecked much of Belize City in 1961.

Burkina Faso.x: Upper Volta renamed 'the land of upright men' by Thomas Sankara in 1984, whose revolution of self-reliance ended with his murder in 1987. Blaise Compaoré ruled until a popular rising in 2014; since 2015 jihadist insurgents have overrun much of the country, and the army seized power twice in 2022.

Namibia.x: The former German South West Africa, ruled by South Africa under a League mandate from 1920, and in defiance of the United Nations until 1990, when after a long guerrilla war by SWAPO it became independent under Sam Nujoma. It is among the driest and most thinly peopled lands on earth.

Republic of Yemen.x: The state formed in May 1990 by the union of North and South Yemen under Ali Abdullah Saleh, who crushed a southern secession in 1994. After the Arab Spring forced him out in 2012, the Zaydi Houthi movement seized Sana'a in 2014, and a war drawing in Saudi Arabia and Iran has divided the country since 2015.
Republic of Yemen.gov: Presidential republic (divided by civil war since 2014)
Republic of Yemen.faith: Sunni Islam (Shafi'i) and Zaydi Shia Islam

Republic of Angola.x: Angola after the end of one-party rule, whose civil war flared again when Savimbi rejected the election of 1992 and ended only with his death in battle in 2002. Oil and diamonds made it one of Africa's largest economies and enriched the family of José Eduardo dos Santos, who handed power to João Lourenço in 2017.

State of Eritrea.x: The former Italian colony on the Red Sea, federated with Ethiopia in 1952 and annexed in 1962, which won independence in 1993 after a thirty-year war led by Isaias Afwerki's EPLF. It fought Ethiopia again from 1998 to 2000 and remains a closed one-party state that has never held a national election.
State of Eritrea.faith: Eritrean Orthodox Christianity and Sunni Islam

British Overseas Territories.x: The remnants of the British Empire, so named in 2002: among them the Falkland Islands, defended against Argentina in 1982, South Georgia, Bermuda, the Cayman and British Virgin Islands, Anguilla, Montserrat, the Turks and Caicos, St. Helena, Ascension, and Tristan da Cunha, Gibraltar, and the British Antarctic Territory.
British Overseas Territories.gov: Overseas territories of the British crown under governors

Dutch Caribbean.x: The Dutch islands of the Caribbean after the dissolution of the Netherlands Antilles in 2010: Aruba, Curaçao, and Sint Maarten as constituent countries of the Kingdom, and Bonaire, Sint Eustatius, and Saba as special municipalities of the Netherlands itself.
Dutch Caribbean.gov: Constituent countries and special municipalities of the Kingdom of the Netherlands

South Sudan.x: The newest nation on earth, independent of Sudan on 9 July 2011 after two civil wars that cost some two and a half million lives, an oil-rich but desperately poor land of the Dinka, Nuer, and other Nilotic peoples. Civil war between the factions of President Salva Kiir and his vice president Riek Machar broke out in 2013.

Turkish-occupied Cyprus.x: The north of Cyprus taken by the Turkish army in July and August 1974, after the Greek junta's coup against Archbishop Makarios. About 160,000 Greek Cypriots fled or were driven south across the new line.

Turkish Federated State of Cyprus.x: The Turkish Cypriot state set up in the north in 1975 behind the Turkish army's lines. In November 1983 it declared itself the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus.

Chechen Republic of Ichkeria.x: The breakaway Chechen state proclaimed by Dzhokhar Dudayev in 1991. It threw back the Russian army in the war of 1994 to 1996 and was independent in all but name until Russia invaded again in 1999 and took Grozny in February 2000.

Transnistria.x: The strip of land east of the Dniester that broke from Moldova in the war of 1992. It has been held since by its own government with a Russian garrison, and no member of the United Nations recognizes it.
Transnistria.gov: Republic, recognized by no member of the UN

UN-administered Kosovo.x: After NATO's air war drove the Serbian forces out in June 1999, Kosovo was governed by the United Nations mission under Resolution 1244 and guarded by NATO's troops until it declared independence in February 2008.
UN-administered Kosovo.faith: Sunni Islam, with a Serbian Orthodox minority

Houthi-held Yemen.x: The north-west of Yemen, with Sanaa and most of the people, held since 2014 by the Zaydi movement Ansar Allah, called the Houthis after its founding family. A Saudi-led coalition has fought it since 2015 without breaking its hold.

Somaliland.x: The former British Somaliland, which declared its independence from Somalia in May 1991 after the fall of Siad Barre. It has kept its own peace, elections, and currency since, though no state recognizes it.
Somaliland.gov: Presidential republic, recognized by no state

Haftar's Libya.x: The east and south of Libya, governed since 2014 by the House of Representatives at Tobruk and held by Khalifa Haftar's Libyan National Army, in rivalry with the recognized government at Tripoli. Haftar's offensive on Tripoli failed in 2020.
rulers: Khalifa Haftar (commander of the Libyan National Army)
Aguila Saleh (speaker of the House of Representatives)

Rapid Support Forces.x: The paramilitary force raised from the Janjaweed of Darfur and led by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, called Hemedti. It turned on the army in April 2023, took Khartoum, most of Darfur, and the Gezira, and was accused of massacring the Masalit at El Geneina.

Wa State.x: The hill country of the Wa on the Chinese border, ruled since the collapse of the Communist Party of Burma in 1989 by the United Wa State Army, the strongest of Myanmar's ethnic armies, with its own administration and Chinese money.

Resistance-held Myanmar.x: Land taken from the junta after the coup of February 2021 by the ethnic armies and the People's Defence Forces, above all after Operation 1027 of October 2023: the Arakan Army in Rakhine, the Kokang and Ta'ang armies in northern Shan, the Kachin, the Chin, and the Karenni.
Resistance-held Myanmar.gov: Ethnic armed organizations and the National Unity Government

Turkish-occupied Syria.x: The strips of northern Syria taken by Turkey and its Syrian National Army allies in three campaigns against the Islamic State and the Kurdish YPG: Euphrates Shield (2016), Olive Branch at Afrin (2018), and Peace Spring (2019).
Turkish-occupied Syria.gov: Military occupation with a Syrian interim administration

Rojava.x: The Kurdish-led Autonomous Administration of North and East Syria, held by the YPG and from 2015 by the Syrian Democratic Forces. With American air power it broke the Islamic State's caliphate, taking Raqqa in 2017 and Baghuz in 2019.
Rojava.faith: Sunni Islam, with Christian and Yazidi minorities
rulers: Mazloum Abdi (commander of the Syrian Democratic Forces)

Kurdistan Region.x: The self-governing Kurdish region of northern Iraq, recognized in the constitution of 2005, with its own parliament and Peshmerga army. Its referendum on independence in 2017 won a large majority but cost it Kirkuk.

Iraqi Kurdistan.x: The Kurdish north of Iraq, free of Saddam's rule after the uprising of 1991 and shielded by the Allied no-fly zone. The parties of Massoud Barzani and Jalal Talabani governed it, and fought each other between 1994 and 1997.

Coalition-occupied Iraq.x: Iraq after the American-led invasion of March 2003 and the fall of Baghdad on 9 April, governed by the Coalition Provisional Authority under Paul Bremer until sovereignty passed to an Iraqi government on 28 June 2004.

Islamic State.x: The jihadist caliphate proclaimed in June 2014 over eastern Syria and western Iraq, its caliph Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi preaching at Mosul. It enslaved and massacred the Yazidis, drove the Christians from Mosul, and lost Mosul in July 2017 and Raqqa in October.

Rebel-held Syria.x: The land held against Assad by the rebels of the civil war that began in 2011, from 2017 chiefly Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham in Idlib. Its offensive of late November 2024 brought down the regime in eleven days.
Rebel-held Syria.gov: Rebel administrations; from 2017 the Syrian Salvation Government in Idlib

Abkhazia.x: The Black Sea coast that broke from Georgia in the war of 1992 to 1993, when most of its Georgian people were driven out. Russia recognized it after the war of August 2008 and keeps a garrison there.
Abkhazia.gov: Republic, recognized by Russia and a few others
Abkhazia.faith: Eastern Orthodox Christianity and Abkhaz folk religion

South Ossetia.x: The Ossetian highlands south of the Caucasus that broke from Georgia in 1991 and 1992. Georgia's attempt to retake them in August 2008 brought in the Russian army, and Russia recognizes and garrisons the republic.
South Ossetia.gov: Republic, recognized by Russia and a few others

Azawad.x: Northern Mali, seized in 2012 by the Tuareg rebels of the MNLA, who proclaimed it independent in April, and then by the Islamists of Ansar Dine and al-Qaeda, who flogged and maimed under sharia and smashed the shrines of Timbuktu. French troops drove them out in January 2013.

(Sumerian City-States).x: The land of Sumer on the lower Tigris and Euphrates, where Ur, Uruk, Lagash, Umma, Kish, Nippur, and their neighbors each served its own god and ruler, fought over water and fields, and at times owned a king of Kish as overlord, until Sargon of Akkad made them one realm.
(Sumerian City-States).faith: Sumerian religion (An, Enlil, Enki, Inanna, and the city gods)

Ur.x: The city of Nanna, the moon god, on the Euphrates near the head of the Gulf, seat of the First Dynasty of Ur, whose royal cemetery held the gold of Queen Puabi and the bodies of servants buried with their masters.

Uruk.x: The greatest city of early Sumer, where writing began in the precinct of Inanna and Gilgamesh ruled in legend. Lugalzagesi governed all Sumer from it before Sargon; Utu-hengal of Uruk drove out the Gutians; and under its own kings it stood apart again in the 19th century B.C.

Lagash.x: Sumerian state of Girsu, Lagash, and Nigin, rich in canals and temple estates. Eannatum fought Umma for the Gu-edina, Urukagina curbed the officials, and in the Gutian years Gudea rebuilt the temple of Ningirsu.

Umma.x: Sumerian city-state north of Lagash and its enemy for a century over the fields of the Gu-edina. Its ruler Lugalzagesi conquered Lagash and Uruk and made himself king of all Sumer, until Sargon overthrew him.

Shuruppak.x: City of the grain goddess Sud on the Euphrates, home in Sumerian tradition of Ziusudra, the hero of the flood story, and source of some of the oldest literary tablets, among them the Instructions of Shuruppak.

Adab.x: Sumerian city-state between Nippur and Umma, whose temple and royal statues were dug up at Bismaya by an American expedition in 1903 to 1905; like its neighbors it bowed by turns to Kish, Lagash, and Uruk.

Nippur.x: The holy city of Enlil, chief god of Sumer. Never the seat of a great dynasty, it was where kingship was conferred: whoever held Nippur and was owned in the Ekur, Enlil's temple, could claim to rule the land.

Kish.x: The northernmost of the early cities, whose kings won such prestige that king of Kish became the title of a ruler over all Sumer and Akkad. Sargon began his rise as cupbearer to its king, Ur-Zababa.

Mari.x: Great trading city on the middle Euphrates, rival of Ebla in the early Bronze Age and in the 18th century B.C. the seat of Zimri-Lim, whose palace archive lights up the age of Hammurabi. Hammurabi took the city in 1761 B.C. and razed it two years later.

Ebla.x: Kingdom of northern Syria whose palace archive, some seventeen thousand tablets and fragments found in the 1970s, revealed a great trading state of the 24th century B.C. Burned in the age of Akkad, it rose again as a vassal of Yamhad until the Hittites destroyed it about 1600 B.C.
Ebla.gov: Monarchy with a council of elders

Third Dynasty of Ur.x: The Sumerian revival founded by Ur-Nammu: a kingdom of provinces under governors, with standard weights, a state calendar, written law, and a bureaucracy recorded on tens of thousands of tablets. It fell when the Elamites sacked Ur in 2004 B.C. and led Ibbi-Sin away captive.

Isin.x: Kingdom founded by Ishbi-Erra amid the fall of Ur, claiming its inheritance and the rule of Sumer and Akkad. Under Lipit-Ishtar it gave the land laws; it lost the south to Larsa, and Rim-Sin of Larsa took Isin itself in 1794 B.C.

Larsa.x: Amorite kingdom on the lower Euphrates that took Ur from Isin under Gungunum and, under Rim-Sin I, ruled all Sumer for three decades, before Hammurabi of Babylon besieged and took it in 1763 B.C.

Eshnunna.x: Kingdom of the Diyala valley east of the Tigris, grown strong on the trade road to Iran, which wrote down its own laws a generation before Hammurabi. Elam seized it in the 1760s B.C., and Hammurabi annexed it soon after.

First Sealand Dynasty.x: A line of kings who held the marshes and the old cities of the far south after Babylon lost them under Samsu-iluna, keeping Sumerian learning alive for some two and a half centuries until the Kassites conquered them.

Khana.x: Kingdom of the middle Euphrates around Terqa that rose from the ruin of Mari after the age of Hammurabi and held the river road between Babylonia and Syria for some two centuries.

Yamhad.x: The Amorite great kingdom of Halab, whose king was followed by twenty kings in the age of Hammurabi, and which dominated northern Syria until the Hittites Hattusili I and Mursili I broke it and sacked Halab about 1595 B.C.

Qatna.x: Wealthy kingdom of central Syria on the road between Mesopotamia and Egypt, ally of Mari and rival of Yamhad, which fell to the Hittite Suppiluliuma I about 1340 B.C. Its royal tomb was found unplundered beneath the palace in 2002.

Ugarit.x: Rich port kingdom of the Syrian coast, trading between Egypt, Cyprus, the Aegean, and Mesopotamia, and writing in an alphabet of its own. A Hittite vassal from the 1340s B.C., it was destroyed by the Sea Peoples about 1185 B.C.

Amurru.x: Kingdom of the Lebanon coast and its hinterland, carved out of Egypt's vassals by Abdi-Ashirta and his son Aziru. Aziru went over to the Hittites, and Amurru remained a Hittite vassal until the end of the Bronze Age.

Byblos.x: Ancient port of the Lebanon coast that shipped cedar to Egypt from the Old Kingdom on and honored its Lady of Byblos. In the Amarna age its king Rib-Hadda wrote Pharaoh some sixty letters begging help against Amurru.

Kadesh.x: Fortified city on the Orontes that led the Syrian princes against Thutmose III at Megiddo, then passed from Egypt to the Hittites. Beneath its walls Ramesses II and Muwatalli II fought the great chariot battle of 1274 B.C.

Kanesh.x: City of central Anatolia where Assyrian merchants kept their chief trading post. Its king Anitta of Kussara conquered Hattusa and wrote the oldest known text in the Hittite language.

Hattum.x: The Hattian kingdom of Hattusa before the Hittites, trading with Assyrian merchants until Anitta of Kussara destroyed the city and cursed its site about 1750 B.C.

Purushanda.x: Anatolian kingdom of the Konya plain whose ruler stood first among the city lords of the age of the Assyrian merchant colonies, until he submitted to Anitta of Kussara and gave him a throne and scepter of iron.

Kizzuwatna.x: Hurrian and Luwian kingdom of Cilicia between Hatti and Mitanni, bound by treaty first to one and then the other, until the Hittites absorbed it about 1400 B.C. Puduhepa, queen of Hattusili III, was a priest's daughter from its town of Lawazantiya.

Arzawa.x: The great Luwian kingdom of western Anatolia, with its capital at Apasa, later Ephesus. Its king corresponded with Amenhotep III as an equal, until Mursili II conquered it about 1320 B.C. and divided its lands among vassals.

Mira.x: Luwian kingdom of the Maeander valley, set up by Mursili II from the ruin of Arzawa and the greatest of the Hittite vassals in the west, its kings bound to Hatti by treaty.

Seha River Land.x: Luwian vassal kingdom of the Hermus valley in western Anatolia, made a Hittite dependency by Mursili II; its kings Manapa-Tarhunta and Masturi appear in Hittite letters and treaties.

Wilusa.x: The kingdom of Troy as the Hittites knew it. Its king Alaksandu swore a treaty with Muwatalli II about 1280 B.C., and Hittite letters tell of quarrels with Ahhiyawa over it, names that recall Homer's Ilios and Alexandros.

Minoan Crete.x: The palace civilization of Crete, named by Arthur Evans for King Minos. Knossos, Phaistos, Malia, and Zakros ruled the island and its seas from great courtyard palaces, wrote in Linear A, and traded with Egypt, until Mycenaean Greeks took Knossos about 1450 B.C.
Minoan Crete.faith: Minoan religion (goddesses, sacred horns, peak sanctuaries)

(Mycenaean Greece).x: The palace kingdoms of the Greek mainland and Crete in their age of power: Mycenae, Pylos, Thebes, Orchomenus, Athens, Iolcus, Laconia, and Knossos, each ruled by a wanax and recorded in Linear B. The Hittites called their great king the king of Ahhiyawa.

Mycenae.x: Citadel of the Argolid, rich in gold in Homer, with Cyclopean walls, the Lion Gate, and the shaft graves. With Tiryns it was the chief power of Mycenaean Greece and, in legend, the seat of Agamemnon.

Pylos.x: Mycenaean kingdom of Messenia, the sandy Pylos of Nestor in Homer, whose palace burned about 1180 B.C. and so baked its Linear B archive: a register of land, flocks, bronze-smiths, and rowers for the fleet.

Laconia.x: Mycenaean kingdom of the Eurotas valley, the land of Menelaus in Homer. A palace with Linear B tablets was found at Ayios Vasileios, south of Sparta, in 2009.

Thebes.x: Mycenaean kingdom of Boeotia, the city of Cadmus and Oedipus in legend, whose palace stores yielded Linear B tablets and a hoard of cylinder seals from Babylonia and Syria.

Orchomenus.x: Mycenaean kingdom of northern Boeotia that drained Lake Copais with dikes and canals and built the fortress of Gla, the largest Mycenaean citadel.

Athens.x: Mycenaean Athens, with a palace on the Acropolis behind Cyclopean walls and a hidden stair down to a spring for times of siege; the city of Erechtheus and Theseus in legend.

Iolcus.x: Mycenaean kingdom of Thessaly on the Gulf of Pagasae, home of Jason and the Argonauts in legend, with a palace at Dimini.

Knossos.x: Crete under Greek-speaking Mycenaean lords after about 1450 B.C., ruled from the old palace of Knossos, whose Linear B tablets Michael Ventris deciphered as Greek in 1952.

Kydonia.x: The chief Mycenaean center of western Crete at Chania after the fall of Knossos, with Linear B tablets of its own.

Herakleopolitan Kingdom.x: The Ninth and Tenth Dynasties of Egypt, ruling from Herakleopolis at the entrance to the Faiyum in the First Intermediate Period, until Mentuhotep II of Thebes overthrew them and reunited the land.

Eleventh Dynasty of Egypt.x: The Theban princes who made themselves kings of the south and fought Herakleopolis for Abydos and Thinis, until Mentuhotep II reunited Egypt about 2040 B.C.

Kerma.x: The kingdom of Kush on the Nile above the third cataract, Egypt's great southern rival, ruled from Kerma with its towering temples of mud brick. At its height it held Lower Nubia and courted the Hyksos, until Thutmose I and his heirs destroyed it.

Dilmun.x: Trading state of Bahrain and the Gulf coast, the land of paradise in Sumerian myth and the market between Mesopotamia, Magan, and the Indus. Under the Kassites it was governed from Babylon.

Magan.x: The copper land of Oman and the southeastern Gulf, with its stone towers and great communal tombs, which shipped copper and diorite to Sumer. Naram-Sin of Akkad claimed to have defeated its ruler Manium.
